Avanzado Every major lab now ships a model that can look at a screen and click on it. Anthropic's computer use tool, OpenAI's computer tool, and Google's computer_use tool all solve the same shape of problem — take a screenshot, decide an action, execute it, screenshot again — and all three are wire-incompatible with each other in ways that are not obvious until your clicks start landing 40 pixels off. This page is the harness-level guide, not the leaderboard. The leaderboard changes monthly; the failure modes below have been the same since the first preview shipped. :::caution Related security reading When the screen an agent drives is a browser, the agent also lands above a boundary the web has relied on for 30 years — see Agentic Browsers Break the Same-Origin Policy for the UW findings on Atlas, Comet, Gemini in Chrome and Claude for Chrome. ::: :::tip Related pattern For the shared-login variant — an agent that drives a real Chromium session with your cookies inherited, via ego lite and its ego-browser skill — the loop above collapses into a JavaScript-per-turn model and the security posture inverts (the agent has your privileges by design). ::: What you'll learn Understand the agent loop all three providers share — and the three places they diverge Fix the coordinate bug that silently breaks most first attempts (Retina, downscaling, and image size limits) Know each provider's safety gate, because it is part of the protocol, not an optional add-on Read OSWorld honestly: what the human baseline actually means Pick reasoning effort correctly — the cheapest setting is not the one you would guess Última verificación: 2026-07-14. Model names, beta headers, pixel limits and benchmark scores in this space move fast, and every provider still labels its computer-use surface as preview or beta. The mechanics below are durable; re-check any specific number, header or model id against the provider docs linked in Sources before you ship. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Strip away the branding and all three are the same state machine: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Send the task plus a screenshot⌄ The model gets your instruction and an image of the current screen. Some providers also want the current URL or a short history of recent actions. ←PreviousNext→ 2The model returns an action, not a result⌄ Click at (x, y). Type this. Scroll here. It is a request for your code to do something — the model cannot touch the machine itself. ←PreviousNext→ 3Your harness executes it⌄ You own this. Anthropic states it plainly: your application must run the tool; Claude cannot run it directly. You implement the screenshot capture, the mouse, the keyboard. ←PreviousNext→ 4Screenshot again, feed it back⌄ The new screen goes back as a tool result. The model sees the consequence of its own action — this is the entire feedback signal. ←PreviousNext→ 5Repeat until no action comes back⌄ Termination is the absence of a further action request, not a 'done' flag. Your loop needs its own step cap and stall detection. ←PreviousNext→ The consequence people miss: the model's only perception of the world is the image you send it. Every failure below is really a failure of that image, or of the coordinate space it implies.

The divergence is not "which one is smarter." It is the contract. Anthropic (Claude) OpenAI (GPT) Google (Gemini) Action space Raw desktop primitives: screenshot, left_click, type, key, scroll, drag, hold_key, wait, plus zoom on the newest tool version Structured UI actions: click, double_click, scroll, type, keypress, drag, move, wait, screenshot Semantic actions: not just click/type but navigate, go_back, go_forward, open_app, long_press — the browser and mobile concepts are first-class Coordinates You send pixel dimensions; the model returns raw pixel coordinates in that space Same pixel contract, with recommended desktop sizes Same, with an intent field explaining the reasoning behind each action Loop plumbing Tool result blocks carrying an image computer_call → computer_call_output keyed by call_id; previous_response_id carries history so you don't resend it Function call → function_result with a fresh screenshot Safety gate Injection classifiers run automatically on screenshots pending_safety_checks you must explicitly acknowledge safety_decision with policy categories Sweet spot General desktop / OS-level control Desktop and browser, plus a code-execution path Browser-first; strong on mobile; explicitly not optimized for desktop OS control That last Anthropic/Google row is the one that decides architecture. Google's action space is semantic — go_back is a concept the model can name. Anthropic's is mechanical — going back means the model must find and click the back button, or press the right key combination. Semantic actions are more reliable inside a browser and useless outside one. Mechanical primitives work anywhere and fail more often. So: porting a computer-use agent between providers is not a model swap. It is rewriting the harness's action executor. Budget accordingly. (Same lesson as Coding Agent CLIs Compared: the harness, not the model, is the thing you're actually married to.)

This is the single highest-value thing on this page, because almost everyone hits it and the symptom looks like "the model is bad at clicking." It is not bad at clicking. Your image and your coordinate space disagree. Three independent causes, which stack:
documents.s: The coordinate bug that eats your first week

documents.t: macOS Retina displays capture screenshots at a device pixel ratio of 2 — the image is twice the resolution of the logical screen coordinates. Send that raw and the model reasons about a 2880-wide image while your click executor thinks in 1440-wide logical points. Every click lands at roughly half the intended position, consistently, in one direction. Fix: downscale by 2 before sending, or halve the coordinates the model returns. Not both.

Models have image size limits — and they differ between models from the same lab. Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7 accept up to 2576 pixels on the long edge; earlier Claude models accept 1568 pixels and roughly 1.15 megapixels total. Here is the trap: if you send something bigger, the API downscales it for you rather than erroring. The model then returns coordinates in the space of the image it saw — and you never learned the scale factor, because the resize happened server-side. Only genuinely enormous images (over ~8,000 px on a side) get rejected outright with a validation error. So the "helpful" behavior is the bug. Always resize client-side, set display_width_px/display_height_px to the dimensions you actually sent, and scale returned coordinates back up yourself.
documents.s: 2. The API silently downscales oversized images

documents.t: On OpenAI's tool, screenshots should use detail: "original" — both "high" and "low" degrade click accuracy for this task specifically. And if you resize without preserving aspect ratio, clicks land in the right region and miss the target. Coordinate scaling — the shape of the fix CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Before sending: shrink to fit the model's image limit, remember the factor. LONG_EDGE_LIMIT = 2576 # check YOUR model's limit; older Claude models: 1568 scale = min(1.0, LONG_EDGE_LIMIT / max(width, height)) sent_w, sent_h = round(width * scale), round(height * scale) # -> send the resized image, and declare display_width_px=sent_w, display_height_px=sent_h # After the model replies: map its coordinates back to the real screen. real_x, real_y = model_x / scale, model_y / scale # On a Retina capture you did NOT pre-downscale, divide by the device pixel ratio too.

Symptom Almost certainly Clicks consistently offset in one direction Your declared display_width_px/display_height_px don't match the image you actually sent Clicks land in the right area but miss small targets Detail lost to downscaling, or aspect ratio distorted on resize Accuracy poor everywhere Resolution too low — try 1280x720 as a floor Model misreads tiny text (tab titles, filenames, line numbers) It needs to zoom, and you didn't enable it Resolution guidance, from the vendors themselves: Anthropic suggests 1024x768 or 1280x720 for general desktop, 1280x800 or 1366x768 for web apps, and explicitly says to avoid going above 1920x1080. OpenAI recommends 1440x900 or 1600x900. Bigger is not better — you pay tokens for pixels and then throw the detail away in the downscale.

Claude's newest computer tool version (computer_20251124) adds a zoom action, off by default — you must set enable_zoom: true. With it on, Claude zooms into a region when it needs to read small text that isn't legible at the screenshot's base resolution: sidebar filenames, tab titles, status-bar text, line numbers, button labels. Non-obvious operational note: if Claude isn't zooming when you expect it to, the fix is usually to ask about a specific region or element rather than about the screen as a whole.

Do not treat this as a bolt-on. In all three APIs, the safety mechanism changes the shape of your loop. Anthropic trained the model to resist prompt injection and runs classifiers over your prompts automatically when the computer-use tools are in play. When a classifier spots a likely injection in a screenshot, it steers the model to ask the user for confirmation before the next action. That is great with a human present and actively wrong for an unattended pipeline — which is why there is an opt-out, gated behind contacting support. OpenAI surfaces pending_safety_checks that your code must explicitly acknowledge (acknowledged_safety_checks) before the loop proceeds. The gate is in your hands, and skipping it is a decision you make in code. Google returns a safety_decision — allowed, require_confirmation, or blocked — driven by policy categories including FINANCIAL_TRANSACTIONS, COMMUNICATION_TOOL, ACCOUNT_CREATION, SENSITIVE_DATA_MODIFICATION and LEGAL_TERMS_AND_AGREEMENTS. Prompt-injection screening of screenshots is available as an opt-in. The threat is real and specific: a screenshot is untrusted input. Text rendered on a webpage, in an image, in a PDF the agent opened — all of it reaches the model through the same channel as your instructions. Anthropic's own docs note that Claude will, in some circumstances, follow instructions found in content even when they conflict with yours. Every provider's mitigation converges on the same three rules: isolate the environment, keep a human on high-impact actions, and treat everything on screen as hostile. If the agent must log in, that risk goes up sharply — credentials plus injectable content is the worst combination in this space. See Securing Local and Hybrid Agents and Prompt Injection for the defensive playbook.
documents.s: Safety gates are part of the protocol

documents.t: OSWorld is the shared yardstick, and it's a good one because it's hard to fake: it drops an agent into a real OS with real applications, and grades with execution-based verification — a script checks whether the file actually got saved, not whether the agent claimed it did. The benchmark spans 369 tasks (361 in the standard evaluation set, since a handful of Google Drive tasks need manual setup) and ships 134 execution-based evaluation functions. OSWorld-Verified is the cleaned-up revision, with community-reported broken examples fixed and evaluation time cut to about an hour on AWS. Two numbers worth holding together: The human baseline is ~72.4%. Not 100%. These tasks are genuinely fiddly, and humans fumble them too. When OSWorld launched, the best model scored 12.24%. Frontier agents now report scores in the 70s and up — which means the headline "agents have reached human level on computer use" is arithmetically defensible and practically misleading. A benchmark score is a model + harness + scaffold result, exactly like a coding benchmark (see The Capability–Reliability Gap). Your harness is not their harness. And a 75% success rate on single tasks compounds brutally: an eight-step workflow where each step is 95% reliable succeeds about 66% of the time. Treat OSWorld as evidence the capability exists, and your own eval set as the only evidence that your product works.

For Claude computer use specifically, Anthropic's internal benchmarking gives guidance that inverts the usual intuition: Opus 4.7: high effort as the default; drop to low for high-throughput or cost-sensitive workloads. Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6: medium is the best accuracy-to-cost ratio. Avoid max — on UI tasks it adds token cost without improving accuracy. The counterintuitive one: on those models, low effort uses fewer output tokens than disabling thinking entirely. A little thinking prevents mistakes, and mistakes cost you retries — and retries cost far more tokens than the thinking did. So "turn thinking off to save money" is, for computer use, often wrong. Cheapest is a little thinking. One more model-selection wrinkle: mechanical click precision is not the same axis as intelligence. Sonnet 4.6 is more mechanically precise at clicking than Opus 4.6, and more robust when screenshots have been heavily downscaled. Opus 4.7 narrows that gap and raises the pixel limit, so it needs less downscaling in the first place. girarTérminoWhy do clicks land at half the intended position on a Mac?DefiniciónRetina captures at device pixel ratio 2 — the screenshot is 2x the logical coordinate space. Downscale the image by 2, or halve the returned coordinates. Not both.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 7 Siguiente→

Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Sandbox first, always⌄ A container or VM with nothing valuable in it. Every provider says this and they all mean it: the agent will eventually click something you did not intend. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pin the coordinate space⌄ Capture, resize client-side to your model's limit, declare the exact dimensions you sent, and keep the scale factor. Write this once and never think about it again. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the loop⌄ Termination is 'no further action returned' — which never fires if the agent is stuck in a modal it can't dismiss. Add a max-step budget and a stall detector (identical screenshots N times running). ←PreviousNext→ 4Decide your safety-gate policy explicitly⌄ Human-in-the-loop, or unattended with an opt-out and a narrower blast radius. Do not discover this by accident when a confirmation prompt deadlocks your cron job. ←PreviousNext→ 5Build a ten-task eval before you build feature two⌄ Execution-verified, like OSWorld does it: check the world changed, not that the agent said it did. This is the only number about your system that means anything. ←PreviousNext→ 6Prefer the API to the pixels where you can⌄ The most reliable computer-use agent is the one that doesn't have to use the computer. If the target has an API, an MCP server, or a CLI, that path is faster, cheaper and orders of magnitude more reliable. Screens are the fallback, not the goal. ←PreviousNext→ That last step is the strategic one. Computer use is the universal adapter for software with no API — legacy desktop apps, vendor portals, anything behind a login with no integration story. It is a magnificent hack, and it is still a hack. Reach for MCP and real tools first. Check yourself 0/5 1Your computer-use agent's clicks are consistently offset in one direction. What is the most likely cause? The model is not intelligent enough for UI tasksThe declared display dimensions don't match the image dimensions actually sentThe screen resolution is too high for the applicationYou need to enable extended thinking 2Why is relying on the API's automatic downscaling of oversized screenshots a bug rather than a convenience? It makes the request slowerIt strips colour information the model needsThe model returns coordinates in the resized image's space, and you never learn the scale factor to map them backIt causes the request to be rejected 3For Claude computer use on Sonnet 4.6, which reasoning-effort setting typically costs the FEWEST output tokens? Thinking disabled entirelylowmaxThey are all identical in cost 4The OSWorld human baseline is roughly 72%. What does that imply about an agent scoring 75%? The agent is superhuman and production-ready for any UI taskThe benchmark is broken and should be ignoredIt cleared a hard bar on average single tasks — but the score is a model+harness result, and multi-step reliability compounds downwardIt means the agent will succeed 75% of the time on your workflow 5Why is a screenshot considered untrusted input? Screenshots can carry malware in the image encodingText rendered on the screen reaches the model through the same channel as your instructions, so page content can act as an injected instructionScreenshots are always too large for the APIThe model cannot read text in images reliably

Intermedio Durante mucho tiempo, la historia de la "buena IA" fue la historia de un puñado de modelos cerrados y de frontera a los que solo podías acceder alquilándolos a través de una API. Eso ya no es toda la historia. Una ola de modelos de pesos abiertos — muchos de laboratorios chinos como DeepSeek y el Qwen de Alibaba, junto al Llama de Meta y el Mistral francés — se volvió lo suficientemente buena, barata y pequeña como para que descargar y ejecutar tu propio modelo capaz se convirtiera en una opción real. Esta página es el mapa duradero de ese panorama: por qué ocurrió, qué significa realmente "pesos abiertos", las concesiones honestas frente a los modelos cerrados de frontera y cómo usar realmente estos modelos hoy. What you'll learn Entender POR QUÉ los modelos de pesos abiertos se volvieron competitivos — capacidad por coste y razonamiento abierto Precisar qué significa realmente 'pesos abiertos' — frente a código abierto y frente a datos abiertos Reconocer los arquetipos: chat general, razonamiento, programación y modelos pequeños/eficientes Sopesar las concesiones reales frente a la frontera cerrada — la brecha de capacidad en las tareas más difíciles, y hacerte cargo de tu propia infraestructura y seguridad Conocer las dos formas de usarlos realmente: una API alojada o autoalojamiento vía Ollama
documents.s: DeepSeek, Qwen y la ola de pesos abiertos

documents.t: Tres cosas cambiaron aproximadamente al mismo tiempo y, juntas, cerraron la mayor parte de la brecha cotidiana. La capacidad por coste se desplomó. Mejores recetas de entrenamiento, curación de datos y arquitecturas de mezcla de expertos (MoE) (donde solo se activa una fracción de los parámetros de un modelo grande por token) permitieron a los laboratorios lanzar modelos que rinden muy por encima de su coste. Para una gran parte de las tareas reales — redactar, resumir, extraer, clasificar, programación rutinaria — un buen modelo abierto es ahora "suficientemente bueno", a una fracción del coste de una API de frontera. Llegaron los modelos de razonamiento abiertos. La línea de razonamiento de DeepSeek fue un punto de inflexión: demostró que la capacidad de "pensar paso a paso antes de responder" — antes el foso de unos pocos modelos cerrados — podía entrenarse y publicarse con pesos abiertos. Una vez que un laboratorio lo demostró, el resto del ecosistema abierto lo siguió. Los modelos pequeños se volvieron genuinamente útiles. Los modelos por debajo de 10B, e incluso por debajo de 1B, se volvieron coherentes y útiles, lo que significa que puedes ejecutar algo capaz en un portátil o un servidor barato. Eso cambia la economía de la privacidad, la latencia y la escala. El efecto neto: la brecha con la frontera cerrada no desapareció, pero para la mayor parte del trabajo dejó de ser el factor decisivo. Los factores decisivos pasaron a ser el coste, el control y dónde viven tus datos.
documents.s: Por qué los modelos de pesos abiertos se volvieron competitivos de repente

documents.t: Este es el punto más confuso de todo el espacio. "Abierto" trabaja mucho de tres maneras distintas, y no son la misma cosa. Término Lo que realmente obtienes Lo que normalmente NO obtienes Pesos abiertos El archivo del modelo entrenado (los pesos). Puedes descargarlo, ejecutarlo, hacerle fine-tuning y autoalojarlo. Los datos de entrenamiento, y a veces el código de entrenamiento completo. El uso puede regirse por una licencia personalizada. Código abierto (estricto) Los pesos más el código de entrenamiento/inferencia bajo una licencia estilo OSI, con libertad para usar, modificar y redistribuir. A menudo, aún no los datos de entrenamiento. Datos abiertos Los conjuntos de datos reales con los que se entrenó el modelo, publicados abiertamente. Raro para modelos a escala de frontera; la mayoría de los modelos "abiertos" son de pesos abiertos, no de datos abiertos. La conclusión práctica: la mayoría de los modelos que la gente llama "código abierto" son en realidad de pesos abiertos. Puedes ejecutarlos y adaptarlos, pero normalmente no puedes reproducirlos desde cero, y debes leer la licencia. Las licencias varían: Algunos se distribuyen bajo licencias permisivas (Apache 2.0, MIT) que son limpias para uso comercial — los modelos Qwen y Mistral, por ejemplo, han usado históricamente Apache 2.0, y DeepSeek ha usado MIT para lanzamientos importantes. Algunos se distribuyen bajo licencias comunitarias personalizadas con condiciones — la licencia de Llama de Meta, por ejemplo, ha incluido históricamente una cláusula que restringe a las empresas más grandes (por usuarios activos mensuales) el uso libre. Comprueba siempre la ficha del modelo concreto para conocer su licencia antes de construir sobre él. Neutral pero importante: que un modelo sea de pesos abiertos te dice que puedes alojarlo tú mismo; no te dice los términos legales, y no hace desaparecer las cuestiones de licencia o residencia de datos — las reubica en ti. Última verificación: 2026-06-28. Las versiones exactas actuales de los modelos, los recuentos de parámetros, las puntuaciones de benchmarks y los precios por token cambian rápido y deliberadamente no se afirman aquí como permanentes. La forma duradera del panorama — los laboratorios, los arquetipos y la distinción entre pesos abiertos, código abierto y datos abiertos — es estable; los números concretos de las tablas de clasificación no lo son. Consulta las páginas de las organizaciones enlazadas para ver lo que está vigente. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Las familias de pesos abiertos casi siempre vienen como un abanico de variantes, no como un único modelo. Aprende los cuatro arquetipos y podrás leer la línea de cualquier laboratorio de un vistazo. Arquetipos de modelos de pesos abiertos girarTérminoChat general / instructDefiniciónEl todoterreno: un modelo ajustado por instrucciones para conversación, escritura, resumen y preguntas y respuestas amplias. El punto de partida por defecto cuando no tienes una necesidad especializada. (p. ej. modelos base Qwen / Llama / Mistral instruct, la serie DeepSeek-V.)Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 4 Siguiente→ Una sola familia — Qwen es el ejemplo más claro — normalmente te da toda la escala: modelos diminutos para el edge y portátiles, modelos de tamaño medio para servidores, un gran buque insignia para las tareas más difíciles, más variantes especializadas en programación y razonamiento. Eliges el peldaño que encaja con tu hardware y tu tarea, no "el modelo".

Los modelos de pesos abiertos no son una mejora estricta. Son un trato distinto. Aquí está el trato de forma neutral. Dimensión Pesos abiertos (autoalojado o alojamiento barato) Frontera cerrada (API alojada) Capacidad en las tareas más difíciles Fuerte y cerrando rápido, pero la frontera cerrada normalmente sigue liderando en el razonamiento más difícil, las tareas agénticas de largo horizonte y los nichos Suele ser el techo en las tareas más duras Coste a escala Puede ser drásticamente más barato, especialmente autoalojado o vía hosts económicos Prima por token; predecible pero se acumula Privacidad / residencia de datos Puedes mantener los datos totalmente dentro de tu entorno Los datos salen de tu red hacia el proveedor Control y personalización Total: fine-tuning, cuantización, fijar una versión, ejecutar sin conexión Limitado a lo que expone la API; las versiones pueden cambiar bajo tus pies Quién se hace cargo de la seguridad y las operaciones Tú — las barreras de protección, el filtrado de abuso, la disponibilidad, el escalado y el parcheado son tu trabajo El proveedor gestiona la infraestructura y ofrece una seguridad base Esa última fila es la que la gente infravalora. Cuando autoalojas un modelo de pesos abiertos también heredas las responsabilidades que un laboratorio de frontera normalmente absorbe por ti: la seguridad de contenidos y la mitigación de abusos, mantener el despliegue parcheado, la capacidad y la disponibilidad, y evaluar tú mismo cada nueva versión del modelo. "Pesos abiertos" te compra control, y el control es tanto un coste como un beneficio. Para intuición de costes en el lado de la API de este trato, consulta Economía de tokens.
documents.s: Las concesiones honestas frente a la frontera cerrada

documents.t: Hay exactamente dos caminos, y la mayoría de los equipos usan ambos en distintas etapas. API alojada — muchos proveedores (incluidos los propios laboratorios y hosts de inferencia de terceros) sirven modelos de pesos abiertos detrás de una API, a menudo compatible con OpenAI. Obtienes la economía del modelo abierto sin trabajo de infraestructura. Mejor cuando quieres bajo coste sin ejecutar servidores, pero ten en cuenta que tus datos siguen saliendo de tu red. Autoalojamiento — descargas los pesos y los ejecutas en tu entorno. Máxima privacidad y control, y la única opción cuando los datos realmente no pueden salir de tu red. La rampa de entrada más fácil es Ollama, que descarga y ejecuta modelos abiertos con un solo comando.
documents.s: Cómo usar realmente un modelo abierto

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Instala Ollama⌄ Descárgalo de ollama.com/download (macOS/Windows) o usa el script de instalación de Linux. Esto te da el comando ollama y un servicio local en segundo plano. Guía completa en la página Ejecutar modelos localmente. ←PreviousNext→ 2Elige un tamaño que tu máquina pueda ejecutar⌄ Los modelos más pequeños necesitan menos RAM/VRAM. Un portátil ejecuta cómodamente variantes pequeñas (unos pocos GB); los grandes buques insignia necesitan una GPU o un servidor de verdad. Empieza pequeño para confirmar que todo funciona, luego escala si la calidad no es suficiente. ←PreviousNext→ 3Ejecútalo con un solo comando⌄ ollama run <model> descarga los pesos en el primer uso (varios GB) y luego te deja en un chat interactivo. La primera ejecución es lenta porque está descargando; las siguientes son instantáneas desde la caché. ←PreviousNext→ 4Llámalo desde tu código⌄ Ollama expone un endpoint local compatible con OpenAI, así que puedes apuntar un SDK existente estilo OpenAI a localhost en lugar de a la nube. Ahora el mismo código se ejecuta contra un modelo privado y local. ←PreviousNext→ Descarga y ejecuta un modelo abierto localmente con Ollama CopyOpen in Claude↗ ollama run qwen3 Ese único comando descarga un modelo Qwen de pesos abiertos e inicia un chat local — sin clave de API, sin datos saliendo de tu máquina. Cambia qwen3 por otra familia (por ejemplo, una etiqueta de Llama, Mistral o DeepSeek) para compararlos en tu propia tarea. Elegir el modelo adecuado para un trabajo dado es una habilidad en sí misma: consulta Elegir un modelo.
documents.s: Prueba un modelo localmente en cuatro pasos

documents.t: No elijas por tabla de clasificación. Elige por restricción: Los datos no pueden salir de tu red → el pesos abiertos autoalojado es la respuesta, punto. Alto volumen, sensible al coste, calidad "suficientemente buena" → los pesos abiertos (alojados o autoalojados) normalmente ganan en coste. Necesitas lo absolutamente mejor en las tareas más difíciles → la frontera cerrada aún tiende a liderar — úsala donde importa y enruta el tráfico más fácil a modelos abiertos más baratos. Quieres hacer fine-tuning, cuantizar, fijar una versión o ejecutar sin conexión → solo los pesos abiertos te dan ese control. El movimiento más duradero es ejecutar una evaluación diminuta sobre tus propios datos reales entre un candidato abierto y uno cerrado. Los benchmarks describen la tarea de otro; tu evaluación describe la tuya. Compruébate 0/3 1¿Qué te garantiza obtener 'pesos abiertos'? Los conjuntos de datos de entrenamiento de los que aprendió el modeloEl archivo del modelo entrenado descargable que puedes ejecutar y ajustarUna licencia permisiva sin condiciones 2Debes procesar datos que legalmente no pueden salir de tu red. ¿Qué camino encaja? Un modelo cerrado de frontera vía API alojadaUn modelo de pesos abiertos que autoalojas en tu propio entornoCualquier API alojada, siempre que sea compatible con OpenAI 3¿Qué nueva responsabilidad asumes cuando autoalojas un modelo de pesos abiertos? Nada — se comporta exactamente como una API alojadaLas barreras de protección de seguridad, la disponibilidad, el escalado y el parcheado pasan a ser tuyosDebes publicar tus pesos ajustados de forma pública Key takeaways Los modelos de pesos abiertos cerraron la mayor parte de la brecha cotidiana gracias a la capacidad por coste, los modelos de razonamiento abiertos y modelos pequeños genuinamente útiles 'Pesos abiertos' = pesos descargables que puedes ejecutar y ajustar — NO necesariamente código abierto, datos de entrenamiento abiertos ni una licencia permisiva; lee siempre la ficha del modelo Lee cualquier línea por arquetipo: chat general, razonamiento, programación y pequeño/eficiente — la mayoría de las familias ofrecen toda la escala de tamaños El trato es real: lo abierto te compra coste, privacidad y control, pero la frontera cerrada normalmente sigue liderando en las tareas más difíciles y heredas la seguridad y la infraestructura Dos formas de usarlos: una API alojada (a menudo compatible con OpenAI) o autoalojar vía Ollama con un solo comando — luego evalúa sobre TUS datos, no sobre una tabla de clasificación

Intermedio At 04:00 UTC on September 10, 2026, DeepSeek flipped its API to a new model and published the weights the same day: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served as deepseek-flash. It is the smallest member of a new architecture family, but it is not a small model: 552 billion parameters, a 1-million-token context, native vision, and a KV cache that costs 890 bytes per token. On DeepSWE v1.1, the long-horizon software-engineering benchmark both Google and Anthropic now headline, DeepSeek reports 74.2, one-fifth of a point above Claude Opus 5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it reports 31.2 against Opus 5's 51.8. Both numbers are true, and the gap between them is the whole story. This page is the field guide for a Claude user: what actually changed, the routing change that quietly re-pointed every deepseek-v4-pro request, the effort dial and what it does to your bill, how to run the weights, and the workloads where Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Read the V4.1-Flash launch numbers the way they deserve: tied with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, far behind on Terminal-Bench, and why that split is not a contradiction Understand the new Causal Encoder-Decoder + CSA2 design well enough to know what the 890-byte KV cache buys you (and what DeepSeek says it has not yet characterized) Use the 1–100 reasoning_effort dial deliberately — 25 vs 100 is an 8-point DeepSWE swing for ~2.5× the output tokens Do the honest cost math: $0.30 / $1.20 peak, half that off-peak, $0.003 per million on an off-peak cache hit — and the UTC peak window that decides which rate you pay Know the September 14 routing change: deepseek-v4-pro now silently serves V4.1-Flash until V4.1-Pro ships Pick a serving path (hosted API, vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner) and the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends Última verificación: 2026-09-15. Model ID, routing dates, and pricing from DeepSeek's September 10 announcement and the API pricing page. Architecture, license, reasoning-effort range, and sampling defaults from the Hugging Face model card. Benchmark comparisons against Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are DeepSeek's own launch table as reported by VentureBeat on September 10; treat them as vendor-run until an independent harness publishes. The 3.0/4.0 Terminal-Bench gaps come from the same table. DeepSeek's statement that the architecture has "robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized" is quoted from the same coverage. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A 1M-Context Open Weight That Ties Opus 5 on DeepSWE (Sep 2026)

documents.t: V4.1-Flash is DeepSeek's first model on a new architecture (a "Causal Encoder-Decoder" with Compressed Sparse Attention 2), released MIT-licensed with native vision, a 1M-token window, 384K max output, and a continuously controllable reasoning effort from 1 to 100. It replaces every V4-era Flash endpoint immediately and, since September 14, also answers every deepseek-v4-pro call at Flash prices until V4.1-Pro lands.

DeepSeek's launch table, in the columns that matter for an agent shop: Benchmark DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (resolved) 74.2 74.0 73.0 Terminal-Bench 3.0 30.0 43.3 — Terminal-Bench 4.0 31.2 51.8 — CyberGym 88.1 — — AutomationBench 54.8 — — DeepSWE rewards a model that reads a repository, plans a patch, and lands it: long context, careful retrieval, a few large edits. Terminal-Bench rewards many short, adaptive shell turns where each decision depends on the last tool result. V4.1-Flash has 1M tokens of context and a cheap cache, so the first shape suits it. It runs 8B active parameters per token at prefill and 16B at decode, which is a lot less "thinking per step" than a dense frontier model, so the second shape hurts. If your work looks like a pull request, the parity claim is credible and worth an eval. If your work looks like an interactive terminal session, the 20-point Terminal-Bench gap is the number to budget around. The same split shows up in Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash launch a week earlier, and for the same architectural reasons. The base-model rows tell a quieter story: MMLU-Pro 74.1 (V4-Flash 68.3, V4-Pro 73.5), HumanEval 79.4 (V4-Flash 69.5), GSM8K 93.0 (V4-Flash 90.8). The new "Flash" is a better base than last month's "Pro", which is why DeepSeek was comfortable routing Pro traffic onto it.
documents.s: 1. DeepSWE parity and Terminal-Bench deficit are the same fact seen twice

documents.t: Unlike Claude's effort (low/medium/high/max), V4.1-Flash exposes an integer from 1 to 100. DeepSeek's own ablation on DeepSWE v1.1: effort 25 scores 66.0%, effort 100 scores 74.2%, and the top setting emits roughly 2.5× as many output tokens. They also say the 60–80 band delivers most of the maximum-effort accuracy at less than half the token budget. Every benchmark row above was run at reasoning_effort=100. So the parity number is the expensive number. Reproduce it at 100 first, then walk down to the cheapest setting your evals still pass at. That is the same discipline we recommend for thinking_level on Gemini and effort on Claude in Reasoning models compared.
documents.s: 2. The reasoning-effort dial is a real dial, and it is on your bill

documents.t: From September 10, deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp route to V4.1-Flash, billed at Flash rates. The V4-Flash-Vision-Exp page's numbers now describe the open weights, not the hosted endpoint. From 04:00 UTC September 14, every deepseek-v4-pro request also routes to V4.1-Flash at Flash rates, "until V4.1-Pro launches". If you have evals pinned to deepseek-v4-pro, your production model changed under you on Sunday morning. Re-run the suite. The upside is that the same call now costs roughly a quarter of the Pro rate; the downside is that any Pro-specific behavior you tuned for is gone. This is exactly the failure mode Porting prompts across models warns about when a provider aliases model IDs.
documents.s: 3. Two routing changes happened without a client-side change

documents.t: Spec DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash API model ID deepseek-flash Release September 10, 2026 (API + open weights same day) Parameters 552B total; 8B active at prefill, 16B at decode MoE layout 384 routed + 1 shared expert per MoE layer; 6 routed experts active per token Architecture Causal Encoder-Decoder, Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2) KV cache 890 bytes per token (FP4, E2M1): ~1/4 of V4-Flash in HBM, ~1/8 in SSD storage; global KV cache lifetime at least 72 hours Context / max output 1M tokens / 384K tokens Vision Native; DeepSeek-ViT trained from scratch, 2D-RoPE, 3×3 pixel-unshuffle downsampling Reasoning control reasoning_effort integer 1–100 License MIT Weights Safetensors in BF16, F32, F8_E4M3, I8 Serving vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, Transformers; reference inference code in the inference/ folder Recommended sampling temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context 1M API concurrency 2,500 The KV-cache line is the architectural headline. A 1M-token conversation at 890 bytes per token is under a gigabyte of cache, which is why DeepSeek can promise a 72-hour cache lifetime and price cache hits at fractions of a cent. Anthropic's answer to the same problem is a cheaper cache-read rate on Claude Fable 5.1; DeepSeek's is to make the cache physically small. Both push you toward the same habit: put the stable prefix first and never edit it mid-run. See Prompt caching.

DeepSeek keeps a two-rate schedule. Peak hours are 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC, Monday through Friday; everything else is off-peak at exactly half the peak rate. Per 1M tokens Peak Off-peak Input, cache hit $0.006 $0.003 Input, cache miss $0.30 $0.15 Output $1.20 $0.60 Two things follow. First, the "$0.003 per million" headline is the off-peak cache-hit price, the cheapest of six cells; a cold, peak-hour agent run pays 100× that on input. Second, the peak window is defined in UTC and covers the European morning and the tail of the U.S. night. A batch job scheduled at 09:00 UTC pays double what the same job pays at 11:00 UTC. If you can shift, shift. For a framework that puts these cells beside Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google list prices, use What AI costs across providers; current Claude list prices live on Models and pricing.

Hosted is right for almost everyone: the model is enormous, and the API is the cheapest thing on this page. Self-host when data cannot leave your network or when you want the effort dial and 1M window without a rate limit. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide hosted vs self-hosted honestly⌄ 552B parameters in BF16 is over a terabyte of weights; the F8_E4M3 and I8 safetensors halve or quarter that but still need a multi-GPU node. If you do not already run Kimi K3 or Colibrì-class MoEs, the hosted endpoint at $0.30 / $1.20 peak will beat your amortized hardware bill. See the hardware math on Running Kimi K3 locally. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a serving stack the card actually names⌄ vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner, and Transformers are the four listed. The card ships no Jinja chat template; it uses a custom encoding implementation, so use the reference code in the repo's inference folder (or the deepseek-recipe toolkit) rather than hand-rolling the prompt format. ←PreviousNext→ 3Set the sampling defaults DeepSeek recommends⌄ temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 or 1.0, context window 1M. These are the settings the benchmark rows were produced with. Do not port a Claude-tuned temperature of 0.2 over blindly. ←PreviousNext→ 4Start at reasoning_effort=100, then walk down⌄ Reproduce DeepSeek's number on your own eval first. Then try 80, 60, 40 and record accuracy vs output tokens. Most teams will land in the 60–80 band the vendor itself points at. ←PreviousNext→ 5Test long-context retrieval before you trust it⌄ DeepSeek says the new architecture has robustness boundaries it has not fully characterized, specifically sparse retrieval over very long contexts. Run a needle-in-haystack and a multi-hop retrieval test at the context length you will actually use. Treat the 1M number as a ceiling, not a promise. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted call with the effort dial (OpenAI-compatible endpoint) CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "deepseek-flash", "reasoning_effort": 70, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Here is the log and the relevant module: ..."} ] }' Self-hosted with vLLM (shape only; check the model card for the exact flags) CopyOpen in Claude↗ # One node, tensor-parallel across all visible GPUs. # The card names vLLM, SGLang, Docker Model Runner and Transformers as supported. vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --max-model-len 1000000 \ --trust-remote-code # Then hit http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions with the same body as above.

Pro tip Reach for V4.1-Flash: repository-scale coding tasks that look like DeepSWE (read a lot, edit a little), where you can run at effort 60–100 and the cost per resolved issue still undercuts Claude by an order of magnitude. Reach for V4.1-Flash: anything that needs a 1M-token window and a warm cache for days — a 72-hour global cache lifetime and 890-byte-per-token KV make 'keep the whole codebase in context' cheap. Reach for V4.1-Flash: self-hosted or data-residency workloads where MIT licensing matters and you already run a multi-GPU MoE stack. Stay on Claude: interactive terminal agents and any many-short-turns loop. A 20-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 gap (31.2 vs 51.8) is not noise, and it is the shape of most real Claude Code sessions. Stay on Claude: work that needs Anthropic's tool-use loop, prefilled assistant turns, structured-output strictness, or the safety and retention guarantees of a first-party API. The DeepSeek API is OpenAI-shaped and the model has documented, uncharacterized long-context failure modes. Cross-check both: for a coding agent, run your own eval at DeepSeek's effort=100 and Claude's default effort, then at the cheapest passing setting on each. The vendor tables were run at maximum effort; your bill will not be. For the durable framework behind that list, How to choose a model. For what changes when you move a prompt between an Anthropic-shaped and an OpenAI-shaped API, Porting prompts across models. For the Claude-side reference these comparisons hang off, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.
documents.s: When to reach for V4.1-Flash, and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 1DeepSeek reports V4.1-Flash at 74.2 on DeepSWE v1.1 (Opus 5: 74.0) and 31.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Opus 5: 51.8). What is the right reading? One of the two numbers must be wrongV4.1-Flash is strong at long-context, few-large-edits work and weak at many short adaptive tool turns — the benchmarks measure different shapesTerminal-Bench is deprecated so only DeepSWE countsV4.1-Flash beats Opus 5 overall 2You pinned production to deepseek-v4-pro in August. What happened on September 14, 2026? Nothing — the model ID still serves V4-ProRequests started returning an error asking you to migrateRequests silently route to V4.1-Flash at Flash rates until V4.1-Pro launchesThe endpoint was retired 3Which price is the '$0.003 per million tokens' headline? Peak-hour input on a cache missOff-peak outputOff-peak input on a cache hitThe flat rate for all tokens 4DeepSeek's DeepSWE ablation: effort 25 → 66.0%, effort 100 → 74.2%, at ~2.5× the output tokens. What should you do? Always run at 100 — accuracy is what mattersAlways run at 25 — cost is what mattersReproduce the vendor number at 100, then walk down to the cheapest setting your own evals still pass at (DeepSeek itself points at 60–80)Ignore the parameter; the default is fine 5What did DeepSeek explicitly say it has NOT fully characterized about the new architecture? Its behavior on imagesRobustness boundaries, particularly sparse retrieval over very long contextsIts tool-calling formatIts performance on math girarTérminoDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash — what and whenDefiniciónSeptember 10, 2026. API model ID deepseek-flash; open weights on Hugging Face same day under MIT. First model on DeepSeek's new architecture family; native vision; 1M context; 384K max output.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→ Key takeaways V4.1-Flash is a repository-shaped model: parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE, a 20-point deficit on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Match it to work that reads a lot and edits a little. The 1–100 effort dial is the price lever. Every launch number is at 100; DeepSeek's own guidance is that 60–80 keeps most of the accuracy at under half the tokens. Six price cells, not one. The $0.003 headline is off-peak cache-hit input; a cold peak-hour token is 100× that. Peak is 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays. Two silent routing changes: V4-Flash endpoints on Sept 10, deepseek-v4-pro on Sept 14. If you pinned Pro, your model changed — re-run evals. The 890-byte KV cache and 72-hour cache lifetime make long-lived 1M-token contexts cheap, but DeepSeek itself flags long-context sparse retrieval as uncharacterized. Test before you trust.

Intermedio At 00:00 UTC on August 31, 2026, DeepSeek quietly pushed a new repository to Hugging Face: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp. Ten days after the same model went live on their API (August 21), the weights are now MIT-licensed and public. This is the first V4-family model with native vision — not a text model with a bolt-on adapter, but a joint-trained multimodal MoE — and its agent scores on the vision side jumped from 26.2 to 36.5 on ApexBench without moving the text-only agent scores at all. On several agent benchmarks it now matches or edges past Claude Opus 4.8 while the API costs $0.22 per million input tokens. This page is the practical field guide the launch didn't come with: what changed architecturally, the numbers that matter, the one hard limit nobody warns you about, how to run it, and when Claude is still the right call. What you'll learn Understand what 'native vision' means here — the V4-Flash backbone plus a vision encoder + aligner trained together, not stapled on after Read the benchmark table the way the release intends: text-only agents preserved, vision agents up sharply, both within striking distance of Claude Opus 4.8 Know the hard 384-tokens-per-image architectural cap and why it changes how you prompt Do the honest cost math: $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 (cached) per million tokens vs Claude Opus 4.8 at $15 / $75 Pick the right serving path — hosted API for almost everyone, vLLM + DSpark for a real self-hosted run
documents.s: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision: First Native-Vision Frontier Open Weight

documents.t: DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is a 305-billion-parameter sparse-MoE multimodal model — 13B active per token, 1.048M-token context — that adds joint-trained vision to the V4-Flash text backbone, ships open under MIT on Hugging Face on August 31 2026, and delivers agent-tier multimodal performance at roughly one-fortieth of Claude Opus 4.8's per-token price.

Every open lab that has bolted vision onto a strong text model has paid a tax on text benchmarks. DeepSeek's release table is the flex: on Terminal Bench 2.1 the vision model scores 83.9 (vs 82.7 for the text-only V4-Flash-0731); on DeepSWE it climbs to 59.3 (from 54.4); on Toolathlon-Verified to 75.9 (from 70.3). None of these are vision tasks — they're pure code and tool-use agent evals. The vision variant is better on text-agent work than the text-only checkpoint, not worse. This matters because it's the "prove-out" the field has been waiting for since Chameleon: you can jointly train a giant MoE for text and vision without the multimodal add causing text regression, as long as the vision head lands late enough and the router gets to keep specializing text experts.
documents.s: 1. Vision was added without breaking the text agents — that's the whole point

documents.t: This is the single most important thing to learn before writing your first prompt. The vision encoder in V4-Flash-Vision-Exp allocates at most 384 tokens per image — and that ceiling is architectural, not a commercial policy. There is no "high-detail" mode that unlocks more. Practical consequences: Big screenshots lose fine text. A 2560×1440 dashboard, a dense CSV rendered as an image, or a long PDF page will be encoded at whatever resolution 384 tokens of visual features can express — meaning small-font text will not survive round-trip. Crop, don't scale. If you need to read numbers off a chart, send the chart cropped to the region of interest, not the whole page. Multi-image beats one giant image. Split large documents into per-region tiles; each tile gets its own 384-token budget. This is why Chartography lands at 64.3 (competitive with Claude Opus 4.8's 65.0) but why the model will still miss a footnote in a 12-point font on a full-page screenshot. Every vision-agent workflow you build should assume this ceiling. Última verificación: 2026-09-01. Esta página cita datos que cambian con el tiempo: toma la fecha de arriba como su grado de actualidad. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: 2. The vision encoder has a hard 384-tokens-per-image budget

documents.t: Most published MoE recipes activate 8 experts of 32 or 64. V4-Flash-Vision-Exp uses a much wider expert bank: 256 routed experts + 1 shared expert, with only 6 routed experts firing per token — a 2.3% activation ratio. The model has 43 layers, hidden size 4,096, and the hybrid attention stack combines two mechanisms: Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) — sparse patterns for long-range reads. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) — an aggressively compressed form for the deep-context tail. Wrapped over that, Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) replace the standard residual with a constrained-manifold projection, which the paper reports stabilizes signal propagation through the 43-layer stack. Together these are the reason the model can advertise a 1,048,576-token context window without the quadratic attention bill.
documents.s: 3. The MoE routing is unusually sparse — 6 of 256 experts fire per token

documents.t: Sticker prices, all per million tokens: Model Input Output Cached read DeepSeek V4-Flash-Vision-Exp (API) $0.22 $0.66 $0.007 Claude Opus 4.8 $15.00 $75.00 $1.50 Kimi K3 (cache-miss / cache-hit) $3.00 / $0.30 $15.00 $0.30 Cached-read at $0.007/M is not a typo — that is roughly one two-hundredth of a cent per thousand tokens. For any workload where a repeating system prompt or long context is re-sent (agent loops, RAG over a static corpus, chat with a fixed persona) the effective input price collapses. This is the reason V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is showing up in agent-cost tables at a fraction of what Claude Opus 4.8 costs per task, even when the raw quality is within a few points. documents.t: V4-Flash-Vision-Exp launched on the DeepSeek API on August 21, 2026, and only landed on Hugging Face as open weights on August 31. This ten-day gap is DeepSeek's new default. Compare Z.ai (GLM), which has been shipping API + weights simultaneously; DeepSeek is deliberately sequencing. The industry read: labs now agree that big open MoEs are shipping. The remaining question is when in the release cycle the weights arrive. For production planning that means: If you need on-prem from day zero, watch for GLM-family releases. If you can start on the API and cut over to self-hosted a week or two later, DeepSeek is the pattern.
documents.s: The release pattern — API first, weights ten days later

documents.t: There are three realistic paths. Pick by the two constraints that actually matter: whether the weights need to live on your infrastructure, and how much VRAM (or RAM) you can pay for. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Path A — DeepSeek's hosted API (default for almost everyone)⌄ OpenAI-compatible endpoint at api.deepseek.com. Model ID is deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp. Pricing is $0.22 / $0.66 / $0.007 per million tokens. This is the right answer unless you have a data-residency or air-gap constraint. ←PreviousNext→ 2Path B — vLLM on 4× GB300 (single-node self-host)⌄ The vLLM container ships day-0 support and the deepseek_v4 tool-call parser. You need one node with 4× GB300 (or equivalent B300 config). DSpark speculative decoding is enabled via --speculative-config. FP8 KV cache and block-size 256 are both required for the throughput numbers DeepSeek published. ←PreviousNext→ 3Path C — Community GGUF via llama.cpp / Ollama (workstation-class)⌄ unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF ships two dynamic quants: UD-Q4_K_XL at 155 GB and UD-Q8_K_XL at 162 GB. Neither fits a single 24/48/80 GB GPU. What works is a fat workstation with 192 GB+ system RAM and offload, or a small multi-GPU rig with CPU spillover. ←PreviousNext→ Hosted API — Python (OpenAI-compatible) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_DEEPSEEK_KEY", base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp", messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "What does this chart claim, and what's the one thing it hides?"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/chart.png"}}, ], } ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) Self-host — vLLM on 4× GB300 with DSpark CopyOpen in Claude↗ docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 \ vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv4-flash-vision \ deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --block-size 256 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --tool-call-parser deepseek_v4 \ --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' Local — Ollama with the community GGUF CopyOpen in Claude↗ ollama run hf.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL # Compact image syntax the model was trained to accept: # <image>path/to/screenshot.png</image> followed by your prompt

Reach for V4-Flash-Vision when: You need multimodal agent quality at roughly Opus-4.8 tier and cost is a factor. Cached-read pricing crushes anything on the closed frontier. The workload benefits from a 1M-token context (long-document VQA, whole-video-frame analysis, big-repo review with screenshots). You need open weights for compliance, air-gapped work, or fine-tuning, and you have (or rent) frontier-class hardware. You're building a chart-heavy or dashboard-parsing pipeline where you can control image tiling. Stay on Claude Opus 4.8 (or Sonnet 5) when: The job is whole-repository code translation or synthesis — NL2Repo is the outlier where the gap is real (57.7 vs 69.7). You need Claude-specific features: Extended thinking under budget, Skills, Sub-agent orchestration in Claude Code, or the Managed Agents session-budget controls. Your prompts contain images with tiny critical text and you cannot tile — you'll hit the 384-token cap and lose accuracy. You want a single vendor / SLA / support contact and are already invested in Anthropic tooling. For a broader model-choice framework, see How to choose a model. For a side-by-side of the whole open-weight wave, DeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave is the durable overview.
documents.s: When to reach for V4-Flash-Vision — and when to stay on Claude

documents.t: You will forget the 384-token cap. The first three vision agents you build will overshoot resolution and quietly lose accuracy on small text. Instrument for it: log per-image dimensions and downscale + tile deliberately. DSpark drops silently if you skip --speculative-config. Without the flag, vLLM will happily serve the model at 1/3 the throughput the release announced. Always pass the speculative config in production. The GGUF is not a laptop model. UD-Q4_K_XL is 155 GB. Community threads that show it "running" on smaller boxes are running it at fractional tokens/s via SSD swap — technically working, not usable. API vs weights version parity is not guaranteed. The API model can be silently updated; the Hugging Face weights are pinned to Vision-Exp. If a benchmark shifts a few points month-to-month on the API, that's why. Exp means experimental. The vision variant is not guaranteed to survive into production V4 releases. Do not build a critical pipeline on the assumption that this specific checkpoint will be around in a year.
documents.s: The gotchas that will bite you first

Intermedio On September 23, 2026 Fireworks published Ember-1: not a new architecture, not a new pre-train — Kimi K3 with its reasoning habit re-trained. Same 2.8-trillion-parameter body, same 1M context, same price per token. It just stops thinking so much. Fireworks reports 35–50% fewer reasoning tokens with no loss of accuracy, and on two of five published benchmarks Ember-1 outscores K3 running at its maximum effort setting while costing less. Four days later it was the top AI story on Hacker News. The interesting part is not the model — it is the claim underneath it: the cheapest way to run a reasoning model is no longer to tell it to think less. This page takes that claim apart, shows you the arithmetic the launch table implies but never prints, and gives you a way to test it on your own traffic in an afternoon. What you'll learn Separate the two things that make an agent expensive: price per token, and number of tokens — Ember-1 changes only the second Read the launch table honestly, including the benchmark where effort buys literally nothing and the one where every model scores under 22% Derive the cost per task the blog does not print (and discover a single benchmark run costs $5–$535) Understand why a 71% cut in reasoning tokens produced only a 39% cut in total tokens — and what that ratio tells you about your own bill Measure reasoning-token share on your workload with one field most SDK wrappers throw away Know the fine print before you migrate: research-preview status, no released weights, a lost input modality, and the revenue-tiered Kimi K3 licence underneath it all Última verificación: 2026-09-28. Benchmark table, training description, token-reduction figures and pricing are Fireworks' own announcement of September 23, 2026 — vendor-run, on vendor-chosen benchmarks, with no independent replication published yet. Context window (1,048,576), model id and rates were cross-checked against the Fireworks model page and the OpenRouter model API on 2026-09-28. Ember-1 shipped as a Research Preview with two weeks of serverless access, kept permanently "based on community demand" — availability is the most perishable fact here; check before you build on it. Licence clauses are quoted from the Kimi K3 LICENSE on Hugging Face. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Ember-1: Kimi K3's Answers for 40% Fewer Tokens (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Kimi K3, like every reasoning model, spends most of its generated tokens on internal reasoning — Fireworks puts it at sometimes more than 90%. In a multi-turn agent that reasoning is replayed into every later call, so context grows roughly quadratically with turn count and early thinking gets re-billed for the rest of the run. Fireworks' customers asked for K3's coding quality at lower cost; turning reasoning_effort down gave up too much quality, so Fireworks trained the behaviour instead — over 50 training runs and 200+ evaluations — teaching the model to keep the self-reflection that recovers from mistakes and drop the rest. The result is served as accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1 at exactly K3's rates: $3 / M uncached input, $0.30 / M cached input, $15 / M output.

This is the part that reframes how you should think about model cost. Ember-1's rate card is identical to Kimi K3's, on Fireworks and on OpenRouter alike ($3 input / $15 output per million, 1,048,576-token context on both). There is no discount. Every dollar saved comes from tokens that are never generated in the first place — and, in an agent loop, from those same tokens never being replayed as input on the next nineteen turns. That has a practical consequence: $/token is the wrong number on your dashboard. Two models at the same list price can differ 2× on the same task, and the model with the higher list price is regularly the cheaper one per finished task. AILmanac's What AI costs across providers makes the same point from the pricing side; Ember-1 is the cleanest natural experiment for it yet, because the price variable is pinned and only the token count moves.
documents.s: 1. Nothing got cheaper. The model just buys less.

documents.t: K3 exposes reasoning_effort at low, high and max. Fireworks ran all three as separate arms, which is what makes their table more useful than most launch tables: Benchmark N K3 low K3 high K3 max Ember-1 Ember-1 vs K3 max Terminal Bench 2.1 89 76.4% 77.6% 80.9% 82.0% −51.9% / −23.1 USD SWE-bench Verified 500 80.4% 86.0% 93.2% 92.2% −15.5% / −68.1 USD SWE-Interact 75 6.7% 13.3% 21.3% 20.0% −32.5% / −60.8 USD DeepSWE 1.1 113 55.8% 62.8% 66.4% 75.2% −23.7% / −126.9 USD τ-2 Bench Airline 50 64% 64% 64% 66% −5.9% / −0.3 USD Read down the K3 columns before you read the Ember column. On SWE-bench Verified, dropping from max to low costs you 12.8 points — that is the "give up too much quality" Fireworks is talking about, and it is why an effort dial alone could not solve their customers' problem. Ember-1 lands above K3 high on every row and above K3 max on two of five, at a lower cost than max on all five. Against K3 low it is strictly better on both axes. Two rows deserve separate attention: τ-2 Bench Airline: 64% / 64% / 64%. Three effort levels, one score. On this benchmark every extra thinking token K3 generates is pure waste — you pay max prices for low results. If your production workload looks like τ²-bench (a scripted customer-service policy, short turns, tool calls against a fixed API), the effort dial is a cost setting with no quality meaning, and you should have measured that rather than defaulted to it. The general habit — sweep effort on your eval before trusting a default — is in Effort tuning and Reasoning models compared. SWE-Interact: nobody breaks 22%. The same models that resolve 92–93% of SWE-bench Verified resolve one task in five when the benchmark requires interacting with a user mid-task. SWE-bench Verified is close to saturated and tells you almost nothing about a frontier model any more; the interactive variant is where the actual capability gap lives. Keep both in mind whenever a launch post leads with a 90-something SWE-bench number. This is the capability–reliability gap showing up as two columns in one table.
documents.s: 2. Turning effort down is not the same thing, and the table proves it

documents.t: Fireworks never labels the two figures in that last column. Read as relative cost reduction and absolute dollars saved over the whole run, they are internally consistent — and dividing one by the other recovers a number nobody publishes: what it costs to run these benchmarks once. The arithmetic below is ours, not Fireworks' — it is inference from their two published figures, so treat it as an order of magnitude, not a quote: Benchmark N Implied K3-max run cost Implied cost per task Terminal Bench 2.1 89 ~$44 ~$0.50 SWE-bench Verified 500 ~$439 ~$0.88 SWE-Interact 75 ~$187 ~$2.49 DeepSWE 1.1 113 ~$535 ~$4.74 τ-2 Bench Airline 50 ~$5 ~$0.10 A single DeepSWE 1.1 sweep on K3 at max effort runs to roughly half a thousand dollars — for 113 tasks. That is the real reason "just run your own evals on every model" is advice people nod at and do not follow, and it is worth knowing before you promise a stakeholder a five-model bake-off. It is also the number that makes a 24% saving matter: repeated nightly, that one benchmark is a $46,000-a-year line item.
documents.s: 3. The "−51.9% / −23.1 USD" column tells you what a benchmark run costs

documents.t: Fireworks' internal validation reports 71.3% fewer reasoning tokens and 39% fewer total tokens on the same traffic. The gap between those two numbers is the most useful thing in the announcement, and it generalises to any efficiency claim you are ever pitched. Reasoning tokens are a share of generated tokens. The rest of your bill is made of things an efficiency post-train cannot touch: System prompt and tool definitions, re-sent every turn (often the largest single block in an agent). Tool results — file contents, search results, HTTP responses — which arrive from the outside world at their own size. The final answer, which you actually wanted. Prior turns, replayed as input. So the ceiling on any "fewer thinking tokens" saving is your reasoning-token share, not the vendor's. An agent whose turns are 80% tool output will see a fraction of the advertised win; a chat workload with a short prompt and long deliberation will see most of it. Before you migrate anything, measure the share — the next section shows how. Why agents burn tokens covers the other three lines in that list. Watch out A vendor's token-reduction percentage is measured on the vendor's traffic mix. Your saving is bounded by your own reasoning-token share — measure it before you estimate anything.
documents.s: Why 71% off reasoning was only 39% off the bill

documents.t: Fireworks returns the model's thinking in a reasoning_content field (the content that would otherwise sit inside think tags) rather than in content. Many OpenAI-compatible wrappers drop unknown fields, which is how teams end up unable to answer "what share of our output is thinking?" — and, worse, how they silently break multi-turn quality. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Capture reasoning_content, do not discard it⌄ Log the length of reasoning_content next to the length of content for every assistant message, for a day of real traffic. The ratio is your reasoning-token share and the ceiling on any efficiency saving anyone can sell you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pass reasoning_content back on the next turn⌄ Fireworks is explicit: if you build the assistant message yourself as a dict and omit reasoning_content, the model loses access to its own previous reasoning. Passing message objects through unchanged handles this for you. A harness that strips the field will look like a quality regression that has nothing to do with the model. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run the same 20 real tasks on K3 max and on Ember-1⌄ Not a benchmark — your tasks, your tools, your system prompt. Record pass rate, total tokens, wall-clock, and dollars. Twenty tasks is enough to see a 35% token difference; it is not enough to see a 1-point quality difference, so treat quality as a gate, not a ranking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Add K3 at low effort as a third arm⌄ This is the arm most teams skip, and it is the one that tells you whether you need an efficiency-trained model at all. If K3-low already passes your gate, you were never going to pay for max in the first place. ←PreviousNext→ 5Compare on cost per completed task, never on $/M tokens⌄ Divide total dollars by tasks that passed your gate. A model that fails 10% more often is more expensive than its token count suggests, because failures are re-run by a human or by the agent. ←PreviousNext→ One call against Ember-1 on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $FIREWORKS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1", "max_tokens": 8192, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior engineer. Reply with a unified diff and one paragraph of rationale."}, {"role": "user", "content": "The test suite in ./tests fails on macOS only. Log and module attached: ..."} ] }' | jq '{ reasoning_chars: (.choices[0].message.reasoning_content // "" | length), answer_chars: (.choices[0].message.content // "" | length), usage: .usage }' The A/B you actually want: same task, three arms, one table CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Arm 1 — the incumbent at full effort MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="max" ./run-evals.sh > k3-max.jsonl # Arm 2 — the cheap way people try first MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k3" EFFORT="low" ./run-evals.sh > k3-low.jsonl # Arm 3 — the efficiency post-train (no effort setting to choose) MODEL="accounts/fireworks/models/ember-1" ./run-evals.sh > ember.jsonl # Then the only comparison that matters: # dollars spent / tasks that passed the gate jq -s 'group_by(.arm)[] | {arm: .[0].arm, passed: (map(select(.passed)) | length), usd: (map(.usd) | add), cost_per_pass: ((map(.usd) | add) / (map(select(.passed)) | length))}' *.jsonl
documents.s: Measure it on your own traffic in an afternoon

documents.t: It is a Research Preview. Fireworks ships new research models with two weeks of serverless access and makes them permanent "based on community demand". Do not put an unbudgeted migration behind that. Build the A/B, keep K3 as the fallback path, and re-check availability before you cut over — this is exactly the case server-side fallbacks and model routing patterns exist for. The weights are not released, and that is legal. The most-upvoted confusion in the Hacker News thread was some version of "they trained on open weights and are not releasing theirs — can they do that?" They can. The Kimi K3 licence grants the right to "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies of the Software; to run, deploy, fine-tune, or otherwise modify the Software and create derivative works from it" — with no copyleft obligation to publish what you build. What it does attach are two revenue-tiered conditions, and they are worth knowing whether or not you care about Ember-1: Model-as-a-Service above $20M. If you (and affiliates) run a MaaS business — giving third parties access to model inference or fine-tuning, e.g. via API, with meaningful control over inputs, parameters or training data — whose combined revenue exceeds $20 million over any consecutive 12 months, you must enter a separate agreement with Moonshot AI before commercial use of the Software or its derivative works. Attribution above 100M MAU or $20M/month. A product or service built on it that passes 100 million monthly active users or $20 million in monthly revenue must display "Kimi K3" prominently in its user interface. Internal use that does not expose the model or its capabilities to third parties is exempt from the MaaS clause. The practical reading: an open-weight licence can be MIT-shaped at the top and still gate the two situations a serious business ends up in. Read the licence before the benchmarks — the same advice applies to every "open" frontier release on DeepSeek, Qwen and the open-weight wave. Check your input modalities. OpenRouter lists Kimi K3 as text+image+video and Ember-1 as text+image. Fireworks' own model page advertises image input for Ember-1 and says nothing about video. If any part of your pipeline sends video frames to K3, verify that path explicitly before switching — a modality that silently disappears is a much worse failure than a quality dip, because it usually surfaces as a malformed request in production rather than a lower score in an eval. Check your sampling parameters too. OpenRouter's parameter list for Ember-1 omits seed and min_p, both of which it lists for K3. If your eval harness pins a seed for reproducibility, confirm the behaviour on the endpoint you will actually call rather than assuming the parent model's surface carried over. Porting prompts across models has the broader checklist.
documents.s: The fine print before you migrate

documents.t: Ember-1's other headline — "sets a new Pareto frontier on Bedside Bench across open and closed models including GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5" — comes from the Specialized Intelligence Index, which Fireworks launched on September 22, 2026, one day before Ember-1. Same company runs the index and ships the model. That is not automatically disqualifying, but it changes how you read it. What the SII does better than the usual leaderboard: Benchmarks come from practitioners, not academia — Doximity's BedsideBench (500 physician-validated clinical cases) for healthcare, Harvey's legal agent benchmarks for law, Sierra's τ-Banking and τ-Voice and Decagon's DuetBench for support, Rogo for finance, Novee's PWNBench and depthfirst's dfbench for security, and a software cluster including Datacurve's DeepSWE and Proximal's FrontierSWE V2. It reports cost per task and wall-clock duration next to score, from provider rate cards — the axes this whole page argues for. It labels every result by who can reproduce it: anyone, Fireworks-with-partner, or partner-only. That single label is the most useful piece of leaderboard metadata published this year; treat a partner-only row as a vendor claim with a nicer table around it. It refuses a composite score. No rollup across domains, no single "intelligence" number — which is the right call, and rare. What to hold in mind anyway: the benchmark suite, the arms chosen, the effort settings, and the model that wins are all selected by the same party. Compare its rows against an index run by someone with no model to sell before you quote them in a design doc. The general discipline is in The verification bottleneck.

Agentic coding on K3 at max effort, at volume: run the A/B this week. This is the exact workload Ember-1 was trained on, the reported savings are 15–52% of cost, and DeepSWE 1.1 suggests you may gain accuracy rather than trade it. Already running K3 at low or high because max was too expensive: strong candidate. Ember-1 beats K3 high on all five published rows and dominates low outright. Workloads shaped like τ²-bench (short turns, scripted policy, heavy tool output): expect modest savings — the effort dial was already doing nothing for you, and your reasoning-token share is small. Anything needing video input, a pinned seed, or a guaranteed 12-month endpoint: stay on K3 for now and re-evaluate when the preview converts. Not on Kimi K3 at all: the transferable lesson is the measurement, not the model. Find your reasoning-token share, sweep the effort dial on your own eval, and start reporting cost per completed task instead of $/M tokens. Every provider's version of this question is the same question. Check yourself 0/6 1Ember-1 costs exactly the same per token as Kimi K3 ($3 in / $15 out per million). Where does the reported 35–50% saving come from? A volume discount Fireworks applies at the invoice levelFewer tokens generated — mostly reasoning tokens — which also means fewer tokens replayed as input on later agent turnsAggressive prompt caching that K3 does not supportA smaller model with fewer parameters 2On τ-2 Bench Airline, Kimi K3 scores 64% at low, high AND max effort. What does that tell you? The benchmark is brokenMax effort is always wasted moneyOn this workload shape the effort dial buys no accuracy — running it at max is paying more for the same resultEffort only matters for models above 1T parameters 3Fireworks reports 71.3% fewer reasoning tokens but only 39% fewer total tokens on the same traffic. Why the gap? The reasoning figure is measured wrongReasoning is only part of what you pay for — system prompts, tool definitions, tool results and the final answer do not shrinkTotal tokens include other customers' trafficCached input tokens are billed twice 4Every model in the launch table scores 80–93% on SWE-bench Verified but 6.7–21.3% on SWE-Interact. What is the right conclusion? SWE-Interact is badly designedThe models regressed between the two evaluationsSWE-bench Verified is near saturation; the interactive variant, where the model must work with a user mid-task, is where the real capability gap still isInteractive tasks need a larger context window 5Fireworks built Ember-1 on Kimi K3's open weights and did not release Ember-1's weights. Under the Kimi K3 licence, is that allowed?
