documents.t: Google's launch post is explicit: $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens is an introductory rate available "through 31 December 2026." Standard pricing kicks in 1 January 2027: $1.50 / $7.50, matching the 3.6 Flash sticker. If you model 2027 cost on the intro number you will be off by 2×. Budgeting rule for a Claude shop cross-checking pipelines: run the A/B at the intro price, but pin the decision to the post-January number, because that is what your Q1 invoice will look like. See What AI costs across providers for the framework.
documents.s: 1. The intro price expires — and doubles — on 1 January 2027

documents.t: Google's launch benchmarks (3.7 Flash vs 3.6 Flash, higher is better): Benchmark 3.6 Flash 3.7 Flash Delta DeepSWE v1.1 (real bug fixes) 49.0% 65.3% +16.3 pts FrontierCode 1.1 Main (production code) 34.4% 43.6% +9.2 pts WebDev Arena (Elo) 1538 1588 +50 Elo AutomationBench (agent workflows) 17.0% 30.4% +13.4 pts GDPval AA v2 (knowledge work, Elo) 1421 ~1525 +~104 Elo The GDPval move is real but it still trails Claude Sonnet 5 at 1598 and GPT-5.6 Terra at 1578 for knowledge work. The DeepSWE and AutomationBench moves are where a workhorse model was previously embarrassed — real-repo bug fixes and multi-step agent runs. Read the shape, not the average: 3.7 Flash closed the coding-agent gap while barely moving on general knowledge work. That tells you what job Google is now willing to point Flash at.
documents.s: 2. The DeepSWE jump is bigger than the GDPval jump — and that asymmetry is the whole story

documents.t: Third-party measurements clock 3.7 Flash at roughly 340 output tokens/second, versus ~110 tok/s for GPT-5.6 Terra on comparable prompts — roughly 3×. For a user typing in a chat UI this is invisible: humans read at ~250 words/minute (~5 tok/s), so anything above ~50 tok/s just streams. For a serial agent loop — 20 calls, each with a couple hundred output tokens — 3× compounds across every step and turns a minute of cumulative generation into ~20 seconds. If you are shopping Flash for a customer-facing chat, throughput is a rounding error. If you are shopping it for a coding agent or a research agent, throughput is often the biggest single win. The physics behind this is on Fast inference and token speed.
documents.s: 3. The ~3× throughput advantage matters for agents, not chat

documents.t: Spec Gemini 3.7 Flash Model ID gemini-3.7-flash Context window 1,048,576 input tokens Max output 65,536 tokens Thinking levels low, medium (default), high Modalities in text, image, audio, video, PDF Modalities out text Tools function calling, structured output (JSON schema), code execution, grounding, computer use Intro price (through 31 Dec 2026) $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens Standard price (from 1 Jan 2027) $1.50 in / $7.50 out per 1M tokens Availability Google AI Studio, Android Studio, Gemini API, Google Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Note the thinking_level default is medium, not low or "auto." A blind port from 3.6 Flash will pay for medium reasoning by default; drop it to low for classification/extraction jobs where the extra planning is wasted. High is only worth it on the hardest coding and multi-step agent problems — Google's own migration guide warns "higher isn't automatically better."

The good news for anyone already on 3.6 Flash: the API surface is unchanged. You swap the model ID and re-run your evals. The bad news for anyone porting from Claude or from older Gemini: the 3.6-era API changes still bite. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Swap the model ID⌄ Use `gemini-3.7-flash`. Do not pin to `gemini-3.6-flash` if you want the new pricing and benchmark deltas. ←PreviousNext→ 2Re-benchmark thinking_level for your workload⌄ Default is medium. For low-variance classification, drop to `low` and measure quality delta. For long-horizon agent runs with tool calls, try `high` on a small sample — but only if your evals show the win. ←PreviousNext→ 3Delete temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count if carried over from Claude⌄ 3.7 Flash inherits the 3.6-era removal of these sampling knobs. A Claude-shaped call that carries them over will fail or be silently ignored depending on the SDK. See the 3.6 migration list on [Gemini 3.6 Flash for Claude users](/docs/models/gemini-3-6-flash-family) — the same list still applies. ←PreviousNext→ 4Stop prefilling the assistant turn⌄ Gemini 3.7 Flash still rejects prefilled model turns (conversations ending on a non-empty `model` role). If you use Anthropic-style prefill to steer output, restructure into a user turn before porting. ←PreviousNext→ 5Budget the 2027 cost, not the intro cost⌄ If your ROI analysis needs 3.7 Flash to be cheaper than Claude Haiku 4.5, do the math with $1.50 / $7.50 — the price that starts 1 January 2027 — not the four-and-a-half-month intro sticker. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal 3.7 Flash call (Python SDK) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from google import genai client = genai.Client() # picks up GOOGLE_API_KEY resp = client.models.generate_content( model="gemini-3.7-flash", contents="Given this diff, list the 3 riskiest lines with file:line and 1-sentence rationale each.", config={ "thinking_level": "medium", # default; drop to "low" for pure extraction, raise to "high" for hardest agent steps # do NOT pass temperature, top_p, top_k, candidate_count "tools": [{"function_declarations": [...]}], # or {"computer_use": {}} }, ) print(resp.text)

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.7 Flash: serial coding-agent loops (DeepSWE-shaped work), web-development scaffolding, and any workflow where the ~3× throughput advantage compounds across many calls. Reach for 3.7 Flash: high-volume tool loops during the intro window — the 2× price gap versus Claude Haiku 4.5 (on Anthropic's current Haiku sticker) is genuine and closes on 1 January 2027. Stay on Claude Sonnet 5: knowledge-work tasks where 3.7 Flash still trails on GDPval AA v2 (1525 vs 1598), and long-horizon agent runs where extended-thinking discipline matters more than raw throughput. Stay on Claude for any workload where you rely on prefilled assistant turns, temperature control, or Anthropic's tool-use loop — you'll fight the Gemini API instead of using it. Cross-check both: for anything customer-facing, run a small eval on both at the tier you actually plan to ship. The DeepSWE headline is genuine but does not survive contact with every codebase. For the broader Claude-vs-Gemini framing predating this release, see Gemini for Claude users, the coding-focused Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding, and Choosing a model. For the OpenAI side of the same week, GPT-5.6 August update. For cross-model porting rules that keep any of these swaps stable, Porting prompts across models.

Intermedio Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, twenty days after 3.7 Flash and its third Flash release in six weeks. Same tier, same 1M window, same $0.75 / $3.75 introductory sticker, same model-ID pattern. What changed is the shape of the model's behavior: Google says 3.8 Flash "works harder," executing extra reasoning steps and calling tools iteratively on complex tasks, and the benchmark table shows what that buys. DeepSWE v1.1 moved from 65.3 to 73.7, within a third of a point of Claude Opus 5. Terminal-bench 2.1 reached 89.4, a hair above Opus 5's 89.1. And on Terminal-bench 4.0, the harder successor, 3.8 Flash posts 19.1 against Opus 5's 51.8. This lesson is for a Claude user deciding whether to route work to it. It covers the numbers that are load-bearing, the token-usage cost of "working harder," the migration checklist that has not changed since 3.7, the gated Cyber variant, and the workloads where Claude is still the right default. What you'll learn Recognize what shipped on September 2, 2026 and why a three-week Flash cadence (3.6 → 3.7 → 3.8) is the real signal Read the benchmark table with the right lens: near-parity with Opus 5 on DeepSWE and Terminal-bench 2.1, a 33-point gap on Terminal-bench 4.0, a lead on domain-agent benchmarks Price the 'works harder' behavior: ~30% more output tokens per task, so the same sticker costs more per task than 3.7 Flash Migrate a 3.7 Flash or Claude call to gemini-3.8-flash without surprises (the 3.6-era API removals still apply) Know what Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is, what the Fairwind Program gates, and why you almost certainly cannot call it Última verificación: 2026-09-15. Launch date, pricing window, "works harder" language, Cyber benchmarks, and Fairwind details from Google's launch post. Model ID, thinking_level values and default, context and output limits, and the migration list from Google AI for Developers: latest model. Knowledge cutoff and the DeepSWE / Terminal-bench 2.1 / LVBench deltas from the DeepMind model card. The full comparison table (Opus 5, Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra columns) is Google's evaluation report as reproduced by Vellum; the "~30% more output tokens per task" figure is Emergent's analysis of that report. Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index and cost-per-task numbers are as reported by The Register on September 2. Note a discrepancy: Google's 3.8 report lists 3.7 Flash at 1482 on GDPval-AA v2, while third-party coverage at the 3.7 launch put it near 1525; we show Google's figure here. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

documents.t: Gemini 3.8 Flash is the same-tier successor to 3.7 Flash, model ID gemini-3.8-flash, 1M-token context, 64K max output, thinking_level of low / medium (default) / high, priced at $0.75 in / $3.75 out per 1M tokens through December 31, 2026 and $1.50 / $7.50 from January 1, 2027. It is live in the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, Android Studio, Stitch, Gemini Enterprise, the Gemini app (AI Pro and Ultra), AI Mode in Search, and Google Sheets. Alongside it, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber replaces 3.5 Flash Cyber for vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program. The cadence is the story again. 3.6 Flash on July 21, 3.7 on August 13, 3.8 on September 2: Google is iterating its workhorse tier every three weeks while the flagship stays quiet (The Register notes 3.5 Pro missed its June date). Read that as a fast developer feedback loop at the tier most teams actually pay for. Anthropic's answer this month is Claude Fable 5.1 at the top of the stack, not a cheaper Sonnet; OpenAI's is GPT-6 Astra.

Google's evaluation report, the rows a Claude shop should care about (higher is better): Benchmark 3.8 Flash 3.7 Flash Claude Opus 5 Claude Sonnet 5 GPT-5.6 Sol DeepSWE v1.1 (real bug fixes) 73.7% 65.3% 74.0% 53.8% 72.7% Terminal-bench 2.1 89.4% — 89.1% — 88.8% Terminal-bench 4.0 19.1% 11.2% 51.8% 12.4% 37.3% OSWorld-2.0 (computer use) 59.0% 50.6% 75.4% 42.6% 62.6% HLE-Verified 54.9% 53.6% 54.4% 31.0% 54.5% GDPval-AA v2 (Elo) 1545 1482 1824 1584 1710 Vals Finance Agent v2 61.4% 59.0% 58.6% 53.9% 53.8% Harvey Legal Agent 10.0% 8.8% 6.7% 5.0% 2.5% BioMysteryBench (hard) 56.5% 43.5% 49.4% 34.1% 44.7% Three reads. First, the DeepSWE +8.4 is the load-bearing number, exactly as the +16.3 was for 3.7 Flash: Google keeps pouring the workhorse's gains into repository-scale coding. Second, Terminal-bench 2.1 vs 4.0 is the same split we flag on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash the following week: a cheap model can saturate the older suite while the harder one, with longer adaptive shell sessions, still separates Opus 5 by more than 30 points. Third, on the domain-agent benchmarks (finance, legal, biology) 3.8 Flash now leads every column, including Opus 5. If your work is a finance or legal agent, that row is worth an eval on its own. If your work is an interactive coding session, the 4.0 row is the one to budget around.

documents.t: Google's own description of the change: on complex tasks the model "exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively." The launch post also says developers can "utilize lower effort levels to minimize token overhead," which is a polite way of saying the default now spends more. Emergent's read of the evaluation report puts it at roughly 30% more output tokens per task; Artificial Analysis measured $0.58 per Intelligence Index task, about 40% more than 3.7 Flash, at the same per-token sticker. For a Claude user this is the familiar effort trade-off wearing a different name: the model reaches for more tool calls and more thinking before it answers. The sticker did not move; the bill per task did. Budget on task cost, not token price. And re-run any latency SLO you had on 3.7 Flash: more iterations means more wall-clock, even at Flash speed. The physics is on Why agents burn tokens.
documents.s: 2. "Works harder" is a token-usage decision Google made for you

documents.t: Artificial Analysis puts 3.8 Flash at 59 on its Intelligence Index (at high reasoning), tied with GPT-5.6 Sol at extra-high and Grok 4.6 at medium, versus Claude Opus 5 at 63 and Claude Fable 5.1 at 66 (both at max). Its cost-per-task figure for Fable 5.1 is about $3.76, roughly 6× 3.8 Flash's $0.58. Against Opus 5 on list price, Vellum's arithmetic is about 6.7× cheaper on both input and output. Against Sonnet 5 the gap is far smaller, and Sonnet 5 still leads on GDPval-AA v2 (1584 vs 1545). So the honest comparison is: 3.8 Flash is a Sonnet-tier price with DeepSWE and domain-agent scores that now reach Opus territory, and Terminal-bench 4.0 / OSWorld scores that do not. Current Claude list prices are on Models and pricing.

List the 3 riskiest hunks as file:line with a one-sentence reason each.", config={ "thinking_level": "low", # start low on 3.8 Flash; it already 'works harder' at medium # no temperature / top_p / top_k / candidate_count "tools": [{"function_declarations": [...]}], }, ) print(resp.text)

Alongside the general model, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, replacing 3.5 Flash Cyber. Google's numbers: CWE-Bench patching at 47.2% pass@1 against "a leading frontier model" at 47.8%; a vulnerability-discovery success rate above 70% across 20 programming languages; 2.6× more correct patches to Chrome vulnerabilities than the best commercial models per Chrome Security; and, per Wiz, 7.5–9.7 points higher recall at 2.3–5.2× lower cost. You almost certainly cannot call it. Access runs through the Fairwind Program, limited to "trusted government authorities, as well as critical infrastructure operators and software maintainers," by application. This is the same shape as OpenAI gating GPT-6 Astra's exploit capability behind a vetted program (see the Astra field guide) and Anthropic's treatment of Mythos-class models. For a Claude user the practical takeaway is that the frontier's cyber capability now ships as a separate, gated SKU on all three stacks, and the general models are deliberately not it. Our security section covers what that means for the agents you can call.

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for 3.8 Flash: repository-scale coding that looks like DeepSWE, where 73.7 vs Opus 5's 74.0 at a sixth of the task cost is a real trade. Reach for 3.8 Flash: finance, legal, and life-science agent workflows — it now leads every column on Vals Finance Agent v2, Harvey Legal, and BioMysteryBench, including Opus 5. Reach for 3.8 Flash: long-video and chart understanding (LVBench 87.8, CharXiv 86.2) where Claude has no equivalent input path. Stay on Claude Opus 5: interactive terminal agents and computer use. Terminal-bench 4.0 (51.8 vs 19.1) and OSWorld-2.0 (75.4 vs 59.0) are the widest gaps on the table. Stay on Claude for knowledge work where GDPval-AA v2 matters: Opus 5 at 1824 and even Sonnet 5 at 1584 are ahead of 3.8 Flash's 1545. Stay on Claude for anything built on prefilled turns, temperature control, or Anthropic's tool-use loop — you will fight the Gemini API rather than use it. Cross-check both, at the effort you will ship: 3.8 Flash's table is at default or high thinking and costs ~30% more tokens per task than 3.7; Claude's is at max effort. Neither is your production setting. For the broader framing, Gemini for Claude users; for the coding-specific comparison, Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding; for the durable decision framework, Choosing a model.

Intermedio On September 15, 2026 Google released two speech-to-speech models: Gemini 3.8 Live (gemini-3.8-live) and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking). Both are generally available today in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Google's launch post is mostly benchmarks and demos. If you are building a voice agent, the details that matter are in the developer docs: tools now run asynchronously by default, one config field now returns an error, and one feature is always on and billed while the model listens. This page collects those details in one place. What you'll learn Pick between the two models using the real API differences, not the marketing names Migrate a gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview agent without hitting the thinkingLevel, affective-dialog, and blocking-tool traps Design around the session walls: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per WebSocket connection Estimate what a voice session really costs, and why cost grows faster than minutes Ship a browser client without leaking an API key Última verificación: 2026-09-15. Launched today. Model IDs, GA status and feature list come from the Gemini API changelog (September 15, 2026). Prices come from the Gemini API pricing page. Token limits and the migration list come from the gemini-3.8-live model page. Thinking, tool-scheduling and VAD details come from the Live API capabilities and tools guides. Session limits come from the session-management guide. Billing gotchas come from the Live API best-practices guide. Benchmarks and consumer availability come from Google's launch post. One discrepancy: the launch post says the models detect and switch between 97 languages mid-conversation, while the Live API overview still says live translation covers "70+ languages." Before quoting either number, check which feature it refers to. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

documents.t: Use gemini-3.8-live as the default for low-latency voice agents. Use gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking when the caller asks hard, multi-step questions and a short delay is acceptable. Both cost $3.00 / 1M audio input tokens (~$0.005/min) and $12.00 / 1M audio output tokens (~$0.018/min), plus $0.75 / $4.50 for text. Both have a 131,072-token input window and 65,536-token output limit, and both have a free tier in the Gemini API.

gemini-3.8-live gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking Google's positioning "Default option for most low-latency voice agent experiences" "High-reasoning audio-to-audio model supporting background reasoning during live audio interactions" Thinking Interleaved reasoning; thinkingLevel is not accepted thinkingLevel = low / medium / high (no minimal); includeThoughts: true for summaries Function calling Async by default (NON_BLOCKING); BLOCKING still available; scheduling INTERRUPT / WHEN_IDLE / SILENT Async only, with no blocking mode and no scheduling control Consumer surfaces Search Live Gemini Live app; Docs, Gmail, Keep for subscribers Headline numbers (Google) 2nd on Artificial Analysis' Speech Agent Arena 82.6 Speech-to-Speech Quality Index (1st); 68.6% τ-Voice; 35.1% τ-Voice-banking; 97.7% Big Bench Audio Look at the 35.1% on τ-Voice-banking, the number Google chose to publish. Even the top-ranked voice model completes only about a third of realistic banking tasks by voice. Treat that as the ceiling for unattended voice agents that handle money, and put confirmation gates on anything consequential (the same rule as in Full-duplex voice AI). Every audio output is watermarked with SynthID. If your product records or re-publishes model speech, AI-audio detectors can identify it.
documents.s: What shipped, and what Google claims

documents.t: Extended Thinking does not go silent while it thinks. Google says it "reasons and speaks simultaneously." It gives early verbal cues ("let me check that") and narrates progress while reasoning continues in the background. That changes how your client decides when the model is finished. On this model turnComplete: true does not mean the session is idle. Background reasoning can still be running. Check interaction_status instead (IN_PROGRESS vs IDLE) before you end a call, hand off to a human, or start the next scripted step. This is the same "fast talker, slow thinker" split OpenAI introduced with GPT-Live. The difference is that Google puts both roles in one model, where GPT-Live delegates the reasoning to a separate frontier model.
documents.s: 1. The "thinking" model narrates while it reasons

documents.t: Google's migration notes for gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview → gemini-3.8-live include four changes that alter what your code does: Remove thinkingLevel. 3.1 Flash Live defaulted to minimal. 3.8 Live does not accept the field, so a config copied from 3.1 must drop it. Tool calls are now asynchronous by default. On 3.1 Flash Live, "the model will not start responding until you've sent the tool response." On 3.8 Live the model keeps talking while your function runs. That is good for latency, but a tool that must finish first (an identity check, a payment) now needs behavior: BLOCKING set explicitly. The Extended Thinking model has no blocking mode, so those flows need a gate in your own code. Proactive audio is always on. The model can decide not to respond when speech isn't addressed to it. You cannot turn this off, and the best-practices guide notes that you are billed input tokens while it listens. Affective dialog is gone. If your agent relied on enableAffectiveDialog to adapt to the caller's tone, remove it and test the new default behavior. Two changes help you. send_client_content now works for the whole session, so you can inject text context (CRM data, a transcript of a transfer) mid-call. Turn coverage now defaults to TURN_INCLUDES_AUDIO_ACTIVITY_AND_ALL_VIDEO.
documents.s: 2. Upgrading from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior, not just the model string

documents.t: Audio accumulates at roughly 25 tokens per second (about 1,500 per minute). That is where the per-minute prices come from: 1,500 × $3/1M ≈ $0.0045 in, and 1,500 × $12/1M = $0.018 out. The trap is that each turn re-processes the entire accumulated context, not only the new audio. The best-practices guide says so directly. Two smaller costs stack on top: enabling transcription bills text output on top of audio output, and proactive audio bills input tokens while the model listens. A rough illustration (our arithmetic, not a Google figure): take a 10-minute call with 20 turns. The context grows from 0 to about 15,000 tokens, so the average turn re-reads about 7,500 tokens of input. That is about 150,000 input tokens (~$0.45), compared with ~$0.045 if only new audio were counted. Longer calls cost more per minute, not just more in total. Context window compression, which you need anyway to get past the 15-minute wall, also limits this cost growth.
documents.s: 3. A voice session's cost grows faster than its length

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Know the three limits⌄ Without compression, audio-only sessions stop at 15 minutes and audio+video sessions at 2 minutes. Separately, each WebSocket connection lasts around 10 minutes. The 2-minute video limit catches most screen-share demos. ←PreviousNext→ 2Enable context window compression⌄ Set ContextWindowCompressionConfig with a sliding window and a token trigger threshold. This removes the session-length limit and also stops per-turn input cost from growing without bound. Choose the trigger deliberately: compression discards the oldest turns, so pin anything the agent must remember (policy, caller identity) in the system instruction or re-send it with send_client_content. ←PreviousNext→ 3Enable session resumption⌄ Configure SessionResumptionConfig and store the latest handle from each SessionResumptionUpdate. A handle stays valid for 2 hours after the session ends, so a dropped connection can resume with its state instead of starting a new call. ←PreviousNext→ 4Handle GoAway before the connection drops⌄ The server sends GoAway with a timeLeft field before it disconnects. Use that time to finish the current sentence and reconnect with the resumption handle, so the caller never hears a gap. ←PreviousNext→ 5Discard buffered audio on interruption⌄ When the server flags an interruption (barge-in), clear your client-side playback buffer immediately. Otherwise the caller hears the model finish a sentence it has already abandoned. ←PreviousNext→ 6Send small, correctly formatted chunks⌄ Input is raw 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz little-endian; output is 16-bit PCM at 24 kHz. Resample microphone input (usually 44.1 or 48 kHz) down to 16 kHz and send 20–40 ms chunks. Large buffers add latency no model can remove. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The session walls, and how to design around them

documents.t: Live sessions work best when the client connects directly to Google, because proxying real-time audio through your backend adds latency. The safe way to do this is an ephemeral token. Your server mints it, and the client uses it once. Defaults: the token expires 30 minutes after creation, it must be used to start a new session within 1 minute, and it allows 1 use. You can lock it with liveConnectConstraints to a specific model, response modality and resumption settings, so a stolen token cannot be used for anything else. Ephemeral tokens work only with the Live API and only on v1beta. System-instruction skeleton for gemini-3.8-live (async tools, always-on proactive audio) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are Ava, a voice assistant for Northwind Travel. You are SPEAKING, not writing. RESPOND IN ENGLISH. YOU MUST RESPOND UNMISTAKABLY IN ENGLISH. Style: - Short sentences, one idea each. Never read lists, markdown, or URLs aloud. - If speech is clearly not addressed to you (TV, side conversation), stay silent. Tools: - lookup_booking: invoke ONLY after the caller has given BOTH booking reference AND last name. - While a lookup is running, tell the caller you are checking. Do not guess the result. - change_booking: before invoking, read back the exact change and wait for a clear spoken "yes". Safety: - Repeat back every number, date, and name before acting on it. - If audio is unclear, say what you think you heard and ask. - Anything involving refunds or payment details: offer a human agent instead. The skeleton follows Google's own guidance for Live agents: state the output language explicitly in capitals, and give each tool a precise condition for when to call it. That second rule matters more with async tools, because the model talks while the tool runs and will fill the silence with a guess unless you tell it not to.
documents.s: Browser and mobile clients: never ship the API key

documents.t: vs Claude. Claude's voice features remain turn-based: voice mode in the Claude apps, push-to-talk in Claude Code. A common hybrid uses a Live model as the conversational front end and calls Claude as a tool for heavy reasoning or coding. Async function calling suits this pattern well, since the call can keep going while the tool runs. vs OpenAI. GPT-Live is a speech-native, full-duplex ChatGPT product. For developers, OpenAI's offering is gpt-realtime on the Realtime API (see Full-duplex voice AI for the landscape). Early community reports (Hacker News launch thread, unverified). Commenters praised latency, voice quality, accent handling and live translation. Others said Extended Thinking reasoned inconsistently and that the model "invents additional requirements" in agentic flows. These are anecdotes, not measurements, but they match the 35.1% banking score: test your own task end to end before trusting it. Check yourself 0/5 1You port a gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview config that sets thinkingLevel: minimal to gemini-3.8-live. What should you do? Can you safely hang up? Yes, the turn is doneOnly if transcription is offNot necessarily; background reasoning may still be running, so check interaction_status for IDLEOnly after a GoAway message 4Why does a 20-minute voice call cost more than twice a 10-minute call? Audio output price doubles after 15 minutesEach turn re-processes the whole accumulated context, so per-turn input grows with call lengthSynthID watermarking is billed per minuteResumed sessions are billed twice 5Your screen-sharing support demo keeps disconnecting at about two minutes. Most likely cause? The ephemeral token expiredAudio+video sessions are limited to 2 minutes without context window compressionThe 131K input window is fullProactive audio ended the call Gemini Live API vocabulary girarTérminoNON_BLOCKING functionDefiniciónA tool that runs asynchronously while the model keeps talking. The default on gemini-3.8-live, and the only mode on Extended Thinking.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→ Key takeaways Two GA models, one price: gemini-3.8-live is the low-latency default; gemini-3.8-live-extended-thinking reasons in the background while it keeps speaking. Migrating from 3.1 Flash Live changes behavior: remove thinkingLevel, mark must-finish tools BLOCKING, expect always-on proactive audio (billed while listening), and drop affective dialog. Plan for the limits up front: 15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video, ~10 min per connection. Compression, resumption handles and GoAway handling are required for production. Cost grows faster than call length because every turn re-reads the whole context. Compression is both the session-length fix and the cost fix. Even Google's best score on voice banking tasks is 35.1%. Keep spoken confirmation gates on anything that moves money or data.

Intermedio Google opened the Gemini 4 generation on September 30, 2026 with a single model, Argon, and a number nobody else has: a 1 million token output limit, up from the previous 64K. Not the context window — that stayed at 1M. The output ceiling went up 16x. It landed at the top of Hacker News and stayed there. It also landed in a strange place commercially: Google's own post says Argon "leads or ties for the highest score in more categories than GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5," while the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index published the same week puts Argon at 53 against Claude Opus 5.5's 58. Both statements are accurate. They measure different things, and the gap between them is the most useful thing on this page. This lesson is for a Claude user deciding whether Argon changes anything about their routing. It covers what the 1M output limit actually buys, how to read two contradictory benchmark stories, the per-task economics that the "40% cheaper" headlines invert, and why your access request will probably be declined. What you'll learn Separate the 1M output limit from the 1M context window — they are different ceilings and only one of them moved Reconcile Google's '13 of 18 categories' claim with the independent index that places Argon 5 points below Claude Opus 5.5 Price a task properly: why 62K output tokens against Astra's 27K means Argon's advantage is its rate card, not its efficiency Read the 15% hallucination rate for what it is — an abstention behaviour, not a knowledge win Understand what the Fairwind Program gates, what it requires of your org, and why Argon is effectively uncallable for most readers Última verificación: 2026-10-01. Launch date, the "1M tokens, up from the previous 64K" output figure, introductory and standard pricing, the internal use-case numbers (quantum 40%, 300+ TiB, Fuchsia Zircon 800K lines, libgav1 32K lines / 2.7x) and the Wiz partnership come from Google's launch post. Fairwind eligibility and the access terms come from the Fairwind Program page; the cyber-specific benchmarks from DeepMind's Gemini cyber page. The Intelligence Index scores, 62K-vs-27K output tokens per task, AA-Omniscience hallucination rates and per-task costs are Artificial Analysis' figures as reported by The Decoder and Trending Topics. The 18-benchmark comparison table is Google's own evaluation report as reproduced by VentureBeat. Two discrepancies, both unresolved and both load-bearing. (1) Artificial Analysis' index is quoted as 53 by The Decoder and as 52.6 by Trending Topics, and Opus 5.5 as 58 and 57.6 respectively — the same numbers rounded or not. We use the unrounded pair where precision matters. (2) Google's framing and the independent index disagree on whether Argon leads the frontier; we present both rather than pick. No API model ID has been published — Google's docs do not yet list an Argon identifier, so anyone showing you one is guessing. Pricing is introductory and explicitly scheduled to double; re-check before you budget. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Gemini 4 Argon: The Field Guide for Claude Users (Sep 30, 2026)

documents.t: Gemini 4 Argon is Google's new frontier model, 1M-token input context and a 1M-token output limit (up from 64K), priced at an introductory $2 in / $10 out per 1M tokens with cached input at 95% off, rising to $4 / $20 after the introductory period. It is not generally available: it is rolling out to vetted cyber defenders through the Fairwind Program, then to paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers. On Google's own 18-benchmark set it leads or ties in 13 categories; on the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scores 53, tying GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 and sitting five points below Claude Opus 5.5.

Almost every summary of this launch says "1 million tokens" and leaves the reader to assume a context window. The context window did not change. Gemini has been at 1M input tokens since the 3.x line — Gemini 3.8 Flash has the same 1M window and a 64K output cap. What moved is the output ceiling, from 64K to 1M. These are separate limits and they fail in separate ways: Limit What it governs Gemini 3.8 Flash Gemini 4 Argon Input context How much you can send — files, transcripts, repo 1M 1M Max output How much the model can emit in one response, including reasoning tokens 64K 1M The practical consequence is about where a long task breaks. With a 64K output cap, a genuinely long-horizon job — refactor this subsystem, draft this filing, triage this codebase — has to be chunked by you, and every chunk boundary is a place where the model loses its own working state. Google's pitch is that Argon can hold a single uninterrupted chain of reasoning and execution across the whole job instead. Three things to keep in mind before you treat that as free: Reasoning tokens come out of the same budget. On Gemini, thinking tokens are output tokens. A 1M output allowance is not 1M tokens of deliverable; it is 1M tokens of thinking plus deliverable. Output is the expensive side. At introductory pricing, output costs 5x input ($10 vs $2). A response that actually used the full million output tokens would cost $10 on its own, and $20 once standard pricing lands. Nothing obliges the model to use it. A raised ceiling changes what is possible, not what is typical. Argon averages 62K output tokens per Intelligence Index task — around 6% of its ceiling.
documents.s: The number that is not what it looks like

documents.t: This is the part worth slowing down for, because the same pattern will repeat at every launch for the rest of the year. Story one — Google's evaluation report. Across 18 disclosed benchmarks, Argon leads or ties in 13 (12 outright leads, 1 tie): Benchmark Argon GPT-6 Astra Claude Opus 5.5 Harvey Legal Agent 19.6% 5.4% 3.8% GraphWalks 84.2% 71.8% 66.8% Vals Finance Agent v2 65.4% 53.5% 58.6% AutomationBench 51.3% 41.4% 42.5% LVBench (long video) 91.7% 87.5% 83.7% DeepSWE v1.1 77.9% 74.1% 74.2% CWE-bench v1 68% 68% (tie) 67% Gray Swan IPI (attack success — lower is better) 0.7% 8.5% 1.0% FrontierSWE v2 55.0% 65.5% — Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 57.6% 68.1% — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4% — 66.4% PostTrainBench 45.3% — 49.3% Story two — Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, an independent aggregate run the same week: Model Intelligence Index Claude Opus 5.5 58 (57.6) Claude Sonnet 5.5 56 Gemini 4 Argon (High) 53 (52.6) GPT-6 Astra (max) 53 Claude Fable 5.1 53 GPT-6.1 Sol (max) 52 Argon ranks #8 of 224 models on that index — excellent, and five points behind Anthropic's flagship. Neither source is lying. They diverge for reasons you can name: Benchmark selection is a choice. Google picked 18 benchmarks that include three domain-agent evals (legal, finance, automation) where Argon's margins are enormous. An aggregate index weights a different basket. Change the basket, change the winner. The losses cluster. Argon's four clear losses — FrontierSWE v2, Terminal-Bench Science, Terminal-bench 4.0, PostTrainBench — are all interactive, multi-turn, tool-driven agent work. Its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. That is a shape, not noise, and it maps cleanly onto routing decisions. Absolute numbers matter more than ratios. Harvey Legal Agent is the launch's most quoted row: 19.6% against 5.4%, a 3.6x lead. It is also a score of 19.6% — Argon fails roughly four out of five tasks on that benchmark. "Best available" and "good enough to deploy unsupervised" are different claims. Vendor benchmarks are not production behaviour. Trending Topics cites Bloomberg reporting that, per Google employees, the model performs worse in practical coding use than its scores suggest. Treat that as a single unverified report — but it is the kind of gap the is the model nerfed? protocol exists to measure. Pro tip When a launch post says 'leads or ties in N of M categories,' the load-bearing question is who chose M. Go find an aggregate index you did not have to be invited into, and compare the two baskets before you re-route anything.

Several outlets led with Argon being around 40% cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. The rate card supports that. Per-task cost tells a more interesting story, because Argon is a heavy token spender. Artificial Analysis measured average output per Intelligence Index task: Gemini 4 Argon: ~62,000 output tokens GPT-6 Astra: ~27,000 output tokens Argon emits roughly 2.3x more tokens to reach the same index score. Its cheaper bill is a pricing artefact, not an efficiency win. The measured cost per task: Model Cost per Intelligence Index task Index score GPT-6.1 Sol (max) $0.74 52 Gemini 4 Argon (intro pricing) $1.99 53 GPT-6 Astra (max) $3.26 53 Gemini 4 Argon (standard pricing) $3.98 53 Claude Opus 5.5 (max) $5.98 58 Read that table twice. Three separate conclusions fall out of it: Argon's advantage over Astra is scheduled to expire. At $2/$10 it costs $1.99 per task against Astra's $3.26 — a 39% saving. When pricing doubles to $4/$20, it costs $3.98, which is more than Astra. The entire cost argument lives inside the introductory window, and Google has not said how long that window is. GPT-6.1 Sol is the actual value pick on this table. One index point below Argon at 37% of Argon's intro cost and 19% of Opus 5.5's. If your work is not in Argon's strong domains, the cheap tier is where the ratio lives — the same lesson as every other month. Opus 5.5 costs 3x Argon's intro price for 5 more points. Whether that is worth it is entirely workload-dependent, which is the honest answer and also the reason choosing a model is a framework rather than a leaderboard. Measure tokens-per-task yourself before trusting any per-task cost claim CopyOpen in Claude↗ For the same 20 representative tasks from my own workload, I want to compare two models on cost, not on benchmark score. For each model, log per task: - input tokens, output tokens (split reasoning vs final answer if the API reports it) - wall-clock latency - a 0-5 quality score I assign blind, without knowing which model produced it Then compute, per model: - mean output tokens per task - mean cost per task at CURRENT list price - mean cost per task at the post-introductory price, if one is announced - cost per quality point Flag any model whose cost advantage disappears at post-introductory pricing. Do not quote vendor benchmark scores back to me — I only want my own 20 tasks.
documents.s: The economics are the opposite of the headline

documents.t: On AA-Omniscience, the component of the index that measures whether a model asserts false things, Argon posts a 15% hallucination rate against 51% for GPT-6 Astra and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol. That is not an incremental improvement; it is a different regime, and it is the most under-reported number in the launch. The mechanism matters. Artificial Analysis' characterisation is that Argon is far more likely to admit it does not know than to produce a confident wrong answer. So the win is in calibration and abstention, not in knowing more. Practical consequences: For retrieval, research and compliance work this is the headline feature, well ahead of any coding number. A model that says "not in the provided documents" is worth more than one that scores two points higher and invents a citation. It will read as less helpful in casual use. A model tuned to abstain refuses to guess, and users experience refusal-to-guess as hedging. Expect "it keeps saying it doesn't know" complaints from exactly the same capability that makes it trustworthy. It does not transfer to your prompts automatically. Abstention is a trained disposition interacting with your instructions. Tell a well-calibrated model "always give a definitive answer" and you have spent the advantage.

This is where most readers' interest ends in practice. Argon is not a public endpoint. It is gated behind the Fairwind Program, the same mechanism Google introduced for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber — but this time it gates the flagship, not a cyber-specific SKU. Fairwind prioritises governments and national cyber authorities, critical-infrastructure operators (healthcare, telecoms, energy, finance) and core technology platforms, and vets applicants for "a proven track record of ethical operations and research." Accepted organisations must agree to: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1User-level authentication with phishing-resistant MFA⌄ Not an org-level API key. Each human using Argon must be individually authenticated behind phishing-resistant MFA, plus applicable access controls. That rules out the usual pattern of one service credential shared by a team or embedded in a deployment. ←PreviousNext→ 2Restrict access to specific internal teams⌄ Only internal cybersecurity, incident response or penetration testing teams may be granted access. Not the platform team, not the product org, not a general-purpose internal assistant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Track employee access and use⌄ The org must maintain records of who accessed Argon and what for. Plan for an audit trail as a deliverable, not an afterthought. ←PreviousNext→ 4No sharing, redistribution or resale⌄ You cannot wrap Argon in a product and sell access, or pass it to a subsidiary or client. This is why no gateway or proxy legitimately offers it — see our note on gray-market AI proxies. ←PreviousNext→ 5Stay inside the dual-use boundary⌄ Authorized threat simulation, reverse engineering and malware analysis for defensive and academic research only. Malware creation and offensive use are prohibited. ←PreviousNext→ 6Then wait for the general rollout⌄ Google says paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers come first after Fairwind, then developers, enterprises and consumers 'as soon as possible.' No date has been given. ←PreviousNext→ For trusted defenders, Fairwind can pair Argon with CodeMender, Google's code-security agent that automates vulnerability fixes, and grants a build of Argon without the cyber guardrails that the eventual public model will carry. The cyber case is strong on its own numbers: real-world vulnerability discovery at 85.8% (against 71.0% for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber), the Wiz penetration-test benchmark at 70.9% (from 58.2%), CWE-bench v1 at 68%, and the best measured prompt-injection resistance of any frontier model — 0.7% attack success at k=15 on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection suite, against 1.0% for Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable, and 8.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That last number deserves its own sentence. An 8.5% success rate means roughly one in twelve indirect injection attempts lands; 0.7% means about one in 143. If you build agents that read untrusted web content, that is a twelve-fold difference in exposure — and it is measured at k=15, meaning fifteen attempts per target, not one. Worth reading alongside prompt injection and coding agents under attack. Watch out Because Fairwind forbids sharing, redistribution and resale, any gateway, proxy or 'unlocked Argon' reseller claiming to offer it is either misrepresenting a different model or violating the program terms. Treat an Argon endpoint you did not get from Google as untrustworthy by default.

The launch post's internal case studies are more informative than its benchmark table, because they describe long-horizon work with verifiable outcomes: Quantum algorithm optimisation — beat the published baseline for spacetime resource cost by 40%. Fleet memory profiling — found optimisations freeing over 300 TiB, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB total once applied. C/C++ to Rust migration — including 800K+ lines of the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. libgav1 video decoder — replaced 32K lines of hand-written SIMD, producing code 2.7x faster than the Rust port while emitting bit-identical output. The libgav1 result is the most instructive one on the list. "Bit-identical output" is the detail that makes it credible: there was a mechanical oracle for correctness, so the model's work could be verified rather than reviewed. That is the shape of task where a 1M output budget genuinely pays — large, mechanical, and checkable by a machine. It is also the shape of task most teams do not have, which is worth being honest about before extrapolating from these numbers to your own backlog.
documents.s: What Google says it did with it internally

documents.t: Short answer for most readers: no, because you cannot call it. When it opens up, here is the honest split based on where the benchmarks cluster. Work Where it should go Why Interactive coding agents, terminal work, computer use Claude (Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5) Argon's four clear losses are all in this family — Terminal-bench 4.0 57.4 vs 66.4, FrontierSWE v2 55.0 vs Astra's 65.5 Legal and financial document reasoning Argon, with review Harvey 19.6% vs 3.8–5.4%, Vals Finance 65.4% — but 19.6% absolute means supervision, not automation Long-video and long-context retrieval Argon LVBench 91.7%, GraphWalks 84.2% Research where a wrong citation is worse than no answer Argon 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% Defensive security, autonomous patching Argon via Fairwind, if you qualify 85.8% vuln discovery, CWE-bench 68%, lowest injection susceptibility High-volume everyday work GPT-6.1 Sol or a Flash/Sonnet tier $0.74 per task for one index point less than Argon Anything you are budgeting past the intro window Re-price it first $2/$10 becomes $4/$20; cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98 Check yourself 0/5 1Gemini 4 Argon's headline '1 million tokens' refers to which limit? The input context window, which doubled from 500KThe maximum output tokens in a single response, up from 64K — the context window stayed at 1MThe combined input plus output budget per requestThe daily token quota for Fairwind participants 2Google says Argon 'leads or ties in more categories' than GPT-6 Astra or Claude Opus 5.5, yet Artificial Analysis scores it 53 against Opus 5.5's 58. What is the best explanation? One of the two sources published incorrect dataArtificial Analysis tested a quantised or throttled version of the modelThey measure different benchmark baskets — Google chose 18 benchmarks including domain-agent evals where Argon's margins are largest, while the index weights a different mixThe index was run before Argon's final weights shipped 3Argon costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task against GPT-6 Astra's $3.26. Why is it wrong to call Argon the more efficient model? Because Astra is faster, so it costs less in engineering timeBecause Argon emits ~62K output tokens per task against Astra's ~27K — the saving comes from the rate card, and it reverses to $3.98 once introductory pricing doublesBecause the index does not include input token costsBecause efficiency can only be measured on coding benchmarks 4Argon's 15% hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience, against 51% for GPT-6 Astra, is primarily the result of what? A substantially larger training corpus with more factual coverageMandatory web grounding on every requestBetter calibration and a willingness to abstain — it admits it does not know rather than guessing confidentlyA post-hoc fact-checking pass that filters the output 5Your company wants Argon access through the Fairwind Program for its internal developer platform. What is the blocking problem? Fairwind requires a minimum annual spend commitmentAccess may only be granted to internal cybersecurity, incident response or penetration testing teams, and requires per-user phishing-resistant MFA rather than a shared service credentialFairwind is limited to organisations headquartered in the United StatesA developer platform would exceed the 1M output token limit girarTérminoGemini 4 Argon — the two 1M numbersDefiniciónInput context 1M (unchanged from Gemini 3.x). Max output 1M, up from 64K — this is the one that moved. Reasoning tokens count as output on Gemini, so the budget covers thinking plus deliverable.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 12 Siguiente→ Key takeaways The 1M is the OUTPUT limit (up from 64K), not the context window, which stayed at 1M. Reasoning tokens spend that budget, and output costs 5x input. Google's '13 of 18 categories' and Artificial Analysis' 53-vs-58 are both true about different baskets. Argon's losses cluster in interactive multi-turn agent work; its wins cluster in single-shot domain reasoning and long-context retrieval. Argon burns ~62K output tokens per task against Astra's ~27K. The cheaper bill is the rate card, not efficiency — and at standard pricing cost per task goes $1.99 to $3.98, above Astra's $3.26. The 15% hallucination rate against 51–54% is the most under-reported number here, and it comes from abstention. It is the strongest argument for routing research and compliance work to Argon, and the first thing a 'always answer definitively' instruction destroys. You almost certainly cannot call it: Fairwind gates it to internal cyber/IR/pentest teams with per-user phishing-resistant MFA and no redistribution. No API model ID has been published. Any third-party 'Argon' endpoint is suspect.

Principiante Ya piensas en Claude. Ahora un proyecto vive dentro de Google Workspace, un compañero comparte un Gem personalizado, o necesitas soltar un vídeo de dos horas y una pila de PDFs en un solo prompt — y la herramienta natural es Gemini de Google. Buenas noticias: casi todo lo que sabes se transfiere. Esta página traza tu modelo mental de Claude sobre Gemini, señala el puñado de cosas que realmente funcionan de forma distinta, y te dice cuándo Gemini suele ser la mejor opción. What you'll learn Traducir conceptos de Claude a sus equivalentes en Gemini (Gems, la app de Gemini, integración con Workspace, AI Studio + la Gemini API) Saber cuáles de tus hábitos de prompting de Claude se trasladan sin cambios (la mayoría) Detectar las pocas cosas que realmente tienes que ajustar Saber cuándo Gemini tiende a brillar — tareas del ecosistema Google, contexto enorme y multimodal nativo Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Los nombres exactos de los modelos y números de versión, los niveles de plan, los límites de archivo/subida, los tamaños de ventana de contexto y los precios cambian constantemente en Google. Esta página enseña el modelo mental duradero y el mapeo de conceptos; para cualquier nombre, límite o precio concreto, consulta la documentación actual de Google (enlazada en Fuentes) en lugar de confiar en un número de aquí. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Si solo lees una sección, lee esta. Así se alinean las cosas que conoces en Claude con Gemini: En Claude lo llamas… En el mundo de Gemini es… ¿La misma idea? Claude.ai (la app de chat) La app de Gemini en gemini.google.com Sí — la superficie de consumidor/asistente Claude Projects (workspace + archivos + instrucciones) + Custom Styles reutilizables Gems (un asistente guardado y reutilizable con instrucciones + archivos de conocimiento) Cercano — mira la distinción más abajo Preferencias de cuenta / "cómo quiero que respondas" Instrucciones del Gem + ajustes de tu cuenta Sí — la misma idea Artifacts / contexto de archivos Archivos de conocimiento adjuntos a un Gem (incl. desde Google Drive) Cercano Selector de modelo (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) El selector de modelo de Gemini (Pro para profundidad, Flash para velocidad) Sí — la misma idea, nombres distintos La Console / API + el banco de pruebas de prompts Google AI Studio + la Gemini API Sí — superficie de desarrollo para prototipar y obtener una clave Uso de herramientas / function calling (API) Function calling Sí — el mismo bucle, distintos detalles de JSON La conclusión: casi no hay ningún concepto nuevo que aprender. Se trata sobre todo de renombrar y reubicar cosas que ya entiendes — más dos áreas donde Gemini realmente se inclina más lejos que Claude: integración con el ecosistema Google y multimodal nativo + contexto muy grande.
documents.s: El mapa de conceptos en 60 segundos

documents.t: Un Gem es un asistente personalizable que construyes una vez y reutilizas: le das un nombre, escribes instrucciones y opcionalmente adjuntas archivos de conocimiento para que los consulte. Si alguna vez guardaste un system prompt de Claude o construiste un Claude Project en torno a documentos de referencia, un Gem es el mismo instinto en un solo objeto. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google describe un Gem como un asistente personalizable definido por instrucciones (comúnmente planteadas como persona, tarea, contexto y formato) más archivos de conocimiento subidos opcionales (PDFs, Word/Google Docs, archivos de Drive); el flujo exacto de creación, los límites de archivo y los tipos admitidos cambian — verifica en la página de ayuda actual de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. La estructura de instrucciones que Google recomienda le resultará nativa a un usuario de Claude, porque no es más que buen prompting: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Persona⌄ Quién es el Gem — su rol y voz. El mismo enfoque 'Eres un…' que usas en un system prompt de Claude. ←PreviousNext→ 2Tarea⌄ Qué debe hacer. Enuncia el objetivo en una frase clara. ←PreviousNext→ 3Contexto⌄ El trasfondo que debe asumir — y los archivos de conocimiento que puede consultar, incluidos documentos vivos de Google Drive. ←PreviousNext→ 4Formato⌄ La forma de la salida: una tabla, una lista, JSON, un documento estructurado. Exactamente como pedirle a Claude un formato específico. ←PreviousNext→ Algo sutil que conviene entender bien: un Gem empaqueta instrucciones + material de referencia en un solo asistente reutilizable, muy parecido a las instrucciones y archivos de un Claude Project, pero está planteado como un especialista compartible que un equipo puede ejecutar, no solo tu workspace privado. Cuando un Gem puede consultar archivos de Drive, tiende a leer la versión más reciente — una diferencia pequeña pero real frente a pegar una instantánea estática en un chat. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google ha descrito los Gems compartibles y la capacidad de consultar archivos de Drive (usando su versión más reciente) para suscriptores de Workspace; la disponibilidad, el alcance de compartición y los límites de archivo cambian — consulta los anuncios actuales de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Los Gems son el "Claude reutilizable" que ya deseabas

documents.t: Aquí es donde Gemini más se aparta de tus hábitos de Claude, y normalmente de forma buena para la tarea adecuada. La app de Gemini está cableada a Google Workspace — Gmail, Docs, Drive, Calendar y más — así que puede extraer contexto y actuar sobre tus datos de Google sin que tengas que copiar y pegarlos. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google describe que Gemini se integra con apps de Workspace (Gmail, Docs, Drive y otras) para mostrar y resumir tu contenido; qué apps están conectadas, y los controles de admin/cuenta sobre ese acceso, cambian — verifica en la documentación actual de Workspace de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Para un usuario de Claude, el cambio mental es este: en lugar de llevar el material al modelo, a menudo puedes apuntar el modelo hacia material que ya vive en tu cuenta de Google. Eso cambia el flujo de trabajo más de lo que cambia el prompting. El prompt sigue siendo "resume esto, extrae aquello, redacta esto" — pero el "esto" puede ser un doc vivo de Drive o un hilo de tu bandeja de entrada en vez de un pegado. Pro tip Si tu trabajo ya vive en Gmail/Docs/Drive, la integración de Gemini elimina el paso de copiar y pegar que Claude requeriría. Trata lo que Gemini puede acceder como algo controlado por cuenta y admin — verifica los permisos actuales en vez de asumirlos. Aun así, acótalo: apunta al doc o hilo concreto que quieres decir, no a todo tu Drive, por la misma razón por la que no vuelcas todo en un prompt de Claude.
documents.s: La integración con Workspace es el verdadero titular

documents.t: Dos capacidades son donde Gemini a menudo realmente merece elegirse por encima de un flujo de trabajo habitual de Claude: Entrada multimodal nativa. Los modelos de Gemini están construidos para tomar texto, imágenes, audio y vídeo juntos en una sola petición — no solo imágenes añadidas a última hora. Si tu tarea implica ver un vídeo, escuchar audio o razonar sobre una mezcla de medios a la vez, ese es un punto fuerte de Gemini. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google documenta que Gemini acepta múltiples modalidades de entrada (texto, imágenes y — para muchos modelos — audio y vídeo) en una petición; qué modalidades admite cada modelo concreto cambia según el modelo — verifica en la documentación actual de modelos y visión de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Ventanas de contexto muy grandes. Muchos modelos de Gemini aceptan entradas extremadamente grandes — Google lo plantea como procesar bases de código enteras, múltiples documentos largos u horas de medios de una sola vez, reduciendo la necesidad de trocear o de soluciones alternativas de recuperación. El techo exacto de tokens es volátil y específico de cada modelo, así que no lo fijes en el código; el punto duradero es que "meterlo todo de una vez" es una estrategia más viable aquí de lo que quizá estás acostumbrado. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google describe muchos modelos de Gemini con ventanas de contexto grandes (cita modelos capaces de 1 millón o más tokens) que permiten documentos largos, bases de código grandes y vídeo/audio largos en una sola petición; el límite preciso por modelo cambia — verifica en la documentación actual de contexto largo de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. El hábito que ajustar: con Claude quizá instintivamente recortas, troceas o construyes recuperación antes siquiera de intentarlo. Con un modelo Gemini de contexto grande, a menudo vale la pena probar primero el documento entero (o el vídeo) en un solo prompt, y optimizar solo si topas con un límite real.
documents.s: Multimodal nativo + contexto enorme — apóyate en ello

documents.t: Cuando pasas de chatear a construir, los usuarios de Claude tienen una analogía limpia: Google AI Studio es el banco de pruebas de prototipado — la forma más rápida de probar prompts, ensayar entradas multimodales, ajustar parámetros y obtener una clave de API. Piénsalo como el sitio al que irías a experimentar antes de conectar nada. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google posiciona AI Studio como el entorno de desarrollo para prototipar con Gemini, probar entradas multimodales, ajustar parámetros y obtener una clave de API; sus funciones exactas y los términos del nivel gratuito cambian — verifica en la página actual de AI Studio de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. La Gemini API es lo que llamas desde tu código una vez que has prototipado — el equivalente a pasar de un playground de consola a llamadas de producción. Una diferencia de enfoque que conviene tener clara: la app de Gemini (gemini.google.com) es el asistente pulido con integración de Workspace; AI Studio es la superficie de desarrollo para probar el comportamiento del modelo y obtener claves. Son puertas distintas, y un usuario de Claude ocasionalmente las confunde igual que uno podría confundir Claude.ai con la consola de API. Elige la puerta según el trabajo: trabajo de asistente → la app; construir → AI Studio y luego la API.
documents.s: AI Studio + la Gemini API — la superficie de desarrollo

documents.t: Si has hecho uso de herramientas con Claude, el function calling de Gemini te resultará inmediatamente familiar, porque el bucle es el mismo: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Declara tus funciones⌄ Describes cada función con un nombre, una descripción y un JSON-schema de sus parámetros (tipos, cuáles son obligatorios). La misma idea que una definición de herramienta de Claude. ←PreviousNext→ 2El modelo pide una llamada⌄ Dado el prompt y las funciones declaradas, el modelo devuelve una llamada de función estructurada — el nombre más los argumentos — en lugar de (o junto a) texto. No ejecuta nada por sí mismo. ←PreviousNext→ 3Tú la ejecutas⌄ Tu aplicación extrae el nombre y los argumentos y ejecuta la función real. El modelo propone; tu código dispone. ←PreviousNext→ 4Devuelve el resultado⌄ Retroalimentas al modelo con la salida de la función. ←PreviousNext→ 5El modelo responde⌄ Usa el resultado para producir la respuesta final — y puede pedir más llamadas antes de terminar. ←PreviousNext→ Lo que es idéntico: el bucle describir → el-modelo-pide → tú-ejecutas → devolver-resultado → responder, y el principio de que el modelo nunca ejecuta tu código. Gemini también admite llamadas paralelas (varias funciones independientes en un turno) y composicionales (encadenar funciones donde las llamadas posteriores dependen de resultados anteriores) — conceptos que ya conoces de Claude. Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Google documenta declarar funciones mediante parámetros de nombre/descripción/JSON-schema y un bucle definir → llamar-al-modelo → ejecutar-localmente → devolver-resultado, más llamadas paralelas y composicionales (secuenciales); los nombres exactos de los campos, las formas de respuesta y las opciones cambian — verifica en la guía actual de function calling de Google. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Lo que difiere y te hará tropezar si copias y pegas: los nombres exactos de los campos JSON, cómo se representan las llamadas de función y los resultados en la lista de mensajes, las convenciones de parámetros/esquema y la forma concreta del endpoint. Como regla entre proveedores, el prompting y la arquitectura se transfieren; los detalles del formato de transmisión no — vuelve a revisar siempre el esquema de cada proveedor. (La misma advertencia aplica si vienes de ChatGPT para usuarios de Claude: el bucle es universal, el JSON no.)
documents.s: Function calling — la misma forma, distintos detalles de JSON

documents.t: Tus hábitos de Claude, ganados con esfuerzo, no se desperdician. Estos se trasladan esencialmente sin cambios: Estructura del prompt — rol claro, tarea explícita, ejemplos, formato de salida solicitado → Fundamentos de prompting Dar contexto deliberadamente — acótalo; apunta al material correcto (ahora posiblemente un doc vivo de Drive) Pedir un formato de salida específico — tablas, JSON, pasos; funciona igual Iterar sobre la marcha — refina con preguntas de seguimiento El bucle de uso de herramientas — describe herramientas, deja que el modelo las llame, devuelve resultados → Uso de herramientas Elegir un modelo por dificultad de la tarea — Flash para rápido/barato, Pro para profundo, la misma decisión que Opus/Sonnet/Haiku System prompt neutral respecto al proveedor — pégalo en las instrucciones de un Gem o en un system prompt de la Gemini API CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a {role}. Goal: {one clear sentence}. Rules: - Use ONLY the context I provide or the files attached; if the answer isn't there, say "I don't know". - Be concise. No preamble. - Output format: {exact format — e.g. a markdown table with columns X, Y, Z}. When you need information you don't have, ask one focused question instead of guessing.

Una lista corta y honesta de cosas que sí son diferentes: La integración cambia el flujo de trabajo, no el prompt. Con Gemini puedes apuntar a datos vivos de Google en vez de pegarlos. Verifica a qué se le permite acceder — eso está controlado por cuenta y admin. Por defecto, "meterlo todo de una vez" para entradas grandes. El contexto grande y el multimodal nativo hacen que a menudo puedas saltarte el reflejo de trocear/recuperar y probar primero el documento o vídeo completo. Dos puertas para quien construye. La app de Gemini (asistente) y AI Studio (playground de desarrollo + claves) son separadas; no busques una clave de API dentro de la app de chat. Formato de transmisión para herramientas. El concepto de function calling es idéntico; los detalles del JSON no — nunca reutilices el JSON de herramienta exacto de Claude tal cual. Detalles volátiles. Los nombres de modelo, números de versión, niveles, límites de contexto y precios se mueven rápido. Adquiere el hábito de confirmar en la fuente, exactamente como deberías hacer también con Claude.

Ambos son excelentes asistentes generales y la brecha en cualquier tarea dada suele ser pequeña y cambiante — así que trata esto como tendencias, no leyes, y deja que tu propia evaluación con tus propios datos decida: Tareas del ecosistema Google. Si el trabajo ya vive en Gmail, Docs, Drive o Calendar, la integración nativa con Workspace de Gemini elimina una fricción que Claude no puede igualar sin pegado manual. Contexto enorme de una sola vez. Documentos gigantescos, bases de código enteras o medios largos sobre los que quieres razonar a la vez — inclínate por un modelo Gemini de contexto grande y sáltate el andamiaje de recuperación. Multimodal nativo. La comprensión de vídeo y audio, o los prompts de medios mixtos, son una fortaleza estructural de Gemini. Un equipo que ya funciona sobre Google. Si tus colaboradores comparten Gems y viven en Workspace, encontrarte con ellos ahí supera a la fricción. La respuesta honesta la mayoría de las veces: aquel en el que tú (o tu equipo) ya estáis instalados. La habilidad es portátil; el coste de configuración es el verdadero coste de cambio. Para la forma neutral respecto al proveedor de elegir, mira Cómo elegir un modelo y ¿Qué Claude debería usar?. Vocabulario de Gemini a Claude girarTérminoLa app de Gemini (gemini.google.com)DefiniciónLa superficie de consumidor/asistente de Google con integración profunda de Workspace. ≈ Claude.ai.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 6 Siguiente→ Compruébate 0/3 1El material de tu proyecto ya vive en Google Docs y Gmail. ¿Cuál es la ventaja duradera de recurrir a Gemini aquí? Siempre escribe mejor prosa que ClaudeSu integración nativa con Workspace le permite trabajar sobre tus datos vivos de Google sin copiar y pegarEs el único asistente con un selector de modelo 2Has usado el uso de herramientas de Claude. ¿Qué es cierto sobre el function calling de Gemini? Un concepto completamente distinto que debes reaprenderEl mismo bucle declarar→llamar→ejecutar→devolver, con llamadas paralelas/composicionales — pero los nombres exactos de los campos JSON difierenIdéntico hasta el JSON, así que puedes pegar las definiciones de herramienta de Claude sin cambios 3Tienes un vídeo de 90 minutos y varios PDFs largos sobre los que razonar juntos. ¿Cuál es la jugada nativa de Gemini? Construir de inmediato un pipeline de recuperación y trocearlo todoProbar a meter todo en un solo prompt, apoyándote en el contexto grande y el multimodal nativo, y optimizar solo si topas con un límiteConvertirlo todo a texto plano primero porque Gemini no puede leer vídeo Key takeaways Casi no hay ningún concepto nuevo — la app de Gemini ≈ Claude.ai, un Gem ≈ un system prompt reutilizable + archivos de Project, el selector de modelo (Pro/Flash) ≈ Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, function calling ≈ uso de herramientas. Las diferencias reales son de apalancamiento, no de reaprendizaje: integración profunda con Google Workspace, contexto muy grande y multimodal nativo (imagen/audio/vídeo). Ajusta tus reflejos: apunta a datos vivos de Google en vez de pegarlos; prueba 'meterlo todo de una vez' antes de trocear; recuerda que la app y AI Studio son puertas separadas. Tus hábitos de prompting, disciplina de contexto, formato de salida y bucle de herramientas se transfieren sin cambios — solo difieren los detalles del JSON de las llamadas de herramienta. Los nombres, versiones, niveles, límites de contexto y precios se quedan obsoletos rápido — verifica los detalles concretos en la documentación de Google, igual que deberías hacer con Claude.
