Principiante La mayor parte de AILmanac trata sobre la IA que escribe y razona — modelos de texto como Claude. Pero toda otra rama de la IA crea medios: imágenes, vídeo, voces y música a partir de un prompt. Esta página es un mapa neutral respecto al proveedor de ese panorama: los arquetipos, las herramientas notables (cada una verificada como existente), en qué se diferencian de los LLM de texto, las habilidades que se transfieren y las reglas de derechos y ética que no puedes saltarte. What you'll learn Conocer los principales arquetipos de los medios generativos — imagen, vídeo, voz/música, voz-a-texto — y una herramienta real en cada uno Entender cómo se diferencian los modelos de medios de un modelo de chat de texto como Claude Aprender las habilidades duraderas: prompting para medios, iteración y entradas de referencia Respetar las líneas rojas: derechos de uso, procedencia/marcas de agua y la ética de deepfakes/consentimiento Última verificación: 2026-06-28. Las versiones concretas de los modelos, las capacidades, las resoluciones, los precios y cuál herramienta es "la mejor" cambian casi cada mes en los medios generativos — incluso más rápido que en el texto. Trata cualquier número de versión o precio de aquí como perecedero. Esta página enseña las partes duraderas (arquetipos + habilidades + ética); para los detalles de hoy consulta la propia página de cada herramienta (enlazada en Fuentes) o un rastreador independiente como Artificial Analysis. Ten en cuenta también que los productos se renombran, fusionan o discontinúan — por ejemplo, la app independiente Sora de OpenAI se retiró aunque su modelo de vídeo siguió vivo a través de la API. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Medios generativos: IA de imagen, audio y vídeo

documents.t: Si solo has usado un modelo de chat, importan cuatro diferencias: Salida diferente, "correcto" diferente. Un modelo de texto devuelve una única mejor respuesta, en su mayoría determinista. Un modelo de medios devuelve un artefacto (una imagen, un clip, una toma de voz) donde no hay una única respuesta correcta — solo unas que te gustan más o menos. Generas varias y eliges. Normalmente no puedes editar la salida editando solo el prompt. Cambiar una palabra puede cambiar toda la imagen. El control real proviene de entradas de referencia (una imagen inicial, una imagen de estilo, una voz de referencia) más los controles específicos de la herramienta, no solo de las palabras. Las semillas y la variación forman parte del flujo de trabajo. Muchas herramientas te permiten volver a tirar, variar o bloquear una "semilla" para la reproducibilidad. La iteración es la norma, no un fracaso. La unidad de coste es diferente. El texto factura por tokens; los medios facturan por imagen, segundo de vídeo o carácter/minuto de audio — y el vídeo en particular puede volverse caro muy rápido. Pro tip Modelo mental: un modelo de texto es un escritor que te da la respuesta; un modelo de medios es una máquina tragamonedas con un volante — tiras de la palanca y luego diriges con referencias y nuevas tiradas hasta que quede bien. Genera un lote y cúralo. Tu buen gusto — saber cuál de 4 salidas es la mejor — es la mitad de la habilidad.
documents.s: En qué se diferencian los modelos de medios de un LLM de texto

documents.t: Piensa en arquetipos — las alineaciones se barajan constantemente, las categorías son estables. Cada herramienta mencionada a continuación fue verificada como existente con una URL real (en Fuentes); las versiones concretas se dejan deliberadamente vagas porque cambian sin cesar.
documents.s: El mapa: arquetipos y herramientas notables

documents.t: Convierte un prompt de texto — y opcionalmente imágenes de referencia — en una imagen fija. Midjourney — cerrado, alojado; conocido por una fuerte estética por defecto y controles de estilo/referencia. Generación de imágenes de OpenAI (la línea DALL·E / GPT Image) — cerrado, alojado; estrechamente integrado en ChatGPT y la API. Generación de imágenes de Gemini de Google ("Nano Banana") e Imagen — cerrado, alojado; integrado en Gemini y Google Cloud. Adobe Firefly — cerrado, alojado; construido para flujos de trabajo creativos y entrenado con el uso comercial en mente (ver derechos, más abajo). Stable Diffusion (Stability AI) y FLUX (Black Forest Labs) — familias de modelos de peso abierto que puedes descargar y ejecutar tú mismo, la columna vertebral del ecosistema local/abierto de imágenes.

Genera clips cortos — cada vez más con audio sincronizado — a partir de un prompt o de una imagen inicial. OpenAI Sora — un modelo de vídeo de frontera (nota: la app de consumo independiente fue discontinuada; el modelo continuó a través de la API — un ejemplo de manual de por qué las versiones/disponibilidad quedan obsoletas). Google Veo — vídeo de frontera, con audio nativo en versiones recientes. Runway — una suite creativa construida alrededor de sus modelos de vídeo de la serie Gen. Kling (de Kuaishou) y Pika — herramientas de vídeo de rápida evolución populares para contenido social/de formato corto.

ElevenLabs — cerrado, alojado; texto-a-voz realista y herramientas de voz (la clonación de voz tiene implicaciones reales de consentimiento — ver ética). Suno y Udio — generan canciones completas (voces + instrumentación) a partir de un prompt de texto. OpenAI Whisper — la dirección contraria: voz-a-texto (transcripción). Es de peso abierto (con licencia MIT), así que puedes ejecutarlo tú mismo o llamar a una API alojada. La voz-a-texto es el caballo de batalla silencioso detrás de los subtítulos, las notas de voz y las transcripciones de reuniones. Pro tip La mayor bifurcación (igual que con los modelos de texto): herramientas alojadas CERRADAS (a menudo la mejor calidad, la menor configuración) frente a modelos de PESO ABIERTO como Stable Diffusion, FLUX y Whisper que puedes autoalojar por privacidad, control y menor coste a escala. No elijas por la tabla de clasificación. Para tu aspecto/sonido real, genera unos pocos ejemplos reales en 2-3 herramientas y juzga con tus propios ojos y oídos.

El flujo de trabajo se parece más a una sesión de fotos que a una búsqueda en Google. Estos pasos son independientes de la herramienta: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Describe el sujeto, luego el contexto⌄ Empieza por el sujeto principal, luego añade escenario, acción y ambiente. 'Un zorro rojo' es débil; 'un zorro rojo acurrucado dormido sobre nieve fresca, suave luz de la mañana' le da al modelo algo con lo que trabajar. ←PreviousNext→ 2Especifica el medio y el estilo⌄ Di QUÉ TIPO de imagen/vídeo/voz es: foto vs ilustración vs render 3D; cámara/objetivo o estilo artístico; para audio, el género, el tempo y el tono emocional. El estilo es donde reside la mayor parte del aspecto. ←PreviousNext→ 3Añade entradas de referencia cuando puedas⌄ Una imagen inicial, una imagen de referencia de estilo o un clip de voz de referencia controla el resultado mucho más fiablemente que los adjetivos. Esta es la habilidad duradera que se pierden quienes solo hacen prompts de texto. ←PreviousNext→ 4Genera un lote, luego cura⌄ Produce varias variaciones. Elige la más cercana — tu buen gusto forma parte de la herramienta. No esperes que la primera tirada sea la definitiva. ←PreviousNext→ 5Itera de forma acotada⌄ Cambia UNA cosa a la vez (la iluminación, o la pose, o la paleta) y vuelve a tirar, o usa las funciones de editar/variar/inpaint de la herramienta. Reescribir todo el prompt cada vez pierde lo que estaba funcionando. ←PreviousNext→ 6Comprueba los derechos y la procedencia antes de publicar⌄ Confirma que la licencia cubre tu uso (¿comercial?), y conserva/adjunta la procedencia (Content Credentials) para que el activo sea rastreable. Revela que es generado por IA donde importe. ←PreviousNext→ Prompt de ejemplo de generación de imágenes (medio → sujeto → estilo → detalles) CopyOpen in Claude↗ A cinematic wide-angle photograph of a lighthouse on a rocky cliff at golden hour, waves crashing below, dramatic storm clouds parting. Style: moody, high dynamic range, shot on a 24mm lens, shallow depth of field. Mood: hopeful, epic. Aspect ratio 16:9. Tip: if the result is close, change ONE element next pass (e.g. "blue hour" instead of "golden hour") and re-roll — or add a reference image to lock the look.
documents.s: Cómo obtener un buen resultado de un modelo de medios

documents.t: La IA de medios plantea problemas que el chat de texto normalmente no. Trátalos como parte del trabajo, no como algo secundario. Derechos de uso y comerciales. Cada herramienta tiene su propia licencia, y difieren mucho. Algunas restringen el uso comercial, algunas lo conceden solo en niveles de pago, y las salidas pueden parecerse a obras con derechos de autor o registradas. Adobe Firefly, por ejemplo, se apoya en datos de entrenamiento elegidos con la seguridad comercial en mente — pero aun así deberías leer la licencia real de la herramienta y el nivel en el que estás en lugar de suponer. Procedencia y marcas de agua. Un estándar en crecimiento, C2PA / Content Credentials, adjunta metadatos de "etiqueta nutricional" a prueba de manipulaciones que registran cómo se creó y editó un activo. Muchas herramientas importantes de imagen y vídeo ahora lo incorporan. Mantén intacta esa procedencia, y prefiere herramientas que la soporten — se está convirtiendo en la norma para los medios fiables. Deepfakes, voces y consentimiento. La generación realista de rostros y voces puede suplantar a personas reales. No clones una voz o un parecido sin consentimiento explícito, nunca uses medios generados para engañar, y cumple con la ley de tu jurisdicción. El consentimiento para la clonación de voz y la divulgación de contenido generado por IA no son solo etiqueta — cada vez más son requisitos legales. Watch out Los medios generados pueden llevar límites de derechos de uso y riesgos de deepfake/consentimiento — comprueba la licencia de cada herramienta y revela el contenido generado por IA.
documents.s: Derechos, procedencia y ética — las líneas rojas

documents.t: Buenas noticias: mucho de lo que ya sabes se transfiere. Prompting claro y específico — ser concreto sobre lo que quieres supera a los deseos vagos, en todas las modalidades. Iteración por encima del disparo único — el mismo bucle de "borrador, crítica, refinamiento" que usarías con Claude aplica, solo que con nuevas tiradas e imágenes de referencia en lugar de mensajes de seguimiento. Ver Fundamentos del prompting. Elegir la herramienta adecuada para la tarea — el marco de Elegir un modelo (primero las restricciones, luego una pequeña prueba del mundo real) funciona igual de bien para los medios. Entender qué es realmente el modelo — saber que son aprendices de patrones, no magia, mantiene rectas tus expectativas y tu ética. Ver Fundamentos.
documents.s: Qué se transfiere de tus habilidades con la IA de texto

Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 6 Siguiente→ Key takeaways Los medios generativos son una rama de la IA separada del chat de texto: crea imágenes, vídeo, voz y música, y lo diriges con referencias y nuevas tiradas, no solo con palabras. Piensa en arquetipos — imagen, vídeo, voz/música, voz-a-texto — y recuerda la bifurcación cerrado-vs-peso-abierto (p. ej. Midjourney vs Stable Diffusion/FLUX; TTS alojado vs Whisper abierto). Las habilidades duraderas se transfieren desde la IA de texto: prompting específico, iteración y elegir la herramienta adecuada para la tarea. Los derechos y la ética son parte del trabajo: comprueba la licencia de tu herramienta y nivel, mantén la procedencia (C2PA/Content Credentials), obtén consentimiento para voces/parecidos y revela los medios generados por IA. Los detalles caducan rápido — verifica versiones, precios y capacidades contra la propia página de cada herramienta antes de confiar en ellos.

Intermedio On June 13, 2026, Z.ai (formerly Zhipu AI) released GLM-5.2 — a 753-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context, published on Hugging Face under a plain MIT license with no regional restrictions. In the two weeks that followed, three things happened that were harder to ignore than the launch itself: it landed within ~1 point of Claude Opus 4.8 on long-horizon coding benchmarks, its API undercut frontier pricing by roughly 6×, and Semgrep's security team quietly reported that GLM-5.2 with almost no scaffolding outperformed Claude Code on a real IDOR vulnerability benchmark. This page covers what's actually non-obvious about GLM-5.2 — the IndexShare architectural change that makes 1M-token inference tractable, the honest benchmark picture against Claude and GPT-5.5, what it costs to self-host today, and where it's genuinely a better tool than reaching for a closed frontier model. What you'll learn Understand what IndexShare is and why it cuts long-context compute by ~2.9× — not a marketing number, an architectural one Read the honest benchmark picture: where GLM-5.2 matches Claude Opus 4.8, where it doesn't, and what to trust in vendor scores Know the effective cost math: ~$1.20–1.40 / $4.10–4.40 per M input/output vs Claude Opus at frontier prices Get GLM-5.2 running via API in three lines, or self-hosted on vLLM 0.23+ (with the FP8 and 2-bit paths spelled out) Decide when to reach for GLM-5.2 vs Claude — the two tasks where it clearly wins, and the two where it clearly doesn't

GLM-5.2 is an open-weight (MIT), 753B-total / ~40B-active sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Z.ai with a 1M-token context and 131,072-token max output, built for long-horizon agentic coding — priced at roughly one-sixth of closed frontier APIs and, on independent evaluations, within one point of Claude Opus 4.8 on the coding benchmarks that matter for autonomous agent work.

The headline change in GLM-5.2 isn't "bigger MoE" — it's IndexShare. Sparse attention needs an indexer that decides which past tokens each query attends to. Running that indexer per layer is expensive at 1M-token context. Z.ai's IndexShare reuses the same indexer across every four sparse attention layers, cutting per-token FLOPs by ~2.9× at the full 1M window. The practical consequence: GLM-5.2 can serve real long-context workloads at prices where doing the same job with a fully quadratic-attention model would be economically absurd. This is also why the FP8 checkpoint (published as zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8) runs on 8× H200 with room for a 131K-token session; without IndexShare, that same hardware would choke on the KV cache long before you got there. GLM-5.2 also ships an improved Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layer for speculative decoding, with Z.ai reporting a ~20% acceptance-length uplift — that shows up as faster tokens/sec in real inference, not just a paper metric. Última verificación: 2026-07-29. Architecture details (IndexShare, MTP acceptance uplift, 753B/40B config) are from the official Hugging Face model card and Z.ai's launch materials. Compute-savings claims (2.9×) are vendor-reported; independent inference-cost measurements at 1M context are still sparse as of late July 2026. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: 1. IndexShare is the real architectural story

documents.t: Vendor tables and news coverage compress this to soundbites. The honest reading: Benchmark GLM-5.2 Claude Opus 4.8 GPT-5.5 Notes Terminal-Bench 2.1 81.0 ~85.0 — Long-horizon shell/agent work; 4-point gap SWE-bench Pro 62.1 — 58.6 Autonomous repo-level fixes; ahead of GPT-5.5, ahead of GLM-5.1 (58.4) GPQA Diamond 91.2 — — Hard science QA; strong AIME 2026 99.2 — — Vendor-reported; extreme number, treat cautiously Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 51 — — Highest score for any open-weight model at launch Code Arena (global) #2 — — Behind one closed model Two things to internalize: On the coding benchmarks that map to agent work (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1, Code Arena), GLM-5.2 is closer to Claude Opus 4.8 than to GPT-5.5. That's a first for any open-weight model. On the hardest reasoning tasks and open-ended knowledge, closed frontier models still lead. The AIME 99.2 headline is vendor-reported and should be read alongside independent evals — Z.ai's Artificial Analysis Index score of 51 is a more calibrated summary. Pro tip When someone links "GLM-5.2 beats Claude Opus" or "GLM-5.2 beats GPT-5.5", check which benchmark and whose measurement. On long-horizon coding: within a point of Opus, clearly ahead of GPT-5.5. On general reasoning: still behind closed frontier. Both statements are true.
documents.s: 2. The benchmark story is stronger than "beats GPT-5.5" and weaker than "beats Opus"

documents.t: GLM-5.2 was reportedly trained on Huawei Ascend accelerators rather than Nvidia H100/H200s. That's not a benchmarking detail — it's a supply-chain fact. Combined with Z.ai being on the US Entity List and the hosted API routing through Chinese infrastructure, it shapes three real decisions: Regulated environments should evaluate the hosted API against export-control policy before wiring it into production. The MIT weights are unrestricted; the API isn't a substitute for a compliance review. Data-sensitive workloads should prefer the self-hosted path (see below) rather than sending prompts to Z.ai's API endpoints. Aggregators (OpenRouter, NVIDIA Build, OpenRelay) offer GLM-5.2 through non-Z.ai infrastructure — if you want the model but not the origin routing, that's the route.
documents.s: 3. It was trained on Huawei Ascend NPUs, not Nvidia

documents.t: Z.ai's own API pricing sits at approximately $1.20–$1.40 per million input tokens and $4.10–$4.40 per million output tokens across providers. Compare that to Claude Opus 4.8 territory ($15/M input, $75/M output at frontier prices) and the ratio is roughly 1:6 on input and 1:15+ on output. Semgrep's IDOR benchmark put the per-vulnerability cost at ~$0.17 for GLM-5.2 vs several dollars for frontier equivalents. The catch that's easy to miss: GLM-5.2 runs "high" or "max" thinking effort at the model level, so output-token counts are higher than a non-thinking model for the same task. Cost per task is still lower, but the ratio isn't as extreme as the per-token prices suggest — you're paying for more tokens per answer, at a lower price each.

GLM-5.2 speaks OpenAI-compatible chat completions. The endpoint URLs and model IDs vary by provider — pick one: Provider Base URL Model ID Env Z.ai (direct) https://api.z.ai/api/paas/v4/ glm-5.2 ZAI_API_KEY OpenRouter https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 z-ai/glm-5.2 OPENROUTER_API_KEY NVIDIA Build https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 z-ai/glm-5.2 NVIDIA_API_KEY OpenRelay https://inference.openrelay.inc/v1 openrelay/glm-5.2 OPENRELAY_API_KEY Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Get an API key⌄ For direct access, sign up at z.ai and create a key. For aggregator access (recommended if you're on the US Entity List side of the fence), use OpenRouter or NVIDIA Build. ←PreviousNext→ 2Point an OpenAI client at the base URL⌄ The official openai SDK works unmodified — change the base_url and the model name. Any framework built on OpenAI's API shape (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vercel AI SDK) works the same way. ←PreviousNext→ 3Use tools and long context normally⌄ Function calling, JSON mode, and 1M-token contexts all work through the standard chat.completions shape. There's no special parameter to 'enable' long context — it's always available. ←PreviousNext→ GLM-5.2 via OpenAI SDK (Python), through OpenRouter CopyOpen in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_OPENROUTER_KEY", base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="z-ai/glm-5.2", messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this 800-line auth module for testability. Preserve behavior; return a unified diff."}, ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) GLM-5.2 via Z.ai direct endpoint (Python) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_ZAI_API_KEY", base_url="https://api.z.ai/api/paas/v4/", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="glm-5.2", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful staff engineer."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Review this repo and list the top 5 risks, with file:line references."}, ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content)
The MIT license and published FP8 weights make self-hosting the whole point for a lot of teams. There are three practical paths, from most-hardware to least:

The reference deployment. Download the official FP8 checkpoint and serve with vLLM 0.23.0+ (or SGLang 0.5.13.post1+). This is the config Z.ai's own inference is closest to; it gives you the full 131K-token max output and stable throughput. Deploy GLM-5.2 FP8 on 8× H200 with vLLM CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1) Download the FP8 weights (~750 GB) huggingface-cli download zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8 \ --local-dir /models/glm-5.2-fp8 # 2) Serve with vLLM 0.23.0+ python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \ --model /models/glm-5.2-fp8 \ --served-model-name glm-5.2-fp8 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --quantization fp8 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --max-num-seqs 32 \ --port 8000
documents.s: Path A — FP8 on 8× H200 with vLLM (production-grade)

documents.t: Unsloth's dynamic 2-bit GGUF compresses GLM-5.2 from ~1.51 TB down to ~239 GB — small enough to fit a 256 GB Mac Studio (Ultra) or a workstation with a 24 GB GPU plus 256 GB system RAM (MoE routing keeps only a few experts hot at a time, so DRAM offload is workable). This is the "actually run it on hardware you can buy at a store" path. Expect slower tokens/sec than an H200 rack but usable for solo agent workloads.
documents.s: Path B — 2-bit GGUF on a Mac Studio or 24 GB GPU + 256 GB RAM

documents.t: Third-party quantizations (e.g., QuantTrio/GLM-5-AWQ, PhalaCloud/GLM-5.2-W4AFP8) target 4-bit weight paths compatible with vLLM's AWQ kernel. These are useful when you want smaller memory footprints than FP8 but more headroom than the 2-bit GGUF. Z.ai has not published an official AWQ variant as of late July 2026 — verify the community version's calibration before using it in production. Watch out Self-hosting GLM-5.2 at any tier still needs care with the tokenizer and the chat template. The Hugging Face model card ships both; use apply_chat_template with add_generation_prompt=True rather than hand-assembling the prompt. Mismatched templates are the single most common cause of "why is my open-weight model so much worse than the API?" reports.
documents.s: Path C — AWQ/W4A16 quantizations from the community

documents.t: Two tasks where it's genuinely the better tool: Long-horizon autonomous coding on a private codebase. Self-hosted FP8 gives you a frontier-adjacent SWE-bench Pro score with no code or context leaving your infrastructure. Claude Opus 4.8 is a hair sharper on Terminal-Bench 2.1, but the compliance win of on-prem inference often outweighs 4 percentage points. Security research on adversarial payloads. Semgrep's IDOR experiment (F1 39% with a bare-prompt harness, ahead of Claude Code at 37%) suggests GLM-5.2 is meaningfully less refusal-prone on defensive security tasks where Claude's safety training triggers false positives. Two tasks where Claude is still the better tool: Open-ended reasoning and factual knowledge questions. GLM-5.2 lags closed frontier models on general knowledge and open reasoning; Claude Opus/Sonnet 5 and Fable 5 stay ahead here. Anything where refusal-mode nuance matters. Claude's harm-avoidance is more nuanced (fewer over-refusals on legitimate work, sharper stops on genuine harm). GLM-5.2's safety layer is thinner and less calibrated for edge cases. Pro tip Cross-link: for the wider open-weight landscape, see DeepSeek, Qwen & the Open-Weight Wave and Kimi K3: World's Largest Open-Weight Model. For the "should this run locally at all?" decision, see Local vs Claude agent.
documents.s: When to reach for GLM-5.2 vs Claude

documents.t: Semgrep held the vulnerability dataset (real open-source IDOR flaws), the F1 scoring, and the system prompt constant, and varied the model + surrounding harness. Their custom Semgrep Multimodal rig with GPT-5.5 scored 61% F1; the same rig with Opus 4.8 scored 53%. When they tested GLM-5.2 with nothing but the prompt (a bare Pydantic AI harness, no endpoint enumeration, no guided navigation), it scored 39% F1 — beating Claude Code on the same task (37% F1) at about $0.17 per vulnerability found, roughly a sixth of the frontier cost. Their own headline: "We have Mythos at home." The important caveat: one task, one dataset, one run — the finding is directional, not a promise it generalizes to SSRF, XSS, or other classes.
documents.s: Semgrep's IDOR result in one paragraph

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 1What does GLM-5.2's IndexShare mechanism actually do? Compresses the model weights by sharing them across layersReuses the same sparse-attention indexer across every four sparse attention layers, cutting per-token compute by ~2.9× at 1M contextShares the KV cache across different requests to save memoryDistributes inference across multiple GPUs via a shared index 2How does GLM-5.2 compare to Claude Opus 4.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1? It beats Claude Opus 4.8 by a wide marginIt scores within ~4 points (81.0 vs ~85.0) — close, but Claude Opus 4.8 still leads on this benchmarkClaude Opus 4.8 is more than double the scoreThey tie exactly 3You want to run GLM-5.2 privately on your own hardware but don't have an 8× H200 rack. What's a realistic path? It's not possible without frontier data-center hardwareRun Unsloth's 2-bit dynamic GGUF (~239 GB) on a 256 GB Mac Studio Ultra, or a workstation with a 24 GB GPU plus 256 GB system RAMOnly the Z.ai hosted API can run at 1M contextYou must use AWQ 4-bit; nothing else works 4Which task did Semgrep's benchmark specifically find GLM-5.2 outperforming Claude Code on? IndexShare is the architectural story: sparse-attention indexer reused across every 4 layers, ~2.9× per-token compute reduction at 1M context — makes long-context serving economical. Effective cost is ~1/6 of Claude Opus per input token, offset partly by higher output-token counts (high/max thinking on by default). Semgrep measured ~$0.17 per IDOR vulnerability found. Three self-host paths: FP8 on 8× H200 with vLLM (production), 2-bit dynamic GGUF on a Mac Studio / 24 GB + 256 GB box (accessible), or community AWQ/W4 quantizations (middle ground). Reach for GLM-5.2 on private long-horizon coding and defensive security research; keep Claude for open-ended reasoning, factual knowledge, and nuanced safety edges.

Avanzado Última verificación: 2026-09-21. Esta página cita datos que cambian con el tiempo: toma la fecha de arriba como su grado de actualidad. Fuentes: github.com/google/ax (README, docs/concepts.md, docs/manifests.md, docs/runner.md, docs/sandbox.md; release tags v0.1.0 of May 20, 2026 through v0.3.0 of Sep 20, 2026; 4.3k stars on Sep 21, 2026); agentexecutor.io; Google Cloud blog posts of May 21, 2026 (Agent Executor; Agent Sandbox GA + Agent Substrate); github.com/agent-substrate/substrate README (2.4k stars); Google Cloud docs 'About GKE Agent Substrate'; Hacker News item 49780797. AX is v1alpha1 and its README promises major breaking changes: re-check field names and commands against the repo before you build on them. What you'll learn Place AX correctly in Google's stack: Kubernetes, Agent Sandbox, Agent Substrate, AX, then your harness Read the four AX resources (Task, Workspace, Gateway, Model) and know what each one buys you Explain what really survives an AX suspend/resume, what does not, and what your runner image must do about it Run a first Task end to end with ax apply, ax watch and ax ssh, and know the three debugging traps Decide when a self-hosted runtime like AX beats Claude Managed Agents or the OpenAI Agents API, and when it does not On the night of September 20, 2026, AX: Google's open agentic orchestrator went to the top of Hacker News with 507 points and 222 comments. Most of those comments were people asking what it is for. That is a fair question, because the project has been public since May 20, 2026 (v0.1.0) and has changed shape twice since, so most of the blog posts you will find describe a CLI that no longer exists. Here is the short version. AX is not a model, not an agent framework and not a hosted service. It is a Kubernetes-style control plane, with a kubectl-shaped CLI, that takes a declared agent Task, gives it a sandbox, clones its repos, wires its MCP servers and skills, fences its network, and can freeze it to a snapshot and thaw it later on any free worker. It sits under whatever harness you already use, whether that is Claude Code, Google's ADK, LangChain, or a Python loop you wrote yourself.
documents.s: AX (Agent Executor): Google's Open Agent Runtime, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: The Google announcements use four names that are easy to confuse. They are four layers, and AX is the top one. Layer What it is Status (Sep 2026) Numbers Google publishes Kubernetes / GKE The cluster — — Agent Sandbox (kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox) A Sandbox CRD: gVisor-isolated pods (Kata pluggable), warm pools, pod snapshots GA on GKE since May 21, 2026 300 sandbox allocations/s per cluster; sub-second start, 90% within 200 ms Agent Substrate (agent-substrate/substrate) A minimal control plane that multiplexes many idle actors onto few warm workers by snapshotting RAM + files to object storage Open source, early, "not an officially supported Google product"; managed flavour on GKE in evaluation ~250 stateful actors on 8 pods; "10x higher density" than plain containers; sub-second activation AX (google/ax) Declarative Tasks/Workspaces/Gateways/Models + CLI on top of Substrate v0.3.0, ax.io/v1alpha1, Apache-2.0, 4.3k stars "billions of tasks per cluster" (marketing claim, not a benchmark) Your harness Claude Code, ADK, LangChain, A2A agents, your own loop — — Two things the table hides. First, Substrate is where the interesting engineering lives (the snapshot and teleport machinery); AX is the ergonomic layer. Second, Substrate lives in its own GitHub org, not under google/, which several HN commenters flagged as a signal about how official any of this is. Treat the whole thing as a serious but pre-1.0 open-source project from a Google team, not a product with an SLA.
Everything in AX is a YAML resource in an atespace (Substrate's tenancy unit; default unless you say otherwise). You ax apply -f them exactly as you would with kubectl.

apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: fix-flaky-test spec: image: "ghcr.io/my-org/my-agent-image" command: ["my-agent", "--goal", "fix the flaky test"] env: - name: ENVIRONMENT value: "staging" resources: requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" } limits: { cpu: "2", memory: "4Gi" } workspaces: - name: golang path: "/workspace" goal: "Ensure the Go toolchain is available and built from source" gateway: name: default-gateway debug: true A Task is deliberately small. The concepts doc describes agents creating many Tasks over their lifetime rather than living inside one long process. Three fields matter more than they look: workspaces[].goal is a plain-English description of the environment the Task needs. AX's "generative" setup tries to complete the workspace from that sentence (install a toolchain, fetch dependencies). It is the one place where a model is in the loop before your agent starts. debug: true is the only way to get ax ssh into the sandbox. Without it the guest services are not exposed and the CLI refuses to connect. gateway is optional in the schema, but if you leave it out you are relying on whatever the substrate's default egress policy is. Declare one.
documents.s: Task: the unit of isolated execution

documents.t: apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Workspace metadata: name: golang spec: git: - name: origin repo: "https://github.com/golang/go.git" branch: "my-fix" mcp: registries: - provider: google query: "mcp.tags:build" servers: - name: git-tools endpoint: "http://git-mcp.default.svc.cluster.local:8080" skills: registries: - provider: google query: "skills.tags:nodejs" path: "/.agents/skills" This is the resource that makes AX more than "Kubernetes Jobs with a sandbox". A Workspace pre-clones repositories, resolves MCP servers (by explicit endpoint or by a registry query), and drops skill packages into a path. Note the default skills path: /.agents/skills is the same directory convention the cross-agent SKILL.md standard uses for Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI, so a Workspace can hand the same skills to whichever harness runs inside the Task.
documents.s: Workspace: git + MCP + skills, materialised before the agent starts

documents.t: apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Gateway metadata: name: default-gateway spec: listeners: - name: http port: 8080 protocol: HTTP egress: allowlist: hosts: - host: "api.anthropic.com" port: 443 The reference manifest ships with host: "*" on 443, which is an allow-everything policy. Change it. Egress allowlists are the single most effective control against the exfiltration patterns in our prompt-injection and what your agent uploads pages, and AX gives you a declarative place to put them. Listeners are how a Task exposes a port (for an A2A endpoint, a dev server, a debug UI); ax tunnel forwards them to your laptop.

apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Model metadata: name: claude-model spec: provider: anthropic model: claude-opus-5 secretKey: name: anthropic-api-secret key: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY parameters: maxTokens: 16000 temperature: 0.9 The reference docs show google and anthropic providers. The credential is a reference to a Kubernetes Secret, so the manifest never contains the key and the key is rotated where you already rotate secrets. AX is not Gemini-only; the runner docs do mention that GEMINI_API_KEY is injected automatically when the atespace has Gemini credentials, which is the one place Google's own model gets a shortcut.
documents.s: Model: provider + model ID + a Kubernetes secret

documents.t: This is the part no launch post covers, and it is where you will lose an afternoon if you skip it. From docs/runner.md: The entrypoint is fixed. Whatever spec.image you supply, the controller starts the container with /usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner as PID 1. Your image must contain an executable at that path (a symlink is fine). The published base image is gcr.io/ax-substrate/ate-images/ax-task-runner, and extending it is the normal route. Your command arrives via environment, not argv. The runner receives AX_TASK_YAML (the whole Task, including status) and AX_WORKSPACES_YAML (every bound Workspace as multi-document YAML), parses spec.command out of the Task, and starts it as a child process with the first workspace as the working directory. It also exposes AX_METADATA_URL, a small local HTTP metadata server. Bootstrap has a 10-minute clock. Workspace materialisation (clones, MCP resolution, skill install, the generative goal step) must finish within AX_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT, default 10 minutes. Large monorepos on a cold worker can blow through it. The control plane does not read your exit code. The runner logs the command's exit status but stays up as PID 1 whether or not your agent is still running. So a Task in phase Running does not mean your agent is alive. Write your own completion signal (a file in the workspace, a message to your own queue, a Task deletion from inside) and watch that. Shutdown is SIGTERM, 10 seconds, SIGKILL. The runner forwards SIGTERM to the command's process group and waits a bounded grace period. Flush state early.
documents.s: What actually happens inside a Task

documents.t: Suspend/resume is the feature that justifies the whole stack. Agents spend most of their wall-clock waiting on a model, a tool, or a human, and Substrate's bet is that an idle agent should cost storage, not a warm pod. ax suspend task fix-flaky-test # Ready=False, snapshot taken ax resume task fix-flaky-test # restored on any free worker What the docs say survives, and what does not: Survives a suspend/resume Does not survive The /workspace volume (files, clones, build artefacts) The process tree: your agent restarts from its entrypoint Substrate-level actor memory snapshot (RAM + files, at the Substrate layer) Open network connections (GKE docs: agents must handle reconnection) Task spec and status Anything written outside the workspace volume The runner doc is explicit about the consequence: after resume, the runner sees the same files but a new process tree, so it must track whether workspace setup already ran (marker files are the suggested mechanism) or it will re-clone every repo. If your agent keeps its plan or its conversation only in process memory, a resume loses it; keep the transcript on disk in the workspace. This is the same lesson as our long-running agent harnesses page, enforced by the infrastructure. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Install the CLI and point it at a cluster⌄ go install github.com/google/ax/cmd/ax@latest. AX follows your active kubeconfig context (kubectx works) and defaults to namespace ax-system and atespace default. For a laptop, the Agent Substrate repo's hack/ scripts stand up a kind cluster with the substrate installed; AX's control plane is then deployed with make deploy AX_IMAGE_REPO=<your registry>, which needs ko and a registry you can push to. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a runner image⌄ FROM the published ax-task-runner image, apt-get or npm install your agent, keep /usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner as the entrypoint. Do not override ENTRYPOINT; put the agent in spec.command instead. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write the four manifests⌄ One Model with a secretKey pointing at an existing Kubernetes Secret, one Gateway with a real egress allowlist (your model provider, your git host, nothing else), one Workspace with the repo and any MCP servers, one Task with debug: true for the first run. ←PreviousNext→ 4Apply and watch⌄ ax apply -f manifests/ then ax watch task <name>. Wait for the WorkspaceReady and GatewayReady conditions before Ready. If Ready never comes and the phase flips to Failed, the 10-minute bootstrap timeout is the first suspect. ←PreviousNext→ 5Get inside⌄ ax ssh <name> -- ls -al /workspace shows what the Workspace actually materialised; ax ssh <name> -- env | grep AX_ shows the runner contract. Both only work because you set debug: true. ←PreviousNext→ 6Suspend, resume, and check your own completion signal⌄ ax suspend task <name>, wait, ax resume task <name>, then confirm your agent picked up from disk rather than restarting the job. Finally ax delete task <name>: the phase goes to Terminating while the sandbox is torn down. ←PreviousNext→ Have Claude draft the manifests for an agent you already run CopyOpen in Claude↗ I run an agent as a container image ghcr.io/acme/triage-agent:1.4. Its entrypoint is "triage --repo REPO_PATH --model MODEL_ID". It needs: the repo github.com/acme/backend on branch main, an MCP server for Linear reachable at http://linear-mcp.tools.svc.cluster.local:8080, outbound access only to api.anthropic.com:443 and github.com:443, and the Anthropic key from the Kubernetes Secret "anthropic-api-secret" (key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). Write the four google/ax v1alpha1 manifests (Model, Gateway, Workspace, Task) for this, following docs/manifests.md in the repo. Then write a Dockerfile that extends the published ax-task-runner base image and installs my agent WITHOUT changing the entrypoint. Finally, list what I must change in the agent so that (a) it treats the first workspace as its working directory, (b) it survives a suspend/resume by keeping its plan and transcript on disk under /workspace and using a marker file to skip re-setup, and (c) it signals completion in a way the AX control plane can't (it ignores exit codes).

The most-upvoted question in the HN thread was "what is the benefit over the OpenAI Agents API?" The honest answer is that they are different layers. AX + Agent Substrate Claude Managed Agents OpenAI Agents API Cloudflare's isolate runtime Who runs the loop You (any harness in the container) Anthropic (the harness is theirs) OpenAI (the Codex harness) You, on Workers/Durable Objects Where it runs Your Kubernetes cluster, any cloud or on-prem Anthropic's infrastructure OpenAI's, or a self-hosted sandbox Cloudflare's edge Isolation gVisor / Cloud Hypervisor sandbox per Task Anthropic-managed environment Hosted or self-hosted sandbox V8 isolate, container on demand Model choice Any provider you put in a Model resource Claude OpenAI models Any (via API) Idle cost model Snapshot to storage, resume on demand Session-based billing Session-based billing Isolates hibernate You own Cluster, upgrades, secrets, egress policy An API key An API key A Workers account Pick AX when you need data sovereignty, want to run more than one vendor's model behind one policy, already operate Kubernetes, or want agents that can sleep for days without paying for compute. Pick a hosted loop when you want a working harness today and do not want to own a cluster. Many teams will do both: a hosted loop for interactive sessions, AX-style infrastructure for fleets of background Tasks.
documents.s: Where AX sits next to the hosted agent loops

documents.t: The June-era docs describe a different tool. The May preview exposed a conversation-centric CLI (ax exec --conversation … --resume, ax fork for trajectory branching, an AgentService protocol with ADK and A2A bridges). The September README's command reference is resource-centric: apply, get, describe, watch, suspend, resume, delete, ssh, tunnel, ctx. If a tutorial shows ax fork, it is from before the redesign. The five headline capabilities from the May blog (durable execution, isolation, single-writer session consistency, connection recovery, trajectory branching) are still the stated goals; how much of the branching story survives in the resource model is not documented as of this writing. v1alpha1 means it. The README warns of major breaking changes before a stable release. Pin the CLI version and the runner image digest, and re-read docs/manifests.md on every upgrade. Kubernetes is not optional. The most-repeated complaint in the thread. The Substrate quickstart runs on kind, so you can try it on a laptop, but production means a real cluster. If you do not already run Kubernetes, AX is not the reason to start. Managed GKE Agent Substrate has hard requirements. GKE 1.37+ (1.36 with beta flags), Workload Identity, beta APIs enabled at cluster creation, uniform machine types per ActorTemplate (no E2), a Cloud Storage bucket for snapshots, gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor isolation, and no GPU passthrough. Production use is behind an allowlisted private GA program. Egress defaults are permissive in the examples. host: "*" on 443 lets an agent reach any HTTPS endpoint. That is the opposite of what you want for a Task that reads untrusted repos. Follow the same rules as securing local and hybrid agents. Two projects, two orgs, one disclaimer. AX is under google/; Substrate is under agent-substrate/ and states it is not an officially supported Google product. Neither is eligible for Google's OSS vulnerability rewards program. Budget for reading source when something breaks. AX vocabulary girarTérminoTaskDefiniciónThe smallest unit of isolated execution in AX: an image, a command, resources, bound Workspaces and a Gateway. Agents create many Tasks; a Task is not a long-lived agent process.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→ Check yourself 0/6 1You supply spec.image with your own ENTRYPOINT. What does AX run as PID 1? Your ENTRYPOINT/usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner, alwaysspec.command directlyA shell that sources spec.env 2Your agent exits with status 1. What does ax get task show? FailedSucceededStill Running: the control plane does not read the command's exit statusTerminating 3After ax resume, your agent re-clones every repository. Why? The workspace volume was lostThe Gateway blocked the cacheThe process tree is new, so the runner ran setup again; it should have checked a marker fileResume always re-materialises Workspaces 4ax ssh refuses to connect to your Task. Most likely cause? Wrong kube contextspec.debug is not true, so guest services are not exposedThe Gateway has no listenerYou forgot -a default 5Which layer actually implements snapshotting idle agents to storage and restoring them on a warm worker? AX itselfAgent SubstratekubectlThe Model resource 6A tutorial from June 2026 tells you to run ax fork to branch a trajectory. What should you expect? It works unchangedIt is deprecated but aliasedThe current README's command reference does not list it; the CLI was redesigned around apply/get/suspend/resumeIt only works on GKE
documents.s: Gotchas and the pushback worth listening to

Intermedio On 6 August 2026 OpenAI shipped a mid-cycle refresh of GPT-5.6 that most coverage collapsed into one sentence: "Sol got smarter, free users got unlimited chats." The real update is more interesting — and more consequential if you are a Claude user who occasionally reaches for the OpenAI stack. Three moving parts changed at once: an effort control now runs both in the ChatGPT UI (as a slider) and the API (as a six-tier parameter); a free-tier Think button ships the following week with unlimited Luna chats; and the long-context pricing cliff at 272K input tokens interacts awkwardly with Fast mode, which only runs on Sol. Each shifts a real decision. This page pulls those decisions out of the release-notes fog and shows what actually changes for a builder who thinks in Claude terms. What you'll learn See exactly what shipped on 6 August 2026 for GPT-5.6 — and what shipped the week of 10 August for free users Understand the six-tier effort parameter (`none, low, medium, high, xhigh, max`) and map it onto Claude's thinking-effort model Learn the 272K input-token pricing cliff — and how it can silently double a job you thought you had budgeted Know when Fast mode helps, when it does nothing, and which requests it silently refuses Decide when the update is a real reason to switch a workload from Claude to Sol — and when it's not
documents.s: GPT-5.6 August 2026 Update: Effort Slider, Free Think Button & the 272K Price Cliff

documents.t: Three concrete things. The rest is polish. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Effort control, both in ChatGPT and the API⌄ Plus and Pro users see a new slider on web, mobile and desktop that sets how much reasoning ChatGPT uses per response. Under the hood, the API exposes the same knob as `reasoning.effort` with six positions — `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` — defaulting to `medium` when omitted. This replaces the previous 'model decides' behavior: you now pick the tier and pay for it. ←PreviousNext→ 2GPT-5.6 Sol behavioral pass⌄ OpenAI updated Sol to give 'more direct responses, use tighter formatting, and avoid extra detail when it does not help', to adapt detail per question, and to be 'less likely to agree when a correction would be more helpful' — the closest OpenAI has come to shipping an explicit anti-sycophancy pass. Internal evals on financial, medical and legal prompts reported factual errors were '68% less common' than the retired GPT-5.5 Instant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Free-tier upgrade the week of 10 August⌄ Free users get unlimited text chats on GPT-5.6 Luna (previously capped) and a new Think button for deeper reasoning on harder questions, 'subject to abuse protections'. The Think button was not live on 6 August — it rolled out the following week. ←PreviousNext→ Última verificación: 2026-08-11. Esta página cita datos que cambian con el tiempo: toma la fecha de arriba como su grado de actualidad. Fuentes: OpenAI GPT-5.6 August Updates PDF; 9to5Mac 2026-08-06; AIToolsReview

If you have been thinking in terms of Claude's five-level effort setting (introduced with Opus 5 in July), the mental model is similar but the labels don't line up cleanly. GPT-5.6 has six tiers where Claude has five, and the semantics differ at both ends. GPT-5.6 tier What it does Roughly like Claude Opus 5 none Skips reasoning entirely; instant answer No direct equivalent — Claude always plans a little low Short chain-of-thought, cheap minimal effort medium (default) Balanced planning; the shipped default low–medium high Deeper planning; slower, dearer medium xhigh Long deliberation; multi-step reasoning high max Full reasoning ceiling — expensive maximum Two practical consequences: The default moved. On the API, if you omit reasoning.effort, you get medium. Previously many wrappers relied on the model auto-selecting effort; that behavior is gone. Explicit is now required for predictable cost. none is a real button. It is genuinely useful for classifier prompts, structured extraction, or tool-router calls where reasoning tokens are pure overhead. Claude has no cleanly-equivalent 'off' switch. A safe request template that pins effort explicitly CopyOpen in Claude↗ { "model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": { "effort": "low" }, "messages": [ { "role": "system", "content": "Extract only. Output JSON." }, { "role": "user", "content": "..." } ] }
documents.s: The effort slider — mapping the six tiers to a Claude mental model

documents.t: This is the change most likely to burn a bill unexpectedly. The rule: if a request's input crosses 272,000 tokens, the entire request is re-priced at 2× the input rate and 1.5× the output rate, not just the tokens above the line. There is no proration. Two things about that rule matter: It's a cliff, not a slope. A prompt at 271,999 input tokens pays the base rate. A prompt at 272,001 pays 2×/1.5× on every input and output token in the call — including the reasoning tokens the model generates. Long conversations creep across it. Multi-turn chats and agent loops accumulate history. A session that starts under 272K can silently cross the line on turn 12 and re-price every subsequent turn. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Do the arithmetic before you commit⌄ GPT-5.6 Sol base pricing is $5 / $30 per million (input / output), with cached input at $0.50. Above 272K input tokens, the same call costs $10 / $45. On a 300K-token document with 4K output, base cost is $1.62. Cross the cliff and it becomes $3.18 — nearly 2× for one extra token past the threshold. ←PreviousNext→ 2Chunk instead of stuffing when you're near the line⌄ Two 200K calls cost $2 in input. One 400K call costs $8 (2× input on the whole request). Chunking is 4× cheaper for input if either chunk stays below 272K. Only stuff when you truly need the model to see everything at once. ←PreviousNext→ 3Watch cache behavior around the cliff⌄ Cached input at $0.50 is still cached at $0.50 up to 272K. Above the cliff, the multiplier applies to every priced token — including uncached input above the cached prefix. A stable 250K cached prefix plus a growing tail can silently push you over. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The 272K token pricing cliff — a real hazard

documents.t: Fast mode is a Sol-only option that trades price for latency: up to 2.5× faster at 2× the API price. Terra and Luna don't offer it. Three things the launch pitch downplays: 'Up to' is a ceiling, not a norm. Wall-clock speedup depends on your workload — tool calls, network hops and streaming rate all cap the realized gain well below 2.5×. Fast mode and long context don't cleanly mix. OpenAI hasn't published a mutual-exclusivity rule, but early guides report Fast mode requests behave badly (or silently degrade) once you cross the 272K input threshold. Treat them as incompatible until OpenAI documents otherwise. Reasoning tokens still count. Fast mode makes throughput faster, but a max-effort call still generates the same volume of reasoning output. The economics only work when you're paying for latency you can actually feel. Pro tip Fast mode's break-even is roughly 25% more throughput per dollar at the 2.5× ceiling — worse when the ceiling isn't hit. Prefer Fast mode for interactive chat where the user waits. Skip it for batch, background agents and long-context RAG. If you were going to switch a batch pipeline from Claude to Sol for cost, don't turn on Fast mode — you'll erase the saving.
documents.s: Fast mode — small print worth reading

documents.t: For a Claude user this matters less than the API changes, but it's the change most likely to show up in a friend's screenshot and start an argument. Unlimited text chats on GPT-5.6 Luna for free ChatGPT users, from the week of 10 August 2026. Previously capped. Think button on free chats, same window. Adds a deeper-reasoning pass to a specific message, subject to abuse protections. It is not the same UI as the Plus/Pro effort slider — it's a per-message toggle, not a session-wide setting. The practical read: OpenAI is aggressively defending the free tier now that Claude and Gemini both have generous free reasoning options. Expect the abuse-protection cap to be tight for the first few weeks.
documents.s: Free tier: unlimited Luna + the Think button

documents.t: For most Claude workloads the answer stays the same. For three specific patterns it moves. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1You are paying for a lot of no-reasoning classifier calls⌄ `reasoning.effort: none` on Sol Luna is now a plausibly cheaper option than a min-effort Claude Haiku call for high-volume routing, tag extraction, or structured labelling — provided your prompts stay well below 272K. Benchmark it on a representative sample before switching. ←PreviousNext→ 2You have a latency-sensitive interactive workflow⌄ Sol + Fast mode is now the fastest quality tier OpenAI ships. If a user is waiting on each response and your prompts fit under 272K, this is the update that most changes the tradeoff. For background agent runs, ignore it. ←PreviousNext→ 3You do long-context RAG or repo-scale reasoning⌄ The 272K cliff means you should design for it. Claude Opus 5's 1M context and Sol's 1.05M context both extend well past 272K, but Claude does not have a cliff of the same shape — its long-context pricing is flat. For repo-wide operations at 400K+ input, Claude currently has the cost advantage. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Where this update actually changes a Claude user's decision

documents.t: If you shipped against Sol before 6 August, two things need to change: Set reasoning.effort explicitly on every call. Omitting it now costs you medium; you probably wanted low for most. Add a 272K guard at the boundary of your pipeline. Reject or chunk requests whose input tokens push past the threshold. A dumb check of len(input) / 4 as an approximation is enough as a first line of defence. A guardrail one-liner for Node.js wrappers CopyOpen in Claude↗ if (estimateTokens(input) > 260_000) { chunkOrReject(input); }

documents.t: Two rumors that were circulating around this update are not part of it: GPT-6 (Astra). As of 11 August 2026 OpenAI had not confirmed a launch date, model card, or pricing. Intermedio You already think in Claude. Then on 9 July 2026 the whole timeline flipped: OpenAI shipped three GPT-5.6 variants — Sol, Terra, Luna — and ChatGPT Work, an agent that takes a goal and works on it in the background for hours. A teammate asks "should we swap to Sol?"; a client wants ChatGPT Work to replace half a workflow you already run in Claude. This page maps the launch onto your Claude mental model and — more usefully — pulls out the parts the news coverage buries: the real prices, the exact benchmark deltas, the 1.05M context nobody expected, and where OpenAI still loses to Anthropic. What you'll learn Learn what actually shipped: Sol, Terra, Luna (plus Sol Ultra), all with a 1.05M-token context window Read the benchmark table the way OpenAI didn't publish it — where GPT-5.6 leads and where Claude Fable 5 still wins Understand ChatGPT Work: not a chat mode, but a background agent that returns a finished spreadsheet, deck, doc, or web app hours later Know when to reach for GPT-5.6 Sol over Claude for coding, agents, browser tasks — and when the answer is still Claude
documents.s: GPT-5.6 & ChatGPT Work for Claude Users

documents.t: GPT-5.6 is a three-tier refresh of the GPT-5 family — Sol (flagship), Terra (mid), Luna (budget) — sharing a 1.05M-token context window, 128K max output, and an OpenAI-published claim of 54% better token efficiency on agentic coding; ChatGPT Work is the new autonomous agent built on top of it, delivered as a merged desktop app that swallowed Codex. The interesting part isn't the model refresh — that was expected. It's the shape of the release: OpenAI is now shipping model + agent + IDE as one product, and pricing the workhorse tier ($1 in / $6 out on Luna) below where "cheap coding models" have historically sat.
Everyone's writing the benchmark recap. Here are the parts most Claude users miss on the first read.
documents.s: Three things about the GPT-5.6 launch that surprise people

documents.t: This is not how OpenAI usually ships. In earlier refreshes, the cheap tier came with a shrunken context window as a way to nudge you upward. In GPT-5.6, Sol, Terra, and Luna all quote a 1.05M-token context and 128K max output — the same shape. That means Luna at $1 input / $6 output per million tokens is a viable long-context option, not just a short-request one, and it changes the maths for RAG pipelines, whole-repo review, and long tool loops. If you were budgeting a Claude Haiku-style tier for high-volume retrieval work, Luna is now the obvious cross-check.
documents.s: 1. All three tiers share the same 1.05M context

documents.t: The framing OpenAI uses is telling: you don't chat with ChatGPT Work, you brief it. It takes an outcome ("build a competitive analysis of these five vendors"), gathers context from your connected apps and files, breaks the job into steps, works independently for minutes or hours, and delivers a finished artifact — a spreadsheet, slide deck, document, report, or working web app. Codex was folded into the same desktop app, so ChatGPT Work also owns the code-writing surface. This is the same "long-running autonomous work" bet Anthropic made with Claude's managed agents, but shipped as an end-user product first and an API second. It rolled out on Pro / Enterprise / Edu on launch day, with Plus and Business following within days.
documents.s: 2. ChatGPT Work is not "a chat mode" — it's a background agent that hands you a finished file

documents.t: Read past the marketing chart and the picture is more mixed than "Sol is the new king". OpenAI's own numbers say Sol reaches 80 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (about +2.8 vs Claude Fable 5) while using less than half the output tokens at roughly a third the cost. That's a real win. But Fable 5 still leads SWE-Bench Pro by a large reported margin — Sol comes in at ~64.6% there — and the launch coverage tends to bury that. Translation: pick by workload, not by press release. For "agent index" style tool-and-browser work, Sol is now the model to beat. For real-repo bug fixes with meaningful context, Anthropic still has the edge.
documents.s: 3. Sol wins the OpenAI-published benchmarks. Claude still leads SWE-bench Pro.

Your prompting instincts still work. Clear instructions, explicit output shapes, few-shot examples, and giving the model tools with good descriptions — all of it moves across, because these are properties of instruction-tuned frontier models, not Claude-specific tricks. For the deep version of that argument see porting prompts across models and the practical guide ChatGPT for Claude users. Two things to reset when you jump: API shape. Anthropic uses a tools block on the messages API; OpenAI uses tools on Chat Completions (or the Responses API), with the OpenAI function-calling schema. Same idea, different wire format. Reasoning as a mode, not just a slider. Claude exposes a thinking/effort parameter; on GPT-5.6, the sharpest gains show up when you pick the right tier (Sol / Sol Ultra) rather than only tuning effort on the cheap one. Cost matters more than it did on GPT-5.5.

documents.t: Neither is strictly better. Reach for GPT-5.6 when: You need a $1/$6 tier with a 1.05M context. Luna is currently the cheapest way to get long-context frontier-adjacent quality; that's a new capability, not a rebrand. The task is browser-heavy or agent-index-shaped. BrowseComp and the Coding Agent Index are Sol's strongest cards. If your agent spends most of its time in a browser or a shell, Sol is the model to beat. You want ChatGPT Work's "brief and forget" workflow for producing finished spreadsheets/decks/reports/apps as end-user artifacts, without gluing an agent framework yourself. Reach for Claude when you want the managed platform around the model — prompt caching, memory and context editing, managed agents, computer use, the desktop app — and specifically when the workload is real-repo software engineering, where Fable 5 still leads SWE-Bench Pro by a large margin. GPT-5.6 August 2026 Update: Effort Slider, Free Think Button & the 272K Price Cliff

Intermedio At DevDay on September 29, 2026 OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Sol (gpt-6.1-sol) one week after GPT-6 Sol, with the pitch "near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price." It went straight to the top of Hacker News. For a Claude user the interesting fact is not the pitch. It is that GPT-6.1 Sol lands on exactly Claude Sonnet 5.5's rate card — $2 in, $10 out per MTok — while charging half of Sonnet 5.5's cached-input rate. Two models, same headline price, different bills, different shapes of work. This page is the specs, the pricing mechanics most write-ups skip, an honest read of the benchmark table, and the rest of what DevDay shipped for developers. What you'll learn Know the exact specs — and the two ceilings that are not the context window Price a workload correctly, including the 272K cliff and the cached-input gap with Sonnet 5.5 Avoid the API-surface trap: tool calling is not available on both endpoints Read the launch benchmarks including the row where Claude still wins Know what else landed at DevDay for developers: Ultrafast, the Decisions API, Codex Security Cloud, Private Intelligence Última verificación: 2026-09-29. Specs, pricing, endpoint support and rate limits from OpenAI's gpt-6.1-sol model page, read the day of launch. Benchmarks are OpenAI's launch figures as compiled by third parties and are not independently reproduced. Three conflicts to know: (1) availability — OpenAI's DevDay resource index lists GPT-6.1 Sol as "coming soon", while launch-day reporting describes it as live in the API, ChatGPT Work and Codex and not yet in general ChatGPT chat; check the model page for your account. (2) One widely shared comparison table lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $5/$25 per MTok; Anthropic's own price is $4/$20 — use Anthropic's. (3) Ultrafast: OpenAI's guide lists broad availability for GPT-6 Astra with preview access for GPT-5.6 Sol, while the DevDay index says Astra now, Sol soon. Prices and limits move; read the source before quoting. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

documents.t: gpt-6.1-sol Context window 1,050,000 tokens Max input tokens 922,000 Max output tokens 128,000 Knowledge cutoff April 30, 2026 Reasoning efforts low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max Input / cached input / output $2.00 / $0.10 / $10.00 per MTok Cache write $2.50 per MTok Long context (>272K) 2× input and cache rates, 1.5× output Fast Mode 2× standard pricing Batch / Flex 50% below standard Rate limits Tier 1: 500 RPM / 500K TPM → Tier 5: 15K RPM / 40M TPM

1,050,000 is the window. 922,000 is the input ceiling. The gap is not slack you can spend on a bigger document — it is the room reasoning and output need. If you size a retrieval step against "1M context" you will hit a limit ~12% earlier than the marketing number, and you will hit it at the worst moment, after you have already paid to assemble the prompt. Then there is the price cliff at 272K. Cross it and input and cached input double, output goes up by half. This is the same cliff GPT-6 Astra has, and it changes the economics of long-context work sharply: a 300K-token prompt does not cost 10% more than a 272K one, it costs roughly twice as much on the input side. If you are near the boundary, compressing to stay under it is worth real engineering effort. Claude prices its 1M window differently — see what AI costs across providers and prompt caching across providers.
documents.s: The two ceilings that are not the context window

documents.t: The model page lists Chat Completions (without tool calling) and Responses API (tool calling). Read that twice if you are porting an existing integration. If your code posts to Chat Completions — the endpoint most third-party libraries, gateways and "OpenAI-compatible" wrappers default to — you do not get function calling on this model. The fix is not a parameter, it is a different endpoint and a different request shape. Also unsupported: Live, Realtime, Assistants, fine-tuning, embeddings, image generation, video, speech and transcription, moderation, and legacy Completions. The supported tool list is broad — web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply patch, skills, computer use, MCP, tool search — but it is a Responses API list. Watch out Check your AI gateway before you switch a model string. A router that normalises everything to Chat Completions will silently drop tool calling on gpt-6.1-sol — the request succeeds, the tools just never fire.
documents.s: The trap: tool calling is not on both APIs

documents.t: Same headline numbers, different mechanics. GPT-6.1 Sol Claude Sonnet 5.5 Claude Opus 5.5 Input / output per MTok $2 / $10 $2 / $10 $4 / $20 Cached read per MTok $0.10 $0.20 $0.20 Context 1.05M (922K input) 1M 1M Max output 128K 128K 128K Long-context surcharge Yes, above 272K No published cliff No published cliff Two consequences that matter more than the headline parity: On a long agent loop, GPT-6.1 Sol's cache read is the cheaper line. $0.10 against $0.20 is a 2× gap on the item an agentic loop re-pays on every single turn. If your prompt is a large stable prefix plus a small delta — which is what an agent is — that is where the bill actually lives. Above 272K the direction flips hard. Anthropic publishes no equivalent cliff on the Claude 5.5 models, so a workload that genuinely needs 400K of context is priced on very different curves. Know which side of 272K you live on before you compare anything.

OpenAI's launch numbers, as compiled at launch. These are vendor-run; nobody has reproduced them independently yet. Benchmark GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-6 Astra Claude Cost per task DeepSWE v1.1 (software engineering) 75.2% (high) 74.8% (high) Sonnet 5.5: 71.0% ~$1.50 vs Astra ~$7.70 OSWorld 2.0 (computer use) 71.4% (max) 73.5% (max) Opus 5: 60.3% (medium) $1.30 vs Astra $9.30 GDP.pdf (document analysis) 32.0% 32.2% Opus 5.5: 28.8% — AutomationBench 1.0.6 (business workflows) 36.0% — Sonnet 5.5: 44.7% $0.30 vs Sonnet ~$1.14 Low-effort factual error rate 7.7% — — (GPT-6 Sol: 11.4%) Three things to take from this table: 1. The cost claim is the strong claim. Beating Astra on DeepSWE by 0.4 points is noise. Doing it at roughly a fifth of the cost per task is not. The interesting comparison in this release is never Sol against Astra on quality — it is Sol against Astra on price for the same quality. 2. AutomationBench is the row OpenAI did not lead with. Claude Sonnet 5.5 scores 44.7% against GPT-6.1 Sol's 36.0% — 8.7 points, on business-workflow automation, at ~4× the cost per task. That is a genuine trade, not a rout in either direction: if a failed workflow costs you more than $0.84, the expensive model is the cheap one. Decide with your own failure cost, not with the leaderboard. 3. Even the best computer-use number is 71.4%. Roughly three in ten tasks fail on the benchmark designed for the capability. Everything in computer-use agents compared about confirmation gates still applies. The factual-error figure is the quietest interesting number: 7.7% at low effort, down from 11.4% on GPT-6 Sol. Error rate improving specifically at the cheap setting is what makes a workhorse model usable as a default rather than as a fallback.

Short version, because several of these deserve their own pages. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Ultrafast speed tier⌄ A paid speed tier: OpenAI describes up to 8x faster token generation in Codex and 6x in the API. The guide notes it is US data residency and global processing only — no EU or other regional processing endpoints — and strongly recommends WebSockets over HTTP, because per-request network overhead eats the latency win on tool-heavy agent loops. On the consumer side it is exclusive to the new $500/month Pro 500 plan. ←PreviousNext→ 2Agents API gains computer use⌄ The Agents API (public beta since September 10) can now operate software through its UI, alongside Codex's multi-agent capabilities, tool search and context compaction. The side-by-side with Anthropic's hosted loop is already written up on this site. ←PreviousNext→ 3Decisions API (limited preview)⌄ Sub-second classification and routing over predefined options, running on the Luna model. This is a direct answer to the decision-model category — the same shape as Jev and Kev: return a choice with calibrated confidence instead of prose. ←PreviousNext→ 4Codex Security Cloud⌄ Scans whole GitHub repositories, reviews new commits continuously, deduplicates findings and prepares fixes for review while your laptop is closed. The CLI is open source at github.com/openai/codex-security, with a TypeScript SDK. ←PreviousNext→ 5Private Intelligence⌄ Zero Data Retention with Private Safety Processing — automated safety checks that run without OpenAI personnel accessing the content. Private Inference, combining confidential computing with verifiable controls, is previewed for later in the fall. ←PreviousNext→ The Decisions API is the one to watch if you have been following the decision-model thread on this site: it takes a research direction that was open-weight and DIY and turns it into a hosted endpoint from the largest vendor. See System One decision models: Jev, Kev and the open clones and train your own decision model for what the category actually guarantees — and what "cannot hallucinate" does not mean.

Above it, input and cache double. Instrument your actual prompt sizes before assuming the window is flat-priced. ←PreviousNext→ Decide the switch on your own data, not the launch table CopyOpen in Claude↗ I am comparing two models for a production workload. Model A: gpt-6.1-sol — $2 in / $0.10 cached / $10 out per MTok, 1.05M context but 922K max input, and input + cached rates DOUBLE above 272K tokens (output x1.5). Model B: claude-sonnet-5-5 — $2 in / $0.20 cached / $10 out per MTok, 1M context, no published long-context surcharge. Here is my workload profile: - average stable prefix (cacheable): <N> tokens - average per-turn delta: <N> tokens - average output per turn: <N> tokens - turns per task: <N> - tasks per day: <N> - share of requests whose total input exceeds 272K: <X>% - cost to me of one wrong answer that ships: $<N> Compute the monthly bill for each model. Then tell me the accuracy gap at which the cheaper model stops being cheaper, given my stated cost of a wrong answer. Show the arithmetic. Do not recommend a model without showing the break-even point.
