Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Si solo lees una sección, lee esta. Así se alinean las cosas que conoces en Claude con el mundo de Grok: En Claude lo llamas… En el mundo de Grok es… ¿La misma idea? Claude.ai (la app de chat) La app de Grok (grok.com, las apps de X, móvil) Sí — la superficie de consumidor/asistente El selector de modelo (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) Las variantes de Grok (un modelo insignia como Grok 4.3, una variante rápida para llamadas a herramientas, una variante de programación) Sí — la misma idea, distintos nombres Claude Code (programación agéntica en la terminal) Grok Build (la CLI de agente de programación de xAI) Cercano — ver abajo La consola / API + el workbench La API de xAI (https://api.x.ai/v1) + la consola de xAI Sí — la superficie de desarrollo para prototipar y obtener una clave Uso de herramientas / llamadas a funciones (API) Llamadas a funciones (con forma compatible con OpenAI) Sí — el mismo bucle, y aquí hasta el JSON es familiar Búsqueda web / citas Búsqueda nativa en tiempo real en X + web integrada en el modelo Cercano — pero notablemente más "en vivo" La conclusión: casi no hay ningún concepto nuevo que aprender. Se trata sobre todo de renombrar y reubicar cosas que ya entiendes — más dos áreas donde Grok genuinamente se inclina más lejos que Claude: acceso en tiempo real a datos de X/web y una API compatible con OpenAI y lista para usar.
documents.s: El mapa de conceptos en 60 segundos

documents.t: Aquí está la diferencia que más cambia para los desarrolladores: la API de xAI sigue la especificación de la API de OpenAI. La URL base es https://api.x.ai/v1, así que si ya tienes código hablando con un cliente compatible con OpenAI, migrar suele ser solo cambiar la URL base y sustituir la clave. Última verificación: 2026-07-01. xAI documenta su API como compatible con OpenAI con la URL base https://api.x.ai/v1; la superficie compatible exacta (qué parámetros y endpoints se mapean limpiamente) evoluciona — verifica contra el quickstart actual de xAI. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Para un usuario de Claude, esto vale la pena interiorizarlo, porque la Messages API de Claude tiene su propia forma (su propio formato de petición/respuesta, sus propios bloques tool_use/tool_result). Viniendo de Claude, ajusta tu reflejo así: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Apunta al SDK de OpenAI, no al de Anthropic⌄ Se llega a Grok a través de clientes de estilo OpenAI. No traduces a un tercer dialecto — reutilizas la forma de petición de OpenAI que tú (o una librería) ya conoces. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cambia la URL base + la clave⌄ Establece la URL base en https://api.x.ai/v1 y usa una clave de xAI. Gran parte de tu infraestructura existente compatible con OpenAI sigue funcionando. ←PreviousNext→ 3Reutiliza el JSON de llamadas a herramientas casi tal cual⌄ Como el formato es compatible con OpenAI, las definiciones de llamadas a funciones se transfieren mucho más directamente que entre Claude y OpenAI — una comodidad genuina, no una trampa. ←PreviousNext→ 4Confirma igualmente el ID del modelo⌄ Lo único que debes establecer correctamente es el nombre del modelo (p. ej. un id grok-4.x actual). Los IDs de modelo son el detalle que se mueve más rápido — consulta la página de modelos en vivo. ←PreviousNext→ Migración directa (Python, SDK de OpenAI) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_XAI_KEY", # an xAI key, not an OpenAI key base_url="https://api.x.ai/v1", # the only structural change ) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="grok-4.3", # confirm the current id in xAI docs messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize today's top AI headline."}], ) print(resp.choices[0].message.content) Watch out Directo ≠ comportamiento idéntico. El formato de cable es compatible con OpenAI, pero el modelo es Grok — su personalidad, sus límites de rechazo y su conocimiento en tiempo real difieren. Vuelve a ejecutar tus evaluaciones; no asumas que un prompt afinado para Claude (o GPT) rinde igual. Nunca pegues una clave de API en vivo en un prompt, un repositorio o un chat. Usa variables de entorno y gestión de secretos, exactamente como harías con una clave de Anthropic.
documents.s: La API es un cambio directo — esto es lo grande para quienes construyen

documents.t: Aquí es donde Grok más se aparta de tus hábitos con Claude. Grok está construido por xAI con acceso nativo en tiempo real a información de X (Twitter) y la web, y xAI posiciona la búsqueda en vivo como una parte de primera clase de cómo responde el modelo. Última verificación: 2026-07-01. xAI describe a Grok con uso nativo de herramientas e integración de búsqueda en tiempo real (incluidos datos de X); el comportamiento exacto de recuperación, la frescura y cualquier límite por plan cambian — verifica en las páginas de producto actuales de xAI. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Para un usuario de Claude, el cambio mental es este: con Claude echas mano de una herramienta de búsqueda, un pipeline de recuperación o un conector cuando necesitas información actual, y razonas con cuidado sobre tu fecha de corte de conocimiento. Con Grok, "qué está pasando ahora mismo en X / en la web" está más cerca de ser un valor por defecto integrado. Eso hace de Grok una opción natural para preguntas en vivo, de actualidad y de pulso social — y cambia lo que deberías desconfiar: los resultados en vivo siguen necesitando la misma disciplina de verificación de fuentes que aplicarías a cualquier contenido web. Pro tip Apóyate en Grok para el eje de la frescura: noticias de última hora, discusión en tendencia, 'qué dice la gente hoy'. Ahí es estructuralmente donde es fuerte. Conserva tus instintos de Claude para la verificación: tiempo real ≠ autoritativo. Pide fuentes y trata una publicación viral como una afirmación por comprobar, no como un hecho. La frescura tiene una vida media. Para material de referencia duradero, una respuesta de búsqueda en vivo puede quedar obsoleta o sobreindexar la opinión reciente más ruidosa — ver la nota de abajo. Para la idea más profunda de por qué la actualidad y la verdad no son lo mismo, ver Frescura y vida media y Alucinaciones — ambas aplican directamente a cualquier asistente de búsqueda en tiempo real.
documents.s: La búsqueda en tiempo real en X + web es el verdadero titular

documents.t: Si vives en Claude Code, Grok Build de xAI es el análogo más cercano: un agente de programación que gobiernas desde la terminal, compitiendo en el mismo carril que Claude Code y la CLI de Codex de OpenAI. Está construido en torno a una variante de Grok afinada para programación y a un enfoque de subagentes en paralelo para trabajar en bases de código más grandes, con un modo autónomo de larga duración para delegar tareas mayores. Última verificación: 2026-07-01. xAI ha lanzado una CLI de agente de programación (Grok Build) y una variante de modelo afinada para programación; la disponibilidad (p. ej. en qué nivel de suscripción), el conjunto exacto de funciones y el id del modelo se mueven rápido — trata los detalles como sensibles al tiempo y verifícalos. Confirma con la fuente oficial. Los conceptos se transfieren casi uno a uno desde Claude Code: Idea de Claude Code Análogo de Grok Build Notas Ediciones agénticas desde la terminal Igual — un agente de programación CLI El bucle central (leer → planificar → editar → ejecutar) es la forma compartida de toda esta categoría Subagentes / trabajo en paralelo Arquitectura de subagentes en paralelo Ambos reparten el trabajo grande entre ayudantes; los detalles de orquestación difieren Tareas autónomas de larga duración Un modo de larga duración de "termina el objetivo" Delega una implementación mayor y déjalo planificar-ejecutar-verificar El punto duradero: la habilidad de gobernar una CLI de programación agéntica es portable. Escribir una tarea clara, mantener el contexto ajustado, revisar diffs y dirigir con puntos de control son las mismas disciplinas ya sea el agente Claude Code, Codex o Grok Build. Ver ¿Qué es Claude Code? para el modelo mental, y Agentes de programación locales para el campo más amplio.
documents.s: Grok Build es la respuesta de xAI a Claude Code

documents.t: La mayor parte de tu conocimiento de Claude se transfiere. Aquí está la lista corta de cosas que son genuinamente diferentes: Dialecto de la API (a tu favor). Grok habla compatible con OpenAI, no la Messages de Anthropic. Si vienes de la API de Claude, cambias a la forma de petición/respuesta de OpenAI — y ganas reutilización fácil de todo lo ya construido para endpoints compatibles con OpenAI. Tiempo real por defecto. El anclaje a la actualidad es más un valor integrado con Grok. Ajusta cuándo echas mano de ello — y sigue verificando fuentes. Persona y límites. La voz y los límites de contenido de Grok están afinados de forma diferente a los de Claude. No asumas que un system prompt calibrado para el estilo de Claude produce el mismo tono o los mismos rechazos. Detalles volátiles. Los nombres de modelos, las variantes, los límites de contexto y los precios se mueven rápido (Grok lanzó múltiples versiones a lo largo de 2026). Adquiere el hábito de confirmar en la fuente — exactamente como deberías hacer también para Claude.

Ambos son asistentes generales capaces y la brecha en cualquier tarea dada suele ser pequeña y cambiante — así que trata esto como tendencias, no leyes, y deja que tu propia evaluación con tus propios datos decida: Trabajo en vivo y de actualidad. "Qué está pasando ahora mismo", temas en tendencia y preguntas de pulso social juegan a favor de la búsqueda nativa en tiempo real en X/web de Grok. Migraciones directas desde OpenAI. Si ya tienes código compatible con OpenAI, apuntarlo a xAI es uno de los cambios de menor fricción del campo. Delegaciones de programación desde la terminal. Si te gusta el flujo de Claude Code / Codex, Grok Build es una tercera opción natural para hacer A/B en tus propias tareas. La respuesta honesta la mayoría de las veces: aquel en el que tú (o tu equipo) ya estáis configurados, y el que gane tu evaluación en la tarea que importa. La habilidad es portable; el coste de configuración es el verdadero coste de cambio. Para la forma neutral respecto al proveedor de elegir, ver Elegir un modelo y Cuánto cuesta la IA en cada proveedor. Vocabulario de Grok a Claude girarTérminoLa app de Grok (grok.com / dentro de X)DefiniciónLa superficie de consumidor/asistente de xAI, estrechamente ligada a X. ≈ Claude.ai.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 6 Siguiente→ Ponte a prueba 0/3 1Tienes un servicio ya escrito contra un cliente compatible con OpenAI y quieres probar Grok. ¿Cuál es el movimiento duradero y de menor fricción? Reescribirlo todo primero al formato de la Messages API de ClaudeCambiar la URL base a https://api.x.ai/v1, sustituir por una clave de xAI y establecer un id de modelo Grok actualNo puedes — xAI tiene un dialecto de API completamente propietario 2Una tarea es 'resume qué dice la gente sobre el anuncio de hoy en X'. ¿Por qué podría Grok ser la opción natural — y qué disciplina sigue aplicando? Grok siempre es más preciso que Claude, así que no hace falta comprobar nadaLa búsqueda nativa en tiempo real en X/web de Grok se adapta a preguntas en vivo/de actualidad, pero deberías verificar igualmente las fuentes y tratar las publicaciones virales como afirmacionesSolo Claude puede acceder a la web, así que es una pregunta trampa 3Te encanta el flujo de Claude Code. ¿Cuál es la forma correcta de pensar en Grok Build? Un paradigma totalmente distinto que debes reaprender desde ceroLa misma categoría de CLI de programación agéntica — las habilidades de gobernarlo se transfieren, solo difieren los detalles de orquestación y el modeloUna herramienta solo con GUI sin flujo de terminal Key takeaways Casi ningún concepto nuevo: la app de Grok ≈ Claude.ai, las variantes de Grok ≈ Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, Grok Build ≈ Claude Code, las llamadas a funciones ≈ el uso de herramientas. La API es la diferencia destacada — es compatible con OpenAI (URL base api.x.ai/v1), así que el código con forma de OpenAI migra con un cambio de URL base + clave, a diferencia de la propia Messages API de Claude. La búsqueda en tiempo real en X/web es más un valor integrado con Grok — échale mano para la frescura y la actualidad, pero conserva tu disciplina de verificación de fuentes de Claude. Grok Build es un agente de programación en la terminal en el carril de Claude Code / Codex; la habilidad de gobernar una CLI agéntica es portable. Los nombres, las variantes, los límites de contexto y los precios quedan obsoletos rápido en xAI — verifica los detalles en la documentación de xAI, igual que deberías hacer para Claude.

Most "agent memory" is a vector store with a nice wrapper: you dump conversation turns in, you cosine-similarity them back out, and the agent recites history it was never going to forget anyway. Hindsight is built around a different claim — that an agent should end the month believing things it did not believe at the start of it — and it is currently the fastest-growing project on GitHub because of it: roughly 4,500 stars in a single day on 2026-09-27, about 37,000 total, MIT-licensed, Python, with a peer-reviewable paper behind the architecture. This page is the practical read: what is actually inside a memory bank, why recall and reflect are two different cost classes, the benchmark result that should change how you budget your stack, and the four defaults that will bite you in production. What you'll learn Tell apart the three operations — retain, recall, reflect — and the third path most people miss: reading a mental model with no LLM call at all Understand why recall is four parallel retrievers fused by reciprocal rank fusion, not a vector search Read the benchmark numbers correctly, including the one where a competitor wins and the 3.2-point gap between the vendor's own two pages Stand a server up and wire it into Claude, an OpenAI-SDK agent, or a coding agent, in three commands Spot the four production defaults that are wrong for you — starting with the security policy that is off until you switch it on Última verificación: 2026-09-28. Hindsight ships fast (last push the day before this page was written) and the live leaderboard changes. Treat every score, star count and pattern count below as a dated snapshot; the architecture and the gotchas are the durable part. Fuentes: github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight README and GitHub API (36,993 stars, MIT, Python, pushed 2026-09-26); github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight-benchmarks (LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo tables); vectorize.io/benchmarks (94.6% headline); arXiv:2512.12818 'Hindsight is 20/20'; hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/memory-defense, /developer/mcp-server, /developer/mental-models, /developer/observations, /developer/retrieval; hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/03/23/agent-memory-benchmark; GitHub trending (daily) 2026-09-27. Benchmark leaderboards here are continuously updated and every non-Hindsight score is vendor-self-reported — re-read the live tables before quoting a number in a decision.

Almost every mistake with Hindsight comes from treating its three verbs as interchangeable. They are not — they sit at wildly different points on the price/latency curve, and there is a fourth path that costs essentially nothing. Path What happens LLM calls Use it for retain An LLM extracts facts, timestamps, entities and relationships, then normalises them into canonical entities, time series and search indexes Yes, on write Ingesting a turn, a tool result, a document recall Four retrievers run in parallel, results are fused and reranked, then trimmed to a token budget No generation — retrieval and a cross-encoder "What do I know about X?" before a turn reflect Walks the hierarchy mental models → observations → raw facts and reasons over it, shaped by the bank's mission, directives and disposition Yes, and more than one "What risks am I missing on this project?" Read a mental model A stored standing answer is fetched from the database None Booting an agent with settled knowledge That last row is the mechanism most readers have never seen. A mental model is a question you register once ("What are this user's preferences?"); Hindsight writes the answer, stores it, and rewrites it in the background as the bank learns. Reading it is a database read — no retrieval, no inference, no tokens. So an agent's session can start already knowing, instead of spending its first three turns rediscovering. The practical rule: reflect is for thinking, recall is for looking up, and a mental model is for what you look up every single session. If you are calling reflect on every turn, you have built an expensive chatbot.
documents.s: The one idea: three operations, three cost classes

documents.t: A bank is one isolated brain — one user, one agent, or one project — with strict isolation and no cross-bank leakage. Inside it, memories are not one flat pile. Hindsight splits them along a biomimetic axis: World facts — how the world is. "The stove gets hot." Experiences — what this agent did and what happened. "I touched the stove and it hurt." Observations — consolidated, evidence-backed beliefs formed from many facts. Mental models — learned understanding synthesised from observations and facts. Knowledge pages — mental models with the mechanics hidden: living wiki-style documents the bank writes about itself, organised in folders, searchable, and projectable onto disk as plain markdown. The world/experience split is doing real work. "The deploy script needs sudo" and "I ran the deploy script and it failed" are different kinds of claim with different lifetimes, and collapsing them into one undifferentiated memories table is exactly what makes a naive vector store answer confidently about a fact it only ever observed once, two months ago, in a failed attempt. Observations are refined, not overwritten. Each one keeps its supporting evidence as exact quotes plus a proof count, and when new evidence arrives it strengthens, weakens or extends the existing belief rather than silently replacing it. This is the difference between a memory system and a cache: a cache's last write wins, and a belief's last write is evidence. Banks also carry a mission (a natural-language identity that directs what to prioritise), directives (hard rules never to violate) and disposition traits (skepticism, literalism, empathy) that shape how reflect reasons. Two banks over identical facts can reach different conclusions on purpose.
documents.s: What is actually inside a bank

documents.t: This is the part worth internalising even if you never run Hindsight. A single recall fires four retrieval strategies in parallel: Semantic — dense vector similarity Keyword — BM25 exact matching Graph — entity, temporal and causal links Temporal — time-range filtering Then the four result sets are merged by reciprocal rank fusion, reordered by a cross-encoder reranker, and trimmed to fit a token limit. Why bother? Because each arm fails in a way the others do not. Semantic search cannot answer "what happened in June" — a date is not semantically similar to anything. BM25 cannot match a paraphrase. A graph traversal is the only thing that answers "who replaced the person who owned the account the user complained about," and none of the three know that the answer must fit in 2,000 tokens. Reciprocal rank fusion is the cheap trick that makes this composable: it scores by rank position, not by each retriever's own score, so you never have to normalise a cosine distance against a BM25 score. If you are hand-rolling hybrid retrieval anywhere in your stack, that one detail is the takeaway. The reranker matters more than the retrievers. Fusion gets the right memory into the top 50; the cross-encoder is what gets it into the top 5 that actually reach the model.
documents.s: Recall is not a vector search

documents.t: On LongMemEval-S (500 questions), the project's own harness reports: System Score Hindsight (Gemini 3) 91.4% Hindsight (OSS-120B) 89.0% Supermemory (Gemini 3) 85.2% Supermemory (GPT-5) 84.6% Hindsight (OSS-20B) 83.6% Full context (GPT-4o) 60.2% Full context (OSS-20B) 39.0% Look at the two bold rows. Same 20B open-weight model, same questions. With Hindsight in front of it: 83.6%. With the whole history stuffed into its context: 39.0%. That is +44.6 points from architecture alone, and it puts a 20B model 23 points above full-context GPT-4o. The paper's framing — memory as "a structured, first-class substrate for reasoning" rather than a retrieval add-on — is exactly this result. If your memory layer is losing, buying a bigger model is the expensive way to not fix it. Now the honest caveats, because they matter more than the headline: A competitor wins the other benchmark. On LoCoMo, Hindsight (Gemini 3) scores 89.61% — and Backboard reports 90.00%. Memobase 75.78%, Zep 75.14%. The ranking flips depending on which benchmark you pick, which is the whole reason to read two. Only one row is independently reproduced. Per the project's own README, Hindsight's figures were reproduced by research collaborators at Virginia Tech's Sanghani Center and The Washington Post; every other system's score is self-reported by its vendor. A table of self-reported numbers is a table of best days. The vendor's two pages disagree. vectorize.io/benchmarks headlines 94.6% on LongMemEval; the benchmarks repo's LongMemEval-S table says 91.4%. Both are Hindsight's own publications. The leaderboard is continuously updated and the configurations differ, but a 3.2-point spread between a marketing page and a repo is a reason to run the harness yourself before you quote either. And then the most interesting critique — which comes from Hindsight's own team. Their benchmark manifesto argues that LoCoMo and LongMemEval were designed for the 32k-context era, when retrieval was the hard part. With million-token windows, stuffing everything in scores competitively, so these benchmarks increasingly measure a model's reading comprehension rather than a memory architecture. Worse, they collapse everything to one axis. Their line is the one to steal: A system that scores 90% and costs $10 per user per day is not better than one that scores 82% and costs $0.10. Which is the correct way to evaluate any memory layer, including the one you already have: accuracy per dollar per user per day, on your own traffic. See Evaluating Agents for how to build that harness.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11. Run the server⌄ One Docker command, one LLM key. It ships an embedded Postgres (pg0) in a named volume, so there is nothing else to provision. API on 8888, UI on 9999. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Pick the provider deliberately⌄ HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_PROVIDER accepts 25+ values — openai, anthropic, gemini, groq, bedrock, vertexai, deepseek, minimax — plus fully local ollama, lmstudio and llamacpp, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and litellm gateways. Existing subscriptions work with no API key at all: claude-code (Claude Pro/Max), openai-codex (ChatGPT Plus/Pro), cursor, github-copilot. Retain calls an LLM on every write, so this choice is your bill. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Retain, recall, reflect from a client⌄ pip install hindsight-client (or npm, Go, CLI). Three methods, one bank_id. Pass a real timestamp on retain — temporal recall is one of the four arms and it cannot filter on a time you never supplied. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Register the questions you ask every session⌄ Turn the lookups your agent repeats into mental models or knowledge pages. Each one converts a recall into a database read. This is the single biggest cost lever in the system. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Turn Memory Defense on before the first real write⌄ It is opt-in, disabled by default, and it does not scan retroactively. Enable it at bank creation — see the gotchas below for why 'later' is the wrong answer. ←PreviousNext→ Server, client, first three calls CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. Server — API on :8888, UI on :9999, embedded Postgres in a volume export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-xxx docker run -it --pull always --name hindsight --restart unless-stopped \ -p 8888:8888 -p 9999:9999 \ -e HINDSIGHT_API_LLM_API_KEY=$OPENAI_API_KEY \ -v hindsight-data:/home/hindsight/.pg0 \ ghcr.io/vectorize-io/hindsight:latest # 2. Client pip install hindsight-client -U Python: the three operations CopyOpen in Claude↗ from hindsight_client import Hindsight client = Hindsight(base_url="http://localhost:8888") # Retain — an LLM extracts facts, entities, relationships, time. # Always pass a real timestamp: temporal recall filters on it. client.retain( bank_id="user-123", content="Alice got promoted to senior engineer", context="career update", timestamp="2026-06-15T10:00:00Z", ) # Recall — 4 parallel retrievers, RRF, cross-encoder, token trim. No generation. client.recall(bank_id="user-123", query="What does Alice do?") client.recall(bank_id="user-123", query="What happened in June?") # temporal arm # Reflect — walks mental models -> observations -> raw facts and reasons. # Costs several LLM calls. Not a per-turn operation. client.reflect(bank_id="user-123", query="What should I know about Alice?") No Docker, or you want it inside a test suite? There is an embedded mode that starts and stops the server in a context manager: Embedded — no server to manage CopyOpen in Claude↗ pip install hindsight-all -U # hindsight-all-slim on Intel Macs Embedded mode in Python CopyOpen in Claude↗ import os from hindsight import HindsightServer, HindsightClient with HindsightServer( llm_provider="openai", llm_model="gpt-5-mini", llm_api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"], ) as server: client = HindsightClient(base_url=server.url) client.retain(bank_id="my-bank", content="Alice works at Google") print(client.recall(bank_id="my-bank", query="Where does Alice work?"))

Three paths, in increasing order of control. The LLM wrapper — two lines, no other changes. Swap your SDK client for a wrapped one and memories are recalled before every call and retained after it. LiteLLM sits underneath, so the same integration reaches 100+ models, and wrap_anthropic() does the same for the Anthropic SDK. Every setting — bank, recall budget, fact types, or reflect instead of recall — is overridable per call with hindsight_* kwargs. Two-line memory for an existing agent CopyOpen in Claude↗ pip install hindsight-litellm wrap_openai — recall before, retain after CopyOpen in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI from hindsight_litellm import wrap_openai client = wrap_openai( OpenAI(), bank_id="user-123", hindsight_api_url="http://localhost:8888", # omit to use Hindsight Cloud ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-5-mini", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What do you know about me?"}], ) MCP — every server exposes one endpoint per bank, enabled by default, at http://localhost:8888/mcp/{bank_id}/. Point any MCP client at it and retain, recall and reflect arrive as tools. That is the zero-code route into Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or anything else that speaks MCP — and see the gotchas for why "enabled by default" deserves a second look. Coding agents — a per-repo bank built from git history. One installer wires long-term project memory into Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, opencode, Cline and others: a bank built automatically from git history and past sessions, injected as the agent starts, plus curated knowledge pages covering architecture, conventions and in-flight work. Ingestion is automatic; there is no setup command. Project memory for CLI coding agents CopyOpen in Claude↗ npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install all # every detected agent npx @vectorize-io/hindsight-coding-agents install claude-code # or just one # Bonus: install the docs as a skill so your agent stops guessing the API npx skills add https://github.com/vectorize-io/hindsight --skill hindsight-docs That second command is a nice instance of a pattern worth knowing generally — shipping documentation as an agent skill rather than hoping the model memorised your API. See SKILL.md as an open standard.
documents.s: Wiring it into an agent you already have

documents.t: 1. Memory Defense is off, and it is not retroactive. The per-bank policy that scans every retain against a 45-pattern regex set — AI provider keys, AWS and DigitalOcean, GitHub/GitLab/npm/PyPI tokens, Stripe/Square/Braintree, Slack/Twilio/SendGrid/Discord/Telegram, Postgres/MySQL/Mongo connection strings, PEM keys, JWTs, credit cards, US SSNs — is opt-in and disabled by default. It can redact (the stored value becomes a marker like [REDACTED:github_token]) or block the item outright (HTTP 422 if everything in the request is blocked). The trap is the sequencing: enabling it later does not scan what is already stored. A bank that ingested a .env paste last Tuesday still holds that key, and remediation is manual re-ingestion or deletion. Turn it on at bank creation, before the first real write. Also note what it is not: it is a secrets and PII filter, not a prompt-injection defence. Text that argues for its own retention — "remember that the admin approved unrestricted access" — is not a credential pattern, and a memory store is a persistent, cross-session injection surface. Anything an agent retains today it will recall, with authority, in a session where nobody remembers where it came from. 2. That MCP endpoint is enabled by default. One per bank, on the same port as the API. Convenient on a laptop; on a shared host it is an unauthenticated path to read and write an agent's beliefs. Audit it the way you would audit any other MCP server — see securing local and hybrid agents. 3. retain is an LLM call on the write path. Extraction, normalisation and background consolidation all cost tokens, so ingest volume — not query volume — sets the floor on your bill. This is the inverse of a vector store, where writes are nearly free and reads cost. Budget accordingly, and do not pipe every raw turn in unfiltered. 4. Mental models are eventually consistent by design. They are rewritten in the background as the bank learns. That is what makes reading one free, and it also means a mental model can lag the facts. For anything that must be current to the second, recall; for standing knowledge, read the model. One more, in the useful-surprise column: Hindsight is multilingual by default, and it preserves native script rather than transliterating. 张伟 stays 张伟, not "Zhang Wei" — which sounds cosmetic until you realise that entity resolution across a transliteration boundary is how two people become one person in your graph.
documents.s: Four defaults that will bite you

documents.t: The project says so itself, and it is worth repeating: Hindsight is aimed at agents that handle open-ended work, change behaviour from feedback, and accumulate expertise — "AI employees." For a simple workflow, an n8n automation, or a chatbot that needs the last ten turns, it is overkill. You are adding a Postgres instance, an LLM call on every write, and a consolidation pipeline to solve a problem that a summary in a text file solves. The ladder in How Agent Memory Actually Works still applies: try full context, then vector, then a graph, and only reach for a system like this when your agent needs to hold beliefs rather than transcripts. Check yourself 0/5 1Which path costs no LLM call and no retrieval at all? recall with a small token budgetReading a registered mental modelreflect with a narrow queryretain with extraction disabled 2Hindsight with a 20B open model scores 83.6% on LongMemEval-S while the same model with the full history in context scores 39.0%. What is the lesson? LongMemEval is brokenThe memory architecture, not model size, drives the result — a bigger model is the expensive way to not fix your memory layer20B models are better at long contextVector search is enough 3Why does recall fuse its four retrievers with reciprocal rank fusion instead of comparing their scores? It is fasterRRF scores by rank position, so you never have to normalise a cosine distance against a BM25 scoreIt guarantees the semantic arm wins tiesIt removes the need for a reranker 4You enable Memory Defense on a bank that has been ingesting production data for a month. What have you protected? Everything in the bank, scanned retroactivelyOnly future retains — existing secrets stay until you re-ingest or deleteOnly recall output, not storageNothing until you restart the server 5Hindsight tops LongMemEval but Backboard reports 90.00% against Hindsight's 89.61% on LoCoMo. What should you conclude? One of the two is lyingRankings flip by benchmark, and only Hindsight's numbers here are independently reproduced — run the harness on your own trafficLoCoMo is the better benchmarkBackboard is the better system Hindsight vocabulary girarTérminoBankDefiniciónOne isolated memory store — a single brain for one user, agent or project. Strict isolation, no cross-bank leakage. Carries a mission, hard directives, and disposition traits that shape how reflect reasons.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 10 Siguiente→

Intermedio On 15 July 2026, Thinking Machines Lab — Mira Murati's lab — released Inkling, its first in-house model, as open weights under Apache 2.0. It hit the front page of Hacker News overnight, and the coverage settled into two lazy shapes: "trillion-parameter open model!" and a benchmark table showing it losing. Both miss the point. Inkling is an unusual release that is deliberately not trying to top the leaderboard, and its most interesting feature — a continuous thinking-effort dial trained into the weights — has been widely mis-described in the first wave of reporting. This page is the practical read. What you'll learn Understand what Inkling actually is: a 975B sparse MoE with 41B active, Apache 2.0, 1M context, natively multimodal across text/image/audio/video Learn what the thinking-effort dial really is — a continuous float trained via RL, not the discrete low/medium/high enum the API wrappers show you See why 'open weights' does not mean 'runs on your machine' — the real VRAM floor is ~600 GB even quantized Know why Inkling loses benchmarks on purpose, and the one metric where it wins that nobody put in a headline

Inkling is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 975B total parameters and 41B active per token, pretrained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video, supporting a 1M-token context window, released under Apache 2.0 — positioned not as the best model available, but as the best base to customize. That last clause is the whole strategy. Thinking Machines says so plainly: Inkling "is not the strongest overall model available today, open or closed." Shipping a model alongside that sentence is not modesty, it's positioning — and it explains every design decision below.

This is the headline feature and it's the most mis-reported detail of the launch. Several outlets described the effort parameter as ranging "0.2 to 0.99," or as a named enum — none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh. The official Tinker documentation says something different. Effort is continuous reasoning-effort conditioning: any float from 0.0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1.0. The default is 0.9. The named levels are just recommended sweep values, not the actual interface: Preset Value none 0.0 minimal 0.1 low 0.2 medium 0.7 high 0.9 xhigh 0.99 The 0.2 floor that got reported is simply the low preset — not a limit. Nothing stops you passing 0.45. Note also how non-linear the presets are: the gap from low to medium is 0.5, while high to xhigh is 0.09. The useful resolution is bunched up at the top of the range. This matters because most people will meet Inkling through an OpenAI-compatible wrapper exposing reasoning_effort="high". That enum is a lossy adapter over a continuous knob. If you're tuning cost against quality, the enum hides most of the dial. Set effort directly via the Tinker renderer CopyOpen in Claude↗ renderer = TmlV0Renderer(get_tokenizer("thinkingmachines/Inkling")) messages = [Message(role="user", content="Solve this problem step by step.")] prompt = renderer.build_generation_prompt(messages, effort=0.9) The same effort argument carries into fine-tuning, which is the part worth pausing on — you can train at a chosen effort level: Fine-tune at a fixed effort level CopyOpen in Claude↗ model_input, weights = renderer.build_supervised_example( messages_with_assistant_response, effort=0.9, ) Última verificación: 2026-07-16. Esta página cita datos que cambian con el tiempo: toma la fecha de arriba como su grado de actualidad. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: 1. The effort dial is a float, and the news got its range wrong

documents.t: The reason the dial is continuous is that it wasn't bolted on at inference time. During reinforcement learning, the team set effort by changing the system message and adjusting the per-token cost — literally taxing the model for thinking. The model learned to spend different token budgets on different rollouts, and the dial is the residue of that training. That's a genuinely different mechanism from "please think step by step, but briefly," and it's why the payoff is real: Thinking Machines reports Inkling matches Nemotron 3 Ultra on Terminal Bench 2.1 while using roughly one-third as many reasoning tokens. It also explains the caveat the docs are careful to state, which you should take seriously: "Larger values generally encourage more reasoning, but do not guarantee longer responses or higher accuracy on every sample." Effort is a learned tendency, not a guarantee. Turning it to 0.99 and expecting monotonic improvement is a misread of what it is. And higher effort "may require a larger generation budget to avoid truncation" — crank effort without raising max tokens and you'll cut the model off mid-thought.
documents.s: 2. Effort isn't a prompt trick — it was trained in with a token tax

documents.t: "975B parameters, Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face" invites an assumption the hardware table demolishes: Numeric Aggregated VRAM floor Example configuration BF16 at least 2 TB 8× NVIDIA B300, or 16× NVIDIA H200 NVFP4 (W4A4) at least 600 GB 4× NVIDIA B300 NVFP4 (W4A16) at least 600 GB 8× NVIDIA H200 Even fully quantized to 4-bit, the floor is roughly 600 GB of aggregated VRAM. This is a multi-GPU-cluster model, not a workstation model, and not remotely a laptop model. The 41B active parameters make it cheap to run a token through; they do nothing to reduce what you must hold in memory. All 975B parameters have to be resident, because the router may reach for any of them on any token. If your interest in open weights is "run it locally," Inkling is the wrong model and running models locally with Ollama is the right page. If your interest is legal freedom to modify and commercialize — Apache 2.0, genuinely permissive — then Inkling qualifies, and you'll rent the GPUs from TogetherAI, Fireworks, Modal, Databricks or Baseten. Those are different reasons to want open weights, and this release serves only the second one.
documents.s: 3. Open weights, but you almost certainly can't run it

documents.t: The benchmark table is unflattering, and Thinking Machines published it anyway: Benchmark Inkling A stronger competitor Terminal Bench 2.1 63.8% GLM 5.2: 82.7% SWEBench Verified 77.6% Kimi K2.6: 80.2% SimpleQA Verified 43.9% DeepSeek V4 Pro: 57.0% FORTRESS Adversarial 78.0% Nemotron 3 Ultra: 77.6% Three losses, one narrow win. But the interesting result isn't in that table at all — it's calibration. The team trained with reinforcement learning based on proper scoring rules, which reward a model for saying "I'm 70% sure" and being right 70% of the time, rather than for sounding confident. The model was rewarded for estimating its own uncertainty well instead of confidently producing wrong answers, and it shows up on forecasting evaluations like ForecastBench and Prophet Arena. For anything where a wrong-but-confident answer costs more than a hedged one — triage, research, routing, extraction with a human reviewer downstream — a well-calibrated 44% is worth more than an overconfident 57%. That property doesn't fit in a leaderboard column, which is roughly why nobody led with it.
documents.s: 4. It loses benchmarks on purpose — and wins the one nobody reported

documents.t: The pieces worth knowing, beyond the parameter count: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Sparse MoE routing⌄ A 66-layer decoder-only transformer. Each layer holds 256 routed experts plus 2 shared experts, with 6 routed experts active per token. The shared experts always fire — they carry general capability — while the router picks specialists per token. ←PreviousNext→ 2Relative positional embeddings, not RoPE⌄ A deliberate departure from the near-universal default. The stated reason is better extrapolation to longer sequences, which is how a 1M-token context window is meant to hold up rather than degrade at the tail. ←PreviousNext→ 3Attention shape⌄ Sliding-window and global layers mixed at a 5:1 ratio with 8 KV heads, plus short convolutions applied at the attention inputs. Five cheap local layers per one expensive global layer is what makes 1M context affordable. ←PreviousNext→ 4Native multimodality⌄ Images enter as 40×40 pixel patches through a four-layer hMLP; audio as dMel spectrograms. Both pass through a lightweight embedding layer and are processed jointly with text tokens — one stream, not a bolted-on vision encoder. Output is UTF-8 text only. ←PreviousNext→ 5Hybrid optimizer⌄ Muon for large matrix weights, Adam for everything else — an unusual choice at this scale, and consistent with the lab's public research interest in optimizer behavior. ←PreviousNext→

Reach for Inkling when: You need to own and modify a capable multimodal model. Apache 2.0 plus real multimodality plus first-class fine-tuning support on Tinker is a rare combination. This is the intended use. Cost per task matters more than peak score. The effort dial at one-third the reasoning tokens is a real lever, and you can tune it continuously rather than in three steps. Calibration matters. If your pipeline can act on "the model isn't sure," this is unusually well-suited. Don't reach for it when you want the strongest coding agent (the table says GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 beat it), when you want to self-host on your own hardware (see the VRAM floor), or when you want maximum factual recall (SimpleQA 43.9% is not competitive). One safety note that the model card states directly: Inkling has a residual "occasional tendency to comply with role-play and indirectly framed prompts concerning harmful topics," and the card explicitly recommends layering external moderation — it names Llama Guard — rather than relying on built-in refusals. VentureBeat framed the model's posture as "resistance to censorship"; read the model card's own language as the operative guidance instead, and budget for a moderation layer if you deploy this. The card also lists the usual residual limits: hallucination, imperfect instruction-following, and degraded performance in long multi-turn conversations. Check yourself 0/4 1What is the actual valid range of Inkling's thinking-effort parameter? A float from 0.0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1.0A float from 0.2 to 0.99One of six named levels: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhighAn integer from 1 to 10 2Inkling has 41B active parameters out of 975B total. What does that mean for memory? You only need enough VRAM for ~41B parametersAll 975B parameters must be resident in memory; the sparsity cuts compute, not memoryThe inactive experts stream from disk on demand at no costMemory scales with context length only 3Why did Thinking Machines train Inkling with proper scoring rules in RL? To make responses shorterTo top the SWEBench leaderboardTo improve calibration — so stated confidence tracks actual accuracyTo enable multimodal input 4Setting effort=0.99 instead of 0.9 guarantees what? A longer responseHigher accuracy on every sampleNothing guaranteed — it encourages more reasoning but the docs warn it may need a bigger generation budget to avoid truncationLower latency

If you already read Kimi K2 for Claude users, the shape is familiar — a trillion-ish-parameter sparse MoE with permissive licensing — but the intent differs. Kimi K2 optimizes for long agentic tool chains. Inkling optimizes for being reshaped: multimodal input, a tunable effort budget, and fine-tuning as a first-class path. For the broader picture, see choosing a model, DeepSeek and Qwen open models for the rest of the open-weights field, and what AI costs across providers for the economics the effort dial is aimed at. Última verificación: 2026-07-16. Inkling was released on 15 July 2026. Benchmark comparisons and competitor scores move quickly, and hosted pricing was not published at launch. Avanzado On 14–16 July 2026, xAI published Grok Build — the coding agent behind its CLI — as a public Apache 2.0 repository at xai-org/grok-build. Not the weights. The harness: the agent loop, the tool implementations, the terminal UI, the extension system. It went to the front page of Hacker News within hours. This is a rare artifact. Almost every serious coding agent — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — ships as a binary or a bundle. Here, roughly 800,000 lines of production Rust are sitting in a repo you can read. That's worth more as a textbook than as a product. This page is the practical read: what's actually in there, what the structure teaches you about building agents, and two things about this release that most of the coverage got backwards. What you'll learn Understand what was published and what wasn't — harness yes, weights no, development history no Read the crate map as a checklist of what a production coding agent actually needs Learn why Apache 2.0 here means source-available, not open-development — and why that distinction is load-bearing See the data-collector code still present in the published tree, and what its constants confirm about the July exfil incident Know what's genuinely reusable from this repo and what is a dead end
documents.s: Inside Grok Build: Reading an Open Agent Harness

documents.t: The repository is 99%+ Rust, licensed Apache 2.0, and describes itself as a coding agent harness and TUI — fullscreen, mouse-interactive, extensible. It builds on macOS and Linux with a pinned Rust toolchain. Three things it is not: Not the model. Grok 4.5's weights are not here and are not open. The harness talks to a hosted endpoint. You can read every line of how the agent thinks about your codebase and still not run it without xAI's API. Not a development history. The repo has two commits: Publish harness and TUI open-source, then Synced from monorepo. There's a SOURCE_REV file at the root containing a single internal revision hash. This is an export of a private monorepo, re-synced periodically — not a repository that was developed in public and not one you can archaeologize for design decisions. Not open to you. CONTRIBUTING.md states plainly that the repository does not accept external pull requests or unsolicited patches, that xAI develops the software internally, and that the tree is published "for source transparency and local builds." GitHub issues are disabled at the repo level. ★ The distinction that matters: Apache 2.0 is a license, and it grants you real rights — read, fork, modify, ship derivatives. It says nothing about governance. Grok Build is source-available under an open-source license with a closed development model. You may fork it; you may not influence it. Read "open source" in the headlines as "you can read the source," because that is exactly and only what is on offer.

Ignore the marketing. The directory listing under crates/codegen/ is the most useful thing in the repo, because it is an honest inventory of what a shipping coding agent needs. A selection: Crate What it tells you xai-grok-agent, xai-grok-shell The agent runtime and its entry points — interactive, stdio, headless xai-grok-tools, xai-grok-tools-api Tool implementations, split from the tool interface — a real boundary xai-grok-workspace, xai-fast-worktree Filesystem, version control, execution, checkpoints — and fast git worktrees xai-codebase-graph Structural understanding of a repo, not just grep xai-grok-memory Memory is a subsystem, not a prompt trick xai-grok-mcp MCP is a first-class integration surface xai-grok-hooks, xai-hooks-plugins-types Hooks and plugins have their own type layer xai-grok-subagent-resolution Resolving which subagent handles what is hard enough to need its own crate xai-token-estimation Counting tokens before you spend them xai-hunk-tracker Tracking diff hunks across an editing session xai-grok-pager, xai-ratatui-inline The TUI — scrollback, prompts, modals, inline rendering xai-acp-lib Agent Client Protocol — editors embed the agent xai-grok-telemetry, xai-mixpanel Telemetry and product analytics, as first-class crates ptyctl, xai-tty-utils, xai-grok-crash-handler Terminals are hostile and processes crash Read that list again as a build plan. The naive mental model of a coding agent is "a loop that calls a model and runs tools." The actual decomposition includes a codebase graph, a memory subsystem, checkpointing, worktree management, hunk tracking, subagent resolution, token estimation, crash handling and a PTY control layer — before you write a single prompt. ★ The scale check. Simon Willison counted 844,530 lines of Rust in the tree, only ~3% of it vendored dependencies, and noted that OpenAI's Codex sits at roughly 950,933 lines. Two independent teams, converging near a million lines, for "a loop around an LLM." If your agent project feels like it's ballooning, this is the calibration: it is not you, and the hard part was never the loop. There's also a xai-grok-mermaid crate — a terminal renderer that draws Mermaid diagrams with Unicode box-drawing characters. It is not important. It is a nice reminder that shipping polish is a large fraction of any real agent. Última verificación: 2026-07-16. Verified directly against the repository (license, commit count, CONTRIBUTING.md, crate listing). The star count, the enabled/disabled state of the upload path, and the crate list all move; the repo is re-synced from an internal monorepo. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: The crate map is the real lesson

documents.t: This is where the repo stops being a textbook and starts being evidence. In July 2026 a researcher's wire capture showed Grok Build uploading entire repositories — full git history, never-read files, .env contents — to a Google Cloud Storage bucket, through a channel unrelated to what the model read. AILmanac covers that incident and the general failure mode in What your agent uploads. xAI disabled the behavior server-side and said the retained data would be deleted. The published source contains that machinery. Verifiable from the repo directly: crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/upload/gcs.rs exists. crates/codegen/xai-file-utils/src/upload_config.rs defines DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX = "repo_changes_dedup". That constant is the interesting one. The researcher's intercepted upload went to object paths of the form gs://grok-code-session-traces/repo_changes_dedup/v2/…. The path prefix captured on the wire is a named constant in xAI's own published source. The same file defines both ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION (v2) and ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION_V3 — meaning the archive format had been iterated to a third version. This was maintained infrastructure, not a stray debug path. The module documentation in gcs.rs is blunter than any press statement. It refers to the upload helpers as "the data-collector helpers," and the file's entire reason for existing is an engineering fix: threading refresh-aware credentials through so that stale tokens stop causing POST /v1/storage 401s. Someone was debugging the reliability of the repository upload path as production work. Simon Willison reports that the upload path is now disabled in the published tree, returning a hard-coded error. That is consistent with xAI's stated position, and we were not able to independently confirm the specific mechanism by code search — treat it as reported rather than verified here. ★ What to take from this. Not "xAI is uniquely bad" — the wider lesson from the security page stands: this class of channel exists in some form in many agents, and reading the source is the only way to know. Take instead the meta-point: this is what source transparency is actually for. You cannot audit a binary's data flows in an afternoon. You can grep a published tree for bucket_url in about ten seconds. The release is genuinely valuable precisely because it makes the uncomfortable parts greppable. Check yourself 0/4 1xai-org/grok-build is Apache 2.0 licensed. What does that tell you about contributing a fix upstream? You can open a PR like any open-source projectNothing — the license grants usage rights, and CONTRIBUTING.md explicitly refuses external PRsYou must sign a CLA first, then contributeContributions are accepted only from xAI API customers 2The repo has two commits and a root SOURCE_REV file containing one hash. What does that mean? The project is only two days oldThe history was squashed to hide a security bugIt is a periodic export of an internal monorepo; SOURCE_REV points at the internal revision it was cut fromGit history is stored in the crates/ subdirectories 3Roughly how large is the Grok Build harness, and what's the comparable figure for OpenAI's Codex? ~30k lines vs ~40k lines~845k lines of Rust vs ~950k lines~5M lines vs ~6M lines~120k lines vs ~2M lines 4What does the DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX constant in upload_config.rs confirm? That the upload path is currently enabledThat the GCS object-path prefix seen in the researcher's wire capture is a named constant in xAI's own source — maintained infrastructure, not a stray debug pathThat user data was never uploadedThat the bucket is publicly readable
documents.s: The data-collector code is still in the tree

documents.t: Be honest about the constraints before you fork: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Read it for architecture, not for code⌄ The crate boundaries are the product of a well-funded team shipping to real users. That decomposition — tools split from tools-api, workspace from agent, subagent resolution as its own concern — is the transferable asset. Copying Rust out of it buys you far less than copying the shape. ←PreviousNext→ 2Treat the tool implementations as a survey⌄ Willison notes the tool implementations show signs of being adapted from competing products including Codex, Claude and Cursor. That makes the tool layer a convergent-design reference: where three or four agents independently landed on the same tool contract, that contract is probably right. ←PreviousNext→ 3Audit before you trust any agent, including this one⌄ The value of a published tree is that you can check claims instead of believing them. Grep for HTTP clients, bucket URLs, telemetry crates and upload call sites. xai-grok-telemetry and xai-mixpanel are first-class crates here — that is not a scandal, but it is a fact you can only learn by looking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Don't plan on upstreaming anything⌄ No PRs, no issues. If you fork, you own your fork forever, and you rebase against monorepo exports on xAI's schedule. Budget accordingly. ←PreviousNext→ If you want to explore the tree without building it: Clone and map the crate structure CopyOpen in Claude↗ git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build cd grok-build # The inventory of what a production coding agent needs ls crates/codegen/ # Where does data leave the machine? Start here, not with the README. grep -rn "bucket_url\|/v1/storage\|upload_bytes" crates/ --include=*.rs | head -30 # Which internal revision was this cut from? cat SOURCE_REV

If you drive Claude Code, Grok Build is the same category of tool with its guts exposed — read it as a second opinion on problems you already have. Coding agent CLIs compared places it against the field, and Grok for Claude users covers the xAI ecosystem around it. For the architecture ideas the crate map gestures at, see long-running agent harnesses and agent memory architectures — xai-grok-memory and xai-grok-subagent-resolution are one team's answers to exactly those problems. And read What your agent uploads alongside this page. That one shows you how to catch a channel like this on the wire with mitmproxy and a canary repo. This one shows you what it looks like in the source. The two techniques together are the whole audit.

Intermedio On 29 September 2026 the top Claude story on Hacker News was not a launch. It was LiveNerf, a repository whose entire purpose is to answer one question — has Claude Opus 5.5 been nerfed yet? — with 745 points and 306 comments. Seven days after a flagship model ships, the community's most engaged conversation about it is whether it has already been quietly made worse. This question is older than any current model and it never resolves, because almost everyone arguing about it is arguing from memory. The useful version of the question is narrower and answerable: what, specifically, is allowed to change between the model you used last Tuesday and the model you are using now — and how would you know which one moved? What you'll learn Know the one thing that cannot silently change on the Claude API — and why the answer is different on claude.ai Recognise the seven mechanisms that really do change output quality without any new model Understand why the most-cited 'the model got dumber' result was an eval-design bug, not a capability loss Run a measurement that could actually detect a 3-point drop, using a paired design and a control arm Triage a bad day in ten minutes before concluding anything Última verificación: 2026-09-30. Model IDs, pinned-snapshot semantics, effort defaults and the system-prompt policy are from Anthropic's own docs, read on 30 September 2026. LiveNerf's methodology and counts are from its repository README, also read that day — the series was 6 of 30 days collected at the time, so it had not yet produced a verdict. One figure here is second-hand: BridgeBench's NerfBench reportedly put Opus 5.5 at ~99.2% of launch power in late September 2026, but bridgebench.ai blocks automated fetching and that number comes from search-result summaries — treat it as unverified and check the source yourself. Everything in the "what can change" section is mechanism, not news, and should age well; the specific model IDs and effort defaults will not. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Is the model nerfed? How to actually tell

documents.t: Start with the claim that the whole argument depends on: they swapped the weights for a cheaper, quantised version and did not tell anyone. On the Claude API, for the current lineup, this is not a thing that can happen — and the reason is a versioning decision, not a promise about intentions. From Anthropic's models overview: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, including the dateless IDs used from the 4.6 generation on. That sentence is easy to skim past and it is the whole ballgame. Historically claude-opus-4-5 was an alias that resolved to a dated snapshot like claude-opus-4-5-20251101 — aliases move, snapshots do not. From the 4.6 generation onward the dateless ID is itself the snapshot. claude-opus-5-5 is not a pointer to whatever Anthropic is serving this week; it is one frozen artefact with a published retirement date (not sooner than 22 September 2027). So if you are calling the API with a current model ID, "they changed the model" is the one hypothesis you can rule out without measuring anything. Which is useful, because it forces the interesting question: then what did change? Watch out This is a statement about weights, not about serving. A frozen model served through a broken inference stack produces worse output than the same frozen model served correctly — and that has demonstrably happened. See mechanism 4 below.
documents.s: The one thing that cannot change

documents.t: # What moves Where it applies Visible to you? 1 The product system prompt claude.ai, iOS/Android apps — not the API Yes, published 2 Thinking depth (adaptive thinking + effort) API, Claude Code, apps Partly 3 Harness-level model swaps Claude Code, any client with fallbacks Sometimes 4 Serving-stack bugs Everything No — until a postmortem 5 Live incidents Everything Yes, status page 6 Conversation length and compaction Everything Rarely 7 Your own prompts and tasks You Almost never
documents.s: Seven things that change without a new model

documents.t: Anthropic publishes the system prompt that claude.ai and the mobile apps prepend to every conversation, with dated entries per model, and states plainly: This prompt is periodically updated to improve Claude's responses. These system prompt updates do not apply to the Claude API. This is the single most under-appreciated fact in the nerf discourse. The same frozen model can behave measurably differently on claude.ai this week than last week, because the several-thousand-token instruction block in front of your message changed — and none of that reaches an API caller. It also means the two populations arguing with each other on Reddit are often not using the same system at all: one group is on a product surface where the framing moves, the other is on a raw endpoint where it does not. If you want to know whether the app got different, the release notes are the primary source, not your memory.
documents.s: 1. The product system prompt is updated, and the API is not

documents.t: On the current lineup, thinking is adaptive: the model decides how much to think, steered by an effort parameter. This is a real, documented source of run-to-run variance that did not exist in the fixed-budget era. The defaults are also not uniform, and they moved: Model Default effort Thinking Claude Fable 5.1 high Adaptive, always on Claude Opus 5.5 medium Adaptive, always on Claude Sonnet 5.5 high Adaptive Claude Haiku 4.5 not supported Extended Anthropic's own note is that Opus 5.5 at medium is calibrated to match Opus 5 at high. Carry a config forward from an older model without re-reading that and you can land on less thinking than you had before, on a newer and nominally better model, and correctly perceive that "it got lazier." Nothing was nerfed. An enum meant something different. Claude Code adds a wider ladder — low, medium, high, xhigh, max, ultracode — settable per session, per model, and overridable by skill and subagent frontmatter. A skill you installed last month can be quietly capping the effort of every run it touches.
documents.s: 2. Adaptive thinking means the same prompt does not get the same effort

documents.t: This is the mechanism that most often produces a genuine "it got dumber mid-session," and it has nothing to do with the model. Claude Code has three independent swap mechanisms: Usage-limit fallback. Hit the Opus cap and the session continues on Sonnet. Users have filed issues asking for it to stop rather than downgrade, precisely because the drop is felt before it is read. Error fallback chains. --fallback-model sonnet,haiku or a fallbackModel array in settings. It fires on overload and non-retryable server errors — never on auth, billing, rate-limit or request-size errors — and lasts only for the current turn. Content-flagged fallback. Fable, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5 run safety classifiers for cyber and bio content. A flagged message can route to a different model rather than refuse: Opus 5.5 falls back to Opus 5 for bio and to Opus 4.8 for cyber; Sonnet 5.5 falls back to Sonnet 5 for cyber and refuses for bio. Toggle it with switchModelsOnFlag. The third one is the sneaky one. Ask about a security topic and your "Opus 5.5 session" may answer on Opus 4.8. The output is not degraded Opus 5.5. It is undegraded Opus 4.8. The opusplan alias does the same thing by design: Opus for planning, Sonnet for execution. If your perception is "it plans brilliantly and then implements sloppily," check whether you asked for exactly that.
documents.s: 3. Your harness swaps models on you

documents.t: The strongest argument that "it's all placebo" is wrong is that Anthropic wrote the counter-example itself. In September 2025 it published a postmortem on three overlapping infrastructure bugs that degraded output quality for weeks: A context-window routing error (5 Aug – 18 Sept) sent ordinary requests to servers configured for an upcoming 1M-token context. At peak, 16% of Sonnet 4 requests on 31 August were misrouted, and roughly 30% of Claude Code users hit at least one degraded response. Routing was sticky: once a conversation landed on a wrong server, follow-ups tended to land there too — which is exactly the "it's broken for me and fine for you" pattern people are told is imaginary. Output corruption from a TPU misconfiguration (25 Aug – 2 Sept) on Opus 4.1, Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 — including Thai characters appearing mid-English-sentence. An XLA:TPU miscompilation of approximate top-k (25 Aug – 12 Sept), a mixed-precision bug in the compiler that translates JAX to TPU instructions, triggered by a change intended to improve token selection. Three details from that document are worth internalising. First, Anthropic states flatly: "We never reduce model quality due to demand, time of day, or server load" — the specific conspiracy theory is denied, while three unrelated real bugs are admitted. Second, the reason detection took weeks is that the internal evals did not catch it: the benchmarks stayed green while users were right. Third, privacy controls meant engineers could not simply read the bad conversations. That is the honest shape of this problem. Degradation is real, it is usually infrastructure rather than intent, and aggregate benchmarks are bad at seeing it.
documents.s: 4. The serving stack breaks, quietly, for weeks

documents.t: Before theorising, check status.claude.com. On 29 September 2026 — the same day LiveNerf hit the front page — Anthropic opened an incident at 14:21 UTC for elevated error rates across claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and the API, expanded it at 14:30 to "degraded performance," and applied a mitigation at 14:41. A week earlier, on 22 September, errors hit several models including Opus 5, Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1. A meaningful share of "it got worse today" posts are filed during a window that is already publicly acknowledged.
documents.s: 5. There is an incident open right now

documents.t: Every current Claude model advertises a 1M-token context window, and quality is not flat across it. Two compounding effects: Long conversations degrade. Attention over a very long prefix is not free, and instructions given 200 turns ago compete with everything since. Compaction rewrites your history. Server-side compaction summarises earlier context when it nears the trigger threshold. Claude Code compacts too. After a compaction, the model is working from a summary of the thing you remember telling it. It did not forget. The transcript changed. Also worth knowing: the tokenizer introduced with Opus 4.7 changed the exchange rate. 1M tokens is roughly 555k words on the current tokenizer, against about 750k words on the older one. The same document is a larger fraction of your window than it used to be.

The least popular mechanism and the most common. Week one you ask for things you already know the model does well. Week four you ask harder questions, on a larger codebase, with a longer CLAUDE.md, having stopped writing the careful prompts you wrote when it was new. The measured quantity — my satisfaction per session — has two moving inputs and you only instrumented one.

If you have seen one piece of evidence that a model got worse, it is probably this: in How Is ChatGPT's Behavior Changing over Time?, Chen, Zaharia and Zou report that GPT-4's accuracy on "is this number prime? think step by step" fell from 97.6% to 2.4% between March and June 2023. It went everywhere. It is still quoted. Then Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor looked at the test set. Every one of the 500 numbers was prime. The March model almost always answered "prime." The June model almost always answered "composite." Against an all-prime set that is 97.6% versus 2.4% — but it measures a bias flip, not reasoning. When they ran 500 composite numbers, the scores inverted. Neither version was checking factors; both listed the divisors to test and then guessed. The behaviour changed. The capability was the same, and it was never good. Pro tip The distinction to keep. Behaviour drift — different formatting, verbosity, willingness, default guess — is real, common, and a documented side effect of fine-tuning. Capability loss is a much stronger claim and needs much stronger evidence. Almost every viral nerf claim is the first dressed as the second. Three statistical traps sit on top of that, and they apply to your own impressions too: An all-one-answer eval measures bias, not skill. If your personal test set is all "should refuse" or all "should succeed," a shift in the model's default posture looks like a collapse. Selection bias in the evidence. Nobody posts "Opus was fine again today." The feed you are reading is a filter that only passes bad days, and it gets denser as a model gets more popular. Regression to the mean. Your baseline is the launch week you were most impressed in — which, being the extreme of your sample, is the thing an unchanged model is least likely to repeat.
documents.s: The most-cited proof is an eval bug

documents.t: LiveNerf is worth studying less for its verdict than for its methodology, because it is the design a credible answer requires. From the repository (662 stars at time of writing, 6 of 30 days collected): Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Give up on determinism, then freeze everything else⌄ You cannot make these models deterministic — sampling parameters are gone on the current lineup and adaptive thinking cannot be switched off. LiveNerf's answer, in its own framing: make everything else deterministic. Frozen prompts, a pinned CLI version, exact graders, raw logs kept forever. You are not removing noise; you are making sure the noise is the only thing left that can move. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick items in the band where the model is unreliable⌄ 2,336 candidates were screened from GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, competition maths and AIME 2025–26. Opus 5.5 gets roughly 93% of them right first try — so 93% of the pool is useless for detection, because a ceiling cannot show a drop. The panel is the 78 questions the model is only sometimes right on. A question everyone always gets right measures nothing. ←PreviousNext→ 3Compare paired, not pooled⌄ Each run is compared item-by-item against the same items in the launch-week baseline, so question difficulty cancels out instead of becoming a confound. This is what lets a 78-item panel detect anything at all. ←PreviousNext→ 4Run a control arm⌄ The same GPQA questions go through the same harness on Claude Opus 5 — a different model — every day. If both arms move together, the change is in the platform, the harness or the grader, not in Opus 5.5. Without a control you cannot distinguish 'the model changed' from 'my measurement changed'. ←PreviousNext→ 5Pre-register the decision rule before you look⌄ LiveNerf declares a change only when three conditions hold at once: a 99% confidence interval excluding zero across two consecutive 10-day windows, an effect of at least 3 points, and no matching movement in the control arm. Deciding the threshold after seeing the data is how noise becomes a finding. ←PreviousNext→ 6Log enough to reconstruct a disputed run⌄ Full prompts, full responses, token usage, latency, CLI version, harness git SHA, task and item hashes, and the plan usage meters before and after each daily run. Thirty days: ten to establish a baseline, then two 10-day windows. ←PreviousNext→ The shortest version of all six: a single bad session is not evidence, and neither is a single good one.
documents.s: How to measure it — the LiveNerf design

documents.t: You do not need 78 GPQA items. You need your own tasks, which is better — you care about your workload, not about MMLU-Pro. The protocol scales down: Personal nerf-check protocol CopyOpen in Claude↗ 1. Collect 20-30 real prompts from your own work. Keep only the ones you sometimes get a good answer to and sometimes don't. Drop anything that always works (ceiling) or never works (floor). 2. Write a grader you can run without thinking about it. Pass/fail is enough. A human rubric you apply inconsistently is worse than nothing. 3. Pin EVERYTHING that is pinnable: - exact model ID (e.g. claude-opus-5-5, never an alias on an older generation) - effort level, explicitly set - never inherited - one frozen system prompt, byte for byte - no tools, or exactly the same tool list every run - fresh conversation per item; no shared history 4. Baseline: run the whole set 5 times over the first week. Save raw outputs. 5. Re-run the identical set on the same schedule later. Compare item by item against the baseline - not set average to set average. 6. Add a control arm: the same items on a DIFFERENT model, same harness, same day. Both move together => your measurement moved, not the model. 7. Decide in advance what counts: e.g. "a drop of 3+ items, twice in a row, with the control flat." Write it down before you look at the numbers. Two failure modes to avoid. Do not use an alias where the generation still has one — you will be measuring whatever the alias points at. And do not let effort be inherited from a session setting, a skill, or subagent frontmatter, or you are measuring your own config drift.

As of 30 September 2026, the public trackers do not support a nerf of Opus 5.5. LiveNerf had collected 6 of its 30 planned days with no missed runs and therefore had not reached a verdict — by its own pre-registered rule it cannot, before two full 10-day windows. A second tracker, BridgeBench's NerfBench, was reported in late September to place Opus 5.5 at roughly 99.2% of launch power, comfortably inside its normal-variance band — a figure we could not verify at source (see the note above). Two honest conclusions from that. The empirical evidence so far points at "no detectable change," and the honest version of "no detectable change" includes the detection floor: a paired 78-item panel with a 3-point minimum effect can miss a real 1-point drop entirely. No evidence of degradation is not evidence of no degradation — and a rigorous tracker will tell you which one it has.
documents.s: What the trackers have actually found

documents.t: Before you conclude anything, in this order: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Check the status page⌄ status.claude.com. An open incident ends the investigation. On 29 September 2026 the degraded-performance window and the peak of the nerf discussion were the same afternoon. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check which model actually answered⌄ In Claude Code, /model. Look for a usage-limit switch, a fallback chain firing, a content-flag swap, or opusplan doing exactly what it says. The API returns the serving model in the response — read it rather than assume it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Check your effort level⌄ /effort, plus any effortLevel or per-model modelSettings in settings, plus the frontmatter of any skill or subagent in play. A carried-forward config is the most common cause of 'it got lazier' with no other change. ←PreviousNext→ 4Check the conversation length⌄ If compaction has run, the model is reading a summary of your earlier turns. Start a fresh session with the context restated and see whether the problem survives. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-run the exact same prompt three times⌄ Adaptive thinking makes single-sample judgements unreliable by construction. If two of three are fine, you sampled a bad draw, not a worse model. ←PreviousNext→ 6Only now, compare against something you saved⌄ If you kept no artefact from the good period, you are comparing against a memory of the week you were most impressed - the least reproducible sample you have. Start saving outputs today so the next time this happens you can answer it. ←PreviousNext→ girarTérminoPinned snapshotDefiniciónA model ID whose weights never change. On the Claude API every current ID is one, including the dateless IDs from the 4.6 generation onward — claude-opus-5-5 is itself a snapshot, not a pointer. Rules out 'they swapped the weights' for API callers. Older generations used aliases that resolved to dated IDs; aliases can move.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→

Check yourself 0/6 1You call the Claude API with model ID claude-opus-5-5 and output quality drops noticeably over two weeks. Which explanation can you rule out first, without measuring anything? A serving-stack bug degrading responsesThat the weights behind claude-opus-5-5 were swapped for a different versionThat the product system prompt was updatedThat your own prompts got harder 2GPT-4's accuracy on 'is this number prime?' fell from 97.6% to 2.4% between two versions. What did the follow-up analysis find? The June model had been quantised to cut serving costAll 500 test numbers were prime, so the score measured a flip in the model's default guess rather than any reasoning abilityThe evaluation harness had a scoring bug that inverted pass and failThe drop was real and OpenAI later confirmed it 3You are building a personal check for model degradation. Your 30 prompts all get correct answers today. Why is that panel nearly useless? Thirty items is too few for any statistical testItems the model always gets right are at the ceiling and cannot show a drop — you need items it is only sometimes right onPersonal prompts are not comparable to standard benchmarksYou need a matched set of prompts the model always fails 4Mid-session in Claude Code your answers get noticeably weaker right after you ask a security question. Most likely cause? The model was nerfed during your sessionA safety classifier flagged the content and routed the turn to a different, older modelPrompt caching expiredYour context window filled up 5A tracker reports no detectable degradation using a paired 78-item panel with a pre-registered minimum effect of 3 points. What does that license you to say? The model provably did not changeNo change large enough for this design to see has occurred — a smaller real drop would go undetectedThe model improvedNothing, because 78 items is too few to conclude anything 6Why did Anthropic's internal evaluations fail to catch the three August 2025 infrastructure bugs that really did degrade output? The evaluations were not run during that periodThe benchmarks stayed green — they were not sensitive enough to separate a working implementation from a broken one, and privacy controls limited access to the affected conversationsThe bugs only affected third-party platforms, which were not evaluatedThe affected models were not yet in the evaluation suite
