Intermedio Un agente de codificación local es un programa que se ejecuta en tu propia máquina, lee tu repositorio y edita tus archivos por ti. Describes un cambio en lenguaje natural; el agente lo planifica, escribe código a lo largo de varios archivos, ejecuta tus pruebas, lee los fallos y vuelve a intentarlo — un bucle, no una única respuesta. El asistente de chat en una pestaña del navegador te entrega un fragmento para que lo pegues; un agente de codificación hace por sí mismo el pegar, el ejecutar y el corregir, dentro de tu repositorio. La idea clave que hace que valga la pena leer esta página: casi todas estas herramientas son agnósticas respecto al modelo. El agente (el bucle que toca tus archivos) está separado del modelo (el cerebro que decide qué escribir). Así que la misma herramienta se puede apuntar a Claude para la mejor calidad de código, o a un modelo local de pesos abiertos vía Ollama para que tu código nunca salga de tu portátil. Eliges el agente por cómo encaja en tu flujo de trabajo, y el modelo por el compromiso entre calidad y privacidad — de forma independiente. What you'll learn Entender el arquetipo del agente de codificación: un bucle de agente que lee tu repositorio, planifica, edita archivos, ejecuta pruebas e itera Conocer las herramientas abiertas reales — Aider, Cline, Continue, OpenHands — y cómo encaja el propio Claude Code de Anthropic Comprender por qué importa que sea 'agnóstico respecto al modelo': apuntar un mismo agente a Claude para calidad O a un modelo local para privacidad Entender el ángulo de la privacidad — un modelo local significa que tu código nunca sale de tu máquina Elegir a lo largo de dos ejes: integrado en el IDE vs CLI vs autónomo, e impulsado por Claude vs totalmente local
documents.s: Agentes de codificación locales (y cómo se combinan con Claude)

documents.t: Cada herramienta de esta página es una variación del mismo bucle. Una vez que ves el bucle, cada herramienta no es más que una forma distinta a su alrededor: Leer — el agente reúne contexto: los archivos que le indicas, la estructura del repositorio, a veces la salida de las pruebas o los registros de errores. Planificar — decide qué cambiar y en qué archivos, a menudo proponiendo un plan antes de tocar nada. Editar — escribe cambios en archivos reales en disco (normalmente mostrados como un diff que apruebas). Ejecutar — ejecuta comandos: tu suite de pruebas, una compilación, un linter, un script. Observar e iterar — lee lo que ocurrió (¿pasaron las pruebas? ¿un stack trace?) y vuelve al paso 2 hasta que la tarea esté terminada o te devuelva el control. Esta es la misma forma que el uso de herramientas agéntico: al modelo se le dan herramientas (leer archivo, editar archivo, ejecutar comando) y decide cuándo llamarlas. La diferencia entre herramientas está principalmente en cuánta autonomía tiene el bucle y dónde vive — tu terminal, tu editor o un entorno aislado que se ejecuta por su cuenta. El modelo en medio de ese bucle es intercambiable. Esa es la razón entera por la que un único agente puede servir a dos usuarios muy distintos: alguien que quiere el código más potente posible (apúntalo a Claude) y alguien que legalmente no puede dejar que el código salga de su red (apúntalo a un modelo local).
documents.s: El arquetipo: un bucle de agente, no una caja de chat

documents.t: El agente y el modelo son piezas separadas. El agente es dueño del bucle — leer archivos, aplicar diffs, ejecutar pruebas. El modelo es dueño del juicio — qué escribir, por qué y cuándo parar. Desacoplarlos te da dos diales independientes: Dial de calidad → Claude. Para razonamiento difícil, refactorizaciones multi-archivo y trabajo de contexto largo, un modelo de frontera como Claude produce ediciones notablemente mejores y se recupera de los fallos de forma más fiable. La mayoría de estas herramientas documentan a Claude como una opción recomendada o predeterminada. (Qué nivel de Claude elegir es una decisión propia — véase Elegir un modelo.) Dial de privacidad → un modelo local. Apunta el mismo agente a un modelo de pesos abiertos ejecutándose bajo Ollama y tu código, tus prompts y tus diffs nunca salen de tu máquina — ninguna llamada a la API, ningún tercero, nada por el cable. Ese es el factor decisivo para bases de código reguladas, aisladas (air-gapped) o confidenciales. El compromiso honesto: un modelo lo bastante pequeño como para ejecutarse en un portátil no está a la altura de un modelo de frontera en las tareas más difíciles. Estás cambiando algo de capacidad por control total de los datos. What you'll learn Agnóstico respecto al modelo no significa que todos los modelos sean igual de buenos. El bucle se ejecuta igual, pero un modelo débil hace peores ediciones, malinterpreta los fallos de las pruebas e itera de forma improductiva. La privacidad y la capacidad realmente se compensan entre sí — elige por tarea, no una vez para siempre.
documents.s: Por qué ser agnóstico respecto al modelo es la característica estrella

documents.t: Cinco herramientas que vale la pena conocer. Las primeras cuatro son de código abierto y agnósticas respecto al modelo; la quinta es el propio agente de Anthropic, incluido para que puedas ver dónde encaja una experiencia nativa de Claude.

Aider se ejecuta en tu terminal y está construido en torno a git: edita archivos en tu repositorio y confirma automáticamente cada cambio con un mensaje sensato, de modo que cada edición de IA es un diff que puedes revisar, deshacer o revertir. Es agnóstico respecto al modelo — funciona mejor con modelos de frontera como Claude, y también se conecta a modelos locales vía Ollama (aider --model ollama_chat/<model>). Si vives en la terminal y quieres una higiene de git estricta, Aider es la opción canónica de CLI.
documents.s: Aider — el programador de parejas en CLI

documents.t: Cline es un agente de codificación de código abierto que vive en tu editor (VS Code y JetBrains) y también ofrece una superficie de terminal/CLI. Crea archivos, ejecuta comandos y usa herramientas con aprobación humana en el bucle — ves y apruebas cada paso. Es agnóstico respecto al modelo y admite explícitamente Claude además de modelos locales vía Ollama o LM Studio. Recurre a Cline cuando quieras un agente casi autónomo sin salir de tu editor. Roo Code es un fork bien conocido de Cline que añadió "modos" personalizados (p. ej. un modo Architect para planificar, un modo Coder para editar). También era agnóstico respecto al modelo. Ten en cuenta su estado más abajo — la extensión se ha discontinuado desde entonces, así que no empieces una configuración nueva con ella. Última verificación: 2026-09-30. Roo Code está cerrado, no es simplemente volátil. El equipo fue retirando progresivamente la extensión de VS Code en favor de un agente en la nube, y el repositorio RooCodeInc/Roo-Code está ahora archivado y en modo de solo lectura, con su último commit el 15 de mayo de 2026. Trátalo como discontinuado: si quieres un agente al estilo de Cline en tu editor, usa Cline mismo (el proyecto original), que sigue siendo la opción local-first mantenida. Verifica en github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Cline — el agente dentro de tu IDE

documents.t: Continue es un asistente de código abierto para VS Code y JetBrains (además de una CLI) que cubre chat, edición, autocompletado y un modo agente. Es completamente agnóstico respecto al modelo: su documentación enumera Anthropic (Claude), Ollama para modelos locales y muchos otros proveedores, con distintos modelos asignables a distintos roles (chat, edición, autocompletado). Esa configurabilidad es su atractivo — pero el proyecto ha dejado de publicar versiones, así que trátalo como una herramienta que funciona hoy y que mañana no se arreglará. Última verificación: 2026-09-30. Continue ya no se mantiene activamente. Su README indica que el repositorio continuedev/continue «is no longer actively maintained and is read-only for all users», tras una versión final 2.0.0 de la extensión de VS Code, la CLI y el plugin de JetBrains. La herramienta y su soporte para Claude/Ollama siguen funcionando y docs.continue.dev sigue en línea, así que una instalación existente no da problemas — pero no estandarices un equipo con ella esperando correcciones o soporte para modelos nuevos. Ten en cuenta que la propia marca de «archived» de GitHub no está activada en el repositorio, así que no verás el banner de archivo habitual; la declaración de mantenimiento del README es la señal autorizada. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Continue — el asistente de IDE abierto

documents.t: OpenHands (antes OpenDevin) es el más autónomo de los cuatro: una plataforma para agentes de desarrollo de software de IA que trabajan en un entorno aislado (sandbox), descomponen una tarea (p. ej. un issue de GitHub) y la llevan a cabo de principio a fin con menos aprobaciones paso a paso. Es agnóstico respecto al modelo — "úsalo con cualquier LLM", Claude incluido — y puede ejecutarse de forma autoalojada. Elige OpenHands cuando quieras delegar una tarea entera y volver a comprobarla, en lugar de aprobar cada edición. Última verificación: 2026-09-30. OpenHands cambió de nombre desde OpenDevin, y su organización de GitHub cambió de nombre de All-Hands-AI a OpenHands (la antigua ruta All-Hands-AI/OpenHands todavía redirige). La documentación se ha movido con él: la ubicación canónica es ahora docs.openhands.dev, y la antigua docs.all-hands.dev redirige allí. Confirma el repositorio canónico actual y las URL de la documentación en github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Claude Code es la herramienta de codificación agéntica oficial de Anthropic: lee tu base de código, edita archivos, ejecuta comandos y pruebas, y funciona en tu terminal, IDE, aplicación de escritorio y la web. A diferencia de las cuatro anteriores, no es "apúntalo a cualquier modelo" — está construido en torno a Claude y ajustado para él, que es exactamente por lo que el bucle se siente más ajustado y las ediciones aciertan más a menudo en tareas difíciles. Si tu prioridad es la mejor experiencia de codificación impulsada por Claude en lugar de la máxima intercambiabilidad de modelos, este es el camino nativo. Todo el detalle en Qué es Claude Code.
documents.s: Claude Code — el propio agente de Anthropic

documents.t: Dos ejes deciden casi todo: Eje 1 — dónde vive el agente: CLI / terminal (Aider, Claude Code) — programable, amigable con git, encauzable hacia otras herramientas. Mejor si vives en el shell. Integrado en el IDE (Cline, Continue, la superficie de editor de Claude Code) — diffs y aprobaciones dentro de tu editor, con tu código ahí mismo. Mejor para la edición diaria. Autónomo / aislado (OpenHands) — delega una tarea entera y revisa el resultado. Mejor para trabajo por lotes o desatendido. Eje 2 — impulsado por Claude vs totalmente local: Impulsado por Claude — la mejor calidad, especialmente en tareas difíciles multi-archivo o de contexto largo. Tu código se envía a la API del modelo. Elígelo cuando la calidad importe más y tu código pueda enviarse a un proveedor. Totalmente local (Ollama) — tu código nunca sale de la máquina; gratis de ejecutar; funciona sin conexión. Elígelo cuando la privacidad, la regulación o el aislamiento (air-gapping) sean innegociables — aceptando que un modelo del tamaño de un portátil es más débil en las tareas más difíciles. El movimiento duradero: elige el agente por la superficie que encaja en tu flujo de trabajo, luego elige el modelo por tarea. Nada te impide ejecutar un agente de IDE sobre un modelo local para el repositorio confidencial y el mismo agente sobre Claude para todo lo demás.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide la superficie⌄ CLI (Aider, Claude Code), integrado en el IDE (Cline, Continue) o autónomo (OpenHands). Ajústalo a donde ya trabajas — terminal vs editor vs delegar-y-revisar. ←PreviousNext→ 2Decide el dial del modelo⌄ Claude para la mejor calidad (el código se envía a la API) o un modelo local de Ollama para privacidad total (el código nunca sale de la máquina). Esto es independiente del agente para todas las herramientas salvo Claude Code, que es nativo de Claude. ←PreviousNext→ 3Instala el agente⌄ Sigue la documentación de la herramienta. Aider se instala vía pip; Cline y Continue se instalan desde el marketplace de VS Code o JetBrains; OpenHands se autoaloja; Claude Code se instala mediante su instalador oficial. ←PreviousNext→ 4Conecta el modelo⌄ Para Claude, configura tu clave de API de Anthropic (o inicia sesión para Claude Code). Para local, instala Ollama y descarga un modelo primero — véase Ejecutar modelos localmente con Ollama — y luego apunta el agente hacia él. ←PreviousNext→ 5Empieza pequeño y mantén humanos en el bucle⌄ Ejecuta una tarea acotada (arreglar una prueba que falla, añadir una función pequeña). Revisa cada diff antes de aprobar. Confía más en la autonomía solo después de haber visto el bucle comportarse en tu repositorio. ←PreviousNext→ Una primera ejecución concreta con Aider apuntado a un modelo local (privado, gratis, sin conexión) — descarga primero el modelo con Ollama, luego: Ejecutar Aider sobre un modelo local de Ollama (el código se queda en tu máquina) CopyOpen in Claude↗ aider --model ollama_chat/qwen3 Para apuntar la misma herramienta a Claude en su lugar (la mejor calidad, el código enviado a la API), configuras tu clave de Anthropic y seleccionas un modelo Claude — el bucle del agente es idéntico; solo cambia el cerebro: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... aider --model sonnet Ese intercambio — una bandera, dos perfiles de privacidad/calidad completamente distintos, el mismo agente — es el propósito entero de esta página. Compruébate a ti mismo 0/4 1¿Qué significa 'agnóstico respecto al modelo' para un agente de codificación como Aider o Cline? Funciona sin ningún modelo en absolutoEl mismo bucle de agente puede apuntarse a distintos modelos — p. ej. Claude para calidad o un modelo local para privacidadSolo funciona con modelos de código abierto 2Tu base de código legalmente no puede salir de tu red. ¿Qué configuración encaja? Cualquiera de estos agentes apuntado a la API de ClaudeUn agente de codificación apuntado a un modelo local de pesos abiertos vía OllamaEs imposible usar un agente de codificación en absoluto 3¿En qué se diferencia Claude Code de Aider, Cline, Continue y OpenHands? No puede editar archivosEs el propio agente de Anthropic, construido en torno a Claude en lugar de ser apúntalo-a-cualquier-modeloSolo se ejecuta en la nube 4¿Qué herramienta es la más autónoma — construida para tomar una tarea entera y ejecutarla en un sandbox con menos aprobaciones paso a paso? AiderContinueOpenHands girarTérminoAgente de codificación localDefiniciónUn programa que se ejecuta en tu máquina, lee tu repositorio y edita tus archivos en un bucle: leer → planificar → editar → ejecutar pruebas → iterar. No es una caja de chat — hace la edición y la ejecución por sí mismo.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→ Key takeaways Un agente de codificación ejecuta un bucle en tu máquina — leer el repositorio, planificar, editar archivos, ejecutar pruebas, iterar — en lugar de entregarte fragmentos para pegar. Casi todas estas herramientas son agnósticas respecto al modelo: el agente y el modelo están separados, así que intercambias el cerebro sin cambiar el bucle. Dos diales: Claude para la mejor calidad de código, o un modelo local de pesos abiertos vía Ollama para privacidad total — tu código nunca sale de la máquina. Aider = CLI/git; Cline = agente en tu IDE; Continue = asistente de IDE configurable, ahora sin mantenimiento; OpenHands = autónomo/aislado; Claude Code = el propio agente nativo de Claude de Anthropic. Elige a lo largo de dos ejes — dónde vive el agente (CLI vs IDE vs autónomo) e impulsado por Claude vs totalmente local — y elige el modelo por tarea, no una vez para siempre.

Intermedio Estás construyendo un agente. La primera bifurcación real del camino: ¿funciona sobre un modelo de pesos abiertos totalmente local (privado, gratis de ejecutar, tuyo), sobre Claude (calidad de frontera, alojado), o sobre un híbrido de ambos? Esta página es un marco de decisión — los factores que realmente lo deciden, un flujo claro de "si X → inclínate por Y", y la realidad honesta de que el híbrido suele ganar: local para el 90% fácil/sensible, Claude para el 10% difícil. What you'll learn Nombrar los factores que realmente deciden entre local, Claude e híbrido Recorrer un flujo de decisión claro de 'si X → inclínate por Y' para tu agente Entender por qué un híbrido (local por defecto + escalada a Claude) suele superar a cualquiera de los extremos Salir con una evaluación diminuta como desempate — no con una tabla de clasificación Última verificación: 2026-06-28. Las afirmaciones duraderas aquí — existe una brecha de capacidad entre los mejores modelos de pesos abiertos y los de frontera, pero se sigue estrechando, y el enrutamiento/cascada (modelo barato primero, escalar en lo difícil) ahorra coste manteniendo la calidad — son estables. Pero las cifras específicas (cuán grande es la brecha este mes, qué modelo abierto lidera, precios de Claude por token, tokens/seg exactos en un hardware dado) cambian constantemente. Trata cualquier cifra específica como perecedera y consulta un rastreador en vivo como Artificial Analysis antes de apostar por ella. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: ¿Agente local o Claude? Una guía de decisión

documents.t: Agente totalmente local — un modelo de pesos abiertos (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, etc.) ejecutándose en tu propio hardware vía Ollama/LM Studio/vLLM. Los datos nunca salen de tu máquina; ningún coste por llamada; funciona sin conexión; limitado por tu hardware y el techo del modelo. → Agentes de IA locales Agente con Claude — llama a la API de Claude. Razonamiento y uso de herramientas de frontera, sin infraestructura que cuidar, escala al instante; pero los datos salen de tu red, pagas por llamada y necesitas conectividad. Híbrido — un modelo local gestiona el grueso rutinario/sensible; los pasos difíciles o de alto riesgo escalan a Claude. El patrón hacia el que convergen la mayoría de los agentes en producción. → Claude + modelos locales
documents.s: Las tres opciones, en un suspiro

documents.t: Pasa tu agente por estos. La mayoría de las decisiones se resuelven solo con los dos o tres primeros. Factor Se inclina hacia local cuando… Se inclina hacia Claude cuando… Sensibilidad de los datos / privacidad Los datos están regulados o no pueden salir de tu red Los datos no son sensibles o tienes un acuerdo de datos conforme Dificultad de la tarea y profundidad de razonamiento Las tareas son acotadas, bien definidas, repetitivas Las tareas requieren razonamiento profundo de varios pasos, contexto largo, uso complicado de herramientas Necesidades de fiabilidad Un reintento o una persona basta ante un fallo Cada paso debe ser correcto; los fallos son costosos Latencia El hardware local responde con suficiente rapidez Prefieres pagar por velocidad que aprovisionar GPUs Coste a tu volumen Volumen alto y constante — el hardware fijo se amortiza Volumen bajo/irregular — el pago por llamada supera a las GPUs ociosas Requisito de funcionar sin conexión Debe funcionar aislado / sin conectividad Estar siempre en línea está bien Hardware del que dispones Tienes GPU(s) capaces / memoria unificada No lo tienes y no quieres comprarlo/alquilarlo Presupuesto de mantenimiento Puedes ajustar, cuantizar, evaluar y mantenerlo Quieres que "simplemente funcione" sin operaciones Los dos que suelen decidirlo: si los datos no pueden salir de tu red, eso por sí solo te empuja hacia local (o hacia un despliegue privado) independientemente de todo lo demás. Si pueden, entonces la dificultad de la tarea es el siguiente factor determinante — el trabajo fácil es barato de hacer localmente; el razonamiento difícil es donde la brecha de frontera todavía muerde. What you'll learn La brecha de capacidad entre pesos abiertos y frontera es real, pero se estrecha rápido — los mejores modelos abiertos son excelentes en tareas rutinarias y en muchas de programación, y todavía quedan por detrás de la mayoría en el trabajo agéntico más difícil, de horizonte largo y de razonamiento profundo. Esa asimetría es precisamente lo que hace potente al híbrido: envía la mayoría fácil/sensible a local y reserva Claude para la porción que genuinamente necesita razonamiento de frontera.
documents.s: Los factores que realmente lo deciden

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1¿Pueden los datos salir de tu red?⌄ Si NO → local (o un despliegue privado/VPC) es tu punto de partida. La privacidad es una restricción dura, no una preferencia — domina a los demás factores. Si SÍ → continúa por el flujo. ←PreviousNext→ 2¿Cuán difícil es lo más difícil que tu agente debe hacer?⌄ Si toda tarea es acotada y repetitiva → un buen modelo local probablemente supera el listón; inclínate por local. Si algunos pasos necesitan razonamiento profundo, contexto largo, o una orquestación delicada de varias herramientas → inclínate por Claude al menos para esos pasos. ←PreviousNext→ 3¿Cuán costosa es una respuesta equivocada?⌄ Si un fallo solo significa un reintento o un vistazo humano → las tolerancias locales están bien. Si un único paso malo es caro o inseguro → favorece la fiabilidad de Claude donde importa. ←PreviousNext→ 4¿Cuál es tu volumen y hardware?⌄ Volumen alto y constante sobre hardware que ya posees → local se amortiza de maravilla. Volumen bajo o irregular, sin GPUs → el pago por llamada de Claude evita el hierro ocioso. ←PreviousNext→ 5¿Realmente quieres operar infraestructura?⌄ Dispuesto a cuantizar, servir, monitorizar y reevaluar modelos → local/híbrido es viable. Quieres cero operaciones → Claude, o un híbrido donde la parte local sea sencillísima. ←PreviousNext→ 6Por defecto híbrido, y luego demuestra que no lo necesitas⌄ Modelo local como trabajador por defecto; Claude como vía de escalada para la porción difícil/de alto riesgo. Empieza aquí salvo que el paso 1 fuerce puro-local o la tarea sea uniformemente difícil (entonces puro-Claude). ←PreviousNext→

La mayoría de las cargas de trabajo reales son desequilibradas: una gran mayoría de las peticiones son fáciles y/o sensibles, y una pequeña minoría son genuinamente difíciles. Un híbrido explota esa forma directamente. Local gestiona el 90% fácil/sensible — rápido, gratis al margen, privado, capaz de funcionar sin conexión. El grueso de tu tráfico nunca toca una API. Claude gestiona el 10% difícil — el razonamiento de varios pasos, los casos límite ambiguos, los pasos donde acertar importa. Pagas precios de frontera solo por la porción que necesita calidad de frontera. Este es el patrón de cascada / enrutamiento: prueba primero el modelo barato (local); escala a Claude cuando una señal de calidad diga que la respuesta local no es lo bastante buena, o enruta de entrada mediante un clasificador de dificultad/sensibilidad. Es una forma bien establecida de conservar la mayor parte de la calidad pagando una fracción del coste de todo-frontera — y funciona además como frontera de privacidad, ya que los casos sensibles pueden fijarse a "solo local". Autocomprobación antes de comprometerte con un extremo CopyOpen in Claude↗ Answer for YOUR agent: 1. Must any data stay on my machine? (yes -> local baseline) 2. What % of tasks are genuinely HARD? (high -> Claude leans heavier) 3. What's a wrong answer cost me? (high -> Claude on those steps) 4. My volume + hardware? (high+own GPU -> local amortizes) 5. Can I babysit infra? (no -> Claude or simple hybrid) If answers conflict -> you've just described a HYBRID. Now build the tiny eval below and let DATA pick the split. La advertencia honesta: el híbrido tiene más piezas móviles — dos rutas de modelo, un enrutador y una señal de calidad que mantener. Si tu agente es uniformemente simple o uniformemente difícil, una configuración de un solo modelo es más sencilla y probablemente la correcta. Recurre al híbrido cuando tu carga de trabajo sea genuinamente desequilibrada. Privado, sin coste por llamada, capaz de funcionar sin conexión; limitado por tu hardware y el techo del modelo.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 5 Siguiente→ Ponte a prueba 0/3 1Tu agente procesa datos que legalmente no pueden salir de tu red. ¿Qué implica eso primero? Usar Claude — es de mayor calidadUn despliegue totalmente local o privado es el punto de partida, independientemente de otros factoresElegir el que sea más barato por token 2¿Por qué un agente híbrido suele ganar en una carga de trabajo típica y desequilibrada? Los modelos de frontera siempre son más baratos a escalaLocal gestiona la mayoría fácil/sensible de forma barata y privada; Claude se reserva para la minoría difícil que necesita razonamiento de fronteraElimina la necesidad de cualquier evaluación 3¿Cuándo es una configuración de un solo modelo (puro-local O puro-Claude) mejor opción que el híbrido? Siempre — el híbrido nunca vale la penaCuando la carga de trabajo es uniformemente simple o uniformemente difícil, de modo que la maquinaria extra de enrutador y señal de calidad no se gana su sustentoSolo cuando no tienes GPUs
documents.s: Por qué el híbrido suele ganar

documents.t: Cada factor anterior estrecha el campo; una evaluación diminuta elige al ganador. No elijas por intuición ni por una tabla de clasificación pública. Recopila de 10 a 50 casos reales de tu carga de trabajo real, con respuestas conocidas como buenas (incluye tus casos más difíciles y más sensibles). Ejecuta tu lista corta — un modelo local candidato, Claude y (si procede) un enrutador híbrido — sobre los mismos casos. Puntúa la calidad, luego sopesa el coste y la latencia a tu volumen real. Una mejora de calidad del 2% que cuesta 10× puede no valer la pena; una mejora del 2% en el paso que debe ser correcto puede ser innegociable. Para un híbrido, la evaluación también te dice dónde trazar la línea — qué se escala a Claude y qué se queda en local. Conserva la evaluación. Cuando aparezca un nuevo modelo de pesos abiertos o cambien los precios, volver a ejecutarla convierte una migración angustiosa en una comprobación de cinco minutos. → Evaluaciones Key takeaways Decide en orden: primero la sensibilidad de los datos (¿pueden salir de la red?), luego la dificultad de la tarea (¿cuán difícil es el paso más difícil?). El resto — latencia, volumen, hardware, presupuesto de mantenimiento — son desempates. Puro-local gana en privacidad, funcionamiento sin conexión y coste a volumen alto y constante; Claude gana en el razonamiento más difícil, la fiabilidad y la escala sin operaciones. El híbrido suele ganar en cargas de trabajo desequilibradas: local para el 90% fácil/sensible, Claude para el 10% difícil — en cascada/enrutando y pagando precios de frontera solo donde se los ganan. La brecha de los pesos abiertos es real pero se estrecha — que es precisamente lo que hace al híbrido tan eficaz hoy. No decidas por intuición: construye una evaluación diminuta sobre TUS datos, sopesa el coste y la latencia a TU volumen, y consérvala para el próximo lanzamiento de modelo.

documents.t: Artificial Analysis — comparaciones independientes y actualizadas con frecuencia de capacidad/precio/velocidad entre modelos abiertos y de frontera (el lugar para volver a comprobar los detalles perecederos). Anthropic — Resumen de modelos — la gama actual de Claude, contexto y capacidades. Anthropic — Precios de la API — costes actuales por token para dimensionar tus cálculos a volumen. Ollama · LM Studio — ejecuta modelos de pesos abiertos localmente para la vía local/híbrida. Meta — Llama · Mistral — Modelos — familias de pesos abiertos usadas comúnmente en agentes locales.

Intermedio On September 22, 2026, Xiaomi published MiMo-V2.6 — three checkpoints on Hugging Face under a plain MIT license, headlined by a 1.02-trillion-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context that takes text, image, video and audio as input. It landed the same day as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna, and it went straight to the top of Hacker News. The headline write-ups all say roughly the same thing: frontier-class open weights, twenty to sixty times cheaper than closed models. That part is true and easy to check. What nobody has written up is the part that decides whether you should actually use it — which benchmark versions the wins came from, why the flagship is not a machine you own, and what the third price tier is for. What you'll learn Read the MiMo-V2.6 benchmark table the way its own model card reports it — including the 14-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 deficit the press coverage did not quote Know why a 33-point generational jump on an agentic benchmark usually means the old model could not drive the harness, not that the new one got smarter Understand the architecture that buys the 1M context: 384 experts with 8 active, and a 6:1 sliding-window-to-global attention ratio Pick between Pro, Flash and the 9B distill by what hardware you actually have — Pro's own launch command wants two nodes See what the 10x-priced UltraSpeed tier sells you (latency, from the same weights) and when that is worth paying for Última verificación: 2026-09-23. Architecture, license, benchmark scores and serving commands here are read from the Hugging Face model card published at launch. Hosted pricing is as reported by launch coverage of the OpenRouter and Xiaomi AI Studio listings; per-token prices move faster than anything else on this page — check the live listing before you budget against it. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

MiMo-V2.6-Pro is an MIT-licensed, 1.02T-total / 42B-active sparse MoE with a 1M-token context and text, image, video and audio input that ties or beats Claude Opus 5 on short-horizon agentic and automation benchmarks, trails it badly on long-horizon terminal work, and costs roughly one-tenth as much per token when you rent it instead of running it.

This is the one to internalise. Launch coverage widely reported MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 89.9 on Terminal Bench 2.1, just ahead of Claude Opus 5's 89.1. Xiaomi's own model card does not report Terminal Bench 2.1 at all. It reports Terminal Bench 4.0, where MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 34.9 against Opus 5's 49.0 — a 14.1-point deficit. Both numbers are real. Terminal Bench 2.1 is an older, largely saturated harness where every frontier model clusters near 90 and a 0.8-point gap is noise. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the current one, and it is where models are still spread out. If you read "beats Claude on Terminal Bench" anywhere, the first question is always which version — because on agentic suites the version change is usually a bigger effect than the model change. The same pattern shows up in AILmanac's coverage of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash: parity on DeepSWE, a 15–20 point hole on Terminal-Bench 4.0. It is becoming the signature shape of the cheap tier.
documents.s: 1. The Terminal-Bench win and the Terminal-Bench loss are the same model

documents.t: The model card's own table includes the previous generation. MiMo-V2.5-Pro scored 19.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 1.5 on Terminal Bench 4.0. V2.6-Pro scores 71.9 and 34.9. A model does not get 23× better at terminal work in one generation. A score of 1.5 means the old model essentially could not complete the benchmark's tool-call protocol — it was failing at the harness, not at the reasoning. Read enormous generational deltas on agentic benchmarks as "we fixed tool calling" first, and only then as capability. The deltas on non-agentic benchmarks are the honest ones: ProgramBench went 12.5 → 26.5, roughly a doubling, which is a large but believable generational step.
documents.s: 2. A 33-point generational jump is a harness story, not an intelligence story

documents.t: MiMo-V2.6-Pro's LLM backbone is 70 layers: 60 sliding-window attention, 10 global attention — a 6:1 ratio. Sliding-window layers only keep a local KV window, so the per-token KV footprint at 1M tokens is a fraction of what a fully global 70-layer stack would need. The ten global layers are what still let information travel end to end. The MoE is 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, giving 42B active out of 1.02T — about 4.1% of the model runs on any given token. Flash uses the same shape at 309–311B total and ~15B active. This is why a trillion-parameter model can be served at all: you pay 1T in memory and 42B in compute. On top of that sits a 5-layer multi-token-prediction speculative decoder that drafts 7 tokens per pass. That is a throughput mechanism, and it matters for the next point.
documents.s: 3. The 1M context is bought with attention layout, not brute force

documents.t: Two things the marketing language blurs: Modalities are input-side. The card lists text, image, video and audio as modalities, with a 681M-parameter MiMo ViT vision encoder and a 308M AudioTokenizer plus a 127M audio patch encoder. The Hugging Face pipeline tag for Pro is text generation. You can feed it a video and ask questions; it answers in text. It is not a speech or image generator. If you want generation across media, that is a different page: generative media. UltraSpeed is the same model at 10× the price. MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed is described as Pro quality at up to 20× the output speed, listed at roughly ten times Pro's per-token price. There is no separate set of weights on Hugging Face for it — it is a serving tier built on the speculative decoder and Xiaomi's infrastructure. That is a perfectly reasonable product, but price it as what it is: you are buying tokens-per-second for interactive and real-time workloads, not accuracy. If your job is a background batch, UltraSpeed is a 10× overpay.
documents.s: 4. "Omnimodal" means omnimodal in, and UltraSpeed sells latency, not quality

documents.t: All figures below are Xiaomi's own runs, from the MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL model card. No independent replication existed at the time of writing. Benchmark MiMo-V2.6 Pro MiMo-V2.6 Flash MiMo-V2.5 Pro Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol Claude Fable 5 DeepSWE v1.1 71.9 67.9 19.0 74.0 73.0 70.0 ProgramBench 26.5 26.0 12.5 37.0 25.0 33.0 MiMo Code Bench 63.2 61.2 40.4 68.6 59.3 — AutomationBench v1.0.6 53.1 52.3 16.0 50.3 45.8 46.2 Toolathlon-Verified 76.9 73.6 49.1 80.6 74.9 77.9 Terminal Bench 4.0 34.9 28.8 1.5 49.0 39.9 42.4 OSWorld-Verified 82.0 80.8 — 83.4 83.0 86.0 CyberGym 94.0 95.1 40.0 — — — MiMo VisualCoding 72.3 71.5 — 70.0 73.4 69.1 Three readings worth having: Flash is within a few points of Pro almost everywhere. 67.9 vs 71.9 on DeepSWE, 52.3 vs 53.1 on AutomationBench, and it beats Pro on CyberGym. At roughly a third of Pro's hosted price and a third of the parameters, Flash is the default unless you have measured a reason otherwise. The competitor columns for CyberGym are empty. Xiaomi reported 94.0 and 95.1 and published no Claude or GPT comparison. Treat an unopposed number as unopposed — it tells you the model is competent at the task, not that it leads. Pro wins exactly one row outright: AutomationBench. Everything else is a near-tie or a loss. "Frontier-class open weights" is fair; "beats Claude" is not. On the aggregate side, Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index v4.3 placed MiMo-V2.6-Pro at roughly 46, reported as first among open-weight models and level with Grok 4.7, against about 53 for the closed frontier. A seven-point index gap for a tenth of the price is the actual pitch.
documents.s: The benchmark table, as the vendor published it

documents.t: Rented, as reported at launch from the OpenRouter and Xiaomi listings, per million tokens: Model Input Output MiMo-V2.6-Flash $0.14 $0.28 MiMo-V2.6-Pro $0.435 $0.87 MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed $4.35 $8.70 For scale, Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4 / $20 (see the Opus 5.5 field guide). Pro is roughly 9× cheaper on input and 23× cheaper on output. UltraSpeed costs about the same as Opus 5.5 on input and less than half on output — which is the honest way to think about that tier. Owned is a different conversation, and the launch commands give it away. The model card's SGLang example for Pro asks for --tp 16 --dp 2 ... --nnodes 2: tensor parallelism across sixteen devices, two data-parallel replicas, two nodes. That is a rack, not a workstation. The vLLM path is lighter at --tensor-parallel-size 8, still eight accelerators for a 1.02T checkpoint in BF16. Flash, at ~309–311B total and ~15B active, is the variant that a serious single-node box can plausibly serve. The MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B checkpoint — a 9B distillation, listed on Hugging Face under image-text-to-text — is the one that fits on a laptop-class GPU. If your goal is "run a capable open model at home", start there and at Run models locally with Ollama, not at Pro. One more ownership caveat: the repositories published are the post-RL checkpoints (-Pro-RL, -Flash-RL). No base checkpoint was released. You can serve, quantise and adapt these, but you cannot start your own post-training from the pre-RL base.
documents.s: What it costs, rented and owned

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide input-side first⌄ If your workload never sends an image, video or audio clip, most of what makes MiMo-V2.6 distinctive is irrelevant to you and a cheaper text-only open model may match it. The omnimodal encoders are the differentiator — use them or discount them. ←PreviousNext→ 2Start on Flash, not Pro⌄ Flash is within a few points of Pro on every published row and ahead on one, at roughly a third of the price. Run your real workload on Flash first. Only escalate to Pro if you can measure the gap on your own task. ←PreviousNext→ 3Re-run the benchmark that matches your shape of work⌄ Short, bounded, tool-using tasks (AutomationBench, Toolathlon) are where MiMo is strong. Long autonomous terminal sessions (Terminal Bench 4.0) are where it is 14 points behind. Build a 20-task private eval in the shape you actually ship, and score it yourself. ←PreviousNext→ 4Test the 1M context at your real length⌄ Sixty of seventy layers are sliding-window. Long-range retrieval rides on ten global layers. Run needle-in-a-haystack and multi-hop retrieval at the context length you will really use before you trust the ceiling. ←PreviousNext→ 5Price the tier, not the model⌄ Flash, Pro and Pro-UltraSpeed are a 1x / 3x / 31x price ladder over the same family. Decide whether you are buying accuracy (Flash to Pro) or latency (Pro to UltraSpeed) — they are different purchases. ←PreviousNext→ Call MiMo-V2.6-Flash through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the failure modes in this log and propose one fix."} ] }' Serve MiMo-V2.6-Pro with vLLM (the model card's own launch line) CopyOpen in Claude↗ vllm serve XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --max-model-len auto \ --reasoning-parser mimo \ --tool-call-parser mimo \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --generation-config vllm Pro tip Note the two parser flags: --reasoning-parser mimo and --tool-call-parser mimo. MiMo emits its reasoning and tool calls in a family-specific format. Omit these and your serving stack will hand the raw markers back to your application as ordinary text — a silent failure that looks like the model ignoring your tools. --trust-remote-code is required because the modelling code ships with the checkpoint. Read it before you run it on anything you care about; that flag executes vendor Python in your serving process. The SGLang path adds EAGLE speculative-decoding flags. That is where the throughput advantage lives — a vanilla launch leaves the multi-token predictor unused.
documents.s: How to evaluate it for your own work

documents.t: Good fit High-volume classification, extraction or automation over mixed media, where $0.14/M input changes what is economically possible at all. Anything you must run on your own hardware for privacy or jurisdiction reasons and that needs vision or audio understanding — few MIT-licensed models offer that combination. See a private local AI stack. Short, bounded agentic tasks with well-specified tools, which is where AutomationBench and Toolathlon scores say it is genuinely competitive. Poor fit Long autonomous coding sessions. The Terminal Bench 4.0 gap is 14 points against Opus 5 and 5 points against GPT-5.6 Sol, and it is the vendor's own number. Anywhere you need a base checkpoint to post-train from. Only RL checkpoints shipped. Single-box self-hosting of Pro. Budget for Flash or the 9B distill, or rent Pro.
documents.s: When to reach for it, and when not

documents.t: Worth noting because it is unusually specific: Xiaomi published the RL training run's shape and cost — roughly a six-day run, 30 RL steps, about 750,000 trajectories, 1,568 prompts with 16 rollouts per step, at a reported ~$2.62M for Pro and ~$850K for Flash, using asynchronous GRPO with the MoE router frozen during RL. Two things to take from it. First, a frozen router during reinforcement learning is a stability choice: it keeps expert assignment fixed so the policy update cannot quietly reshape which experts fire. Second, and more useful: a frontier-adjacent post-training run now costs single-digit millions, not hundreds. That is the number that explains why four labs shipped in the same week. Check yourself 0/5 1Press coverage said MiMo-V2.6-Pro beat Claude Opus 5 on Terminal Bench; the model card shows it 14 points behind. What explains the contradiction? The press used a different model variantThe two figures are from different Terminal Bench versions — 2.1 (saturated, near-90 scores) versus 4.0 (current, spread out)The press quoted Flash, not ProOne of the two numbers is fabricated 2MiMo-V2.5-Pro scored 1.5 on Terminal Bench 4.0; V2.6-Pro scores 34.9. What is the most likely reading? The new model is roughly 23 times more intelligentThe benchmark was made easier between runsThe previous generation largely could not drive the benchmark's tool-call protocol, so the jump is mostly harness compatibilityThe old score was a typo 3What does the MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed tier actually sell at roughly 10x Pro's price? A larger model with higher accuracyA longer context windowThroughput and latency from the same quality, built on the speculative decoder and Xiaomi's serving stackAccess to the base checkpoint 4Why does MiMo-V2.6-Pro's 1M-token context not require a proportionally enormous KV cache? It compresses the context into a summary60 of its 70 backbone layers use sliding-window attention, so only 10 global layers hold full-range KVIt offloads the KV cache to disk by defaultIt only attends to the most recent 128K tokens 5You want to run a capable open-weight model with vision on one workstation GPU. Which MiMo-V2.6 checkpoint is the realistic starting point? MiMo-V2.6-Pro beats Opus 5 on Terminal Bench 2.1 and trails it by 14 points on 4.0 — same model, same vendor, opposite headline. Flash, not Pro, is the default. Within a few points on every published row, ahead on CyberGym, roughly a third of the price, and actually servable on one node. Omnimodal is input-side. Video and audio go in, text comes out. If you never send media, a cheaper text-only open model may do the same job. UltraSpeed is a latency product at 10x the price of identical quality. Buy it for interactive work; never for a batch. Intermedio On August 3, 2026 MiniMax pushed the weights of MiniMax-H3 (consumer name: Hailuo 3.0) to Hugging Face — a 33-billion-parameter, single-stream Transformer that turns text, images, video and audio references into 4–15 second clips at up to 2K/24fps with native stereo audio, all generated in one pass. That last part is the interesting one: there is no separate TTS stage, no bolted-on SFX pipeline. Dialogue, room tone and picture come out together, from the same model. Three days earlier the paid API had opened at $0.1625/second for 2K (~$9.75/minute of video), roughly half the cost of Kling 3.0 or Seedance 2.0 at comparable resolution. On the Artificial Analysis leaderboards single-run scores put H3 #1 in video editing with audio, top-three in text-to-video and image-to-video. That combination — frontier-tier video quality, open weights, and honest sub-$10/minute pricing — is what put H3 on every generative-media feed this week. This page is what most other write-ups miss: the parts that determine whether H3 is actually useful to you. What you'll learn Understand the H3 architecture — single-stream Transformer, H3-VAE, MM-RoPE — and why it produces video and audio in one forward pass Know the three self-hosting gotchas nobody puts on the landing page: the geo-restricted license, the 768p ceiling on the open base, and the AdaLN parameter-skip trick Get a working self-hosted path: minimum 42.5 GB of weights, quantization choices, and how a 12 GB card runs it with offloading Try H3 from the API with a real cURL you can copy, and know the input-shape limits (12 files max, ≤64 MB body, public URLs only) Pick between H3 and the closed alternatives (Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, Veo, Sora) with clear tie-breakers on price, control and licensing Última verificación: 2026-08-08. Video-model prices, license terms and quantized checkpoints churn weekly in this space. Anything with a dollar sign, a GB count or a benchmark rank on this page is a snapshot — re-check the official model card and the vendor's pricing page before you commit. The architecture facts (33B / single-stream / MM-RoPE / native audio) are the durable part. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

documents.t: The Hugging Face model card links a MiniMax H3 Community License Agreement whose text is application-gated for four regions: the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea. In practice that means: if you or your organisation is in any of those places and you want to run H3 on your own hardware (or serve it to your users), you need to complete the H3 licence application at platform.minimax.io/h3-license first. The restriction extends to outputs, not just the weights — a detail most reblog posts skip. If you are outside those regions the standard Community License applies. If you are in them, treat the API as your default path until your application clears, or use the license reviewer at your org before shipping anything that touches the weights. This is a real, enforceable restriction — not the usual "please don't do bad things" clause.
documents.s: 1. The Community License blocks self-hosting in the US, EU, UK and South Korea

documents.t: Every "up to 2K" headline about H3 elides a key detail: the open-weight base models (Base FL2VA for text-to-video / first-last-frame, Base Ref2VA for multi-reference) generate at 768p. The 2K output people are marveling at on the Hailuo app comes from H3-Regenerate-2K, an in-context upsampler that runs after the base model and that MiniMax has not open-sourced. H3-Context-IR, the multimodal instruction preprocessor, is also API-only. The consequence for self-hosters is simple: you get the same generation quality the frontier system is built on, but you top out at 768p unless you chain your own upscaler (Topaz, ESRGAN, a diffusion upsampler) after the fact. This is fine for many use cases — 768p at 24fps is more than enough for social clips, storyboards, and rapid iteration — but it's not the same product as the paid tier.
documents.s: 2. The open base tops out at 768p — 2K only exists inside the API

documents.t: The model card breaks the H3-Omni-Transformer down as a 33 B dense single-stream Transformer of which roughly 13 B parameters live in AdaLN-related branches. AdaLN (Adaptive Layer Norm) is how diffusion-style transformers absorb conditioning signals (timestep, class, text embedding) — and its outputs, per conditioning slot, are precomputable. That's how third-party providers hit a minimum 42.5 GB working configuration even though naive BF16 weights are much larger: they combine a pruned INT8 checkpoint (~20 GB) with an NVFP4 AWQ text encoder (~16 GB) and both VAEs (~5.8 GB), and skip the cached-branch weights at inference time. The rule of thumb from the ComfyUI ecosystem: a 12 GB card can run H3 with CPU/RAM offloading, at the cost of longer render times per clip. If you have 24 GB or more, offload isn't needed.
documents.s: 3. About 13 B of the 33 B parameters are AdaLN branches you can precompute and skip

documents.t: H3 is a single-stream, modality-agnostic Transformer. There is one attention stack, one FFN stack, and video/audio/text tokens all pass through it. The four components you actually load are: Component Role Open-sourced? H3-Omni-Transformer 33 B dense generator (video + audio) ✅ (BF16, INT8, pruned INT8) H3-Encoder Multimodal text/vision encoder — reuses Qwen3-VL-32B layer-50 hidden states ✅ H3-VisualVAE Temporal-causal video autoencoder, f16t4d24 compression ✅ H3-AudioVAE Stereo audio, 32 kHz output, 40 Hz temporal rate ✅ H3-Context-IR Multimodal instruction preprocessor ❌ API-only H3-Regenerate-2K In-context upscaler to 2K ❌ API-only Two design choices are worth calling out for anyone comparing H3 to other video models: 3-D MM-RoPE positional embeddings. Rotary positions are extended to three axes (spatial x, spatial y, time), so temporal coherence is baked into the attention pattern rather than added by a separate temporal module. This is one of the main reasons H3 keeps subject identity and lighting stable across 15-second clips. H3-VAE gives a 4× effective sequence-length gain. The custom tokenizer packs more pixels per token than the standard VAEs used by prior open video models — that's what makes 2K output tractable at all in this parameter class. The native audio pass is the other differentiator. Because dialogue, SFX and room tone are generated in the same forward pass as picture, lip-sync and diegetic audio come out coherent by default. Reference audio (WAV/MP3, 2–15s per clip, up to 3 clips) enables voice cloning; but audio references must accompany an image or video reference — the API rejects audio-only inputs.
documents.s: What H3 actually is (the architecture in one page)

documents.t: If you're planning to run H3 locally, these are the numbers that determine what fits: Checkpoint Diffusion model Text encoder Both VAEs Minimum working total BF16 (reference) 61.7 GB 48.0 GB 5.82 GB ~115 GB INT8 31.7 GB 25.3 GB 5.82 GB ~63 GB Pruned INT8 + NVFP4 AWQ TE 19.5 GB 14.6 GB 5.82 GB ~42.5 GB VRAM: 24 GB comfortably, 12 GB with offload (slower per clip). SGLang example configs use 4 GPUs for serving. Pull the latest and the new H3 nodes appear automatically. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a checkpoint that fits your VRAM⌄ 24 GB+ card → INT8 or BF16. 12–16 GB card → pruned INT8 + NVFP4 AWQ text encoder + CPU offload. Below 12 GB, use the API — you won't have a good time. ←PreviousNext→ 3Load one of the six official workflow templates⌄ Three local (text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video) and three API-backed (text-to-video, reference-to-video, first/last-frame-to-video) ship in ComfyUI's built-in gallery. The API is REST + polling. You post a job, receive a task_id, and poll a query endpoint until status == "succeeded". Only public URLs work — Base64 payloads are rejected, and the total request body is capped at 64 MB. Reference limits: ≤9 images, ≤3 video clips, ≤3 audio clips, 12 files total, ≤7 000-character prompt. H3 text-to-video with a voice reference (Python) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import os, time, requests headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['MINIMAX_API_KEY']}"} payload = { "model": "MiniMax-H3", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "Wide shot: a lighthouse keeper walks onto the balcony and says, 'Follow the wind, live free.' Voice follows reference audio 1."}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": "https://example.com/voice-ref.mp3"}, "role": "reference_audio"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/lighthouse.jpg"}, "role": "reference_image"}, ], "resolution": "2K", # 2K is the only value the API accepts right now "duration": 8, # seconds, 4–15 "ratio": "16:9", } task_id = requests.post( "https://api.minimax.io/v2/video_generation", headers=headers, json=payload, ).json()["task_id"] while True: time.sleep(10) task = requests.get( f"https://api.minimax.io/v2/query/video_generation/{task_id}", headers=headers, ).json()["task"] if task["status"] == "succeeded": print(task["video_url"]) break if task["status"] == "failed": raise RuntimeError(task) H3 locally via diffusers (self-host, 768p) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline import torch pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained( "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3", dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda", ) video, audio = pipe( prompt="Slow dolly-in on a neon-lit ramen shop at night; steam rising; jazz sax outside.", num_frames=24 * 8, # 8 seconds at 24 fps height=768, width=1344, generator=torch.manual_seed(42), ) video.save("ramen.mp4"); audio.save("ramen.wav")

What AI Actually Costs (Across Providers)

Intermedio Once your product does more than one kind of thing, one model stops being the right answer for every request. Classify the ticket, extract the fields, draft the reply, review it — those are four jobs with four different cost/latency/quality budgets. The pattern the whole field has converged on in 2026 is to route each request to the model that fits the job, and to escalate when the cheap model isn't good enough. This page is the editorial guide to those patterns: what they are, when each one ships, the recipes that work, and the failure modes to avoid. What you'll learn Know the six routing patterns that ship in production and when to reach for each Understand the difference between routing (one decision up front) and cascading (escalate on failure) Build your first classifier router with a copy-paste prompt and a one-week rollout plan Read the cost math: when routing saves real money, and when the overhead eats the savings Recognize the anti-patterns that turn a router into an outage waiting to happen Última verificación: 2026-08-10. Anthropic's own "Building Effective Agents" guide defines Routing as a first-class workflow: "Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task. This workflow allows for separation of concerns, and building more specialized prompts." Two of the examples they give are exactly the ones covered here — splitting customer-service categories into distinct downstream flows, and "routing easy questions to smaller models like Claude Haiku... and difficult ones to Claude Sonnet." Model names, prices and quality gaps drift; always check the current per-provider docs before hard-coding a threshold. Prices/limits in this page: check Models & pricing before you build. documents.s: Model Routing Patterns: Cascades, Classifiers, and What Actually Ships

documents.t: The "one big model for everything" era is quietly over. Three forces drove the shift: A wide, well-behaved price curve. Every major provider now ships a family — Anthropic (Haiku / Sonnet / Opus), OpenAI (small / mid / frontier), Google (Flash / Pro), plus open-weight tiers. Cheap tiers are 10–100× cheaper than the frontier and, on narrow tasks, only marginally worse. Leaving the cheap tier idle is money you're setting on fire. Real latency budgets. A classify step in front of a support agent needs to answer in under 300 ms. A frontier model is often the wrong tool for reasons other than cost — it's just too slow for the step. Specialization. Different models genuinely lead on different tasks — one is better at structured JSON, another at long context, another at code, another at multilingual. The rankings shuffle monthly (see Choosing a Model), but the shape — "different tools for different jobs" — is durable. The result: a router in front of your models, deciding per-request where to send the work. The rest of this page is the design vocabulary for that router.
documents.s: Why routing is the default pattern in 2026

documents.t: Almost every pattern below is a variation on two ideas. Get the difference right and the rest is naming. Routing makes one decision up front, before any model runs. A classifier (a rule, a small model, or a bigger model) reads the request, picks a target, and hands off. Fast, cheap in the steady state, but wrong when the classifier is wrong — and you don't find out until later. Cascading runs the cheap model first and escalates to a stronger one only when a defined signal says "this answer isn't good enough." Robust because the signal is grounded in the actual output, but every escalation pays both models — so the win only survives when the cheap tier handles most traffic on its own. They compose. A production system usually does both: route to the right lane based on task type, then cascade inside a lane based on the cheap model's confidence. Anthropic's taxonomy calls the up-front decision "Routing" and the dynamic decomposition "Orchestrator-Workers"; cascading is the industry name for the "try small first, escalate on failure" variant of the same idea.
documents.s: The two big families: routing vs cascading

documents.t: A hand-written rule (regex, keyword, request field, message length) decides the target. No model runs to make the decision. When it wins. The signal is unambiguous and cheap: "if the request contains a code fence, send to the coding model", "if the customer is on the Enterprise plan, send to the frontier tier", "if the input is > 200k tokens, send to the long-context model." When it breaks. The rule silently rots as the domain shifts — new phrasing, new intents, edge cases the regex never anticipated. Every "if X then Y" is a small piece of tech debt. Ship it when. You have one or two high-value carve-outs (a paying tier, a code path, a language) and want zero latency overhead.

A small, fast model reads the request and returns a label — "billing" | "technical" | "sales" | "other" — which picks the downstream handler. Anthropic gives this as one of their canonical examples: easy questions to Haiku, hard ones to Sonnet. When it wins. You have a small, stable set of categories and each one deserves its own prompt/tool set/model. A single specialized prompt per category beats one giant do-everything system prompt. When it breaks. Categories overlap (many real requests are "billing and technical"), the classifier misroutes silently, or your label set explodes past ~10 categories and picks become noisy. Ship it when. You can enumerate the top 5–8 request types and each one materially benefits from a different handler. Classifier-router prompt (portable across Claude/GPT/Gemini) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a request classifier for a support product. Read the CUSTOMER MESSAGE below and return a JSON object with: - "category": one of ["billing", "technical", "account", "sales", "other"] - "confidence": a number from 0.0 to 1.0 - "reason": one short sentence explaining the pick If you are less than 0.7 confident, use "other" and say why. Return ONLY the JSON, no prose, no code fence. CUSTOMER MESSAGE: """ {{message}} """

Instead of what the request is about, you estimate how hard it is — length, entity count, whether it references numbers/code, whether tool use is likely — and pick a tier accordingly: cheap for easy, mid for medium, frontier for hard. When it wins. The task type is roughly homogeneous (say, "answer a coding question") but the individual requests vary wildly in difficulty. Instead of paying frontier prices for a two-line syntax question, you pay Haiku prices for those and reserve the frontier for the multi-file refactors. When it breaks. The "difficulty score" is really "prompt length", and long prompts aren't always hard prompts. A user pastes a huge stack trace and asks a trivial question about it — your router upgrades needlessly. Ship it when. You have measurable variance in difficulty within a task type and clear signals (length, presence of code, number of subquestions) that correlate with it.

Try the cheap model first. Check the answer against a failure signal. If it fails, retry on the stronger model. This is the pattern the industry ships more than any other, because the "signal" is grounded in what the model actually said — not a guess about what it will say. What counts as a signal? Anything cheap and reliable: schema validation on JSON output, a "does this answer the question?" check by an LLM judge, an explicit "needs_help": true field the model can emit when unsure, a downstream test that runs the code, a low logprob on the answer token when the provider exposes it. Cost math. The savings survive only when the cheap tier handles most traffic. If 90% of requests get resolved by the cheap model and 10% escalate, you pay 0.9 × cheap + 0.1 × (cheap + strong) ≈ mostly cheap. If half escalate, you're paying more than always using the strong model. When it wins. Tasks with a clear "did this work?" signal — code that runs or doesn't, JSON that validates or doesn't, extraction where the field either matches the source or doesn't. When it breaks. No cheap failure signal, or the cheap model thinks it succeeded when it didn't (silent failure — the worst case). Ship it when. You can name the failure signal in one sentence and it doesn't require the strong model to check.

Run the same request against N models in parallel and reconcile the answers — take a majority vote, take the first schema-valid one, or send all N to a judge model that picks the best. When it wins. Quality matters more than cost or latency: legal research, medical summarization, high-stakes financial extraction, "review this contract for red flags." Also useful for hard math and code, where different models make different mistakes and their intersection is more reliable than any single one. When it breaks. You pay N× the cost and inherit the slowest model's latency for every request. Ensembles are a tax you accept for quality, not a way to save money. Ship it when. The cost of getting the answer wrong is at least an order of magnitude larger than the cost of N model calls — which is almost never true for consumer traffic and often true for enterprise workflows.

Try the primary; on 429/5xx/timeout, transparently retry on a secondary from a different provider. This is the pattern every serious multi-model app needs even if it uses none of the others. When it wins. Every time your primary provider has an outage or throttles you at exactly the wrong moment. Fallback is a reliability pattern, not a cost-optimization pattern — the secondary is usually a different provider's equivalent tier, not a cheaper model. What to watch. The fallback path is untested code most of the time; it will regress. Run at least a small share of live traffic through the secondary continuously so you find out the response shape drifted before you're relying on it in an outage. Ship it when. Your uptime SLO is higher than any single provider's, or a single-provider dependency is a business risk (contracts, region availability, geopolitics).

Pattern Decision made Adds latency? Adds cost? Main risk Rule-based Before the model runs No No Rules silently rot as inputs shift Classifier Before, by a small model + one fast call + one cheap call Misroutes when categories overlap Complexity-based Before, by a heuristic Negligible Negligible "Difficulty" often means "length" Cascade After the cheap model tries + retry when escalating Mostly-cheap in steady state Silent success on wrong answer Ensemble Runs N in parallel, reconciles Slowest-of-N N× You are buying quality, not saving money Fallback Only on primary failure 0 in the happy path 0 in the happy path Untested until it matters

The patterns above are Lego. In production they compose. Three recipes we see repeatedly: Customer support agent. Classifier router picks a lane (billing / technical / account / sales), each lane has its own system prompt and tool set, inside the technical lane a cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates to the frontier when a "needs escalation" tool call fires. Fallback across providers wraps everything. Result: 70–90% of traffic never touches the frontier model. Coding assistant. Rule-based routing on file type and diff size sends small edits to a cheap tier and multi-file refactors to a coding-specialist. A cascade on the output — "does the patch apply cleanly and pass the smoke test?" — escalates failures to a stronger model. Compare against the field guide in Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding. RAG QA over a document corpus. Classifier picks between "answer from context" (cheap) and "needs cross-document reasoning" (mid). An ensemble of two models cross-checks the answer for high-stakes documents (contracts, filings). Compare with Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Day 1 — Pick one workload and log a week of it⌄ Instrument the *real* prompts your product already sends. You need at least a few hundred, ideally categorized by outcome (resolved / escalated / wrong). Without ground-truth traffic you're guessing at where the router should send things. ←PreviousNext→ 2Day 2 — Cluster by hand⌄ Read 100 requests and write down the 5–8 categories they naturally fall into. If you can't do this in an afternoon, the workload isn't ready for a classifier router — start with rule-based routing on the one or two obvious carve-outs (paying tier, long context, code). ←PreviousNext→ 3Day 3 — Write the classifier prompt⌄ Use the PromptCard above. Run it against yesterday's clusters on a cheap model (Haiku, Gemini Flash, GPT-nano). Measure accuracy against your hand-labels. If it's below ~85%, either merge categories or add few-shot examples — don't ship a router that's wrong 1-in-5. ←PreviousNext→ 4Day 4 — Route + shadow-log⌄ Wire the router into the request path but do NOT change the downstream model yet — every request still goes to the current model, and you *also* log where the router *would* have sent it. Compare against real outcomes for a day. ←PreviousNext→ 5Day 5 — Turn it on for one lane⌄ Flip routing live for the highest-value lane (usually the easiest one, where cheap-tier savings are biggest). Watch quality metrics — retry rate, thumbs-down rate, escalation rate — for 24 hours. ←PreviousNext→ 6Day 6 — Add a cascade inside a lane⌄ For the lane where the cheap tier is 'usually right but sometimes wrong', add an escalation signal (schema validation, judge check, explicit `needs_help` flag) and retry on the strong model. Confirm the fallback path with a chaos test — kill the cheap model and check the escalation works. ←PreviousNext→ 7Day 7 — Write the runbook and hand it off⌄ Document the router's rules, the classifier prompt, the escalation signal, and — critically — the metrics dashboard. If the router silently misroutes a category next month, someone needs to notice. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: How to build your first router in a week

documents.t: Cascades ship far more than learned routers. Research systems like RouteLLM train a router on preference data and can cut cost 2× or more on standard benchmarks (see the RouteLLM paper) — but training and maintaining a learned router is real engineering. Most teams get most of the wins from cheap-first + explicit escalation. The classifier is almost always a cheap chat model, not a fine-tune. Haiku-class or Flash-class models with a good prompt hit the accuracy bar for 5–8 categories. Fine-tune only if you're at scale and the cheap classifier is your bottleneck. The evaluator matters more than the router. A router without a metrics loop is a guess. Instrument every routing decision with request → chosen model → outcome, and review weekly. You can't tune what you don't measure. Infrastructure and design are separable. The patterns above are language- and provider-neutral. The plumbing — one endpoint per provider, virtual keys, per-team spend caps, prompt caching — is what an AI gateway gives you. Once you know the pattern you want, see AI gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel for the concrete choice.
documents.s: What actually gets deployed (2026 field notes)

documents.t: The classifier that calls the frontier model. If picking a lane costs as much as running the strong model would have, you saved nothing and added latency. Classifiers must be cheap. Cascade without a failure signal. "The cheap model returned something, so we're done" is not a signal — it's a bet. Every cascade needs a defined check the cheap model can fail. Rule proliferation. Ten rules is manageable. A hundred is a hand-coded classifier without the tests. When your rule set drifts past ~15 branches, rip it out and use a small model. Ensembles as a cost strategy. Running three models in parallel to save money is a category error — ensembles cost N× to buy quality, not to save cost. If you're using an ensemble to make up for a bad primary model, fix the primary instead. No fallback path. Every model provider goes down eventually. A single-provider product will inherit that outage. See AI gateways for the plumbing. Routing without observability. A router that quietly sends everything to the wrong lane looks fine until quality craters two weeks later. Log every decision with the input hash, the chosen model, the outcome, and the cost — and review weekly.

Check yourself 0/3 1You have a support product where 90% of requests are answered correctly by a cheap model, but the remaining 10% need the frontier. What pattern gives you the biggest cost win? Ensemble — run cheap + frontier in parallel and take the better oneCascade — try cheap first, escalate to frontier on a failure signalAlways route to the frontier, since 10% need it anywayFallback — send to cheap, then to frontier when cheap has an outage 2Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' guide defines Routing as: Running the same request against multiple models and voting on the answerClassifying an input and directing it to a specialized followup taskFailing over to a secondary provider when the primary is downEscalating to a stronger model when the cheap one returns low confidence 3You're building a classifier router. Your classifier prompt runs on a frontier model because 'accuracy matters'. What's the problem? Nothing — accuracy is what matters, so pay for itThe classifier now costs as much as the downstream work — you've paid for the routing decision without saving anything, and added latency on topFrontier models are less accurate at classification than cheaper modelsThe classifier must always be a fine-tuned model, not a chat model

Pick a target: Choosing a Model — the archetype framework the router leans on. Wire it up: AI gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel — the plumbing every router needs. Move a prompt to the model you routed to: Porting Prompts Across Models. Coding-specific routing signals: Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding. A purpose-built classifier stage: System One decision models: Jev, Kev and the open clones — calibrated probabilities in under half a second, and how to threshold them honestly. Anthropic's canonical workflow taxonomy: Building Effective Agents.

Anthropic — Building Effective Agents — canonical definitions of the Routing and Orchestrator-Workers workflows. RouteLLM paper (arXiv 2406.18665) — a learned router trained on preference data; demonstrates the pattern's headroom, though most production teams still ship rule + classifier + cascade rather than learned routing.

Intermedio On 5 August 2026 Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped Muse Code — a terminal coding agent — alongside Muse Spark 1.2, the model co-trained with it. Two products, one release, and the pairing is the interesting part: Meta claims tools that are trained together with the model produce fewer retries and higher-quality output than a generic model steered by a generic harness. Whether or not you buy that claim, the launch is worth reading closely — Muse Code is the closest structural analogue to Claude Code that any competitor has shipped, and a few of its design decisions (the append-only event log, the contributor tier pricing, the three bundled skills) are non-obvious enough to be worth stealing regardless of which agent you actually use day to day. This page is the practical read: what Muse Code actually is, how it compares to Claude Code on the numbers Meta itself published, the pricing trap that shows up on the second read of the pricing table, and where it fits into the AILmanac tour. What you'll learn Understand what Muse Code is architecturally: a terminal agent with a local append-only event log, persistent async background agents, and three shipped skills (/plan, /grill, /goal) Read the Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 numbers correctly — including the vendor-run caveat that the source review itself flags Know the pricing tiers: $1.25/$4.25 standard vs. $0.10/$0.20 contributor, and what the 12.5×/21.25× discount actually costs you in data terms Get the install command, the platforms supported, and the beta-status caveats before you point this at anything sensitive Place Muse Code next to Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the rest of the coding-agent CLI landscape
documents.s: Muse Code + Muse Spark 1.2: Meta's Terminal Coding Agent

documents.t: Muse Code is a beta terminal coding agent for macOS and Linux, powered by Muse Spark 1.2 — a 1M-token multimodal-input, text-output model — with async background agents, a local append-only event log for crash-safe resume, and three bundled skills (/plan, /grill, /goal); Meta prices the standard tier at $1.25/M input and $4.25/M output, and offers a contributor tier at $0.10/M input and $0.20/M output in exchange for permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions.

Muse Code's runtime records every model call, tool run, approval, and edit to a local append-only event log before it executes. Meta describes this as "replay-exact and restart-safe." If the agent crashes mid-task — segfault, laptop lid, expired token, anything — you resume from the log without losing work or having to re-prompt the model to reconstruct state. That's a write-ahead log pattern from database engineering, applied to the harness rather than the storage layer. Two things follow that are worth internalising: Failures during 24-hour runs become recoverable rather than expensive. Meta's own kernel-optimisation case study executed 1,000+ tool calls over 24 hours on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. Without a durable log, one crash in hour 22 costs the whole run. With one, the model resumes from the last committed event. Post-hoc auditing is trivial. Every decision is on disk, in order, with the tool inputs and outputs. You can inspect what the agent thought, why it called a particular tool, and what came back — without instrumenting anything. The comparable pattern in Claude Code is checkpoints and rewind, which snapshots the workspace so you can step backwards through interactive edits. The Muse Code event log is a different tool for a different problem: rewind lets you undo, while the event log lets the agent resume.
documents.s: 1. The event log is a write-ahead log, and it's what makes long runs safe

documents.t: Two pricing tiers, publicly disclosed: Tier Input ($/M) Cached input ($/M) Output ($/M) You give up Standard $1.25 $0.15 $4.25 Nothing Contributor $0.10 — $0.20 Permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions The math on the discount: 12.5× cheaper on input, 21.25× cheaper on output. For a real coding session that reads more than it writes, the effective cost drop lands closer to 15×. The catch is not that Meta will look at your prompts (all frontier vendors log for abuse review by default). The catch is training rights — Meta explicitly retains permission to train future models on your inputs and completions. That means: Anything that would leak trade secrets, PII, licensed code, or a customer's data through a future model output is off-limits. Anything under a share-alike or similar restrictive licence you don't own is off-limits. Anything covered by an NDA is off-limits. Read Meta's exact terms before flipping the toggle — the source reviews are clear that "confirm exact terms and toggle settings in Meta's official docs before running it on anything sensitive." A 12.5× cost reduction on personal side-projects is a genuinely good deal. A 12.5× cost reduction on your employer's monorepo is a legal problem waiting to happen. Última verificación: 2026-08-06.
