documents.t: Jev is API-only and early-access, with no weights. Within days the community produced three different answers to "how would you build this", and each teaches something about the category. Project How it works Reported numbers License / stars (Sept 21) Kev (Jared Palmer) Qwen3.5 0.8B / 4B / 9B base models with rank-16 LoRA adapters; supervised on 10,000 examples from ten public datasets plus 2,576 generated policy and rule examples, two epochs, base weights frozen; same request/response shape as TypeSafe accuracy on unseen sources (dev / test): 0.652 / 0.684, 0.797 / 0.837, 0.822 / 0.852 — versus 0.83–0.87 on sources seen in training; Kev-9B trails Jev by 3.5 points on the new-source dev set (0.822 vs 0.857) and by far more on knowledge-heavy sets (MMLU 0.74 vs 0.90, MMLU-Pro 0.52 vs 0.84) Apache-2.0 · 1.8k Nimble (Bespoke Labs) Qwen3.5-9B, LoRA applied only to answer tokens; 2,676 contrastive examples across ten domains — near-identical pairs where one changed fact flips the label 90.12% agreement on 324 held-out cases vs Jev 1.13.0 at 93.21% and the untuned base at 66.36%; ~106 ms median on an H100, ~444 ms on a Mac 1.4k openjev-sglang (Eric Zhang) No training at all: serves the TypeSafe HTTP API over Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on SGLang by prefilling the shared prefix once, then issuing one single-token request per question and reading the logprobs of the label tokens; N+1 one-token calls for N questions up to 64 questions with 2–64 answers each; radix-cache reuse is "opportunistic, not a pinned per-request KV session" 246 Three things these repos tell you that the launch post does not: The architecture is probably ordinary; the data is not. openjev reaches a usable System One API with zero training by reading first-token logprobs — which is what every "poor man's classifier" on an open model has always done. Nimble's jump from 66% to 90% on the same 9B base came from 2,676 carefully contrastive examples. The moat, if there is one, is RLCD-style training data, not a secret block diagram. Small clones are over-confident in exactly the way the pilot measured Jev to be. Kev's README states that Kev-9B assigns at least 0.9 probability to a wrong answer on 8.7% of questions from unseen sources. Raising the softmax temperature (KEV_TEMPERATURE=2.0) drops that to 4.4% at no accuracy cost. Whatever you deploy, calibrate it on your own labels before a threshold is allowed to skip a human. Local latency depends on the base model's attention kernels. Kev measured 329 ms (0.8B), 779 ms (4B) and about 2 s (9B) per request on an Apple M5, because Qwen3.5's DeltaNet layers have no optimized macOS kernels; the same requests take tens of milliseconds on an H100 with flash-linear-attention installed. The README's own advice for a Mac is the previous-generation Qwen3 bases. Claude has no logprob endpoint, so you cannot build the openjev shim on it. What you can do is structured output with an explicit confidence field — but that number is generated, not calibrated, and the whole point of this model class is that the difference matters. Run Kev locally and ask it three questions CopyOpen in Claude↗ git clone https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev.git && cd kev uv sync --extra serve # Python 3.12+, transformers >= 5.17; add flash-linear-attention on CUDA KEV_DTYPE=bf16 KEV_TEMPERATURE=2.0 uv run --extra serve python -m kev.serve --run jaredpalmer/kev-4b --port 8009 curl -s localhost:8009/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "kev-latest", "state": "Customer on the Pro plan says the export button has been broken for two days and their board deck is due tomorrow.", "questions": { "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "The customer needs a response within hours, not days."}, "department": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team owns this?", "criteria": {"billing": "", "engineering": "", "sales": "", "other": "none of these"}}, "sentiment": {"type": "score", "instructions": "How frustrated is the customer?", "criteria": {"calm": "", "annoyed": "", "angry": ""}} }}' Then generate the labels you will calibrate against. Nimble's contrastive recipe is the one to copy, and Claude is good at producing it: Claude: build a contrastive calibration set for a decision model CopyOpen in Claude↗ I am calibrating a small decision model that answers typed questions about support tickets. Question under test: "urgent" (noul) — "The customer needs a response within hours, not days." Produce 40 ticket pairs as JSON lines. In each pair the two tickets are nearly identical, but exactly one fact changes and flips the correct label. Vary the flipping fact across pairs: explicit deadlines, implied deadlines, plan tier, tone that sounds urgent but is not, negations ("this is not urgent but..."), dates expressed as text, and tickets that try to talk their way into urgency. Fields per line: {"ticket": "...", "label": true|false, "flipped_fact": "..."}. No commentary. Score the model on those 80 tickets, bucket by confidence, and you have the calibration curve that decides your thresholds. If the "tries to talk its way into urgency" bucket scores badly, you have also just measured your injection exposure. Check yourself 0/5 1Why does adding a tenth question to a Jev request add almost no latency? The API caches previous answersEvery question is read out in parallel from one shared encoding of the state, with no autoregressive decodingQuestions are batched across customersJev only answers the first five questions 2What does 'cannot hallucinate' actually guarantee? The answer is correctThe output is always a valid value of the declared schema; it can still be the wrong valueThe model refuses when unsureProbabilities are perfectly calibrated 3The independent BANKING77 pilot found Jev's mean confidence was 87.4% at 75.3% accuracy. What should you do with that? Trust probabilities above 0.9Measure calibration on your own labelled data and set thresholds from that curveUse Jev only for generationSwitch to sequential single-question calls 4Which of these is NOT a good job for a System One model? Scoring a proposed tool call for risk before it runsDeciding whether a retrieved passage is relevantComputing how many days remain before a deadline stated in the ticketRouting a ticket to a department 5How does openjev-sglang provide a Jev-style API with no training? It distils Jev's answersIt prefills the shared state once and reads the logprobs of the label tokens with one single-token request per questionIt fine-tunes Qwen at request timeIt proxies to TypeSafe Decision-model vocabulary girarTérminoSystem One modelDefiniciónTypeSafe's term for a model that returns typed probabilistic decisions instead of text: state plus typed questions in, a probability per question out, all evaluated in one parallel pass.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Avanzado On 17 September 2026, PrismML published Ternary Bonsai 2 27B: a 27-billion-parameter model whose weights are only -1, 0 and +1, packed into a 5.95 GB file, released Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face GGUF repo passed 2.5 million downloads inside five days. The headline everywhere was the same — a 27B model that fits on a laptop. The headline is true. Almost everything people assume follows from it is not. Stock llama.cpp will load the file and produce fluent nonsense without raising an error. Ollama and LM Studio refuse it outright. The 5.95 GB file needs roughly 12 GB of VRAM at default settings. The larger 7.21 GB build is faster on a datacenter GPU and slower on a 4090. And the widely-quoted "98.2% of full precision" is an average across fourteen benchmarks that hides a 6-point collapse in multimodal reasoning and, in one independent test, complete failure on low-resource languages. This page is the practical layer: what ternary quantization actually buys you, how to run this model without silently corrupting your output, and how to read a compression retention number honestly. The technique outlives the model — the same reasoning applies to every low-bit release that follows. What you'll learn Understand why ternary weights are 1.75 bits in practice, not the 1.58 bits the theory promises Recognise the silent-garbage failure mode: stock loaders ignore the Hadamard rotation and never error Pick between PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 using the bandwidth-vs-unpack crossover, not file size Budget real memory: 5.95 GB of weights, ~64 KiB per token of cache, and why defaults blow past 12 GB Read '98.2% retention' correctly — which capabilities survive compression and which quietly do not
documents.s: Ternary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: A normal model stores each weight as a 16-bit float. A ternary model stores each weight as one of three values — -1, 0, +1 — with a single shared FP16 scale per group of weights. Reconstruction is w = scale_g * t, where t is the trit. Three states need log₂(3) ≈ 1.58 bits. That is the number the research literature uses, from Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 onward. It is not the number you get on disk. Bonsai 2 27B ships at 1.75 bits per weight for its densest build. The extra 0.17 bits per weight is the part nobody explains: Group scales. One FP16 scale per group of 128 weights is 16 bits amortised over 128 weights — 0.125 bits per weight before anything else. Packing waste. Trits do not divide neatly into bytes. Dense packing recovers most but not all of the theoretical density. Unquantized components. Embeddings, output projections and normalisation layers stay at higher precision. On a 27B model these are a small fraction of parameters but a noticeable fraction of bytes. So the real ratio is not 16/1.58 ≈ 10×. It is 53.8 GB → 5.95 GB, or about 9× — which is exactly what the model card reports. :::tip Why ternary is fast, and it is not the maths The intuition most people have is that ternary multiplication is cheap: multiplying by -1, 0 or +1 is a sign flip, a skip, or nothing. True, but that is not where the win comes from on real hardware. Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Every generated token requires streaming the entire weight matrix from memory. Cut the bytes by 9× and you cut the dominant cost by 9×. The arithmetic was never the bottleneck. This matters practically: a CPU or GPU without native ternary support must dequantize back to a normal format to use its existing multiply-accumulate units, which throws away the arithmetic saving while keeping the bandwidth one. Which is why the packing format you pick changes performance in a direction that looks backwards — see below. :::

This is the single most important thing on this page, and it appears in almost no coverage of the release. Bonsai 2's weights have a blockwise Hadamard rotation folded into storage. A matching inverse transform must be applied to the activations at runtime. The rotation is a standard trick for low-bit quantization — it spreads outlier magnitudes across a block so the ternary grid has less to lose — but it means the stored weights are not directly usable by a loader that does not know about it. A stock llama.cpp build does not know about it. Depending on version it will either reject the tensor types or, worse, load the file successfully and generate fluent, confident, completely wrong output. There is no error, no warning, no degraded-quality flag. The model card states this plainly: stock llama.cpp will not run these files, and standard builds produce garbage because the Hadamard activation transform is missing. Downstream tools inherit the problem in different ways: Runtime Behaviour with Bonsai 2 27B GGUF PrismML's llama.cpp fork (branch prism) Works — the only local GGUF path today Stock llama.cpp Rejects the tensor types, or loads and emits nonsense Ollama Import fails with a tensor size overflow error LM Studio Rejects ggml tensor types 142 and 143 MLX (Apple) Separate mlx-2bit build required; larger footprint The Ollama and LM Studio failures are the safe outcome. The stock-llama.cpp silent success is the dangerous one, because a benchmark script or an eval harness will happily record the nonsense as a result. :::warning If you are evaluating a low-bit model, verify the loader first Run one known-answer prompt before you run anything else. If a model that scores 95+ on HumanEval cannot answer "what is 2+2" coherently, you have a loader problem, not a model problem. This applies to every exotic quantization format, not just this one. :::
documents.s: The trap: stock llama.cpp loads it and lies

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Build PrismML's fork, not mainline⌄ git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp, then cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j for NVIDIA. On Apple Silicon drop the CUDA flag — Metal is on by default. On AMD use -DGGML_HIP=ON. The default branch is prism; the README explicitly warns against building from prism-v6 and against mixing this fork's libraries with a stock llama.cpp install on the same machine. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick the right GGUF before downloading 7 GB⌄ PTQ1_0 is 5.95 GB at 1.75 bits per weight — dense trits. PQ2_0 is 7.21 GB at 2.13 bits per weight — each trit gets its own 2-bit slot. Same weights, same quality, different packing. The choice is a throughput decision, not a quality one. See the crossover table below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Download, and check the byte count⌄ hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . — PTQ1_0 is 5,946,648,928 bytes and PQ2_0 is 7,206,168,928 bytes. A truncated download is another way to get plausible-looking garbage. Add the mmproj file (629 MB at Q8_0, 931 MB at BF16) only if you need vision. ←PreviousNext→ 4Serve it with an explicit context size⌄ ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080. The -c flag is not optional in practice: -c 0 defaults to the full 262K window and will try to allocate roughly 16 GB of attention cache before it has generated a single token. ←PreviousNext→ 5Verify with a known-answer call, then wire up your tooling⌄ The server exposes an OpenAI-shaped /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so anything that speaks chat-completions can point at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1. Send one trivial prompt and read the answer with your own eyes before you point an eval harness or an agent loop at it. ←PreviousNext→ 6If PQ2_0 crashes on CPU, disable repacking⌄ PQ2_0 can crash during llama.cpp's CPU repack step. Pass --no-repack, or set LLAMA_ARG_REPACK=0 in the environment. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal end-to-end: build, fetch, serve, verify CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. Fork only — stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j # 2. Fetch (PQ2_0 = 7.21 GB, faster on big GPUs; PTQ1_0 = 5.95 GB, fits 8 GB cards) hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \ Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . # 3. Serve — always set -c explicitly, never leave it at 0 ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \ --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 # 4. Verify the loader BEFORE trusting any output curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bonsai-2-27b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer with one number."}]}' # Coherent "4" => loader is correct. Fluent nonsense => wrong build, stop here.

Two builds of the same weights. PTQ1_0 packs trits densely at 1.75 bits. PQ2_0 gives each trit its own 2-bit slot at 2.13 bits — 21% more disk, but the unpacking is far cheaper because slots are byte-aligned. Measured generation throughput, tokens per second: GPU PQ2_0 (7.21 GB) PTQ1_0 (5.95 GB) Winner RTX 5090 129.9 120.5 PQ2_0 RTX 4090 81.2 91.1 PTQ1_0 L4 (24 GB) 29.8 32.1 PTQ1_0 M5 Pro (Metal) 28.1 — — The pattern generalises: PTQ1_0 wins on Ada-generation and lower-end GPUs, PQ2_0 wins on H100, A100 and Blackwell. That is the opposite of the usual quantization rule of thumb, where smaller is always faster. The reason is the bandwidth-versus-unpack tradeoff from earlier. On a bandwidth-starved card, moving 21% fewer bytes dominates and the dense packing wins. On a card with enormous memory bandwidth, bandwidth stops being the constraint and the bit-shuffling cost of dense unpacking becomes the bottleneck instead — so the fatter, byte-aligned format runs faster. Prompt processing tells the same story more loudly: on an RTX 5090, PQ2_0 processes prompts at 3,893 tok/s against PTQ1_0's 1,805 — more than double, because prefill is compute-bound, where unpacking cost hits hardest. Rule of thumb: below 12 GB of VRAM you have no choice, take PTQ1_0. Above it, take PQ2_0 unless you are on a 4090 or an L4, where PTQ1_0 measurably wins.
documents.s: PTQ1_0 vs PQ2_0: the crossover that looks backwards

documents.t: Three different "size" numbers are circulating for this model — 5.9 GB, 7.2 GB and 8.6 GB — and all three are defensible, because they measure different things. Here is the actual budget: Weights: 5.95 GB (PTQ1_0) or 7.21 GB (PQ2_0). Vision projector: +629 MB (Q8_0) or +931 MB (BF16), if you need images. Attention cache: roughly 64 KiB per token. That is ~0.5 GB at 8K context, ~2 GB at 32K, and ~16 GB at the full 262K window. Parallel slots: llama.cpp allocates cache per slot. Defaults allocate several. One independent test measured just over 12 GB of VRAM at default settings, dropping to about 8 GB when the server was restricted to a single parallel slot. The disk footprint they measured — around 7 GB — corresponds to the PQ2_0 build, which is where part of the number confusion comes from. Practical context headroom by card, using PQ2_0 unless noted: VRAM Build Usable context 8 GB PTQ1_0 ~16K tokens (~6K with vision) 12 GB PQ2_0 ~56K tokens 16 GB PQ2_0 ~118K tokens 24 GB PQ2_0 ~240K tokens 32 GB+ PQ2_0 Full 262K window The "runs on a laptop" claim survives all of this — but "runs on a laptop with an 8 GB GPU and a 16K context" is the honest version, and that is a materially different product.
documents.s: File size is not memory requirement

documents.t: PrismML reports an aggregate of 84.78 against the full-precision base model's 86.32 across fourteen benchmarks — the 98.2% figure. Averages are where compression damage goes to hide. The per-benchmark spread: Benchmark Bonsai 2 27B FP16 base Delta AIME26 95.83 94.58 +1.25 MATH-500 98.80 99.80 −1.00 LiveCodeBench 90.07 90.05 +0.02 HumanEval+ 95.12 93.29 +1.83 MMLU-Redux 89.09 91.46 −2.37 MMMU-Pro 75.49 81.73 −6.24 Three things to take from this table. First, the damage is not uniform — it is structural. Maths and code are essentially untouched. Knowledge recall drops (composite knowledge-and-reasoning lands near 79.9 versus 85.6 for full precision). Multimodal reasoning takes the real hit: MMMU-Pro falls 6.24 points, and OCR Bench v2 drops from 60.99 to 56.88. Compression costs you breadth of stored fact, not procedural skill — which is exactly what you would expect when you crush the precision available to store long-tail associations. Second, be suspicious of the positives. The compressed model "beating" its own full-precision base by 1.83 points on HumanEval+ and 1.25 on AIME26 is not evidence that compression helps. It is evidence that these benchmarks have run-to-run variance of a couple of points. Which should also make you discount the small negatives. Third, the vendor's own numbers do not fully agree. The model card's benchmark table aggregates to 84.78, while PrismML's launch post reports an aggregate of 83.9. Both are described as the same 98.2% retention. The discrepancy is small and unexplained; we report it rather than pick one. :::danger The failure mode benchmarks did not catch One independent hands-on test found behaviour no benchmark row predicts: asked to translate into low-resource languages including Tamil, the model entered a repetitive loop and never completed the task — worse than the previous Bonsai generation. The same test found it identified a real timezone bug and then talked itself out of the correct conclusion, and failed to produce a working reset button in a small HTML task across three correction rounds. This is the characteristic signature of aggressive quantization: aggregate scores hold, while the long tail — rare languages, long-horizon self-correction — degrades in ways that only show up in use. Community reports also describe recall and coherence degradation past roughly 200K tokens of the advertised 262K window. :::

There is a parallel effort to get ternary Bonsai into upstream llama.cpp, and its current state is a useful lesson in how low-bit formats fragment. PrismML proposed group-128 ternary packing for the smaller Bonsai models. The llama.cpp maintainer pushed back in favour of group size 64, on the grounds that it costs under 6% extra memory while supporting more tensor shapes and giving better quality. Q2_0 with group-64 became the official format and has been merged into multiple backends including CUDA and Vulkan. PrismML kept their group-128 variants in the fork. So "does llama.cpp support ternary models" has two correct and opposite answers: Yes — Q2_0_g64 builds run on mainline across backends, and the fork's own README points at them as the portable path. No, not for this model — as of verification, the published Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf repo contains F16, PQ2_0, PTQ1_0 and the two mmproj files. There is no Q2_0_g64 build of the 27B. The fork is the only path. Two older ternary formats, TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, already exist in ggml but use group size 256, which is incompatible with how these models are natively packed. TQ2_0 is also the tightest faithful ternary layout in ggml at roughly 2.06 bits per weight — and in current mainline it implements a CPU-only dot product with no CUDA, Metal or Vulkan path. Seeing "ternary supported" in a changelog tells you very little about whether your GPU will use it. For the next low-bit model you evaluate, the question to ask is not is it quantized but which group size, which packing, which backends have kernels, and is there a portable build — because that determines whether you are running on mainline or maintaining someone else's fork.
documents.s: The mainline story, and why it matters for the next release

documents.t: Worth it when: You need a capable maths or coding model on hardware that cannot hold a 27B at higher precision. That is where retention is near-perfect and the value is highest. You are bandwidth-constrained — a laptop GPU, an edge box, a shared L4 — and 9× fewer bytes per token is the difference between usable and not. Energy matters. PrismML reports 0.714 mWh per token on an RTX 4090, which they put at 40% more efficient than a full-precision 8B model. The Apache 2.0 licence and fully local execution are requirements, not preferences. Not worth it when: The work is knowledge-heavy or multimodal. That is precisely where the compression bill lands. You need non-English long-tail language coverage. The independent evidence here is bad and benchmarks did not predict it. You cannot maintain a forked inference runtime. Ollama and LM Studio do not load it today, and a stock build fails silently rather than loudly. You were going to run it past ~200K tokens of context on the strength of the 262K spec. girarTérminoWhat is Bonsai 2 27B, precisely?DefiniciónA ternary-quantized compression of Qwen3.8-27B (27.36B parameters) published by PrismML on 17 September 2026 under Apache 2.0. Architecture unchanged from the base model; only the weight representation differs.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 10 Siguiente→
documents.s: When this is the right tool

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 1You download Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf, run it on a recent stock llama.cpp build, and it generates fluent text that is subtly wrong. What is the most likely cause? The download was corruptedStock llama.cpp does not apply the required Hadamard activation transform, so it loads the file and produces garbage without erroringThe temperature is too highThe model needs a system prompt 2You have an RTX 4090 with 24 GB. Which GGUF build gives higher generation throughput? PQ2_0 — it is larger so it must be higher qualityPTQ1_0 — 91.1 tok/s vs PQ2_0's 81.2 on that cardThey are identical; the files only differ in disk sizeNeither runs on a 4090 3Your card has 8 GB of VRAM. The weights file is 5.95 GB. You launch llama-server with default settings and it runs out of memory. Why? The file is secretly larger than advertisedAttention cache costs roughly 64 KiB per token and llama.cpp allocates it per parallel slot — defaults push total usage past 12 GBTernary models require double the VRAM of their file size by designThe vision projector is always loaded 4A teammate cites '98.2% of full-precision performance' to argue the compressed model is a drop-in replacement for a document-understanding pipeline. What is the strongest objection? 98.2% is within benchmark noise so the number is meaninglessRetention is highly uneven — maths and code are at parity while MMMU-Pro drops 6.24 points and OCR Bench v2 falls from 60.99 to 56.88, which is exactly the workload in questionThe model is not licensed for commercial use27B models are never suitable for document understanding 5A changelog says llama.cpp 'supports ternary quantization'. What must you still check before assuming your GPU will use it? Nothing — ternary support is a single feature flagGroup size, packing format, and which backends have kernels — TQ2_0 is CPU-only in mainline, and the Bonsai 2 27B repo ships no Q2_0_g64 buildOnly whether the file is under 8 GBWhether the model is Apache 2.0 licensed Última verificación: 2026-09-22. Esta página cita datos que cambian con el tiempo: toma la fecha de arriba como su grado de actualidad. Avanzado Última verificación: 2026-09-29. Every accuracy, latency and training-time figure on this page is self-reported by the project that published it, on benchmarks that project chose. Nothing here has been independently replicated. Both repositories are days old and moving fast — star counts, model names, checkpoint ids and CLI flags are the most perishable facts here; read the current README before you copy a command. Neither project is affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe, the makers of Jev. Fuentes: README of firelex/jeff (created 2026-09-28, 895 stars at time of writing) and PostHog/jeeves (created 2026-09-29, 107 stars); denis-pplx/autojev README; Hacker News items 49883844 (Jeff, 536 points / 204 comments) and 49891290 (Jeeves, 105 points / 44 comments). What you'll learn Explain the actual training recipe behind an open decision model — cross-entropy over option letters, one epoch, and a temperature fitted afterwards — and why calibration is a separate step from accuracy Read the published benchmark tables honestly: the three rows where a 0.8B model beats the commercial API, and the two rows where it loses by 20–26 points Decide between four options — hosted API, zero-shot open weights, your own fine-tune, or a plain embeddings classifier — using the one baseline number that kills most of these projects Train and serve a Jev-compatible model yourself in an afternoon on a single GPU, including the checkpoint-selection rule that keeps the result honest Know when adding reasoning back to a decision model is worth 11x the latency, and how a confidence threshold buys most of the accuracy for a third of the wait System One decision models explained the category: you send program state plus typed questions, and you get calibrated probabilities back instead of text. That page ended where the open recreations were in mid-September — Kev, Nimble, a logprob shim. In the last week of September the story changed shape. The question stopped being "can we clone the API" and became "should you train your own?" On September 28 a project called Jeff shipped 0.8B and 2B fine-tunes that land within four points of Jev's overall benchmark score and run in ~22–28 ms on a laptop-class GPU, trained in about two hours on one workstation card. It was the top AI story on Hacker News that day. Twelve hours later PostHog published Jeeves, which does the opposite thing — bolts reasoning onto a decision model — and reports beating Jev on Jev's own hard tier. Both are MIT code with Apache-2.0 weights. Both are honest enough in their READMEs to publish the rows where they lose. This page is about what those rows mean for you.
documents.s: Train Your Own Decision Model: Jeff, Jeeves and the DIY System One Stack (Sep 2026)

documents.t: Date (2026) What shipped Why it matters Sep 15 Jev (TypeSafe AI), API-only Defined the category and the /v1/systemone request shape Sep 21 Kev, Nimble, openjev-sglang Proved the interface was reproducible on open weights — AutoJev (denis-pplx) The recipe: full-weight SFT of Qwen3.8-27B, 73,000 examples, one H200, 84.60% vs a 69.83% base Sep 28 Jeff (firelex) Shrank it — 0.8B/2B students, ~2 h on one workstation GPU, MLX serving, game evals Sep 29 Jeeves (PostHog) Reversed the premise — a thinking decision model, LoRA + RL on Qwen3.5-9B The through-line: in two weeks a category went from a closed API with undisclosed training to a recipe you can run overnight. AutoJev is the hinge — it published the loss function, and everything after it is a variation on that one idea.
Strip the marketing and a decision model is a startlingly small change to a normal LLM.

The model is not taught to "make decisions". It is taught to put probability mass on a single letter token — A, B, C — at one specific position. You lay the options out as a lettered panel, you train with plain cross-entropy on the correct letter, and at inference you read the logits for the letter tokens and renormalise them over just the options you offered. That one implementation detail explains the headline limitation. Jeff caps you at 26 options, and the README is blunt that positions past that are "effectively never selected" — because the alphabet ran out, not because of anything architectural. (Jev itself advertises up to 255 options, which tells you it encodes options differently.) Jeeves takes the other road: a pointer head that scores a projected hidden state against each option's embedding with a scaled dot product. No letters, no alphabet ceiling. It marks the structure with rare tokens borrowed from Qwen's tokenizer that real text essentially never uses — <|fim_prefix|> for state, <|fim_middle|> for questions, <|box_start|>/<|box_end|> around options, <|fim_suffix|> at the decision point. Reusing dead tokens as delimiters is the cheap trick that avoids growing the vocabulary or colliding with content.
documents.s: 1. The loss is cross-entropy over option letters

documents.t: This is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the output trustworthy. Accuracy and calibration are different properties. A model can rank the right answer first almost every time and still say "91%" when it is right 75% of the time — the independent BANKING77 pilot on Jev found exactly that shape of over-confidence. So all three projects fit a single scalar temperature on a held-out development set after training, and ship it alongside the checkpoint. Divide the logits by it, softmax, done. AutoJev publishes what that buys, and it is the cleanest before/after in the whole stack: Metric Base Qwen3.8-27B AutoJev-27B Accuracy 69.83% 84.60% ECE (expected calibration error — lower is better) 0.06483 0.04282 Brier score (lower is better) 0.40834 0.22027 Note that all three moved, but by different amounts. Accuracy climbed ~15 points while ECE fell ~34% — training made the model both righter and more honest, and the honesty is measurable separately. If you train your own and only report accuracy, you have not finished.
documents.s: 2. The calibration is a separate, one-parameter stage

documents.t: One epoch. Batch 256. Full-weight (Jeff, AutoJev) or LoRA r=16 (Jeeves). Checkpoint selection on a development set, never on the benchmark panel — Jeff states this explicitly, and it is the single line that separates a credible small-model result from a leaked one. Jeff also keeps at least half of each training family in the same panel layout it will see at inference, which matters more than it should; see the wording section below. Train a 0.8B decision model (Jeff's own recipe) CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. Build the training mix from public datasets uv run autojev-mix ... # 2. One epoch, full-weight, lr 5e-6 scripts/train.sh RUN data/mix/public.jsonl data/mix 5e-6 40 Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B <revision> --epochs 1 # 3. Evaluate the SELECTED checkpoint against a held-out panel uv run autojev-evaluate --data data/panel.jsonl --local \ --checkpoint checkpoints/RUN/selected --output runs/eval/RUN.json Reported cost of step 2: ~2 hours for 0.8B, ~3.5 hours for 2B, on one RTX PRO 6000. That is the number that made this a front-page story.

Here is Jeff's published panel — 4,599 questions across five public datasets plus JevBench's hard tier — with the commercial API in the last column. Read it by row, not by the overall line. Benchmark Jeff-0.8B Jeff-2B Jeff-Gemma4-E2B Jev (API) Overall 79.1% 83.1% 81.6% 83.0% Financial PhraseBank 96.4% 96.3% 96.1% 77.0% RAGTruth 86.1% 88.9% 87.4% 77.3% WinoGrande 68.6% 79.0% 77.4% 90.7% JudgeBench 62.6% 64.6% 60.6% 78.6% BBH 64.0% 68.0% 66.4% 94.3% JevBench Hard 47.6% 53.3% 48.6% 73.3% The overall scores are nearly tied. The rows are not close at all: Where the tiny model wins, it wins big. Financial PhraseBank: 96.4% against 77.0% — a 0.8B model beating a commercial API by 19 points. RAGTruth (does this answer stay faithful to the retrieved passage?): 86.1% against 77.3%. Both are narrow, high-volume, pattern-shaped jobs — sentiment on a fixed vocabulary, groundedness on a supplied passage. If your agent's hot path is that shape, a local 0.8B is not a compromise, it is the better tool. Where it loses, it is not close. BBH is 30 points down. JevBench Hard is 26 points down. Those are the rows that need multi-step reasoning, and the README says so plainly: small decision models give you "fast, calibrated choices between the options you describe" and no reasoning chain. The overall number is the average of those two facts and therefore describes nothing. This is the most transferable lesson on this page, and it is not specific to decision models: any single headline score is a weighted average over a benchmark mix that is not your mix.

Jeff also evaluated zero-shot game play — 20 episodes each of Doom, Frogger and Pac-Man — and the result is uncomfortable enough that publishing it earns trust: Model Doom (kills) Frogger (crossings) Pac-Man (pellets / 98) Random −0.05 0 11.2 Hand-coded rule bot 6.55 10.25 94.1 Jeff-0.8B 6.55 10.3 57.0 Jeff-2B −0.9 6.0 41.2 The 2B is worse at all three games than the 0.8B it outscores on every benchmark row. The README's read is that the bigger model came out more risk-averse. Whatever the cause, the pairing of those two tables is the point: benchmark rank did not predict behaviour in a loop. And the hand-coded rule bot still wins Pac-Man by 37 points — the reminder that "can a model do it" and "should a model do it" are different questions.
documents.s: The games table is the honest one

documents.t: Median latency per decision, ~200-token questions: Model RTX PRO 6000 Apple M4 Max (MLX) CPU (32 threads) Jeff-0.8B 22 ms 28 ms 463 ms Jeff-2B 24 ms 60 ms 708 ms Jeff-Gemma4-E2B 29 ms — 1.0 s Two things to take from this: "Tiny model" does not mean "runs anywhere fast." The same 0.8B checkpoint is 22 ms on a GPU and 463 ms on 32 CPU threads — a 21x gap. A decision model is only a decision model at GPU latency; on CPU it is a slow API call you happen to host. If your plan was "sprinkle these calls everywhere in the request path", the CPU column is the plan's budget. 2.5x the parameters cost 2 ms on the big GPU. 22 → 24 ms. At this size a single forward pass over ~200 tokens is dominated by overhead and memory bandwidth, not by arithmetic, so on a fast card the 2B is nearly free relative to the 0.8B — while on the M4 Max the same step costs you 2.1x (28 → 60 ms). Pick your model per deployment target, not from the parameter count. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Serve one locally before you train anything⌄ Install with uv, pull a checkpoint from Hugging Face, start the server. You want the zero-shot number on YOUR data before you decide training is necessary — the most common outcome reported by practitioners is that zero-shot is not good enough, and that is much cheaper to discover in twenty minutes than after a training run. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a labelled dev set of a few hundred real examples⌄ Real traffic, real label distribution, including the ambiguous ones you would normally throw out. This set does double duty: it selects your checkpoint and it fits your temperature. It must never overlap the panel you report numbers on. ←PreviousNext→ 3Measure the boring baseline first⌄ Embeddings plus a logistic-regression head, on the same dev set. On BANKING77 this approach was reported in the Jeff discussion at 93.0% with a model roughly 15x smaller. If it wins on your data, stop here — you have saved yourself a fine-tune and a GPU. ←PreviousNext→ 4Fine-tune only the gap you measured⌄ One epoch, batch 256, cross-entropy over the option letters, lr around 5e-6. Keep at least half your training examples in the exact panel layout you will use at inference. Select the checkpoint on the dev set. ←PreviousNext→ 5Fit the temperature, then report both numbers⌄ One scalar on the dev set, stored with the checkpoint. Then publish accuracy AND calibration error to yourself. An uncalibrated decision model is a classifier with a confidence field you are not allowed to trust — which defeats the entire purpose of the category. ←PreviousNext→ 6Set the threshold from the reliability curve, not from a round number⌄ Find the confidence at which observed accuracy is actually good enough to skip a human or a frontier model. Everything below it escalates. That number is a property of your data and will not be 0.9 just because 0.9 looks tidy. ←PreviousNext→ Serve a Jev-compatible model locally and send it a real request CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Apple silicon (MLX backend) uv sync --no-default-groups --extra mac uv run --no-default-groups hf download mstrasser/Jeff-Qwen3.5-0.8B --local-dir checkpoints/jeff-0.8b JEFF_BACKEND=mlx JEFF_CHECKPOINT=checkpoints/jeff-0.8b PORT=8765 \ uv run --no-default-groups --extra mac jeff-serve # Two independent questions, one request, one parallel pass curl -s localhost:8765/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{ "model": "jeff-latest", "state": "Refund request: the customer says the parcel arrived crushed and wants their money back.", "questions": { "route": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": {"1": "Refunds and payments", "2": "Damaged or lost parcels", "3": "Account and login problems"}}, "angry": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer angry?"} } }'

The sharpest criticism in the Hacker News thread was not that Jeff performs badly. It was structural: if you have to fine-tune it on your own labelled data anyway, you have not bought a zero-shot classifier — you have bought a somewhat awkward way to train a classifier, and the field already has cheaper ones. The numbers in that thread support taking it seriously. A commenter reported testing the 0.8B zero-shot on job-ad classification and finding it unusable, with the 2B still missing categories. Another reported that plain embeddings plus a logistic-regression head reached 93.0% on BANKING77 using a model about 15x smaller than the decision models being compared — against the 87.4%-confidence/75.3%-accuracy shape the independent Jev pilot found on the same dataset. So the honest decision table: Situation Use Handful of fixed labels, plenty of examples, latency matters Embeddings + logistic regression. Smallest, fastest, trains in seconds. Beat this before considering anything else. Labels change often, or questions are written in prose per request Zero-shot decision model — the schema is the interface, which is the actual product One high-volume domain, you have labels, you have a GPU for an afternoon Fine-tune. Jeff's chess run went 15.5% → 55.8%; a voice-navigation fine-tune on ~11,000 examples went 31.7% → 95.8% in under 30 minutes Genuinely hard, multi-step judgements Reasoning — Jeeves, or a frontier model behind a cascade You need it working this afternoon and the volume is low Hosted API. Your own GPU is not free either The general rule underneath: a decision model earns its place when the schema is the valuable part — arbitrary typed questions, in prose, resolved in one pass. When your label set is fixed and known, you are paying model-shaped costs for classifier-shaped work.
documents.s: The uncomfortable question: do you need a model at all?

documents.t: Jev's founding pitch was that this class of model does not generate text. PostHog's Jeeves tests that premise directly by letting a decision model think first, then decide, on Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA r=16 and a pointer head. Training runs in three stages: SFT (19,126 questions from 12 public datasets plus synthetic policy data, half carrying reasoning chains, 2 epochs / 596 steps on 8 GPUs), then CISPO reinforcement learning (9,992 questions, 8 rollouts each at temperature 1, thinking capped at 2,560 tokens — a 624-step schedule deliberately stopped at step 402 because calibration was degrading past it), then the same scalar temperature fit. Reported results: Benchmark Jeeves Jev Kev-9B Test overall 0.889 0.857 0.822 JevBench overall (231 items) 0.935 0.866 0.715 JevBench hard (111 items) 0.865 0.730 0.451 And the ablation that matters more than any of those rows: 0.804 without reasoning, 0.840 with it. Thinking is worth about 3.6 points on this model. Now price it. On one H100, Jeeves answers in ~0.3 s with reasoning off and 3.3 s median with it on — 17.1 s at p90. That is roughly 11x the median latency and a tail an order of magnitude worse, for 3.6 points. The README's own mitigation is the interesting engineering: cap thinking at 2,560 tokens and add a 0.9 confidence threshold that stops early when the model is already sure, which brings the median to 2.0 s. Reasoning becomes something you spend only on the items that need it. Two caveats Jeeves publishes about itself: it is worse than Jev on knowledge-heavy tasks (MMLU 0.793 vs 0.900) — reasoning does not add facts — and its reasoning chains were never rewarded for language consistency, so they are not reliably readable. If you wanted the chain as an audit trail, check that it is legible before you promise anyone it is.

Wording consistency beats wording quality. Jeff reports Frogger crossings going from 15 to 23 purely by phrasing every option the same way as its siblings. Options are compared against each other in one pass — asymmetric phrasing is a thumb on the scale. Keep keys short and put the description in the text. Prompt formats do not port between decision models. Jev's bearing-number style did not transfer to Jeff; consequence-focused wording was needed instead. Treat a switch of decision model as a re-tuning job, exactly like porting prompts across models. The 26-option ceiling is silent. Nothing errors. Options 27+ simply never win. Chunk large label sets into a two-stage decision instead. English, text-only for Jeff. AutoJev accepts base64 images; Jeff does not. Zero-shot quality is workload-shaped and often disappointing. Multiple practitioners reported the small models being unusable on their own real classification tasks. Measure on your data on day one. Training-data leak filtering is your job. Jeff generates synthetic data locally with leak filtering precisely because a decision model trained near its eval panel produces a number that means nothing. Both repos are days old. Flags, checkpoint names and defaults are moving. Nothing here substitutes for the current README. DIY decision-model vocabulary girarTérminoOption-letter cross-entropyDefiniciónThe Jeff/AutoJev training objective: lay options out as a lettered panel and train plain cross-entropy on the correct letter token, then read and renormalise the letter logits at inference. Cheap — and the reason the option count stops at 26.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 8 Siguiente→ Check yourself 0/5 1Jeff-0.8B scores 96.4% on Financial PhraseBank against Jev's 77.0%, but 64.0% on BBH against Jev's 94.3%. What is the right conclusion? Jeff is better than Jev overall, since it wins the more practical benchmarkThe overall score averages two very different regimes — pick per workload shape: narrow pattern tasks favour the small fine-tune, multi-step reasoning does notThe benchmarks contradict each other, so neither is usableJev is only better because it is larger, so a larger Jeff would beat it everywhere 2Why does Jeff cap you at 26 options per question? Attention over more than 26 options becomes numerically unstableIt is a licensing restriction inherited from Qwen3.5Options are encoded as single letter tokens A–Z and trained with cross-entropy on that letter, so the alphabet is the ceiling26 is the largest option count present in any public benchmark 3Your fine-tuned decision model hits 88% accuracy on your dev set. What still has to be done before you let it skip human review? Nothing — 88% accuracy is the relevant number for an automation thresholdFit a temperature and check calibration, then set the threshold from the reliability curve rather than from a round numberRetrain for more epochs until accuracy exceeds 95%Switch to the 2B model, since larger models are better calibrated by default 4Jeeves reports 0.804 accuracy with reasoning off and 0.840 with it on, at 0.3 s versus 3.3 s median (17.1 s p90). What is the engineering takeaway? Always enable reasoning — 3.6 points is a large gain for a classifierNever enable reasoning — an 11x latency cost can never be justifiedSpend reasoning selectively: a confidence threshold that stops early on easy items recovered most of the gain at 2.0 s medianThe 9B model is simply too small, and reasoning would be free on a larger one 5Before training your own decision model on a fixed label set, which baseline should you measure first? The largest open-weight model you can fit, zero-shotSentence embeddings plus a logistic-regression head — reported at 93.0% on BANKING77 with a roughly 15x smaller modelA hand-written regular-expression rulesetThe hosted API at its lowest confidence threshold

Intermedio "¿Cuánto cuesta la IA?" no tiene una única respuesta: depende de qué arquetipo de precios estás comprando y cuánto lo usas en realidad. Las cifras en dólares cambian cada pocos meses; la estructura del coste apenas se mueve. Esta página enseña la forma duradera: las tres maneras en que se cobra la IA, cómo estimar una carga de trabajo antes de construirla, las palancas que reducen la factura y la verdadera bifurcación entre alquilar una API y autohospedar. What you'll learn Distinguir los tres arquetipos de coste: API por token, suscripción plana y abierto/autohospedado Estimar el coste de cualquier carga de trabajo a partir de tokens × tarifa × volumen, antes de lanzarla Accionar las grandes palancas que reducen el gasto sin dañar la calidad Saber cuándo lo abierto/autohospedado gana en coste a la API, y cuándo gana la API Saber qué números caducan rápido, y dónde comprobar la verdad de hoy Última verificación: 2026-06-28. Las tarifas por token, los niveles de suscripción, los descuentos de caché y batch, y cuál es el modelo más barato cambian casi cada mes: trata cada cifra concreta en dólares como perecedera. Esta página enseña el modelo duradero (arquetipos + cómo estimar + las palancas); para los números de hoy consulta la propia página de precios de cada proveedor (enlazada en Fuentes), un tracker independiente como Artificial Analysis, y haz las cuentas en nuestra Calculadora de coste. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Cuánto cuesta realmente la IA (entre proveedores)

documents.t: Casi todas las formas de pagar por IA se reducen a una de tres formas. Aprende las formas, no los precios. API por token (basada en uso). Llamas a un modelo alojado a través de una API y pagas por token, y la entrada y la salida se cobran por separado, con la salida casi siempre como la más cara de las dos. Los modelos más grandes/inteligentes cuestan más por token; los más pequeños cuestan mucho menos. La mayoría de los proveedores también ofrecen descuentos: una tarifa reducida para la entrada en caché que reenvías, y un descuento por batch fijo para trabajos asíncronos no urgentes. Así es como pagas cuando construyes un producto sobre Claude, GPT o Gemini. El coste escala directamente con el uso: céntimos a pequeña escala, la partida dominante a gran escala. Suscripción plana de consumidor/asiento. Una cuota mensual fija por una app de chat o un asistente de IDE (los planes de consumidor de Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini, los asientos tipo Copilot). No ves tokens; obtienes un cupo de uso y límites de tasa. Predecible y barato para un humano ante un teclado, pero no escala a trabajo programático/de alto volumen, y los costes por asiento se acumulan en un equipo. Abierto / local (autohospedado). Ejecutas un modelo de pesos abiertos (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) en tu propio hardware o en una GPU alquilada. No hay precio por llamada: pagas por el hardware (o alquiler de GPU por hora) + electricidad + operaciones, esté el modelo ocupado o inactivo. El coste marginal de una llamada más es prácticamente casi cero a escala, pero cargas con el coste fijo y la carga operativa. Mira Ejecutar modelos localmente con Ollama. Pro tip La división clave: la API y las suscripciones son coste MARGINAL (pagas por uso); el autohospedaje es sobre todo coste FIJO (pagas por mantener la capacidad disponible, se use o no). En la API, la mayor sorpresa es que los tokens de SALIDA normalmente cuestan varias veces más que los de entrada: las respuestas verbosas cuestan dinero real. Una suscripción plana es la herramienta correcta para un humano chateando; la API por token es la herramienta correcta para una app llamando al modelo en un bucle.

Puedes dimensionar una factura de API antes de escribir una línea de código en producción. Todo el modelo es una fórmula: coste ≈ (tokens de entrada × tarifa de entrada) + (tokens de salida × tarifa de salida), por llamada × número de llamadas Las tarifas se cotizan por millón de tokens, y la entrada y la salida tienen tarifas diferentes, así que estima las dos mitades por separado y súmalas. Una regla aproximada de tokens: ~1 token ≈ 4 caracteres de inglés, o ~0,75 palabras. Para conteos exactos, usa el área del Estimador de tokens y lee Tokens y precios. La mecánica completa de dónde se esconden los tokens vive en La economía de los tokens. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Dimensiona los tokens de UNA llamada⌄ Suma la entrada: prompt de sistema + herramientas + contexto recuperado + historial + el turno del usuario. Luego estima la salida que pides. Cuenta entrada y salida por separado: se cobran distinto. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiplica cada lado por su propia tarifa⌄ tokens de entrada × tarifa de entrada, más tokens de salida × tarifa de salida. Usa los números por millón de hoy de la página de precios del proveedor (no confíes en una cifra que memorizaste; mira VerifyNote). ←PreviousNext→ 3Escala por el volumen real⌄ Multiplica el coste por llamada por llamadas al día × días. Un coste trivial por llamada (fracciones de céntimo) se convierte en tu mayor partida con millones de llamadas: modela tu tráfico REAL, no una sola petición. ←PreviousNext→ 4Aplica los descuentos que usarás de verdad⌄ Si una gran parte de la entrada se repite en cada llamada, cótizala a la tarifa de CACHÉ, no a la de entrada completa. Si el trabajo es offline, aplica el descuento por BATCH. Estos cambian la respuesta drásticamente a escala. ←PreviousNext→ 5Contrasta con un tracker, luego recorta⌄ Compara tus supuestos por token con un tracker independiente y nuestra Calculadora de coste, luego ataca la factura con las palancas de abajo. ←PreviousNext→ Estimación de servilleta (rellena las tarifas de hoy) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.
documents.s: Cómo estimar el coste de una carga de trabajo

documents.t: La mayoría de las cargas de trabajo reales llevan peso muerto. Estas palancas, aproximadamente en orden de apalancamiento, reducen el gasto sin tocar la calidad: acciona primero las estructurales baratas. Ajusta el tamaño del modelo. No pagues tarifa de buque insignia por un trabajo que hace bien un modelo pequeño/barato. Clasificación, extracción, enrutamiento y formateo simple suelen ir genial en el nivel más pequeño a una fracción del precio por token. Reserva el modelo grande para razonamiento genuinamente difícil, y considera el enrutamiento: el modelo barato maneja la mayoría fácil, escala solo los casos difíciles. Mira Elegir un modelo. Recorta el contexto que envías. El token más barato es el que nunca envías. Poda prompts de sistema inflados, compacta historiales largos en un resumen continuo, y expón solo las herramientas que la tarea necesita: cada una es entrada que vuelves a pagar en cada llamada. RAG en vez de meter un contexto enorme. Pegar un documento de 50 páginas para responder una pregunta paga 50 páginas en cada llamada. La recuperación trae solo los pocos pasajes relevantes: muchos menos tokens de entrada para la misma respuesta (a menudo mejor). Recurre a una ventana de contexto gigante solo cuando realmente necesites todo el corpus a la vista a la vez. Caché de prompts. Si muchas llamadas comparten un prefijo grande e invariable (prompt de sistema, catálogo de herramientas, documento de referencia), la caché lo procesa una vez y lo vuelve a servir con un fuerte descuento en cada llamada posterior. El cambio estructural de mayor apalancamiento para cargas de chat y agente, porque se paga solo en cada turno. Agrupa lo no urgente. Evals, etiquetado masivo, resumir un archivo: cualquier cosa donde no necesites la respuesta en segundos corre por una vía batch asíncrona con un descuento fijo en la mayoría de proveedores. Cambia inmediatez por una factura materialmente menor. Acorta la salida. La salida es el lado más caro. Pide JSON o un esquema ajustado en lugar de un párrafo charlatán: menos tokens de salida y sin adivinanzas de parseo aguas abajo. Modelos más pequeños / abiertos para la parte fácil. Para la mayoría de llamadas de alto volumen y baja dificultad, un modelo abierto o pequeño puede ser drásticamente más barato por llamada, a veces casi gratis si ya autohospedas. Reserva el modelo de frontera para los casos que realmente lo necesitan. Pro tip Estas se multiplican entre sí: entrada en caché × modelo bien dimensionado × salida más breve × descuento por batch se compone en un gran recorte total en una tarea fácil, con la calidad intacta. Acciona las palancas estructurales (dimensionar, cachear, RAG, batch) antes de microoptimizar la redacción: mueven la factura mucho más. SIEMPRE MIDE el cambio contra la factura real, no contra una suposición. El manual profundo es La economía de los tokens.
documents.s: Las grandes palancas para reducir el coste

documents.t: Esta es la decisión que de verdad mueve tu presupuesto de IA. Es un cruce de coste fijo frente a marginal, y el volumen es la variable que lo decide. Lo abierto/autohospedado gana con volumen ALTO y estable. Una vez que ejecutas suficientes llamadas para mantener una GPU ocupada la mayor parte del tiempo, el coste marginal casi cero por llamada supera pagar por token para siempre. Amortizas el coste fijo de hardware/alquiler entre un número enorme de llamadas, ganas privacidad de datos y personalización total, y aceptas la carga operativa (aprovisionamiento, escalado, disponibilidad, MLOps) como precio de entrada. La API gana con volumen BAJO o irregular, o sin infraestructura. Si el tráfico es pequeño, a ráfagas o impredecible, pagar por token significa que pagas solo por lo que usas y nada cuando está inactivo: ninguna GPU caliente a las 3 de la mañana. También te saltas todas las operaciones. Para la mayoría de equipos que lanzan un producto, prototipan o tienen tráfico a ráfagas, la API es a la vez más barata y mucho menos trabajo. Watch out El autohospedaje rara vez es 'gratis'. Los pesos del modelo pueden ser gratis, pero las GPU, la electricidad y las horas de ingeniería para mantenerlo en marcha no lo son: cuéntalos con honestidad antes de proclamar un ahorro. Las GPU inactivas son pura pérdida: la infraestructura de coste fijo solo supera al precio por token cuando la utilización es ALTA. El tráfico bajo o a ráfagas favorece a la API cada vez. El punto de cruce se mueve cada vez que bajan los precios de API o se abarata el hardware: rehaz las cuentas periódicamente, no decidas una vez y lo olvides. Vocabulario de coste de IA girarTérminoPrecios por token (basados en uso)DefiniciónPagas por token en una API alojada, con entrada y salida cotizadas por separado (la salida normalmente más cara). Escala directamente con el uso: barato en pequeño, dominante a escala.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 6 Siguiente→ Compruébate 0/3 1En una API por token, ¿qué lado de la factura es casi siempre más caro? Tokens de entrada (lo que envías)Tokens de salida (lo que genera el modelo)Siempre se cobran igual 2Tienes tráfico bajo, a ráfagas e impredecible y ninguna infraestructura de ML. ¿Qué suele ser más barato? Autohospedar un modelo abierto en tu propia GPUUna API por token donde pagas solo por lo que usasComprar una suscripción plana de consumidor por desarrollador 3¿Cuál es la forma más fiable de reducir una factura de API en una tarea fácil y de alto volumen? Cambiar cada llamada al mayor modelo buque insigniaAjustar a un modelo más pequeño, cachear el prefijo repetido y agrupar el trabajo no urgenteAñadir más ejemplos al prompt de sistema Key takeaways Tres arquetipos: API por token (basada en uso, entrada vs salida cotizadas por separado), suscripción plana (predecible, no escala a alto volumen) y abierto/autohospedado (coste fijo, casi cero por llamada). Estima antes de construir: (entrada × tarifa de entrada) + (salida × tarifa de salida), por llamada × volumen, luego aplica los descuentos de caché y batch. Mayores palancas: dimensionar el modelo, recortar contexto, RAG sobre contexto enorme, caché de prompts, agrupar lo no urgente, acortar la salida. El autohospedaje gana con volumen ALTO y estable (amortiza el coste fijo); la API gana con volumen BAJO/irregular o sin infraestructura (pagas solo por uso). Cada cifra en dólares caduca rápido: verifica en la página de precios del proveedor y en un tracker, y haz tus propias cuentas en la Calculadora de coste.

Intermedio A chat turn costs a fraction of a cent. The same question handed to an agent — one that reads files, calls tools, and loops until done — can cost dollars. Teams are discovering this the hard way: a coding agent left running racks up a bill that a human at a keyboard never would. The scary part isn't the average; it's that you can't predict it in advance, and the cost of the same task can swing wildly. This page explains why agents burn tokens (the mechanism is not what most people guess), shows the numbers that surprise even experienced builders, and gives you the four levers that actually cut the bill — the same levers whether you're on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or a home-grown loop over any model. What you'll learn Explain the context snowball — why agent cost grows roughly QUADRATICALLY with steps, not linearly Cite the real multipliers: agentic tasks ~1000x a chat's tokens, and the SAME task varying up to 30x Know when a second agent is worth it — and the benchmark showing it usually isn't Pull the four cost levers that work: budget caps, prompt caching, model-tier routing, context pruning Diagnose a runaway agent bill and put a hard ceiling on it Última verificación: 2026-07-15. Per-token prices, per-developer monthly spend, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every dollar figure here as perishable and illustrative. The mechanism (context snowball, re-read tax) and the levers are durable; the exact ratios come from 2026 benchmarks and research linked in Sources. Confirm today's rates on each provider's pricing page before quoting a bill to anyone. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: Why AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Here's the trap. A chat is one turn — one input, one output, done. An agent is a loop: it reads a task, takes an action, reads the result, takes the next action, and so on until the job is finished. The catch is that on every step, the model re-reads the entire accumulated conversation so far — the original prompt, every prior action, and every tool result — before deciding what to do next. So the input grows on every step, and you pay for the whole snowball again each time it rolls forward: Step 1 processes the prompt. Step 2 re-reads the prompt + step 1's action + result. Step 3 re-reads all of that + step 2's action + result. …and so on. Add up the input across a run and the total scales roughly with the square of the number of steps, not linearly. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab found agentic tasks to be "uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat" — and crucially, it's the input tokens that dominate, not the output. The agent isn't writing more; it's re-reading more. What you'll learn The cost driver is re-reading, not thinking. Each loop step re-processes the full transcript, so a 20-step run pays for early context ~20 times over. This is why 'just let the agent figure it out' is expensive: every extra step it takes multiplies against everything before it. Output-heavy tasks (write me an essay) are cheap by comparison; input-heavy loops (explore this repo, then fix the bug) are where the money goes.
documents.s: The context snowball: why cost grows quadratically

documents.t: Three figures reset most people's intuition: ~1000x. Agentic tasks can consume roughly a thousand times the tokens of an equivalent chat or code-completion, per the Stanford analysis — driven by the snowball above, not by a bigger model. Up to 30x variance on the same task. The same agent, run on the same task, can cost up to 30x more one time than another — because the path it takes (how many tools it calls, how far it wanders) is non-deterministic. You genuinely cannot know the bill until it's done. This is why "result-based pricing" for agents is so hard: you only see the cost after everything runs. More agents rarely pay for themselves. 2026 production benchmarks found that a multi-agent setup added only ~2.1% accuracy at 2x the cost versus a well-configured single agent on 64% of tasks. A hierarchical-supervisor pattern pushed a document task from 85% → 95% accuracy — but at roughly $0.15/task vs $0.003 for the single agent (~50x). More agents buys a little accuracy for a lot of money. Watch out Because the same task varies up to 30x, an average-based budget WILL be blown by the tail. Cap the ceiling, don't budget the mean. Adding agents to 'be safe' usually multiplies cost far faster than it adds accuracy. Reach for a second agent only when the task genuinely decomposes into parallel, independent subtasks.

Before the loop even starts, how the agent reaches its tools sets a floor on cost. Connecting a set of MCP servers can inject tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions into every step of the snowball. A rough comparison many builders hit: a plain CLI command averages ~200 tokens, while the equivalent MCP operation can cost 32k–82k tokens once tool schemas and wrapping are counted. That gap rides along on every loop step. That doesn't make MCP wrong — it's the right choice for auth, multi-tenancy, and governed access. It means the tool surface is a cost lever you chose at design time. AILmanac has a dedicated deep-dive: The MCP Token Tax covers Tool Search, deferred loading, and code execution as the three fixes.
documents.s: Your tool surface is part of the bill

documents.t: Optimization advice is endless; only four levers move the number materially. In rough order of leverage: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Cap the budget — a hard ceiling, not a hope⌄ Set a per-run or per-user token/dollar cap that HARD-STOPS the agent. Because the same task can cost 30x more on a bad run, a ceiling is the only thing that bounds the tail. Most agent harnesses expose a max-tokens or max-steps limit — use it. This is the single most important control. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cache the stable prefix⌄ The system prompt, tool definitions, and house rules are re-sent on every loop step (the snowball). Prompt caching charges those repeated tokens at a fraction of the input rate. On a long agentic run this is often the biggest single saving, because the cached part is exactly what gets re-read the most. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route by model tier⌄ Don't run one frontier model for the whole loop. Use a cheap, fast model (Haiku-class, or a small open model) for the grunt work — reading files, formatting, routine tool calls — and reserve the expensive frontier model for the hard reasoning or the orchestrator role. Orchestrator-worker splits with cheaper workers cut cost 40–60% in production benchmarks at near-parity accuracy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prune the context aggressively⌄ The snowball is the problem, so shrink it. Compact old turns, drop tool outputs the agent no longer needs, summarize instead of carrying raw transcripts, and start fresh sub-tasks with a clean context instead of one ever-growing thread. Every token you remove is a token you stop paying for on EVERY remaining step. ←PreviousNext→ Audit a runaway agent (paste your run's token breakdown) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a cost engineer. Here is a token-usage breakdown of one agentic run (input vs output tokens per step, tool calls, model used). Diagnose where the money went, in priority order: 1. Is input or output driving cost? (Agents are almost always input-heavy.) 2. Which repeated content should be prompt-CACHED (system prompt, tools, rules)? 3. Which steps could run on a CHEAPER model without losing correctness? 4. Where is context snowballing — what can be pruned, compacted, or summarized? 5. What is a safe per-run token CAP that stops the worst tail without hurting the median run? Give me the estimated % saving per fix and the ONE change to make first.
documents.s: The four levers that actually cut the bill

documents.t: The cheapest agentic run is the one you don't make. If a task is a single, well-specified transformation — summarize this, classify that, rewrite this — a plain chat/completion call does it at a fraction of the cost, with no snowball at all. Reach for an agent when the work genuinely requires reading, deciding, acting, and re-checking in a loop against a changing environment (explore a repo, debug across files, drive a browser). If you can write the exact steps yourself, script them — don't pay a model to re-derive them every run. girarTérminoContext snowballDefiniciónThe accumulated transcript an agent re-reads on every loop step. It grows each step, so total input cost scales ~quadratically with the number of steps.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 5 Siguiente→ Check yourself 0/3 1Why does an agentic run cost so much more than a single chat turn for the same question? Agents use a bigger, more expensive model by defaultEach loop step re-reads the whole accumulated transcript, so input cost grows roughly quadratically with stepsOutput tokens are priced far higher for agentsAgents disable prompt caching 2A teammate wants to add a second and third agent 'to be safe' on a task a single agent already handles at 85% accuracy. What do the 2026 benchmarks suggest? Always add agents — accuracy scales linearly with agent countExtra agents typically buy a little accuracy for a lot of cost (e.g. +10 points but ~50x/task); add them only when the task truly decomposesMulti-agent is always cheaper because each agent is smallerIt makes no difference to cost 3Given that the SAME task can cost up to 30x more on one run than another, what's the right way to control spend? Budget for the average run costSet a hard per-run token/dollar cap that stops the agent, since the tail — not the mean — blows the budgetTurn off tool useOnly run agents overnight
