Intermedio On September 28, 2026 AMD announced it is acquiring World Labs for about $8.2 billion in stock — its second-largest deal ever, behind only Xilinx — and Fei-Fei Li will join as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting to Lisa Su. A day later OpenAI's DevDay took the front page. Between them, "world model" became the phrase of the week. Here is the problem with the phrase. Two products that share it are architecturally opposite. One keeps the world inside the model and streams you frames as you move; it is interactive, it cannot be exported, and a session is capped in seconds. The other generates a 3D scene you download, own and render yourself for free; it is persistent, engine-ready, and completely inert. Picking the wrong one is not a preference mistake, it is a re-architecture. This page is the practical split: what each family really produces, the verified API and export details, the one benchmark that settles a common assumption, the open weights you can run on your own GPU, and the five things neither family will do for you. What you'll learn Tell the two families of world model apart, and pick by what you need to persist Know the real limits: the 60-second wall, the physics disclaimer, the export tier that gates commercial rights Read the World API correctly — async operations, the WLT-Api-Key header, and which splat formats come out Use the WorldScore evidence instead of vibes when choosing between a video model and a 3D model Run an open world model yourself, and understand why inverse dynamics is the part worth $8.2 billion Última verificación: 2026-09-30. Deal terms from AMD's own newsroom release: approximately $8.2 billion, all stock, announced September 28, 2026, expected to close by the end of 2026 subject to regulatory approval — so it is not closed, and product roadmaps may move once it is. Project Genie access, Marble plan tiers and World API pricing are all live commercial surfaces that change without notice; the resolution and frame-rate figures for Genie 3 come from third-party reporting, not from Google's Project Genie post, which states only the 60-second generation limit. WorldScore leaderboard positions move as teams submit. Read the linked primary sources before you quote any number here. Confirma con la fuente oficial.
documents.s: World Models: What You Can Actually Build Today

documents.t: Frame generators 3D generators Examples Genie 3 / Project Genie, driving world models Marble (World Labs) What it outputs A video stream, frame by frame, conditioned on your actions A scene: Gaussian splats, panoramas, optionally a mesh Where the world lives Inside the model's rolling context In a file you download Interactive? Yes — that is the whole point No. You navigate it, but it does not react Exportable? No geometry to export Yes — SPZ, PLY, GLB, collider meshes Cost shape Per second of interaction, per viewer, forever Once at generation. Rendering is then yours Fails by Drifting, forgetting, running out of session Being static and not simulating anything If you need a world that responds — a player pressing a key, a robot policy taking an action and seeing what happens — you need a frame generator. If you need a world that persists — an asset in your game, a set in your render pipeline, a scene five users load next month and see identically — you need a 3D generator. Almost every confused "why can't it just…" question on this topic is someone holding one and asking for the other.

Google's Project Genie went from research preview to a public-ish product on January 29, 2026. The access shape is narrow and worth knowing before you plan around it: Google AI Ultra subscribers, United States only, 18+, and explicitly not available on Google AI Ultra for Business. Google calls it an "experimental research prototype". The limit that teaches you the most is Google's own: generations are limited to 60 seconds. That is not a billing decision, it is a state problem. In a frame generator the world is not stored anywhere — it is implied by the model's context. Every frame is predicted from the prompt, the accumulated frames and your actions. Consistency is therefore bounded by the same thing that bounds a long chat: how much history the model can hold and keep coherent. Walk away from a wall and back, and whether the wall is still there is a memory question, not a rendering one. Google's stated caveats are the rest of the honest spec sheet: generated worlds "might not look completely true-to-life or always adhere closely to prompts or images, or real-world physics", and characters "can sometimes be less controllable, or experience higher latency in control". Read that physics line carefully if you were planning to use a frame generator as a simulator. It is a plausibility engine, not a solver. Nothing guarantees momentum is conserved between frame 300 and frame 301.
documents.s: The frame generators, and the 60-second wall

documents.t: Interactive generation at the commonly reported 24 fps gives you about 41.7 ms per frame, end to end, including your input reaching the server. That single number explains most of the product decisions in this family: why sessions are short, why access is gated to a paid tier, why there is no public API yet, and why the cost curve is per viewer-second rather than per asset. You are not buying a file. You are renting a GPU that must beat a 42-millisecond deadline for as long as someone is looking.

World Labs' Marble turns text, an image, a panorama, multiple views or a video clip into a navigable 3D scene. The important engineering fact is the representation: the output is 3D Gaussian splats, not a mesh. Splats are millions of small, oriented, semi-transparent blobs with colour and view-dependent shading. They photo-reconstruct beautifully and render fast on commodity GPUs. They also have no surfaces, no edges and no faces — which is why the next section matters more than it looks. What Marble's own export docs say you get: Export Availability Gaussian splats — SPZ and PLY Standard plan 360 panoramas Standard plan Collider meshes Standard plan Textured mesh (GLB) + commercial rights Pro plan only Anything at all Not on Free — generate only Two gotchas live in that table. First, collider meshes are a separate export — you need them because you cannot raycast, collide or do physics against splats directly. The splats are what the player sees; the collider mesh is what the engine tests against. Ship only the splats and your beautiful world has no floor. Second, commercial rights are tied to the Pro tier, not to the act of exporting. Check the plan before you put a generated world in a product. Marble's docs also note that lower-resolution exports are "optimized to be as perceptually similar as possible to the higher-resolution files" — a hint that you should test the small tier before paying to ship the big one.
documents.s: The 3D generators, and what you actually receive

documents.t: A detail several write-ups get wrong: SPZ is Niantic's format, open-sourced by Niantic Spatial, not a World Labs invention — Marble simply exports to it. It is worth using anyway. SPZ stores each spherical-harmonics coefficient as an 8-bit signed integer with optional further quantisation, landing at roughly 10× smaller than the equivalent PLY with no perceptible quality loss. Niantic's own testing puts around 5 bits as the sweet spot for most scenes, with essentially-zero MSE at 8 bits and about 18× compression at 3. SPZ 4, released in 2026, splits compression into six parallel ZSTD streams — one per attribute class — for roughly 3–5× faster compression and 1.5–2× faster end-to-end loading at the same ~10× size advantage. If you are shipping splats over the web, that is the difference between a scene that loads and one that does not.
documents.s: SPZ: the 10× that is not World Labs'

documents.t: The World API exposes Marble's generation to your own code. The verified shape, from World Labs' docs index and its official Python client: Inputs: text, images, panoramas, multi-view inputs, video. Outputs: splats in SPZ, PLY, SOGS, KSPLAT and SPLAT. Auth: an API key passed in the WLT-Api-Key header; the Python client reads WORLDLABS_API_KEY from the environment. Execution model: asynchronous. You submit a generation, get an operation back, and poll until it is done. There is also a credit-balance endpoint, media upload/retrieve, and world create/retrieve/list/export/delete. Client: worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python, Python 3.12+. A CUDA GPU is only needed for local rendering, not for API use. Pricing: usage-based. Generate a world from text and poll for it CopyOpen in Claude↗ # github.com/worldlabsai/worldlabs-api-python (Python 3.12+) # export WORLDLABS_API_KEY=... from worldlabs_api.client import WorldLabsClient from worldlabs_api.models import WorldTextPrompt, WorldsGenerateRequest client = WorldLabsClient(api_key="your-key-here") request = WorldsGenerateRequest( display_name="Mystical Forest", world_prompt=WorldTextPrompt(text_prompt="A mystical forest"), ) op = client.generate_world(request) # returns an operation, not a world done = client.poll_operation(op.operation_id) # poll until done is true world = done.response Design your integration around that async boundary from day one. World generation is a job, not a request — the same lesson as batch inference or video generation. If your handler waits inline for a world, you will rewrite it.

World Labs also maintains Spark, an MIT-licensed 3D Gaussian splatting renderer for THREE.js / WebGL2, so a generated world can ship as a web page. It loads .PLY, .SPZ, .SPLAT, .KSPLAT and .SOG, fuses splats with ordinary meshes in the THREE.js pipeline, and targets the ~98% of devices with WebGL2. Spark 2.0 (April 15, 2026) is the release that makes big scenes viable in a browser: a level-of-detail splat tree that renders a fixed number of splats per frame regardless of scene size, a streaming .RAD format that supports HTTP Range requests so a coarse proxy appears almost instantly and refines progressively, and virtual splat paging against a fixed GPU memory pool so scenes larger than GPU memory still render — including on phones and Quest 3. Put a generated world on the web CopyOpen in Claude↗ npm install @sparkjsdev/spark three # docs and live examples: https://sparkjs.dev # repo: https://github.com/sparkjsdev/spark # # Export from Marble as .spz (≈10x smaller than .ply), serve it as a # static file, and load it into a THREE.js scene with Spark. # For scenes over a few hundred MB, convert to .RAD so the viewer can # range-request a coarse proxy first. Note what just happened to your cost curve. After generation, you are serving a static file from a CDN and rendering on the user's GPU. Serving the world is free. That is the inverse of the frame-generator model, where every viewer-second is inference.
documents.s: Rendering it without a game engine

documents.t: "Just use a video model" is the most common shortcut here, and there is now a benchmark that answers it. WorldScore (Stanford, arXiv:2504.00983) is a unified benchmark for world generation across 3D, 4D, text-to-video and image-to-video models — about 3,000 examples, with metrics for controllability, consistency, perceptual quality and motion, and explicit 3D consistency and camera-control measures. The result that should change a decision: on WorldScore-Static, dedicated 3D scene generators lead — WonderWorld at 72.69 and LucidDreamer at 70.40 — clearly above the video models. If your requirement is a geometrically consistent world you can move a camera through, a video model is the wrong tool even when its individual frames look better. Two caveats. The leaderboard is live and moves as teams submit. And WorldScore-Static measures exactly what its name says — a static world; strong static consistency tells you nothing about dynamics.

You do not need a vendor's API to have a world model. NVIDIA published Cosmos 3 — an open omnimodel for physical AI — with weights on Hugging Face: Model Size Runs on nvidia/Cosmos3-Edge 4B Edge devices, robots, vision agents nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano 16B = 8B reasoner + 8B generator Workstation class, e.g. RTX PRO 6000 nvidia/Cosmos3-Super 64B = 32B reasoner + 32B generator Hopper / Blackwell, large-scale synthetic data Architecturally it is a Mixture-of-Transformers handling text, image, video, audio and action in one model, pairing an autoregressive subsequence for reasoning with a diffusion subsequence for generation. It is wired into Hugging Face Diffusers, so the entry point is ordinary Python. Run an open world model locally CopyOpen in Claude↗ pip install --upgrade diffusers transformers accelerate # Cosmos3-Nano is 16B (8B reasoner + 8B generator); check the model # card on Hugging Face for the licence and the exact torch version # before you build on it. import torch from diffusers import Cosmos3OmniPipeline pipe = Cosmos3OmniPipeline.from_pretrained( "nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 ) Now the part that explains the price tag. Cosmos 3's task table is not a list of video tricks: Input Output What it is Text / image / video Video Video generation Text / video Text Vision-language reasoning Action + image + text Video Forward dynamics — "if I do this, what happens?" Text + video Action Inverse dynamics — "what actions produced this?" Image + text Video and action Policy generation Inverse dynamics is the quiet one. It turns footage into labelled actions — which means ordinary video becomes robot training data, and a generated world becomes a place to train and evaluate a policy without hardware. AMD's own release describes World Labs as building models that "generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments" plus technology for "robotic learning and simulation", and frames the deal around reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI informing its future silicon roadmap. Read as a compute story rather than a graphics story, $8.2 billion for a training-environment flywheel is a different kind of bet than $8.2 billion for a text-to-3D tool.
documents.s: Open weights: Cosmos 3, and what AMD actually bought

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1It is not a reasoning model, and your prompting does not transfer⌄ None of your chain-of-thought, XML-tag or tool-use technique carries over. Conditioning a world model is closer to directing a camera than to instructing an assistant: what matters is the input image, the viewpoint, the described lighting and the action sequence. The one habit that does transfer is source discipline — a clean, well-framed conditioning image beats an elaborate paragraph. ←PreviousNext→ 2It will not give you physics you can trust⌄ Google states plainly that generated worlds may not adhere to real-world physics. Cosmos-style forward dynamics predicts a plausible next observation, which is not the same as solving for one. Use a world model to generate scenarios and a real physics engine to adjudicate them. If a wrong answer costs money or safety, a solver has to be in the loop. ←PreviousNext→ 3Splats will not collide, and a mesh export is a separate thing⌄ Gaussian splats have no surfaces. Raycasts, character controllers, navmeshes and physics all need geometry, which is why Marble exports collider meshes separately and gates high-quality textured GLB to the Pro tier. Plan for two assets per world — the one you see and the one you hit — and budget the mesh export in the tier you actually pay for. ←PreviousNext→ 4A frame-generated world cannot be saved, diffed or versioned⌄ There is no file. The world exists for the length of the session and then it is gone, and a re-run of the same prompt is a different world. That rules out the whole class of workflows built on persistent state: reviewing a level, shipping a fix to it, having two users load the same scene, or asserting in a test that the scene has not changed. If you need any of those, you need exportable geometry. ←PreviousNext→ 5It will not tell you which plan you are allowed to ship on⌄ The export matrix is the licence. Free generates but cannot export at all; splats, panoramas and colliders sit on Standard; textured mesh and commercial rights sit on Pro. For open weights the equivalent step is reading the Hugging Face model card's licence before shipping, not after. This is the cheapest failure on the list to avoid and the most expensive to discover late. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Five jobs a world model will not do for you

documents.t: Game or product asset, multiple users, must look the same tomorrow → 3D generator. Export SPZ for the web or GLB for an engine, and remember the collider. Interactive exploration, one user, novelty is the point → frame generator, and design inside a 60-second session. Training or evaluating a policy → open weights with forward and inverse dynamics, on your own GPU, with a real simulator for anything safety-relevant. A camera moving through a consistent scene → not a video model. WorldScore says so. A frame generator like Project Genie, because it is interactiveA 3D generator like Marble, because the world is an exportable fileA text-to-video model, because it produces the best-looking framesEither — they produce the same thing with different interfaces 2Why is Project Genie's 60-second generation cap a design consequence rather than a pricing choice? Todos los niveles Para fundadores y equipos pequeños, la IA es un multiplicador: hace a la vez el trabajo de un marketer junior, un analista y un asistente. Dirígela bien y reserva el criterio para lo que de verdad importa.

Posicionamiento y mensajes — clava la propuesta de valor y luego deriva el copy a partir de ella. Contenido de marketing — landing pages, correos, anuncios, redes sociales, preguntas frecuentes (consulta Escritura). Comunicación con clientes — redacta respuestas, gestiona quejas, escribe anuncios. Investigación — análisis de mercado y de la competencia (¡verifica!), conjuntos de preguntas para entrevistas con clientes. Antes de cualquier copy, acierta con la frase resumen: Write 3 versions of a value proposition using: for {audience} who {need}, {product} is a {category} that {key benefit}, unlike {alternative}. Then critique each in one line. Todo lo que viene después (anuncios, correos, landing pages) se vuelve más fácil una vez que esto está afinado.

:::warning No inventes pruebas, y cuida las afirmaciones Nunca inventes testimonios, métricas, casos de estudio ni premios — usa marcadores de posición como [insert real number] y rellénalos con datos reales. Vigila las afirmaciones reguladas o no fundamentadas (salud, finanzas, "el número 1", garantías). Verifica los datos y cifras de mercado antes de actuar (Alucinaciones). Protege los datos — no pegues PII de clientes ni cifras confidenciales en herramientas no verificadas (Privacidad). :::

Avanzado Última verificación: 2026-09-23. Runner concurrency caps, queue timeouts and merge-queue settings are platform limits that GitHub changes without much noise. The mechanisms below are stable; re-check the exact numbers against the limits page before you size a pipeline on them. Confirma con la fuente oficial. What you'll learn Know why the merge queue — not the runner budget — is the first thing that breaks under agent PR volume Do the batching arithmetic: how a few points of failure rate collapse speculative merging Rank the four levers correctly, because 'add more runners' is the weakest one Ship a gate that proves an agent's test actually fails without the agent's fix Quarantine flakes on evidence instead of vibes, and know the caching gotcha that silently poisons CI Your coding agents work. That is the problem. A team that merged 5 pull requests a day and now merges 40 has not changed its test suite, its runner budget, or its branch protection rules. It has changed the arrival rate into a queueing system that was tuned for the old one. Everything downstream — merge queue, flaky-test noise, runner concurrency, review attention — was sized for human throughput, and queueing systems do not degrade gracefully. They hold, hold, hold, then fall over inside a week. This page is the pipeline side of the verification bottleneck. That page asks who checks the code. This one asks whether your CI can physically absorb the volume, and what to do when it can't.

−7.2%. DORA's 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps report modelled a 25% increase in AI adoption and estimated a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability alongside a 1.5% decrease in throughput. Individual productivity and job satisfaction went up. Delivery-level outcomes went down — the report ties this to larger changesets and weaker batching discipline. The 2025 follow-up reframes it: AI is an amplifier, magnifying whatever your delivery system already is. A pipeline that was fragile at 5 PRs/day becomes unusable at 40. 19%. METR's randomised trial (July 2025) took 16 experienced open-source maintainers and 246 real issues from their own repositories, randomising whether AI tools were allowed. With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The gap that matters for CI planning is the perceptual one: developers predicted a 24% speed-up, and after the slowdown still believed they had been sped up by 20%. Nobody on your team will tell you the pipeline is the constraint, because nobody experiences it as one — they experience it as "waiting", which feels like weather. 1.5% / 16% / 84%. Google's published flakiness data: roughly 1.5% of test runs report a flaky result; about 16% of their 4.2M tests have shown flakiness at some point; and around 84% of observed pass→fail transitions involve a flaky test rather than a real regression. Hold onto that 1.5% — it is small enough to ignore at 5 PRs/day and load-bearing at 40.
documents.s: Three numbers that frame the whole problem

documents.t: Most teams assume the ceiling is compute. It isn't. It's the merge queue, and the reason is a mechanism most people have never read the docs for. GitHub's merge queue does speculative checking. Queue PRs #1, #2, #3 and it builds temporary branches: main + #1, main + #1 + #2, main + #1 + #2 + #3 — and tests all of them in parallel. If every check passes, all three land in one round. That is the whole value proposition: batching turns N serial validations into one. Now read the failure path. When a check fails for the group containing PR #1, GitHub removes #1 from the queue — and every group behind it contained #1's changes, so those groups are invalid and get rebuilt without it. One bad PR does not cost you one slot. It costs you the rest of the batch's CI round. That makes queue throughput a function of your pass rate, and it's steeper than intuition suggests. Model it: batch size N, each PR independently failing with probability p, and you merge the run of PRs up to the first failure. Expected merges per round is a geometric expectation: E[merges] = (1 − p) · (1 − (1 − p)^N) / p With N = 10: Per-PR failure rate p Expected merges per round Rounds to clear 10 PRs 2% 8.9 ~1.1 5% 7.6 ~1.3 10% 5.9 ~1.7 20% 3.6 ~2.8 30% 2.3 ~4.4 Two consequences most teams get backwards: A flaky suite is a throughput tax, not a nuisance tax. Flakiness adds directly to p. Going from 5% real failures to 5% real + 5% flake takes you from 7.6 merges per round to 5.9 — roughly 23% of your merge capacity, lost to tests that were never testing anything. Raising the batch size is the wrong lever when p is high. Bigger N only helps when (1 − p)^N stays near 1. At p = 0.2, a batch of 10 delivers 3.6 merges; the fix is lowering p, not queueing more optimism. And agent volume pushes p the wrong way — DORA's stability finding is exactly a statement about p rising.
documents.s: Why the merge queue breaks first

documents.t: Do this on a napkin before you buy runners. Assumptions stated, because they're what make it wrong for your team: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Count job-minutes, not wall-clock⌄ A 45-minute suite fanned out into 15 parallel jobs still costs ~45 job-minutes. Parallelism buys latency, never cost. Take your suite's total job-minutes from a recent run, not from the slowest job. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply by validations per PR, not by PRs⌄ With a merge queue every PR is validated at least twice: once on the PR branch, once inside a merge group. Reruns and rebuilds from the p-math above add more. Budget 2.5x as a floor, not 1x. ←PreviousNext→ 3Divide by the burst window, not the day⌄ 40 PRs x 2.5 validations x 45 job-min = 4,500 job-minutes. Spread over 24 hours that is trivial. It does not arrive over 24 hours — it arrives in two or three hours around review time. 4,500 job-min into a 2-hour window needs ~37 sustained concurrent jobs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compare against your plan's hard ceiling⌄ GitHub-hosted standard runners cap total concurrent jobs at 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team) and 500 (Enterprise). The napkin above quietly exceeds Free and sits on top of Pro — during the burst, which is the only window that matters. ←PreviousNext→ 5Find the silent failure⌄ A queued job is cancelled after 24 hours. On a saturated queue this shows up as jobs that never ran rather than jobs that failed, which is far harder to notice and does not page anyone. ←PreviousNext→ The takeaway is not "buy Enterprise". It's that the constraint is burst concurrency, and the daily-average number that makes your pipeline look fine is the number hiding the problem.

Teams reach for these in almost exactly the reverse of the useful order. 1. Lower p (highest leverage, lowest cost). Every point of failure rate removed pays off nonlinearly in the batching math. Concretely: make agents run the fast suite locally before opening a PR, require a green pre-merge check before a PR is allowed into the queue, and quarantine flakes aggressively (below). This costs no compute. 2. Cut the work per validation — test selection. This is the only lever that changes the exponent rather than the constant. Instead of running everything, run what the change can plausibly break: Develocity Predictive Test Selection builds a model from your own Build Scan history plus cross-project patterns, and ships a simulator so you can measure the savings and the missed-failure rate before enabling it. Two safety details worth stealing even if you never buy it: you can pin must-run tests by class pattern or annotation, and it always selects recently flaky tests, because a flaky test is by definition unpredictable from the change. Pair it with a "remaining tests" run post-merge or nightly so nothing is skipped forever. Bazel / Buck2 get this structurally: the build graph knows which targets depend on the changed files, so bazel test on affected targets is target determination for free. No build graph? Python has pytest-testmon, which records which tests cover which code and re-runs only the affected ones. Jest ships --changedSince out of the box. Test selection, three ecosystems CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Bazel — test only what the diff can reach bazel test $(bazel query "rdeps(//..., set($(git diff --name-only origin/main)))" --output=label 2>/dev/null) # Python — coverage-based impact analysis pip install pytest-testmon pytest --testmon # first run builds the DB, later runs select # Jest — built in, no plugin npx jest --changedSince=origin/main 3. Cache aggressively — and know the gotcha. Remote caching stores action results keyed by a hash of inputs, command line and whitelisted environment. Bazel's own docs flag the trap: tools outside the workspace are not tracked, so two machines with different compiler versions can get a cache hit on work that would have produced different outputs. Whitelist what matters with --action_env, and keep write access to CI only — developer machines should read: Remote cache, CI-writes-only CopyOpen in Claude↗ # CI: read and write bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 # Developer machines: read only, never poison the shared cache bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 \ --remote_upload_local_results=false 4. Add runners (last). Linear cost, linear benefit, and it does nothing about p. Do it after the first three, when you actually know your burst concurrency number.

Everything above applies to any high-volume pipeline. This one is specific to agent-written code, and it is the gap most CI setups have. When the same agent writes the fix and the test for the fix, "tests pass" carries much less information than you think. Two failure shapes show up constantly: The test asserts the behaviour of the implementation rather than the requirement — it passes because it was written by reading the code it is testing. The agent, when a pre-existing test fails, edits the test to match the new behaviour instead of fixing the code. The diff is green and the regression shipped. That behaviour has a name and a literature — see reward hacking in coding agents for why models do it and which defenses have measured effect sizes. What follows is the pipeline-side control, not the model-side one. The cheap structural gate: a new test must fail against the pre-change code. That's the red-green discipline of TDD turned into a machine check, and it's what mutation testing formalises at scale. You do not need a mutation-testing framework to get most of the value — you need one CI job: CI gate: new tests must fail without the change CopyOpen in Claude↗ #!/usr/bin/env bash # must-fail-first.sh — run in CI on PRs that add tests set -euo pipefail NEW_TESTS=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- 'tests/**' 'test/**') [ -z "$NEW_TESTS" ] && { echo "no new tests, skipping"; exit 0; } # Keep the new tests, revert everything else to the base commit git stash push --keep-index -- $NEW_TESTS git checkout origin/main -- src/ git stash pop # The new tests MUST fail now. If they pass, they prove nothing. if pytest $NEW_TESTS -q; then echo "FAIL: new tests pass against unmodified source — they do not test the change." exit 1 fi echo "OK: new tests fail without the fix." Two honest caveats. It only works when source and tests live in separate trees, and a test that fails for the wrong reason (import error, missing fixture) passes this gate. It is a floor, not a proof — but it catches the single most common way an agent-authored PR is green and worthless. The complementary review-side control is a reviewer that doesn't share the author's context: see the hybrid AI code reviewer and the PR-review GitHub Action.
documents.s: The AI-specific failure mode: the agent grades its own homework

documents.t: Given 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes, "rerun it" is the default human response and it is the most expensive one available — it burns a full validation on a test that was never going to tell you anything. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Measure before you judge⌄ A flaky test is one that produces different results on the same commit. Run the suite N times on an unchanged main and record per-test failure counts. That is your evidence; developer memory is not. ←PreviousNext→ 2Quarantine on a threshold, not an argument⌄ Anything above your threshold moves to a non-blocking job that still runs and still reports. It stops gating merges immediately — that is the throughput win — and it stays visible so it does not become dead code. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the quarantine and give it an owner⌄ An uncapped quarantine is a graveyard. Fixed budget (say 1% of tests), a name attached, an expiry date. Over budget means the next flake evicts the oldest one back into blocking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Never let test selection skip a flake⌄ This is the counter-intuitive rule Develocity encodes: recently-flaky tests are always selected, because the model cannot predict them from the diff. Selecting away your flakes hides the signal you need to fix them. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-derive p after each round⌄ Recompute your per-PR failure rate monthly and put it on the dashboard next to merge-queue throughput. It is the one number that tells you whether the pipeline is getting better or the agents are just getting louder. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Flake quarantine that survives contact with agents

documents.t: merge_group is not automatic. GitHub's docs are explicit: you must add the merge_group event to your workflow triggers, or your checks never fire inside the queue and merges fail on missing required checks. This is the single most common merge-queue misconfiguration. The 24-hour queue cancellation is silent. Saturated queue → jobs vanish rather than fail. Alert on queue depth, not just on red builds. Matrix jobs cap at 256 per workflow run. Generated matrices (a common agent-scaffolding pattern) hit this without a useful error. Cross-machine cache hits can be wrong. Untracked external toolchains produce false hits. Pin toolchains, whitelist environment with --action_env. Branch protection with wildcard patterns is incompatible with merge queues. If your protection rules use wildcards, the queue will not engage. Agent PRs touching CI are a security boundary, not a style question. A PR that can edit workflow files can exfiltrate CI secrets — see GitHub issue → CI secrets and hardening autonomous runs.
documents.s: Gotchas that cost a day each

documents.t: There is no configuration that makes a pipeline absorb unbounded agent output. What the levers above buy you is a system whose cost grows with the size of the change rather than the number of pull requests — test selection and caching are sublinear, runners are linear, and merge-queue batching is only sublinear while your pass rate stays high. Which puts the real constraint back where DORA's 2025 framing puts it: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. If small batches, fast suites and low flakiness were already your practice, agents make you much faster. If they weren't, agents find out. Check yourself 0/6 1Your merge queue has batch size 10 and your per-PR failure rate rises from 5% to 20%. Roughly what happens to expected merges per round? It drops slightly, from about 9 to about 8It roughly halves, from about 7.6 to about 3.6It is unchanged — batching absorbs failuresIt doubles, because failures free up queue slots 2A merge group fails because of PR #1. What does GitHub do to the groups queued behind it? Nothing — they were tested independently and merge as-isIt merges them anyway and opens a revert PR for #1It removes #1 and rebuilds the groups behind it without #1's changesIt clears the entire queue and every author must re-queue 3Which lever changes how CI cost scales, rather than just shifting the constant? Adding more concurrent runnersIncreasing the merge-queue batch sizeTest selection driven by what the diff can reachRetrying failed jobs automatically 4Why does Develocity's Predictive Test Selection always run recently flaky tests, even when the diff does not touch them? Flaky tests are usually the slowest, so they parallelise wellA flaky test's outcome is not predictable from the change, so the model cannot safely skip itContractual compliance requirements demand full suitesFlaky tests have the highest historical code coverage 5An agent's PR adds a fix and a test, and CI is green. What does the 'must fail first' gate check? That the new test achieves at least 80% line coverageThat the new test fails when run against the pre-change sourceThat the agent did not modify any existing test filesThat the test runs in under one second 6Two machines get a Bazel remote cache hit on the same action but would produce different outputs. What is the most likely cause? The content-addressable store dropped an output fileOne machine used --disk_cache and the other did notA toolchain outside the workspace differs and is not part of the action hashThe action cache stores only stdout, never metadata girarTérminoSpeculative checking (merge queue)DefiniciónGitHub builds temporary branches for base+PR1, base+PR1+PR2, … and tests them in parallel. All green means the whole batch lands in one round. A failure removes that PR and forces every group behind it to be rebuilt.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 12 Siguiente→ Key takeaways The merge queue breaks before the runner budget does. Speculative batching is a bet on your pass rate, and one failing PR invalidates every group behind it. Compute E[merges] = (1 − p)(1 − (1 − p)^N)/p once for your real numbers. It turns 'CI feels slow' into a decision about which lever to pull. Flakiness is throughput, not hygiene. At Google's published rates the noise is bigger than the signal — 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes. Size for burst concurrency, never daily average. The daily number is the one hiding the problem, and a saturated queue cancels jobs silently at 24 hours. Test selection is the only sublinear lever: Bazel/Buck2 target determination, Develocity PTS with its simulator, pytest-testmon, or jest --changedSince. When the agent writes both the fix and the test, green means less than you think. Gate on the test failing against pre-change source. DORA's framing holds: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. Small batches, fast suites and low flake were always the advice — agents just made ignoring it expensive.

Todos los niveles Tanto si estás aprendiendo a programar como si despliegas software en producción, la IA cambia el ciclo de trabajo. Quienes ganan la tratan como un compañero rápido y experto — y verifican todo lo que produce.

Explicar código o errores que no conoces en lenguaje llano. Generar código repetitivo (boilerplate), tests y primeros borradores de funciones. Refactorizar para ganar claridad y depurar razonando sobre una traza de pila. Traducir entre lenguajes y frameworks. Revisar un diff en busca de errores y malos olores de código. Para bases de código reales, hazlo dentro de tu repositorio con Claude Code, que puede leer archivos, ejecutar tests y editar con tu aprobación.

Da contexto — el código relevante, el error, lo que esperabas frente a lo que obtuviste. Si entra vago, sale vago. Pide un plan para cambios no triviales antes de editar (Modo Plan). Genera el cambio. Léelo — entiéndelo antes de aceptarlo. El código es tuyo. Ejecútalo — tests, lint, build. Nunca te fíes de un "esto funciona" sin ejecutarlo. El paso que separa los buenos resultados de los malos es la flecha que vuelve al inicio: cuando una prueba falla, no parchees a ciegas — vuelve a introducir el fallo como contexto nuevo.

Explain what this function does and any edge cases it mishandles: {code} Write tests for {function}. Cover the happy path and the edge cases. {code} This throws {error}. Here's the code and stack trace. Find the root cause and propose a minimal fix. {context}

:::warning Verifica y protege tus secretos Ejecuta y revisa el código generado — puede estar sutilmente equivocado o inventar APIs que no existen. Nunca pegues secretos ni claves en un prompt (Privacidad). Para programación agéntica o automatizada, restringe los permisos y lee Proteger agentes. :::

Todos los niveles No necesitas ser científico de datos para obtener respuestas a partir de tus datos con la IA — pero sí tienes que mantenerla honesta. La IA escribe la consulta y explica el resultado; tú confirmas que las cifras son reales.

Escribir SQL / fórmulas de hoja de cálculo / pandas a partir de una pregunta en lenguaje llano. Explicar qué significa una consulta o un resultado en términos de negocio. Limpiar y transformar datos desordenados (describe el desorden y obtén los pasos). Sugerir el gráfico adecuado para la pregunta. Interpretar los resultados y proponer la siguiente pregunta.

Describe tus datos — columnas, tipos y la granularidad (¿una fila = qué?). No des por hecho los nombres. Plantea la pregunta que debe responder el análisis. Obtén la consulta + una explicación de una línea de lo que hace y sus supuestos. Ejecútala tú mismo sobre los datos reales. Devuelve los resultados para una interpretación en lenguaje llano y sus salvedades. My table `orders` has columns: order_id, customer_id, created_at, total_eur, status. One row per order. Write SQL for monthly revenue from completed orders in 2025, and explain any assumptions.

:::warning Nunca te fíes de cifras que no haya calculado Si la IA expone un resultado sin ejecutar la consulta sobre tus datos, ese número puede estar inventado. Ejecuta tú mismo las consultas; trata como no verificada cualquier cifra que no hayas calculado tú. Y recuerda que correlación ≠ causalidad — pídele que señale las afirmaciones de tipo asociativo. Consulta Alucinaciones. ::: Comprueba el orden de magnitud — ¿resultado inverosímil? Investiga, no lo publiques. Declara los supuestos (nulos, deduplicación, zonas horarias, moneda). No pegues datos sensibles ni PII en herramientas que no hayas verificado (Privacidad).

Avanzado Última verificación: 2026-07-24. Anthropic's evaluation guide is the source of truth for methodology (SMART criteria, exact-match, LLM-graded Likert/binary). Agent-trajectory eval is an emerging discipline — treat framework names as illustrative and confirm APIs at each vendor's docs. Confirma con la fuente oficial. What you'll learn Understand why agent evals differ from prompt evals — trajectory matters, not just the final answer Build a golden set of 20–100 real cases with clear pass criteria Score four layers: tool-call correctness, trajectory quality, task success, production drift Use LLM-as-judge safely: rubric first, calibrate against humans, spot-check verdicts Ship an eval that runs in CI and fails a bad change before it reaches users An agent eval answers a harder question than "did the prompt return the right words?" It asks: did a model running in a loop pick the right tools, in the right order, with the right arguments, arrive at the right outcome — and stay within budget and safety bounds? Skip this step and you'll ship a "helpful" agent that quietly regresses every time you tweak the system prompt.

A single-prompt eval scores one input → one output. An agent produces a trajectory: a chain of reasoning, tool calls, intermediate observations, and revisions across many turns. Two failure modes make this hard: Right answer, wrong path. The agent stumbles onto the correct output after wasteful loops, unsafe actions, or lucky guesses. Final-answer-only evals mark this a pass; production won't. Wrong answer, plausible path. Every step looks reasonable in isolation, but the agent misused a tool, ignored a constraint, or hallucinated an intermediate fact. You need to look at the trace, not just the reply.
documents.s: Why agents need their own evals

documents.t: Layer them cheapest-first so a bad change fails fast without waiting for expensive graders. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Layer 1 — Tool-call correctness (deterministic)⌄ For each expected step, check tool name matches, required parameters are present, and types validate. Pure code, milliseconds, no model needed. Catches 'called search when it should have called write_file' before anything else runs. ←PreviousNext→ 2Layer 2 — Trajectory quality (rubric + LLM-judge)⌄ Score the full trace: did the agent take a sensible path, or wander, loop, or backtrack? Number of steps vs. minimum needed, redundant calls, retries after tool errors, whether it stopped when done. Use an LLM judge with an explicit rubric here. ←PreviousNext→ 3Layer 3 — Task success (end-to-end)⌄ Did the goal get met? Deterministic where possible (schema valid, file written, test passes), LLM-judged where fuzzy (summary faithful, answer helpful). This is your headline number. ←PreviousNext→ 4Layer 4 — Production drift & safety⌄ In prod, sample real traces and re-grade a slice. Watch intervention rate (how often a human had to step in), refusal rate, and cost per successful task. When these shift, your model, tools, or inputs changed underneath you. ←PreviousNext→

Not every metric belongs on the dashboard. These five drive shipping decisions in 2026: Metric What it measures Why it matters Task success rate % of golden-set cases the agent finishes correctly The headline. Everything else is diagnostic. Cost per successful task $ / passing case (tokens in + out, tool costs) Success at 10× the cost is a regression. Latency (p50 / p95) Wall-clock per task, tail included p95 is what real users feel — averages lie. Tool-call accuracy % of expected tool calls with correct name + args Predicts trajectory quality; cheap to compute. Intervention rate % of tasks needing human takeover in prod The autonomy number. Rising = trust falling. Track them together — one moving without the others is usually a leading signal, not noise.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Mine real inputs⌄ Pull 20–100 tasks from actual usage (logs, support tickets, user requests). Cover the frequent easy path, the tricky middle, and the edge cases that already bit you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Write pass criteria per case⌄ For each: what does 'done' look like? Exact expected output, required facts, valid JSON schema, files that must exist, or a rubric for fuzzy cases. If you can't write the criterion, the case is unusable — cut or clarify it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Annotate the ideal trajectory⌄ For a subset, sketch the tool sequence a good agent would take. This is what Layer 1 checks against. ←PreviousNext→ 4Freeze it, version it⌄ Commit the set to your repo. Never edit a case in place — add v2 alongside v1 so score history stays comparable. ←PreviousNext→ 5Grow it from failures⌄ Every prod bug becomes a new eval case before you fix it. That's how the set stays predictive instead of decaying. ←PreviousNext→

Grading fuzzy outputs by hand doesn't scale. A capable model reading against an explicit rubric does — Anthropic's own eval methodology guide recommends this pattern for tone, faithfulness, helpfulness, and safety. Judges have well-documented biases: they prefer longer answers, the first option shown, and outputs that echo their own phrasing. Three habits keep them honest: Rubric, not vibes. "Rate helpfulness 1–5" is useless. Anchor every point on the scale to observable behavior. Calibrate on a human-labeled sample. Have humans grade 30–50 cases; measure judge-vs-human agreement (aim for Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6). If it disagrees, tighten the rubric. Use a different model as judge. Grading with the same model that produced the output leaks bias in both directions. Spot-check verdicts weekly. Read 10 random judge scores and their reasoning. It's the cheapest way to catch drift. LLM-as-judge rubric template CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are grading an AI assistant's response against a rubric. Be strict. Cite exact evidence from the response. <task>{task}</task> <response>{response}</response> Rubric (rate 1–5 per dimension): - Task completion: 1 = ignored task; 3 = partial; 5 = fully done, no gaps. - Faithfulness: 1 = contains false claims; 3 = mostly grounded, one soft claim; 5 = every claim traceable to input/tools. - Efficiency: 1 = wandered/looped; 3 = extra steps; 5 = minimum viable path. Output JSON only: {"task_completion": N, "faithfulness": N, "efficiency": N, "evidence": "<quote>", "verdict": "pass"|"fail"} Trajectory review prompt (Layer 2) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are auditing an AI agent's tool-call trajectory. The goal was: {goal} Expected minimum steps: {n_min} <trajectory> {list of tool_name(args) -> result, in order} </trajectory> Answer in JSON: {"steps_taken": N, "wasted_steps": N, "wrong_tool_calls": [<indices>], "unsafe_actions": [<indices>], "verdict": "pass"|"fail", "reason": "<one sentence>"} Adversarial case generator (grow the set) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Generate 5 new eval cases that are likely to break an agent whose current failures cluster around: {failure_pattern}. For each case give: input, expected output OR pass criterion, ideal tool sequence, and why this case is hard. Return YAML.
documents.s: LLM-as-judge — cheap, fast, but calibrate it

documents.t: The eval only pays off when it blocks regressions automatically. Wire it into CI as a check on every prompt / model / tool change: # tests/eval_gate.py — runs on every PR import json, sys from anthropic import Anthropic from my_agent import run_agent client = Anthropic() golden = json.load(open("evals/golden.v3.json")) results = [] for case in golden: trace = run_agent(case["input"]) layer1 = tool_calls_match(trace, case["expected_tools"]) # deterministic layer3 = judge(client, case, trace.final_output) # LLM rubric results.append({"id": case["id"], "layer1": layer1, "layer3": layer3["verdict"]}) pass_rate = sum(r["layer3"] == "pass" for r in results) / len(results) tool_acc = sum(r["layer1"] for r in results) / len(results) # Gates — tighten over time assert pass_rate >= 0.85, f"Task success dropped to {pass_rate:.0%}" assert tool_acc >= 0.90, f"Tool-call accuracy dropped to {tool_acc:.0%}" print(f"PASS: task={pass_rate:.0%} tools={tool_acc:.0%}") Store per-run scores so you can chart the trend. A drop of 3+ points between merges is a real regression, not noise. Anti-patterns that make evals under-deliver Judging the final answer only — misses every trajectory bug. Score Layers 1 and 2 too. Static golden set — if it doesn't grow with every prod failure it stops predicting prod. Budget time monthly. Same model as agent and judge — bias in both directions. Rotate to a different model for grading. No cost or latency in the gate — a prompt tweak that adds 8 tool calls can 'pass' the eval while 10×-ing the bill. Vibes-only scoring — 'feels better' is not a metric. If you can't diff two numbers, you can't ship confidently. Key takeaways Agents produce trajectories, not answers — evaluate the path, not only the outcome Layer cheapest-first: tool-call correctness → trajectory quality → task success → production drift The five metrics that ship decisions: task success rate, cost per success, p50/p95 latency, tool-call accuracy, intervention rate LLM-as-judge scales, but only with an explicit rubric, a different model, and calibration against human labels A golden set that doesn't grow from prod failures stops predicting prod — grow it monthly Wire the eval into CI as a hard gate — the check that catches a regression before users do
documents.s: CI gate: fail the bad change before it ships

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4 1Why do agents need trajectory evals, not just final-answer evals? Final-answer evals are too slow to run in CIAn agent can arrive at the right answer via wandering or unsafe steps (right answer, wrong path) — and produce a plausible-looking path to a wrong answerTrajectory evals are the only kind that support LLM-as-judgeFinal-answer evals only work for classification tasks 2You're layering your evals. Which order is cheapest-to-most-expensive and correct? LLM-judged task success → deterministic tool-call checks → production drift → trajectory rubricDeterministic tool-call correctness → trajectory quality (LLM-judge) → task success → production driftProduction drift → task success → trajectory rubric → tool-call checksTrajectory rubric → task success → tool-call checks → production drift 3Which pair of habits actually keeps LLM-as-judge trustworthy over time? Grade with the same model as the agent, and rewrite the rubric each runUse a rubric with observable anchors, and calibrate the judge against a human-labeled samplePrefer vibes-based prompts to avoid over-specifying, and never spot-check verdictsAlways use the largest available model as judge, no calibration needed 4Your CI gate passes task success rate but latency and cost per task doubled. What's the right call? Todos los niveles La IA puede ser el tutor paciente y disponible a todas horas que la mayoría nunca tuvimos — siempre que la uses para comprender, no para delegar el pensamiento. La diferencia entre aprender y hacer trampa está en el flujo de trabajo.

Explícamelo como si fuera novato. "Explica [concepto] de forma sencilla, con una analogía y un ejemplo." Luego profundiza por capas. Tutoría socrática. "No me des la respuesta — hazme preguntas que me lleven a ella." Enseñanza inversa (teach-back). Que te lo explique y luego tú lo reformulas; la IA corrige tus lagunas. Aquí es donde el aprendizaje se fija de verdad. Ponme a prueba. "Genera 5 preguntas sobre [tema], luego califica mis respuestas y explica los fallos." Plan de estudio. "Tengo 2 semanas para [examen]. Crea un plan y ejercita mis puntos débiles."

Tutor me on {topic}. Start by asking what I already know, then teach one step at a time and check my understanding before moving on. Don't just give answers. I'll explain {concept} back to you. Point out anything wrong or missing, kindly and specifically. Here's my explanation: {your attempt}

:::warning Para trabajos calificados, pide orientación — no el solucionario Si pegas la tarea y copias la salida, no lo has aprendido (y puedes infringir las normas de tu centro). Pide pistas, comprobaciones y explicaciones que te lleven a la respuesta. Hazte dueño del resultado. ::: Verifica los hechos — los tutores pueden equivocarse con total seguridad; contrasta las afirmaciones clave (Alucinaciones). Un concepto cada vez — la profundidad gana a la amplitud. Práctica espaciada — vuelve y vuelve a ponerte a prueba; eso es lo que lo fija.
documents.s: Úsala para aprender, no para hacer trampas

documents.t: Para la dislexia, el aprendizaje de idiomas o las diferencias de concentración, la IA puede reformular, simplificar, traducir y marcar el ritmo con paciencia — consulta Accesibilidad.
Pack de skills de Estudiante y Aprendizaje ¿Qué es un LLM? Accesibilidad: Claude como herramienta de apoyo
Principiante Cinco cosas que casi cualquiera puede usar hoy mismo. Cada una incluye un prompt de partida — pégalo, cambia lo que va entre corchetes y refínalo en lenguaje llano.

"Aquí tienes un correo que he recibido. Redacta una respuesta cortés y concisa que [acepte la reunión pero proponga el jueves en su lugar]. Que no pase de 80 palabras. Correo: [pegar]" Seguimientos que ayudan: "más formal", "añade una línea de agradecimiento", "dame dos versiones".

"Resume esto en 5 puntos que un responsable ocupado pueda leer en 30 segundos, y luego enumera por separado cualquier decisión o tarea pendiente. Texto: [pegar]" Funciona con artículos, notas de reuniones, hilos e informes. Para textos muy largos, pide primero el resumen y luego profundiza.

"Necesito [organizar un offsite de 30 personas] para [octubre]. Dame un plan paso a paso con tiempos aproximados y señala las 3 cosas que con más probabilidad saldrán mal." Estupendo para planes de proyecto, listas de verificación y para convertir un objetivo difuso en próximas acciones.

"Estoy decidiendo entre [la opción A] y [la opción B] para [situación]. Expón las ventajas y desventajas en una tabla y dime qué más debería considerar antes de decidir." Úsalo como compañero de entrenamiento — pídele que defienda el caso contrario para poner a prueba tu razonamiento.

"Escribe un primer borrador de [una publicación de LinkedIn que anuncie nuestra nueva función]. Imita esta voz: [pega un párrafo que hayas escrito tú]. Luego sugiere una frase de apertura más contundente." Dar una muestra de tu escritura es el secreto para que las salidas no suenen genéricas.

:::tip Da contexto y luego itera Cada prompt de arriba nombra el objetivo, el formato y las restricciones — eso es Fundamentos del prompting. Y ninguno tiene que salir perfecto al primer intento; refínalo en lenguaje llano. ::: :::warning Verifica cualquier dato factual Fechas, números, nombres, citas y "hechos" pueden estar equivocados con total seguridad. Para cualquier cosa que importe, compruébalo — consulta Alucinaciones. :::

Todos los niveles La IA es un magnífico acelerador de la investigación — y uno peligroso si confías en ella a ciegas. Bien usada, comprime horas de lectura en minutos; usada con descuido, inventa fuentes con total seguridad. Aquí tienes la versión disciplinada.

Resumir un documento o artículo largo en puntos clave + implicaciones. Comparar varias fuentes en una tabla (en qué coinciden o discrepan). Construir un panorama — mapea los actores, los enfoques o los argumentos de un tema. Extraer datos o cifras concretas de un documento (con citas). Poner a prueba — "¿cuál es el contraargumento más sólido frente a esto?".
documents.s: Movimientos de investigación de alto valor

documents.t: Using ONLY the text I provide, summarize the key findings and quote the exact sentence supporting each one. If something isn't in the text, say "not stated." Text: """{paste}""" Dale las fuentes. No le pidas que recuerde datos de memoria para nada importante — pega el material o usa una herramienta que lo recupere (RAG). Exige citas. "Cita la frase que respalda cada afirmación." Las afirmaciones sin respaldo quedan a la vista. Separa el hecho de la inferencia. Pídele que etiquete lo que está afirmado frente a lo interpretado. :::warning Las citas fabricadas son la trampa clásica Los modelos inventan artículos, autores y URLs de aspecto realista. Verifica que cada cita existe antes de fiarte de ella. Consulta Alucinaciones. :::

Reúne tú mismo las fuentes (o mediante una herramienta de recuperación). Resume cada una con fundamentación + citas. Sintetiza todas en una comparación por temas. Identifica las lagunas o discrepancias y el "y qué". Comprueba los hechos críticos contra los originales.
Generación aumentada por recuperación (RAG) Alucinaciones y cómo reducirlas Pack de skills de Analista de investigación

Todos los niveles La IA es una compañera de escritura excepcional si la diriges. El objetivo no es pulsar un botón y publicar — es pasar de la página en blanco a un buen borrador rápido, con tu voz, y luego afinar.

Bríefala. Objetivo, audiencia, formato, longitud, tono. ("Una introducción de blog de 600 palabras para fundadores primerizos, alentadora, sin jerga.") Esquema primero para cualquier cosa más larga que unos pocos párrafos — aprueba la estructura antes de la prosa. Redacta y luego edita por pasadas ("aprieta", "ejemplos más concretos", "elimina los preámbulos"). Imita tu voz. Pega una muestra de tu escritura: "imita esta voz". Esta es la mayor palanca de calidad de todas. Reutiliza. Una pieza → hilo, fragmento para boletín, publicación de LinkedIn, correo.
documents.s: El flujo de trabajo que funciona

documents.t: Brief: blog intro, 150 words, for {audience}, tone {tone}. Hook in the first line. Here's my voice to match: """{paste a paragraph you wrote}""" Edit this for clarity and concision without changing meaning. Show a bullet list of the changes. Text: """{paste}"""

:::warning No dejes que invente hechos La IA producirá encantada estadísticas, citas, nombres y fuentes plausibles pero erróneas. Nunca publiques una afirmación factual que no hayas verificado. Pídele que marque con [verify] todo lo que necesite una fuente real y rellénalo tú mismo. Consulta Alucinaciones. ::: Tú eres el editor. Conserva el criterio, el gusto y la responsabilidad. Evita la genérica "voz de IA". Los detalles, los ejemplos y una muestra real de tu estilo lo arreglan. Declara la asistencia de IA donde importe.
Biblioteca de patrones de prompts Generar archivos reales (docx/pptx/pdf) Negocios, marketing y estrategia

Avanzado Ajustaste un prompt y parece mejor, ¿pero lo es? Sin evals (evaluaciones) vuelas a ciegas: cada cambio es un volado, y te enteras de que se rompió por un usuario enojado, no por una prueba. Las evals convierten el "a ojo" en un número en el que puedes confiar, que puedes defender y observar a lo largo del tiempo. Esto es lo más importante que separa los prompts de afición del trabajo con Claude de grado producción. What you'll learn Por qué "a mí me parece bien" no es una prueba, y qué medir en su lugar Construir un golden dataset a partir de fallos REALES (de abajo hacia arriba), no imaginados Puntuar con código donde puedas, y con un LLM-as-judge donde no puedas Conectar las evals al CI para que un cambio de prompt o modelo nunca regrese en silencio Última verificación: 2026-06-24. Las herramientas de eval y el comportamiento de los modelos avanzan rápido: vuelve a revisar las guías enlazadas y recalibra tu juez cada vez que cambies el modelo bajo prueba. OWASP sigue colocando equivocarse en esto (y la inyección de prompts) entre los principales riesgos de LLM para 2026. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

Tres reglas que te salvan: De abajo hacia arriba supera a de arriba hacia abajo. Recolecta primero los fallos reales, luego diseña la métrica para atraparlos. Una eval construida a partir de roturas reales predice roturas reales; una eval inventada en una pizarra mide sobre todo tu imaginación. Un número que puedes volver a ejecutar. Una eval es repetible: las mismas entradas → una puntuación comparable. Eso es lo que te permite comparar honestamente el prompt v1 frente al v2, o claude-haiku-4-5 frente a claude-sonnet-5. Barata de ejecutar, ejecútala a menudo. Si a una persona le toma una tarde, no va a pasar. Automatízala.

Tu golden dataset es el corazón de toda eval: un conjunto curado de entradas con expectativas correctas conocidas. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Recolecta primero los fallos reales⌄ Empieza por las salidas malas reales: trazas de producción, reportes de bugs, tickets de soporte. Estos son los casos que importan. ←PreviousNext→ 2Ancla con 50-100 casos hechos a mano⌄ A mano, escribe casos que cubran tus escenarios más críticos y más propensos a errores. Este es tu conjunto ancla estable. ←PreviousNext→ 3Expande hacia ~500+⌄ Añade muestras de producción anonimizadas (elimina los PII) y casos sintéticos para los escenarios poco representados. No confíes en métricas agregadas sobre un conjunto diminuto. ←PreviousNext→ 4Hazlo crecer cada semana⌄ Cada nueva regresión de producción se convierte en un nuevo caso de prueba. Un golden dataset está vivo, no congelado. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Construye un golden dataset (de abajo hacia arriba)

documents.t: Recurre primero a la comprobación fiable más barata. Comprobaciones programáticas (deterministas) — úsalas siempre que la respuesta tenga estructura: coincidencia exacta/por palabra clave, "JSON válido contra este esquema", "¿llamó a la herramienta correcta con los argumentos correctos?", "por debajo de N tokens / por debajo de X ms". Rápidas, gratuitas y nunca inestables. LLM-as-judge — para dimensiones difusas (utilidad, tono, fidelidad a una fuente) que se resisten al código. Dale al juez una rúbrica, no un "a ojo", y calíbralo contra etiquetas humanas antes de confiar en él. :::warning Los jueces tienen sesgos Los jueces LLM se inclinan hacia respuestas más largas (sesgo de verbosidad) y hacia la opción que se muestra primero (sesgo de posición). Defensas: una rúbrica estricta, comparación por pares en lugar de puntuación absoluta, intercambiar el orden de las respuestas y volver a verificar al juez contra una porción etiquetada por humanos. Un juez es una capa, no toda la prueba. ::: Rúbrica de LLM-as-judge (inicial) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a strict grader. You are given a QUESTION, a REFERENCE answer, and a MODEL answer. Score the MODEL answer from 1-5 on (a) faithfulness to the reference and (b) helpfulness. Output ONLY JSON, nothing else: {"score": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"} QUESTION: {{question}} REFERENCE: {{reference}} MODEL: {{model_answer}}

Un agente puede llegar a la respuesta final correcta por el camino equivocado: entrando en bucles, llamando a una herramienta destructiva o quemando tu presupuesto. Así que evalúa el camino, no solo el destino: ¿llamó a las herramientas correctas, en un orden sensato, sin bucles, dentro del presupuesto? La corrección de las llamadas a herramientas y las comprobaciones de trayectoria detectan fallos que una eval centrada solo en la respuesta final nunca ve.
documents.s: Para los agentes, prueba también la trayectoria

documents.t: Aquí es donde las evals rinden frutos: hacer imposible fusionar regresiones. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Ejecuta el golden set en cada pull request⌄ Puntúa de forma programática donde sea posible; ejecuta el juez en el resto. ←PreviousNext→ 2Haz fallar el build ante una caída⌄ Fija un umbral (p. ej. la puntuación no debe bajar respecto a main). Un cambio de prompt que degrada la calidad no puede publicarse. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cierra el ciclo en producción⌄ Cuando un juez marca una respuesta en vivo, enrútala a una cola de revisión humana; el revisor confirma, añade el caso al golden set y vuelve a probar tras el arreglo. ←PreviousNext→ Vocabulario de evals girarTérminoGolden datasetDefiniciónEntradas curadas con expectativas correctas conocidas: el ancla contra la que puntúas cada cambio.Pulsa Intro o Espacio para girar la tarjeta. Usa las flechas izquierda y derecha para moverte entre las tarjetas.Término mostrado. ←Ant. 1 / 4 Siguiente→ Compruébate 0/3 1¿Cuál es la primera opción más fiable para puntuar una eval? Usar siempre un LLM-as-judgeUna comprobación determinista/programática donde la respuesta tiene estructuraEchar un ojo a unas cuantas salidas 2¿De dónde deberían provenir mayormente los casos de un golden dataset? Casos extremos imaginados en una pizarraFallos reales: trazas de producción, reportes de bugsTexto generado al azar 3Para un AGENTE, ¿qué deberías evaluar más allá de la respuesta final? Nada más importaLa trayectoria: qué herramientas llamó, en qué orden, dentro del presupuestoSolo la longitud de la respuesta Key takeaways Sin eval = publicar a ojo. Construye una antes de confiar en un prompt o agente. Golden dataset a partir de fallos reales; hazlo crecer cada semana con las nuevas regresiones. Comprobaciones basadas en código primero; LLM-as-judge (con una rúbrica, calibrado) para las partes difusas. Para los agentes, califica la trayectoria, no solo la salida. Ejecútalo en el CI y haz fallar el build ante una caída: así es como la calidad deja de regresar.

Intermedio What you'll learn See exactly what changed in July 2026 — categorized entries replace the daily summary in the app, and a new beta header rewires the API Learn how to view, edit, and delete individual entries in Settings without wiping everything Understand the four behavior changes the agent-memory-2026-07-22 header brings to memory_store endpoints, and why the old cursors stop working Meet the memory_store.* webhooks and Dreams — the parts nobody documents Apply five practical patterns for teaching Claude what to remember (and what to forget) For a year, "Claude's memory" meant a single evolving paragraph the model rewrote each day — good for a bio, bad for anything with structure. Between June and July 2026 Anthropic replaced that with an entry-based model: dozens of small, categorized notes Claude reads and writes in real time. Same idea powers the app and the Managed Agents memory API. This page connects them so you understand both surfaces from one mental model. Última verificación: 2026-07-24. The agent-memory-2026-07-22 beta header, the memory_store webhook events, and Dreams model support all changed within the last four weeks. Confirm current beta status and pricing on the platform release notes before shipping. Confirma con la fuente oficial.

documents.t: Both sides work the same way now: many small entries at named locations, each rewritable in isolation. The old model (one blob per user, rewritten wholesale) is gone in the app and has never been the API surface. Once you internalize "entries at paths, listed by prefix, edited one at a time", both surfaces stop feeling like separate features. documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1July 9, 2026 — Monthly recap arrives⌄ A new Settings › Reflect surface starts showing topics you spent time on, your most active day, peak hour, and observations about how you work with Claude. Beta on Free, Pro, and Max (web + Claude Desktop). Requires memory enabled. ←PreviousNext→ 2July 10, 2026 — Categorized entries replace the daily summary⌄ Memory becomes a set of individual, categorized entries that Claude reads and updates during conversations, instead of one rolling daily summary. Announced in the Claude Apps release notes. ←PreviousNext→ 3Rollout — Free / Pro / Max, with Team & Enterprise following⌄ Third-party coverage places availability across Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise, but plan-by-plan wording shifts between Anthropic's help center and news posts. When it matters (compliance, audits), verify in-product for your plan. ←PreviousNext→

The old daily summary had a single failure mode: unrelated context leaked into each other. Fix a fact about your work project and Claude might overwrite something about your writing style. Small, categorized entries fix that structurally — each edit is scoped to one lane. Three consequences most users miss: Retrieval is now targeted, not associative. Claude can pull "your communication preferences" without dragging in the rest of your context. Prompts that used to need "remember I prefer X, not Y" to break through the summary now hit an existing entry directly. You can prune surgically. Delete a single wrong entry in Settings instead of wiping everything and re-teaching Claude who you are. The "burn it all down" tax on correcting one mistake is gone. Categories act as an invisible schema. When Claude decides where an entry belongs (e.g. "communication style" vs. "current project"), it's implicitly choosing whether that fact will be recalled in future personal chats, future work chats, or both. Naming things well up front nudges better recall later.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Open Settings › Memory⌄ You'll see entries grouped by category (professional context, communication preferences, ongoing projects, and similar buckets). ←PreviousNext→ 2Edit or delete individual entries⌄ Each entry has its own controls. Fix a wrong fact without touching the rest — the whole reason for the redesign. ←PreviousNext→ 3Steer writes in-chat⌄ Ask Claude to remember, forget, or update specific things ("remember I use Bun, not npm") and it will update the matching entry live. ←PreviousNext→ 4Use incognito for one-offs⌄ An incognito chat is excluded from memory writes and chat history. Use it for anything you don't want persisted — sensitive drafts, one-time explorations, credentials you'd rather not have summarized. ←PreviousNext→ 5Check the monthly recap⌄ Settings › Reflect surfaces what Claude has been talking to you about. Skim it to catch memory drift — if a topic you no longer care about keeps showing up, prune the entries. ←PreviousNext→ Watch out Memory is best-effort recall, not authoritative storage. Never treat it as a source of truth for anything you'd audit (contracts, credentials, medication, legal facts). Restate hard requirements in the prompt or in a Project's instructions.
documents.s: View and manage your own entries

documents.t: 1. Set standing preferences explicitly, once CopyOpen in Claude↗ Please remember these as standing preferences for our chats: - Language: Italian for prose, English for code and error strings. - Units: metric. - Coding style: TypeScript strict, no default exports. - Voice: direct, no filler, no closing "let me know if…". Store each as its own entry in the right category. 2. Correct a single fact without a wipe CopyOpen in Claude↗ Update the memory entry that says I use Vercel for hosting — I moved everything to Cloudflare Workers last month. Leave every other project fact alone. 3. Deliberately forget CopyOpen in Claude↗ Delete any memory entries about the "Project Nightingale" launch — that work is finished and I don't want it surfacing in future chats. 4. Audit what Claude thinks it knows CopyOpen in Claude↗ Before we start, list every memory entry you have about me, grouped by category. Flag anything that looks outdated so I can decide whether to keep or delete it. 5. Sandbox exploratory chats CopyOpen in Claude↗ (Open the chat in Incognito.) Don't try to remember anything from this conversation — I'm just exploring a sensitive draft I don't want stored.

The Managed Agents platform exposes memory as memory stores — collections of memories addressed by path, listed with a path_prefix, and paged with cursors. On July 2, 2026 Anthropic shipped agent-memory-2026-07-22, a beta header that changes the semantics enough to break naive migrations. On July 22, 2026 the older managed-agents-2026-04-01 header adopted the same list behavior — so the "new" rules are now the only rules on memory-store endpoints.
documents.s: Part 2 — In the API: memory_stores and the new beta header

documents.t: # What changed Old behavior New behavior under agent-memory-2026-07-22 1 List order Client-controlled via order_by / order Stable, server-defined order. order_by and order are ignored — sorting client-side if you need it 2 depth parameter Free-form integer Accepts only 0, 1, or omitted. Any other value returns 400 3 path_prefix matching Substring match Must end with /, matches whole path segments only 4 Pagination cursors Interchangeable Cursors issued without the new header aren't valid with it. Restart from page 1 when you adopt it Two more gotchas: Header collision. On memory-store endpoints, agent-memory-2026-07-22 replaces managed-agents-2026-04-01. Sending both returns 400. Migrate the memory-store calls only; leave the other managed-agents endpoints on the original header. SDKs already switched. Python 0.116.0, TypeScript 0.110.0, Go 1.56.0, Java 2.48.0, Ruby 1.55.0, PHP 0.36.0, C# 12.35.0, and the CLI 1.16.0 all send agent-memory-2026-07-22 on memory-store calls automatically. If your code passes betas explicitly, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 there — don't add both.
documents.s: The four behavior changes you must know

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Bump the SDK⌄ Upgrade to at least Python 0.116.0 / TS 0.110.0 / Go 1.56.0 / Java 2.48.0 / Ruby 1.55.0 / PHP 0.36.0 / C# 12.35.0 (CLI 1.16.0). The header switch happens for you on memory-store calls. ←PreviousNext→ 2Drop dead parameters⌄ Remove order_by / order — the server ignores them. If your code sorts on the returned list order, move the sort client-side. ←PreviousNext→ 3Fix depth⌄ Replace any depth other than 0 or 1 with the value that best matches your intent, or omit the parameter. ←PreviousNext→ 4Normalize path_prefix⌄ Ensure every path_prefix ends with a slash. Remove any substring-style prefixes that relied on partial-segment matches — they will silently return fewer results now. ←PreviousNext→ 5Reset pagination⌄ On the first request after upgrade, don't reuse a stored cursor. Start from page 1 and re-derive the next cursor from the new response. ←PreviousNext→ 6Fix explicit betas⌄ If you pass betas manually, replace managed-agents-2026-04-01 on memory-store calls with agent-memory-2026-07-22 — never send both. ←PreviousNext→

Shipped July 22, 2026 alongside the header default: three memory_store.* webhook event types now cover the memory store's lifecycle, and four environment.* events cover the sandbox environment. This is the piece most integrators miss — you can now react to a memory store being created, updated, or removed by an agent run instead of polling GET /v1/memory_stores on a timer. Subscribe on the Managed Agents webhooks endpoint and route the events into your own audit trail or dashboard.
documents.s: Webhooks: react to memory-store lifecycle without polling

documents.t: Announced in the May 6, 2026 release notes and extended on July 10 to support Claude Fable 5 and Sonnet 5, Dreams is a research preview that reads an existing memory store plus past session transcripts and produces a reorganized output memory store: duplicates merged, stale entries replaced, new insights surfaced. Endpoints are gated by the dreaming-2026-04-21 beta header; access is by request. Treat it as the API-side analogue of the app's monthly recap — a scheduled reflection pass that keeps the store from silting up.
documents.s: Dreams: reorganize memory in the background
